en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-five Thousand Lines. Homage to the Blessed One, the Noble Perfection of Wisdom!
Homage to you, the immeasurable Prajñāpāramitā, who are free from conceptual construction;
you, whose limbs are entirely faultless, behold all things with faultless vision.
Like space, it is unstained, free from conceptual proliferation, and beyond syllables.
But he who perceives you with his whole being, he perceives the Tathāgata.
The virtuous perceive no difference between you, who possess noble qualities and the like, and the Buddha, the teacher of the world, just as they see no difference between the moon and its moonlight.

O you who are compassionate by nature and fond of devotion, those whose souls are filled with mercy, having approached you who are preceded by the Buddha and the Dharma, attain incomparable greatness with ease.
O you of unfailing vision, even one who beholds you according to the prescribed rite with a pure heart— even once—
will certainly attain perfection.
To all heroes who have restrained their selves for the sake of others,
you are the compassionate mother, both their nourisher and their progenitor.
Since the Buddhas, the compassionate teachers of the world, are your sons, you,
O auspicious one, are therefore the grandmother of all sentient beings.
O blameless one, you are always followed by all the stainless perfections,
just as the crescent moon is followed by the stars.
Having encountered those to be trained here and there, you alone, though manifold in form, are praised by the Tathāgatas under various names.
Just as droplets of dew inevitably perish upon encountering the radiance of the blazing sun,
so too do the faults and the arguments of disputants come to an end upon encountering you.
You alone are the source of terror for the ignorant, appearing with a fearsome aspect; yet you are the source of consolation for the wise, appearing with a gentle aspect.
But for one who possesses no attachment even toward you, O Mother, since you are his sole protector— how could passion and hatred arise in him toward anything else?
O mind, you do not come from anywhere, nor do you go anywhere;
even in all places, you are not apprehended by the wise.
But those who do not perceive you in this way, yet take refuge in you with sincere devotion, and having taken refuge, are liberated— this is a great marvel.
Seeing you alone, one is bound; not seeing you, one is also bound. Seeing you alone, one is liberated; not seeing you, one is also liberated.
Oh, how wonderful you are! You are profound and glorious;
you are extremely difficult to comprehend, appearing like an illusion, yet not truly seen.
Cultivated by Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas alike, you alone are the path to liberation; there is no other—this is certain.
Placing worldly convention at the forefront for the sake of designating embodied beings,
you are both spoken of and not spoken of by the Lords of the World out of compassion.
Who here is capable of praising you, who are without cause and stainless;
you who transcend the scope of all speech and are never dependent on anything?
Even though this is so, by means of such paths of speech as these, we have offered praise to you who are beyond praise; thus desiring to praise you, we are perfectly at ease.
Whatever merit has been accumulated by me through praising the Perfection of Wisdom—
Therefore, may you quickly lead this entire world to the perfection of wisdom.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great saṅgha of monks, about five thousand monks in number, all of whom were arhats.
[They were] those whose taints were exhausted, who were free from afflictions, who had attained mastery, whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated,

who were noble steeds, great elephants, who had done what was to be done, accomplished their task, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, and who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states.
Together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, as well as upāsakas and upāsikās, all of whom had seen the Dharma;
together with hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom had attained the dhāraṇīs,
dwelt in emptiness, moved within the signless, were unconditioned by vows, and had realized the equality of patience—

They had attained the *dhāraṇīs* of non-attachment, possessed infallible superknowledges, and their words were authoritative. They were free from hypocrisy and frivolity; their minds were devoid of pride regarding their kin or gain. They taught the Dharma without worldly motives and had reached the further shore of patience toward the profound Dharma.
Having attained fearlessness, they had transcended the works of Māra and laid to rest the obscurations of karma. They were skilled in the analytical discernment of the Dharma.
They were skilled in exposition; they had well undertaken vows for incalculable eons; they possessed smiling faces and were the first to speak;

their countenances were free from frowns; they were skilled in singing and conversing in verses; they were devoid of a dejected mind; they possessed unassailable eloquence; they were endowed with the fearlessness that overcomes infinite assemblies; and they were skilled in the means of escape throughout infinite millions of eons.
Those who are devoted to the teachings that are like an illusion, a mirage, the moon reflected in water, a dream, an echo, an optical illusion, a reflection, and a magical creation;
who are skilled in entering the various subtle inclinations and the conduct of beings within the realms of existence; whose minds are unimpeded;
who are endowed with the highest degree of patience; who are skilled in leading others to enter into the true nature of reality; and [who possess] the infinite arrays of all Buddha-fields—

They were embraced by the vows of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) and the application of practice (*prasthāna*); they were constantly and perpetually absorbed in the meditative concentration of the recollection of the Buddhas of incalculable world-systems; they were skilled in supplicating immeasurable Buddhas; they were skilled in pacifying the afflictions of various views, latent tendencies, and active outbursts; and they were skilled in manifesting hundreds of thousands of playful displays of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as follows:

and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, and by the caravan leader Ratnākara, and by Naradatta, and by Varuṇadatta, and by Śubhagupta, and by Indradatta, and by Uttaramati, and by Viśeṣamati, and by Vardhamānamati, and by Amoghadarśin, and by Susamprasthita, and by Suvi...
And with Krāntavikramin, Nityodyukta, Anikṣiptadhura, Sūryagarbha, Anupamacintin, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
Mañjuśrī, Vajramati, Ratnamudrāhasta, Nityokṣiptahasta, and Maitreya...
Together with that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other Bodhisattvas headed by him,
the Blessed One himself prepared a lion throne and sat down, having assumed the cross-legged posture.
Having straightened his body and established mindfulness directed toward the front, he entered the meditative absorption called the King of Samādhis,
wherein all samādhis enter, are included, and converge.
Then the Blessed One, mindful and clearly comprehending, arose from that samādhi,

surveyed all the world-systems with his divine eye, and smiled from his entire body. From beneath him, from the two thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of his feet, sixty times ten million rays of light—
From his ten toes, sixty-six hundred thousand *niyutas* of rays issued forth; likewise, from his two ankles and from his two shanks, sixty-six [hundred thousand *niyutas* of rays] issued forth.

Sixty-six [rays] from each of the two kneecaps; likewise, sixty-six from the two thighs, from the hips and navel, from the two sides, and from the heart—the *śrīvatsa*, the mark of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Thus, sixty-six [rays] from each of the ten [parts].

From the fingers of the hands, sixty-six [rays]; from the two arms, sixty-six; from the two shoulders, likewise; from the forty teeth of the neck, from the two nostrils, from the two ears, from the two eyes, from the middle of the ūrṇā-hair above, and from the uṣṇīṣa, sixty-six koṭīs of niyutas of rays [emerge].
Hundreds of thousands [of rays] issued forth, by which this trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-system was illuminated and completely suffused.
In the eastern direction, [worlds as numerous as] the sands of the river Gaṅgā—
The world-systems were pervaded and illuminated by that great radiance of light. In this way, in the southern direction,
the western, the northern, the northeastern, the southeastern,
the southwestern, the northwestern, the downward, and the upward directions, world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—
By that great radiance of light rays, [the worlds] were pervaded and illuminated.
And those beings who were pervaded and illuminated by that great radiance of light rays all became fixed in their destiny toward [enlightenment].
[regarding] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One again smiled from all his pores, and from that very [smiling], [light was emitted].
From each pore of his skin, sixty times sixty hundred thousand *niyutas* of millions of light rays issued forth,
by which this great trichiliocosm was illuminated and made manifest;
and by those [rays], in the eastern [direction]...

In that direction, world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were illuminated and pervaded by light. Likewise, in the southern direction, the western, the northern, the northeastern, the southeastern,
the southwestern, the northwestern, the downward, and the upward directions, world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā [were likewise illuminated].
The world-systems were pervaded and illuminated by that great radiance of light rays;
and those beings who were pervaded and illuminated by that great radiance of light rays all became destined for unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete awakening.
Then indeed, the Blessed One once again caused the great trichiliocosm world-system to be illuminated by that natural radiance which belongs to the Blessed Buddhas;
[this extended] as far as all [the worlds].
In each of the ten directions, world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges were illuminated by that light;
and all those beings who were touched by that light—
They became destined for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One extended his tongue-faculty,
by which he covered this great trichiliocosm world-system with his tongue-faculty.
The trichiliocosm—
Having pervaded the great trichiliocosm with his tongue-faculty, he emitted a smile from that tongue-faculty,
from which hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of light rays issued forth.
And upon each of the tips of those light rays, there appeared thousand-petaled lotuses made of the finest jewels and shining like gold.
Lotuses had arisen,
and upon those lotuses there were seated and established forms of Buddhas,
teaching the Dharma— namely, this very Dharma associated with the six perfections.
They went to world systems in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of more than a Ganges river’s worth of incalculable worlds, and there they taught the Dharma to sentient beings.
Likewise in the southern and western directions...
In the north, below, above, in the intermediate directions,
and indeed in each single direction throughout the ten directions— having gone to immeasurable world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā— they teach the Dharma to sentient beings.
It was this very teaching of the Dharma associated with the six perfections;
and those beings who hear that teaching of the Dharma become fixed in their destiny toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One, seated upon that very lion-throne, entered the samādhi called "Lion’s Play" (Siṃhavikrīḍita) and performed such a miraculous feat of supernatural power (ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra).
By means of such a miraculous feat (*ṛddhy-abhisaṃskāra*) as was performed, this great trichiliocosm world-system shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways; it moved, it swayed,
and it vibrated.
It moved;
it shook, it shook violently, it shook all over;
it resounded, it resounded loudly.
It trembled,
it quaked, it shook, it shook violently;
it roared, it thundered.
It roared;
it rose at the edges and sank in the middle,
and it rose in the middle and sank at the edges.
It bent down; it became soft, smooth, and a source of joy for the faces of all sentient beings.
Then, indeed, in that very instant, moment, and second, all the hells, animal births, and worlds of Yama within this great trichiliocosm were completely cut off.
They became empty;
all unfavorable conditions came to an end;
and those beings who...
Having passed away from the states of hell, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, they were all reborn among the company of humans through that very same joy and gladness;
and likewise for those of the Four Great Kings.

They were reborn into the fellowship of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods. Then, indeed, by the very power of the Blessed One, those humans and those gods [recalled] their previous births.
They remembered;
and having remembered, with that very same joy and gladness, they approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood with palms joined in reverence before the Blessed One.
In this same manner, [those from] the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—
In those world-systems— in the south, west, north, in the intermediate directions, above, below,
and all around throughout the ten directions— in every single directional sector, within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges,
all hells, all animal births, and all realms of Yama were completely severed and became empty.
All unfavorable conditions came to an end;
and those beings who had passed away from those states of hell, the animal realm, and the world of Yama were all reborn among gods and humans.
And those who had been reborn among the gods, through the very power of the Blessed One, recollected their former births; and having recollected them, they...
With that very same joy and gladness, they approached the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who had appeared in their respective Buddha-fields.
Having approached, [they prostrated at] the feet of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Having paid homage and with palms joined, they all bowed down to the Blessed One.
Then, indeed, those beings in this triple-thousand great thousandfold world system who were blind from birth saw forms with their eyes.
Deaf beings heard sounds with their ears,
and those who were insane regained their mindfulness.
Those with distracted minds became single-minded;
those who were hungry had their bowls filled.
Those who were thirsty became free from thirst;
those afflicted by disease became free from disease;
and those with impaired faculties became possessed of complete faculties.
They were not separated from unwholesome modes of bodily, vocal, and mental action, nor were they separated from unwholesome livelihoods consisting of unwholesome bodily, vocal, and mental actions.
And all sentient beings came to possess minds equal toward their mothers and fathers,
minds equal toward their brothers and sisters, and minds equal toward their friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations, [abiding] in the ten paths of wholesome action.
And they became practitioners of celibacy, pure, and free from foul odors; and all sentient beings,
endowed with every happiness, attained such bliss as that of the third dhyāna.
At that very moment, while the monk was in meditative absorption, he became endowed with such wisdom that the Buddhas,
the Blessed Ones, residing in other Buddha-fields, uttered this exclamation:
"Excellent is self-restraint; excellent is self-control; excellent is the fulfilled dwelling in the holy life; excellent is non-violence toward living beings.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, seated on that very same seat, [addressed] this trichiliocosm great...
Having surpassed a thousandfold world-system, the Tathāgata stands, shines, blazes, and radiates with light,
color, splendor, and brilliance;
[so too] in the eastern, southern, and western directions.

In the northern direction, above and below, and in the cardinal and intermediate directions, the Tathāgata remains and shines forth, surpassing world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā;
just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, [surpasses] all other mountains.
He stands surpassing [them], shining, glowing, and radiating with splendor, color, glory, and brilliance.

In the very same way, the Blessed One stands surpassing all world-systems, shining, glowing, and radiating with splendor, color, glory, and brilliance. In this very manner, the Blessed One, having surpassed all world-systems...
It stood, shone, blazed, and radiated with splendor, color, glory, and brilliance.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One once again manifested an ordinary physical body equal to the bodies of sentient beings within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system. Then, indeed...

Those gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host in this trichiliocosm, the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Ābhāsvaras, the Brahmakāyikas, the Paranirmitavaśavartins, the Nirmāṇaratis, the Tuṣitas, the Yāmas, the Trāyastriṃśas, and the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods— these [were there].

Having seen that unsatisfiable physical form of the Tathāgata, they took divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and victory standards; they took divine blue lotuses, white lotuses, fragrant lotuses, yellow lotuses, and red lotuses; and they took divine saffron and tamāla leaves.

Having taken them, they approached the Tathāgata’s most beautiful physical form. And those humans here in this great trichiliocosm world-system, having seen that most beautiful physical form of the Tathāgata, took flowers grown on land and in water and [approached] where the Tathāgata was—
They approached that showering body.

Then those gods and humans [honored him] with those divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards, as well as with those [flowers] growing on land and in water.

They scattered flowers over the body of the Tathāgata and showered them down upon it. Then, all those showers of flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and victory standards— both those born on land and those born in water— with which the Blessed One was strewn, [all vanished].
Above in the sky, through the Blessed One’s supernatural power, a single gabled pavilion appeared, equal in size to a great trichiliocosm;
and from that gabled pavilion, those divine [objects]...
Garlands of flowers and silk ribbons hung down and dangled; and by means of those flower garlands and silk ribbons,
this trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-system was exceedingly beautified.

And by that golden-colored radiance of the Blessed One’s majesty, which spread throughout the ten directions, world-systems in each direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges were illuminated and made manifest. And in this...
In the great trichiliocosm, in all the world-systems consisting of four continents, it occurred to each one of those gods and humans:
"The Tathāgata is seated before me."
"He teaches the Dharma.
Then, while seated upon that very lion-throne, the Blessed One once again smiled.
By the radiance of that smile, this great trichiliocosm world-system was suffused with light.
As far as world-systems in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges,

were filled [with light], all those beings within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system saw the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of śrāvakas, in world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

And in that eastern direction, all those beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā saw this Sahā world-system and the Tathāgata Śākyamuni together with the community of monks.
In this way, in the southern direction, the western, the northeastern, the southeastern, the southwestern,

the northwestern, the nadir, and the zenith— in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in each of these directions— they beheld the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of śrāvakas. Among them...
And all those beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā beheld this Sahā world-system and the Tathāgata Śākyamuni together with the community of monks.
Then, having passed beyond world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, [they saw...]

Among those [world-systems], there is a world-system at the very end called Ratnāvatī; therein dwells, remains, and maintains his life a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnākara. He teaches this very Prajñāpāramitā as the Dharma for the Bodhisattvas.
Then, in that world-system,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Samantaraśmi, having seen that great radiance,
that great earthquake, and having seen the Bhagavat’s most pleasing physical form, approached where the Bhagavat was.
He approached the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnākara; having approached and bowed at the feet of that Blessed One, he said this to the Tathāgata Ratnākara:
"O Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason?"
"This is the sign for the manifestation in the world of this great radiance, of this great earthquake of the earth,
and for the display of this Tathāgata’s wondrously beautiful body. When this had been said,
the Tathāgata Ratnākara spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi:
"Noble son, to the west of here, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges,
there is a world-system named Sahā; therein dwells the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni."
It endures and persists;
it is such its power that it reveals the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to the bodhisattvas, the great beings (mahāsattvas).
Then the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Tathāgata Ratnākara:
"Blessed One, I shall go to that Sahā world-system to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and also those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who are for the most part there."
[He saw] those who were youthful, who had attained *dhāraṇīs*, who were skilled in the production of *samādhis*, and who had reached the perfection of mastery over all *samādhis*.
The Blessed One said: "Go, noble son, now to whomever [it may be]."
"Do you consider it the right time?
Then the Tathāgata Ratnākara gave to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi thousand-petaled lotuses made of various jewels and shining with gold, saying, "With these, you..."
"Noble son, scatter those lotuses over the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and speak thus:
'The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, lightness of body, vigor, and well-being.'"
He inquires after the Blessed One’s strength and his state of dwelling in comfort;
and these lotuses have been sent by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, to the Blessed One.
"Thus, noble son, may you be one who acts with clear comprehension in that buddha-field.
For what reason?
Because those bodhisattvas who have been born there in this Sahā world-system are difficult to approach."
Then, indeed, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, having taken from the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnākara those lotuses made of various jewels, shining like gold and possessing a thousand petals,
together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas— both householders and renunciants, as well as boys and girls— [departed].
Surrounded and escorted by them, he proceeded toward the east through those world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā,

honoring, revering, respecting, and worshipping the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and victory-pennants, until he reached this Sahā world.

He arrived at that world-system and approached the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, he...

And the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, standing there, addressed the Blessed One Śākyamuni: "The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, ease of movement, vitality, strength, and whether you dwell in comfort."
And these thousand-petaled lotuses, made of various jewels and shining with the luster of gold, were sent by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, took those lotuses and cast them toward those world-systems in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā;
and by those lotuses, those world-systems were completely filled.
And upon those lotuses, forms of Buddhas were seated; and in those Buddha-fields, they taught the Dharma, namely, this very teaching of the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom.
And those beings by whom that Dharma was heard became fixed in their destiny for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then indeed, those bodhisattvas, those householders, those renunciants, and those boys—

And those maidens, having come from that world-system Ratnavatī together with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaraśmi, honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Blessed One Śākyamuni by means of their respective roots of merit, and sat down to one side.

Then, indeed, having passed beyond world-systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, there is a world-system that is the very last of them, named Sarvaśokāpagata (Free from All Sorrow). There dwells, remains, and maintains himself a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Aśokaśrī (Glorious Freedom from Sorrow).
He teaches this very Dharma of the perfection of wisdom to the Bodhisattvas. Then...
In that world-system, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Vigataśoka, having seen that great radiance, that great earthquake, and having seen that most beautiful physical form of the Blessed One,
approached the place where the Blessed One Ratnākara, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha was; having approached, he...
Having prostrated at the feet of that Blessed One, he addressed the Tathāgata Ratnākara as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the appearance in the world of this great radiance, of this great earthquake, and of this Tathāgata’s most wondrous physical form?
When this was said, the Tathāgata Ratnākara spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi: "There is..."

"O son of good family, to the north of here, beyond as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, there is a world-system named Sahā. There, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni resides, stays, and maintains himself.
He thoroughly proclaims the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; such is his majestic power."
Then the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Tathāgata Ratnākara:
"Blessed One, I shall go to that Sahā world-system in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who for the most part are youthful."
[They were] those who had attained the *dhāraṇīs*, who were skilled in the production of meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and who had reached the perfection of mastery over all concentrations.
The Blessed One said, "Go, noble son, whenever you deem it the right time.
Then the Tathāgata Ratnākara gave to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi lotuses made of various jewels, shining with gold, each having a thousand petals.
"O son of good family, scatter these lotuses over that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and speak thus:
'The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, well-being, strength, and comfortable dwelling.
And these lotuses have been sent by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Ratnākara, to the Blessed One.'"
"And may you, noble son, be one who acts with clear comprehension in that buddha-field.
For what reason? Because those bodhisattvas who have been born there in this Sahā world-system are difficult to approach.
Then, indeed, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi [received] from the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnākara those [objects] made of various jewels.

Holding lotuses that shone like gold and had a thousand petals, he was surrounded and escorted by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas— both householders and renunciants, as well as boys and girls— and while honoring and revering the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in those world-systems in the eastern direction that were as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he proceeded.
Honoring and revering [the Buddha] with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards,
he arrived at this Sahā world-system and approached the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Blessed One Śākyamuni:
"The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, vigor, well-being, strength, and whether you dwell in comfort."

Then, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, having taken from the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnākara those lotuses made of various jewels—shining with the luster of gold and possessing a thousand petals—together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, departed.

Surrounded and escorted by householders and renunciants, as well as by boys and girls, he proceeded toward the eastern direction, honoring, revering, respecting, and worshiping the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in those world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and victory standards.
He arrived at this Sahā world-system and approached the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi addressed the Blessed One Śākyamuni as follows:
"The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from ailment, freedom from distress, ease of movement, vigor, strength, and well-being.
And the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, has sent these thousand-petaled lotuses made of various jewels and shining with gold to the Blessed One."

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, took those lotuses and cast them toward the northwestern direction, toward as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges. By those lotuses, those world-systems were completely filled. Within those lotuses, forms of Buddhas sat, and in those Buddha-fields they taught the Dharma—namely, this very teaching of the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom.
And those beings by whom that Dharma was heard became fixed in their destiny for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then indeed, those bodhisattvas, those householders, those renunciants, those boys,
and those girls [departed] from that world-system Ratnavatī together with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantaraśmi.
Having arrived with their respective roots of merit, they honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Blessed One Śākyamuni,
and then sat down to one side. Then,
having passed beyond world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the direction below, there was a world-system called Padmā, which was the very last of them.
The Tathāgata named Padmaśrī—Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—dwells, remains, and maintains himself.
He teaches this very Dharma of the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattvas.
Now, in that world-system, there is one named Padmottara...
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, having seen that great radiance, that great earthquake,
and having seen that most pleasing physical form of the Blessed One, approached the place where the Blessed One Ratnākara,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was; having approached, he bowed down at the feet of that Blessed One.
He addressed that Tathāgata Ratnākara as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the appearance in the world of this great radiance, of this great earthquake, and of this Tathāgata’s most wondrous physical form?
When this was said, the Tathāgata Ratnākara spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi:

"Noble son, beyond this, in the direction above, after crossing world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, there is a world-system named Sahā. There, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni resides, stays, and maintains himself.
He fully reveals the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas; such is his majestic power."
Then the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Tathāgata Ratnākara:
"Blessed One, I shall go to that Sahā world-system in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who for the most part are youthful."
"They have attained the *dhāraṇīs*, are skilled in the production of meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), and have reached the perfection of mastery over all meditative absorptions.
The Blessed One said, "Go, noble son, at whatever time you deem appropriate.
Then, the Tathāgata Ratnākara gave to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi lotuses made of various jewels, shining with gold, each having a thousand petals.
"O son of good family, scatter these lotuses over that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and speak thus:
'The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, ease of movement, vigor, strength, and well-being;
and these lotuses have been sent by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One Ratnākara, to the Blessed One.'"
"And may you, noble son, be one who acts with clear comprehension in that buddha-field.
For what reason? Because those bodhisattvas who have been born there in this Sahā world-system are difficult to approach.
Then, indeed, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi [received] from the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnākara those [objects] made of various jewels.
Taking lotuses that shone like gold and had a thousand petals, he was surrounded and escorted by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas—

both householders and renunciants, as well as boys and girls— and while honoring and revering the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in those world-systems in the eastern direction that are as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he proceeded.
Honoring and worshipping with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards,
he arrived at this Sahā world-system and approached the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi addressed the Blessed One Śākyamuni as follows:
"The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, vigor, well-being, strength, and whether you dwell in comfort."
And these lotuses, made of various jewels, shining with the luster of gold, and each having a thousand petals, were sent by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, for the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, took those lotuses and cast them toward those world-systems in the direction below, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
Those world-systems were filled with those lotuses,

and upon those lotuses sat forms of the Buddha, who taught the Dharma in those buddha-fields— namely, this very teaching of the Dharma connected with the perfection of wisdom. And those beings by whom that Dharma was heard became fixed in their destiny for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then indeed, those bodhisattvas, those householders, those renunciants, those boys, and those girls,
having come from that world-system Ratnāvatī together with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantaraśmi,
honored, revered, and venerated the Blessed One Śākyamuni by means of their respective roots of merit.
Having paid homage, they sat down to one side.
Then, indeed, having passed beyond world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the direction above, there is a world-system at the very limit of them called Nandā.
There, a Tathāgata named Nandaśrī—worthy and perfectly enlightened—dwells, remains, and sustains himself.
He teaches this very Dharma of the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattvas.
Then, in that world-system, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Nandadatta, having seen that great radiance and...
Seeing that great earthquake and the most enchanting physical form of the Blessed One,

he approached the place where the Blessed One Ratnākara, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha was; having approached and bowed at the feet of that Blessed One, he addressed the Tathāgata Ratnākara as follows:
“Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the appearance of this great radiance in the world, for this great earthquake, and for this Tathāgata’s most wonderful physical form?
When this was said, the Tathāgata Ratnākara spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi:
“Noble son, there is, below from here in the direction of the nadir, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā...”
There is a world-system named Sahā; therein dwells, remains, and maintains his life the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni.
He fully elucidates the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, and such is his majestic power.
Then, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Tathāgata Ratnākara:
"O Blessed One, I shall go to that Sahā world-system to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and those Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who for the most part are youthful,
have attained the dhāraṇīs, are skilled in the production of meditative absorptions, and have reached the perfection of mastery over all samādhis."
The Blessed One said, "Go, noble son, at whatever time you deem appropriate.
Then the Tathāgata Ratnākara gave to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi thousand-petaled lotuses made of various jewels and shining with gold,
saying, "With these lotuses, noble son, you should scatter them over that Tathāgata Śākyamuni."

And you should say this: "The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, vigor, well-being, strength, and comfortable dwelling.
These lotuses have been sent by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One Ratnākara, to the Blessed One.
And may you, noble son, be one who acts with full awareness in the Buddha-field."
For what reason? Because those bodhisattvas who have been born there in that Sahā world-system are indeed difficult to approach.

Then, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, having taken from the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnākara those lotuses made of various jewels, shining with the luster of gold and possessing a thousand petals, [departed] together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas.

Surrounded and escorted by householders and renunciants, as well as by boys and girls, he proceeded toward the eastern direction, honoring, revering, respecting, and worshiping the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in those world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and victory standards.
He arrived at this Sahā world-system and approached the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Blessed One Śākyamuni:
"The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, vigor, well-being, strength, and comfortable dwelling.
And these thousand-petaled lotuses, made of various jewels and shining with gold, have been sent by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, to the Blessed One."
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, took those lotuses and cast them toward those world-systems in the direction above, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā;
and by those lotuses, those world-systems were completely filled.

And upon those lotuses sat forms of the Buddha, and in those buddha-fields they taught the Dharma—namely, this very teaching of the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom. And those beings by whom that Dharma was heard became fixed in their destiny for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then indeed, those bodhisattvas, those householders, those renunciants, those boys, and those girls...
Then those maidens, together with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantaraśmi from the world-system Ratnāvatī,
arrived; having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Blessed One Śākyamuni according to their respective roots of merit, they sat down to one side.
Then, at that very moment, instant, and second, this great trichiliocosm world-system became composed of the seven precious gems, strewn with flowers,
and hung with bundles of silk streamers and garlands.
It was adorned with wish-fulfilling trees whose branches were bent low by fruits that were various ornaments, as well as flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, fragrant trees, and garland trees;
it was, for example, just like the world-system Padmāvatī.

The Buddha-kṣetra of the Tathāgata Samantakusuma, where Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta resides, as well as the Bodhisattva Susthitamati and other Bodhisattvas of great majesty. And the Blessed One beheld the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, together with the community of recluses and brahmins, all assembled there.
And he saw that assembly of subjects and those Bodhisattvas who were in the state of youthful princes.
[Thus is the introduction.]
Then, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects must [practice] the perfection of wisdom."
One should apply oneself to the practice of mindfulness.
[Thus, in brief, is the production of the thought of enlightenment accompanied by the desire for perfect awakening.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"How, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects apply himself to the perfection of wisdom?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
"In this regard, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-abiding, [should practice] giving..."

The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is to be fulfilled by means of non-renunciation, based on the non-apprehension of the gift, the giver, and the recipient. The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is to be fulfilled by means of neither transgression nor non-transgression.
The perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) should be fulfilled by means of remaining unshakable;
the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) should be fulfilled by means of not relaxing physical or mental vigor.
The perfection of meditation is to be fulfilled by means of non-savoring;
the perfection of wisdom is to be fulfilled by means of the non-apprehension of wisdom and lack of wisdom.
[Thus ends the detailed explanation of the production of the thought of enlightenment accompanied by the desire for awakening.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for all those beings in each of the world-systems in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— to lead them all to final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder—
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires this should train in the perfection of wisdom. [Thus, in brief, is the production of the thought of awakening that has the welfare of others as its objective.
Likewise, one who desires to establish miserly beings in generosity, and those of immoral conduct...

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to establish those who abound in ill-will in ethical discipline, those who are indolent in patience, those with distracted minds in vigor, and those with poor wisdom in the perfection of wisdom,
should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus, in detail, the production of the thought of awakening has its objective support for the sake of others.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, by a bodhisattva who desires to perfectly awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects...
A mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus is the earth-like simile associated with the poetic meter.
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having stood in the perfection of wisdom—
By means of non-abiding, the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is to be fulfilled, based on the non-apprehension of the gift, the giver, and the recipient. In the same way,
the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), and the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).
The perfection of meditation and the perfection of wisdom are to be fulfilled by means of the non-apprehension of wisdom and lack of wisdom.
[Thus, accompanied by intention, it is like fine gold.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having thus stood in the perfection of wisdom...
The four foundations of mindfulness must be fulfilled; the four right efforts,
the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path must be fulfilled.
The concentration on emptiness should be cultivated; the concentration on signlessness should be cultivated;
the concentration on wishlessness should be cultivated.
In this way, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations,
the nine successive meditative attainments, and the nine perceptions of impurity are to be cultivated. Which are they?

Nine: namely, the perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a gnawed corpse, the perception of a scattered corpse, the perception of a burned corpse, and the perception of a skeleton.
The perception of repulsiveness regarding food should be cultivated;
the recollection of the Buddha should be cultivated.
The recollection of the Saṅgha should be cultivated;
the recollection of ethical discipline should be cultivated; the recollection of relinquishment should be cultivated.
The recollection of the deities should be cultivated;
the recollection of inhalation and exhalation should be cultivated; the recollection of world-weariness should be cultivated.
The recollection of death should be cultivated;
the perception of impermanence should be cultivated;
the perception of suffering should be cultivated.
The perception of non-self should be cultivated;
the perception of impurity should be cultivated;
the perception of death should be cultivated regarding the entire world.
The perception of non-delight should be cultivated;
the perception of lack of trust in all the world should be cultivated; the perception of mastery—
One should cultivate the perception of conventional reality; one should cultivate the perception of things according to their literal expression.
One should cultivate [this].

One should cultivate concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*). One should cultivate concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only (*avitarko-vicāramātra*).
One should cultivate concentration free from applied thought and sustained thought; one should cultivate the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown";
one should cultivate the faculty of knowing.
The faculty of one who has already known should be cultivated; the bases of mastery should be cultivated;
the bases of totality should be cultivated.
The knowledge of the omniscient one is to be cultivated;
calm abiding and insight are to be cultivated; and the three types of higher knowledge are to be cultivated.
The four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) are to be cultivated;
the four grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya) are to be cultivated; they are unshakable.
The five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā) are to be cultivated;
the six perfections (ṣaṭ pāramitā) are to be cultivated;
the seven riches (sapta dhana) [are to be cultivated].
These are to be cultivated:
the eight thoughts of a great person (mahāpuruṣavitarka) are to be cultivated; the ten powers of a Tathāgata (tathāgatabala) are to be cultivated.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikā buddhadharmāḥ*) should be cultivated;
great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) should be cultivated; great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) should be cultivated.
Great sympathetic joy is to be cultivated; great equanimity is to be cultivated.
[Thus, accompanied by resolute intention, he is like the new moon.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who, having observed omniscience through both knowledge and vision, desires to transcend it, should cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva who desires to fulfill the knowledge of the paths,

who desires to attain the knowledge of all aspects, who desires to fulfill the state of knowing the modes of the mental activities of all sentient beings, and who desires to uproot the afflictions along with their underlying tendencies and habitual traces.
A mahāsattva should apply himself to the perfection of wisdom;
in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.

One who wishes to enter the stage of the bodhisattva’s certainty, one who wishes to transcend the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one who wishes to abide on the stage of non-retrogression,
one who wishes to completely transcend the stage of the youth, one who wishes to attain the six supernormal knowledges, and [one who wishes to understand] the minds of all sentient beings...
By one who desires to understand the movements of conduct, who desires to surpass the knowledge of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and who desires to attain the bliss of dhāraṇīs and samādhis.
[Thus, this application accompanied by the second stage is like a blazing fire.
Desiring to establish beings who are miserly in the practice of giving, [one should surpass] all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas...

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to surpass the gifts being given to the Buddhas by means of a single mental arousal accompanied by sympathetic joy (anumodanā) should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
[Thus, it is like a great treasure-trove accompanied by the perfection of generosity.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish those of immoral conduct in morality, and who wishes to surpass the morality of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas with a single thought-moment accompanied by sympathetic joy, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus, the perfection of ethical discipline,
accompanied by the jewel-mine simile:
one who desires to establish those with malevolent minds in patience— surpassing all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— should practice.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to surpass patience by means of a single thought-moment accompanied by rejoicing should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus, having attained patience, he is like a great ocean.
For one who desires to establish those who are indolent in vigor, [the vigor of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...]
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to surpass [all those] by means of a single thought-moment accompanied by sympathetic joy should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus, this diamond-like [samādhi] is accompanied by vigor.
It is for one who desires to establish those with distracted minds in meditative concentration, [surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas].
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to surpass meditative absorption by means of even a single thought-moment associated with sympathetic joy should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus, this is] the mountain-like [state] accompanied by the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā).
[It is for one] who desires to establish beings of deficient wisdom in wisdom— [surpassing] all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to surpass wisdom by means of a single thought-moment accompanied by rejoicing should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, accompanied by wisdom,
it is like a great medicine;
for, by means of skillfulness, it takes even a single production of a wholesome thought and applies it toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to make even a small gift or even a small observance of morality immeasurable and incalculable through dedication should train in the perfection of wisdom.
By one who protects even a slight degree of patience, cultivates even a slight degree of vigor,

enters even a slight degree of meditative concentration, and cultivates even a slight degree of wisdom— dedicating it through skillful means toward the knowledge of all aspects for the sake of all sentient beings— one makes it immeasurable and incalculable.

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who desires [this] should train in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of giving should train in the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, [the perfection of] ethical discipline...

A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience, practicing the perfection of vigor, practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, and practicing the perfection of wisdom must train in the perfection of wisdom. This is for the sake of all sentient beings, by one who desires to endure the sufferings of the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, throughout [countless] eons.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to relinquish even morality accumulated for hundreds of thousands of eons out of regard for sentient beings, who wishes to be reborn in the family of the Buddhas, and who wishes to bring to perfection the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two marks of a great man, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus, accompanied by skillful means, it is like a friend.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to bring the Buddha-body to perfection should train in the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to enter the stage of a youth (kumārabhūmi) should train in the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes not to be separated from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, with a single voice, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should address] the eastern direction...
One who wishes to make known world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, [one who wishes to do so] in the south, the west, the north, the intermediate directions, below, and above— [should train in the perfection of wisdom].

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to make known as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges with a single sound should train in the perfection of wisdom. Moreover, Śāriputra, for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is not interrupted, [the bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom].
One who wishes to remain [in this state] should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with whatever roots of merit he desires,
wishes to honor, revere, and respect the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: 'May those various roots of merit of mine flourish so that they may be honored.'"

[Thus it is like a wish-fulfilling gem, accompanied by aspiration. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fulfill the heart's desires of all sentient beings— [namely,] food, drink, clothing, perfumes, garlands, flowers, incense, powders, ointments, beds, and seats—

One should train in the perfection of wisdom by means of such requisites as houses, wealth, grain, ornaments, jewels, gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, silver, and even kingdoms. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train] in this world, which has the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) as its limit...
One who desires to establish all sentient beings, as far as the limits of the realm of space, in the perfection of generosity;

one who desires to establish them in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom— [should practice] in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to make even a single arising of a wholesome thought inexhaustible until the moment of perfect awakening at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) should train [in this way].
One should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the ten directions, speak my praises. [Thus ends the section on] power.
[It is] accompanied [by light] and is like the sun.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in internal emptiness should train in the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, [he trains] in external emptiness,

internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, absolute emptiness, and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end— ana-...

One who wishes to train in the emptiness of the letter *va*, in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, in the emptiness of all phenomena, in the emptiness of specific characteristics, in the emptiness of non-apprehension, in the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, in the emptiness of existence, in the emptiness of non-existence, in the emptiness of self-nature, and in the emptiness of other-nature [should practice] for the sake of awakening.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize the suchness of all phenomena should train in the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize the suchness of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-tathatā*) should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
[likewise] one who wishes to realize the suchness of the limit of all that exists (*sarvabhūtakoṭi-tathatā*) should [train in the perfection of wisdom].
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know all the atoms of earth, water, fire, and air in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system should [train] in the perfection of wisdom.
One should train in the perfection [of wisdom].
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows that giving such a gift results in great fruit.
Thus, when this gift is given, it causes one to be reborn among the great kṣatriya clans,
among the great brahmin clans, or among the great householder clans.
[He] causes [beings] to be reborn in families of great *śāla* trees;
likewise, when a gift is given, it causes [them] to be reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*).
Likewise, when a gift is given...
He causes [the donor] to be reborn among the gods of the Thirty-three;
likewise, by giving such a gift, he causes him to be reborn among the Yāma gods;
likewise, by giving such a gift, he causes him to be reborn among the Tuṣita gods.
Giving a gift in this way causes one to be reborn among the Nirmāṇarati gods;
giving a gift in this way causes one to be reborn among the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
Thus, giving such a gift conduces to the attainment of the first dhyāna;
thus, giving such a gift conduces to the attainment of the second dhyāna.
Giving a gift in this way conduces to the attainment of the third dhyāna;
giving a gift in this way conduces to the attainment of the fourth dhyāna.
Thus, giving such a gift conduces to the attainment of the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space;
thus, giving such a gift conduces to the attainment of the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Thus, giving such a gift conduces to the attainment of the sphere of nothingness;
thus, giving such a gift conduces to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In this way, giving a gift conduces to the attainment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
in this way, giving a gift conduces to the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry.
In this way, giving a gift conduces to the attainment of the fruit of once-returning;
in this way, giving a gift conduces to the attainment of the fruit of non-returning;
in this way, giving a gift conduces to the attainment of the fruit of arhatship.
Thus, giving such a gift conduces to the attainment of the state of a Pratyekabuddha;
thus, it conduces to the attainment of the state of a Samyaksambuddha.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should know that by giving a gift with such skillful means, he fulfills the perfection of giving; and by giving a gift in this way,
he fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline.
In this way, giving such a gift fulfills the perfection of patience;
in this way, giving such a gift fulfills the perfection of vigor;
in this way, giving such a gift...
[He] fulfills the perfection of meditative concentration;
giving a gift in this way, he fulfills the perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while giving gifts, fulfill the perfection of generosity? How, while giving gifts, does he fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline?
How is the perfection of patience fulfilled by one giving a gift?
How is the perfection of vigor fulfilled by one giving a gift?
How is the perfection of meditative concentration fulfilled by one giving a gift?
How, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom fulfilled by a bodhisattva giving a gift?
The Blessed One said:
"By means of non-apprehension of the gift, the giver, and the recipient, the perfection of generosity is fulfilled."

The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is fulfilled by virtue of [distinguishing between] transgression, non-transgression, and the absence of committing a transgression; the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) is fulfilled by virtue of being unshakeable and not provoking agitation;
and [the perfection of vigor is fulfilled] by virtue of the non-laxity of physical and mental vigor.
The perfection of vigor becomes fulfilled;
by means of non-distraction and non-conceptualization, the perfection of meditation becomes fulfilled;
[of] all phenomena—
By means of the yoga of non-apprehension while fully cognizing [the gift], the perfection of wisdom is fulfilled.
In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, all six perfections are fulfilled.
In this way, within the perfection of ethical discipline, all six perfections are fulfilled;
likewise, within the perfection of patience, all [six perfections are fulfilled].

In this way, the six perfections are fulfilled; thus, within the perfection of vigor, all six perfections are fulfilled; thus, within the perfection of meditative concentration, all six perfections are fulfilled; thus, within the perfection of wisdom, all six perfections are fulfilled. [Thus, it is like the sound of sweet singing accompanied by knowledge.]

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with a single production of the thought of awakening, desires to transcend world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā— and likewise in the southern, western, northern, intermediate directions, below, and above— [desires to transcend world-systems] as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā...
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to transcend world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Moreover,
Śāriputra, whatever mass of water there is in the great oceans within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system—

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to lift up with the tip of a single hair split a hundredfold all the water in the great rivers, small streams, springs, lakes, and ponds, and who wishes not to harm the living beings dependent upon it, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to extinguish with a single breath from his mouth the fire of the conflagration at the end of the aeon that blazes throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system should train in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore,
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [who wishes to pacify] the whirlwinds that cause agitation...

When the wind-destruction is occurring, it shakes, scatters, and grinds to powder all the mountains— including Sumeru, Mahāsumeru, Cakravāḍa, and Mahācakravāḍa— as well as the entire great earth, up to the very limits;
yet he holds that whirlwind of agitation with the tip of a single finger-joint.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to cover [the entire space] with a single outstretched hand should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Moreover, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to pervade the entire realm of space within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system with a single cross-legged posture should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to bind together with a single hair all the mountains in the trichiliocosm— the Sumerus, Mahāsumerus, Cakravāḍas, Mahācakravāḍas, and so forth— and carry them across incalculable and immeasurable world-systems;
"One should train in the perfection of wisdom [with the thought]: 'I shall cause them to step forward; I shall cast them away.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to see with the divine eye the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in every single Buddha-field throughout the ten directions, and who wishes to hear their teaching of the Dharma with the divine ear..."
One who wishes to know the mental activities of all sentient beings, one who wishes to recollect their former abodes,
one who wishes to bring forth the supernormal knowledge of the cognition of the exhaustion of outflows, and one who wishes to realize the limit of reality, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

[Thus, accompanied by the superknowledges, he is like a great king. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should, with a single morsel of food, [satisfy] as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as there are in each of the ten directions throughout world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
One who wishes to present [offerings] with a vessel should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one should [train] in order to honor those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas with clouds of flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.

One who wishes to revere, honor, respect, and worship [the Buddha] should train in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish all those beings in the world-systems of the eastern direction— as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— in the aggregate of ethical discipline, in the aggregate of concentration, and in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation...

One who wishes to establish [beings] in the aggregate of vision; one who wishes to establish them in the fruit of stream-entry; one who wishes to establish them in the fruit of once-returning; one who wishes to establish them in the fruit of non-returning; one who wishes to establish them in arhatship; one who wishes to establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; and even one who wishes to establish them in the realm of nirvana without remainder, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Just as in the eastern direction, so too in the southern, western, northern, intermediate, downward, and upward directions— in each of these world-systems, which are as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— whatever sentient beings there may be, [he establishes them] in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish [others] in this should train in the perfection of wisdom.

[Thus, accompanied by merit and wisdom, it is like a storehouse. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the qualities of a Buddha— the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present— should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to reach the further shore of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [who wishes to reach the further shore] of all phenomena— past, future, and present— [should train in the perfection of wisdom].
One who desires to awaken to the Tathāgatas, and who desires to reach the limit of non-arising of all phenomena,
should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus, this is like the great path accompanied by the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to become a leader for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to become an attendant to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to become a member of the inner retinue of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, [should train in the perfection of wisdom].
One should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to have a great retinue and who wishes to obtain a retinue of bodhisattvas should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to purify his offerings should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to subdue a mind of stinginess should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes not to give rise to a mind of immorality should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [who wishes not to give rise to a mind of ill will]—

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not wish to give rise to [such thoughts] should train in the perfection of wisdom. Moreover, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to cast off a mind of indolence should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to eliminate a distracted mind should train in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes not to proliferate a mind of faulty wisdom should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish all sentient beings in the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, who wishes to establish them in the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline,
who wishes to establish them in the basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation, and [who wishes to establish them] in that which is accompanied by service and based on material things—
One who wishes to establish others in the bases of meritorious action should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to generate the five eyes should train in the perfection of wisdom.
What are these five?
That is to say, one who wishes to produce the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the divine eye, [should see] as many [beings] in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā...
One who desires to see the Blessed One should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, one who desires to see with the divine eye as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges in the southern direction should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, one who desires to see with the divine eye Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the western direction, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, one who desires to see with the divine eye Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the northern direction, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, one who desires to see with the divine eye Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the northeastern direction, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, one who desires to see with the divine eye Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the southeastern direction, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, one who desires to see with the divine eye Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the southwestern direction, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, one who desires to see with the divine eye Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the northwestern direction, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, one who wishes to see with the divine eye the Blessed Buddhas in the downward direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, one who wishes to see with the divine eye the Blessed Buddhas in the upward direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
And whatever dharmas those Blessed Buddhas proclaim, those dharmas [one should hear] with the divine [ear].
One who wishes to hear with the ear; one who wishes to understand, as it truly is, the minds of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, by means of their own mind;

one who wishes to recollect the state of a bodhisattva associated with the former lives of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; and one who wishes to see the miraculous transformations of the supernatural powers of those Buddhas—such a person should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, having heard the teachings that those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim throughout all world-systems in the ten directions, desires to retain them all through the power of an unbreakable retention of mindfulness until they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to see the buddha-fields of the past blessed buddhas,

and who wishes to see the buddha-fields of the future blessed buddhas as well, should train in the perfection of wisdom. This applies also to those blessed buddhas who currently reside, stay, and maintain themselves throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Those who desire to see the Buddha-fields of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus, accompanied by calm abiding and insight, it is like a vehicle.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, whatever has been spoken, is being spoken, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the ten directions—namely, this:

the discourses (sūtra), the songs (geya), the prophecies (vyākaraṇa), the verses (gāthā), the inspired utterances (udāna), the introductory narratives (nidāna), and the historical accounts (itivṛttaka)—[all of this is contained therein].

One who wishes to take up, retain, recite, practice in accordance with reality, and extensively proclaim to others all that has been taught in the Jātakas, Vaipulyas, Adbhutadharmas, Avadānas, and Upadeśas— which was not heard by the Śrāvakas— should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to take up, retain, and recite everything that has been spoken, is being spoken, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the eastern direction— in accordance with suchness— [should train in this perfection of wisdom].
One who wishes to practice and wishes to reveal it in detail to others should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to take up, retain, recite, and practice according to reality everything that has been spoken, is being spoken, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the southern direction.
One who wishes to reveal it in detail to others should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to take up, retain, recite, and practice according to reality everything that has been, is being, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the western direction.
One who wishes to reveal it in detail to others should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to take up, retain, recite, and practice in accordance with reality everything that has been, is being, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the northern direction.
One who wishes to reveal it in detail to others should train in the perfection of wisdom;
