likewise, one who wishes to take up, retain, recite, and practice in accordance with reality everything that has been, is being, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the northeastern direction.
One who wishes to reveal it in detail to others should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to take up, retain, recite, and practice in accordance with reality everything that has been, is being, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the southeastern direction.
One who wishes to reveal it in detail to others should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to take up, retain, recite, and practice according to reality everything that has been spoken, is being spoken, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the southern and western directions.
One who wishes to reveal it in detail to others should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to take up, retain, recite, and practice according to reality everything that has been spoken, is being spoken, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the northwestern direction.
And by one who wishes to reveal it in detail to others, one should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, by one who wishes to take up, retain, recite, and practice in accordance with suchness everything that has been, is being, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the direction below.
And by one who wishes to reveal it in detail to others, one should train in the perfection of wisdom;
by one who wishes to take up, retain, recite, and practice in accordance with reality everything that has been, is being, or will be spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the upward direction.
And by one who desires to reveal it in detail to others, one should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus, accompanied by dhāraṇīs and eloquence,
it is like a flowing spring.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, whatever [dharmas] there are in the worlds of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—

One who wishes to illuminate all those realms within the world-systems that are shrouded in blinding darkness, where even the light of the sun and moon does not reach, should train in the perfection of wisdom;
[so too for those] in the southern direction.

One who wishes to illuminate all those world-systems in the western direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, which are shrouded in blinding darkness where even the light of the sun and moon does not reach,

should train in the perfection of wisdom. [The same applies to] those world-systems in the western direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, which are shrouded in blinding darkness where the sun and moon...

One who wishes to illuminate all those places where even the light of the sun and moon has no reach— the regions of blinding darkness in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the northern direction— should train in the perfection of wisdom. One who wishes to illuminate all those places where even the light of the sun and moon has no reach should train in the perfection of wisdom.

One who wishes to illuminate all those regions in the northeastern direction—world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—which are shrouded in blinding darkness where even the light of the sun and moon does not reach, should train in the perfection of wisdom. One who wishes to illuminate all those regions in the southeastern direction—world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—which are shrouded in blinding darkness where... [the light of the sun and moon does not reach], should train in the perfection of wisdom.

One who wishes to illuminate all those places where even the light of the sun and moon does not reach— those regions of blinding darkness in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the southern and western directions, where even the radiance of the sun and moon has no access— should train in the perfection of wisdom. One who wishes to illuminate all those places where even the light of the sun and moon does not reach should train in the perfection of wisdom.

One who wishes to illuminate all those world systems in the northwestern direction— as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— which are shrouded in blinding darkness where even the light of the sun and moon does not reach, should train in the perfection of wisdom. One who wishes to [illuminate] all those world systems in the downward direction— as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— which are shrouded in blinding darkness where [the light of the sun and moon...]
One who wishes to illuminate all those places where even the light of the sun and moon has no reach—
the regions of blinding darkness in world-systems in the upward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to cause all those beings born in various buddha-fields within the world-systems of the eastern direction— as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— to hear the sound of the Buddha,
the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Saṅgha, and who wishes to establish those beings in right view...
One who wishes to establish [beings] [in the path] should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to cause all those beings in the southern direction— in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā who have been born in various Buddha-fields— to hear the sound of "Buddha," the sound of "Dharma," and the sound of "Saṅgha," and to [establish] those beings [therein], should train in the perfection of wisdom.
One who wishes to establish [beings] in right view should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to cause all those beings— who have been born in various Buddha-fields within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the western direction— to hear the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Saṅgha, should train in that same perfection of wisdom.
One who wishes to establish [beings] in right view should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to cause all those beings—who have been born in various Buddha-fields within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the northern direction—to hear the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Saṅgha, should [train in the perfection of wisdom]. And those beings...
One who wishes to establish [beings] in right view should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Likewise, one who wishes to cause all those beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the northeastern direction— who have been born in various Buddha-fields— to hear the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Saṅgha, and to cause those beings [to hear them], [should train in the perfection of wisdom].
One who wishes to establish [beings] in right view should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to cause all those beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the southeastern direction—who have been born in various Buddha-fields—to hear the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Saṅgha, should [train in the perfection of wisdom]. And those beings...
One who wishes to establish [beings] in right view should train in the perfection of wisdom.

One who wishes to cause all those beings— who have been born in various Buddha-fields within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River in the southern and western directions— to hear the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Saṅgha, and to [establish] those beings...
One who wishes to establish [beings] in right view should train in the perfection of wisdom.

One who wishes to cause all those beings— who have been born in various Buddha-fields within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the northwestern direction— to hear the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Saṅgha, and to lead those beings [to that state], should train in the perfection of wisdom.
One who wishes to establish [beings] in right view should train in the perfection of wisdom.

One who wishes to cause all those beings— who have been born in various Buddha-fields within world-systems in the downward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— to hear the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Saṅgha, and to [establish] those beings...
One who wishes to establish [beings] in right view should train in the perfection of wisdom;

likewise, one who wishes to cause all those beings born in various Buddha-fields throughout world-systems in the upward direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, to hear the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, and the sound of the Saṅgha, should [train in the perfection of wisdom].
One who wishes to establish others in right view should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus it is like the sound of joy accompanied by the summary of the Dharma.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should think]: "By my power, may all those beings who are blind in all the Buddha-fields within the world-systems in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, behold forms with their eyes."
One should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Likewise, [one should train] thinking that those who are deaf will hear sounds with their ears; that those who are insane will regain their mindfulness; that those who are naked will obtain clothing; and that those who are hungry...

"Sentient beings shall have their bowls filled; those sentient beings born in the miserable realms shall be liberated from all miserable realms and obtain a human body. [Thinking,] "I shall establish those of immoral conduct in the aggregate of morality," and "I shall establish those who are not concentrated in the aggregate of concentration," [he resolves upon] the wicked...

"I shall establish those with wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom; I shall establish those who are not liberated in the aggregate of liberation; I shall establish those who lack the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not yet seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry; I shall establish them in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and in arhatship."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought, "I shall establish them in individual enlightenment," and "I shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment.

[He should train] with the thought: "By my power, those beings who are blind in all the Buddha-fields within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the southern direction shall see forms with their eyes" through the perfection of wisdom.

Thus, it would be like saying that the deaf will hear sounds with their ears, the insane will regain their mindfulness, the naked will obtain clothing, hungry beings will have their bowls filled to the brim, and that beings born in the states of woe will be liberated from all miserable realms and regain a human body— even though they are of immoral conduct.

"I shall establish those who lack morality in the aggregate of morality; I shall establish those who are unconcentrated in the aggregate of concentration; I shall establish those with poor wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom; I shall establish those who are unliberated in the aggregate of liberation;

I shall establish those lacking the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not yet seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "I shall establish them in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship; I shall establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; I shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, [a bodhisattva should train] in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "By my power, those beings who are blind in all buddha-fields within the world-systems in the western direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, shall see forms with their eyes."

Thus, it would be like saying that the deaf will hear sounds with their ears, the insane will regain their mindfulness, the naked will obtain clothing, hungry beings will have their bowls filled, and those born in the states of woe will be liberated from all miserable realms and regain a human body— yet this would apply even to those of immoral conduct.

"I shall establish those who have not yet established themselves in the aggregate of ethical discipline; I shall establish those who are unconcentrated in the aggregate of concentration; I shall establish those with poor wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom; I shall establish those who are unliberated in the aggregate of liberation;

I shall establish those who lack the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not yet seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "I shall establish them in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship; I shall establish them in pratyekabodhi; I shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Furthermore, [he should train] with the thought: "By my power, those beings who are blind in all the buddha-fields within the world-systems of the northern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, shall see forms with their eyes. Thus should one train in the perfection of wisdom.

Thus, it would be like saying that the deaf will hear sounds with their ears; that the insane will regain their memory; that the naked will obtain clothing; that hungry beings will have their bowls filled; that beings born in the states of woe will be liberated from all miserable rebirths and obtain a human body; and [that] those of immoral conduct...

"I shall establish those who lack the aggregate of ethical discipline in the aggregate of ethical discipline; I shall establish those who are not concentrated in the aggregate of concentration; I shall establish those with impaired wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom; I shall establish those who are not liberated in the aggregate of liberation;

I shall establish those who lack the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "I shall establish them in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship; I shall establish them in pratyekabodhi; I shall establish them in unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, [a bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom] with the thought: "By my power, those beings who are blind in all the buddha-fields within the world-systems in the northeastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, shall see forms with their eyes."

Thus, it would be like saying that the deaf will hear sounds with their ears; that the insane will regain their mindfulness; that the naked will obtain clothing; that hungry beings will have their bowls filled to the brim; that beings born in the states of woe will be liberated from all those states of woe and regain a human body; and [that] those of immoral conduct...

"I shall establish those who lack the aggregate of ethical discipline in the aggregate of ethical discipline; I shall establish those who lack concentration in the aggregate of concentration; I shall establish those with poor wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom; I shall establish those who are not liberated in the aggregate of liberation;

I shall establish those who lack the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "I shall establish them in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship; I shall establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; I shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, [he should train] with the thought: "By my power, those beings who are blind in all the buddha-fields within the world-systems of the eastern direction—as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—shall see forms with their eyes," thus in the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, they will say: "The deaf shall hear sounds with their ears; the insane shall regain their mindfulness; the naked shall obtain clothing; hungry beings shall have their bowls filled;

beings born in the states of woe shall be liberated from all states of woe and regain a human body"; and [they will say] that those of immoral conduct [shall be established] in the aggregate of morality.
"I shall establish them"—that is, "I shall establish those who are not concentrated in the aggregate of concentration; I shall establish those with poor wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom;

I shall establish those who are not liberated in the aggregate of liberation; I shall establish those who lack the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "I shall establish them in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship; I shall establish them in pratyekabodhi; I shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, [he should train] with the thought: "By my power, those beings who are blind in all buddha-fields within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the southern and western directions shall see forms with their eyes" through the perfection of wisdom.

Thus, it would be like saying that the deaf will hear sounds with their ears; that the insane will regain their mindfulness; that the naked will obtain clothing; that hungry beings will have their bowls filled; that beings born in the states of woe will be liberated from all states of woe and obtain a human body; and [that] those of immoral conduct...

"I shall establish those who lack the aggregate of ethical discipline in the aggregate of ethical discipline; I shall establish those who lack concentration in the aggregate of concentration; I shall establish those with poor wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom; I shall establish those who are not liberated in the aggregate of liberation;

I shall establish those who lack the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "I shall establish them in the fruit of a once-returner, in the fruit of a non-returner, in arhatship; I shall establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; I shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, [he should train] with the thought: "By my power, those beings who are blind in all buddha-fields throughout the world-systems in the western and northern directions—as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—shall see forms with their eyes," and thus in the perfection of wisdom.

Thus, it would be like saying that the deaf will hear sounds with their ears, the insane will regain their mindfulness, the naked will obtain clothing, hungry beings will have their bowls filled to the brim, and those born in the states of woe will be liberated from all miserable rebirths and regain a human body— yet this applies even to those of immoral conduct.

"I shall establish those who lack morality in the aggregate of morality; I shall establish those who are unconcentrated in the aggregate of concentration; I shall establish those with poor wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom; I shall establish those who are unliberated in the aggregate of liberation;

I shall establish those who lack the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "I shall establish them in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship; I shall establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; I shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, [he should train] with the thought: "By my power, those beings who are blind in all the buddha-fields throughout the world-systems in the downward direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, shall see forms with their eyes through the perfection of wisdom."

Thus, it would be like saying that the deaf will hear sounds with their ears, the insane will regain their mindfulness, the naked will obtain clothing, hungry beings will have their bowls filled to the brim, and that beings born in the states of woe will be liberated from all miserable rebirths and obtain a human body— yet this applies even to those of immoral conduct.

"I shall establish those who lack the aggregate of ethical discipline in the aggregate of ethical discipline; I shall establish those who are not concentrated in the aggregate of concentration; I shall establish those with deficient wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom; I shall establish those who are not liberated in the aggregate of liberation;

I shall establish those who lack the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "I shall establish them in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship; I shall establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; I shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment.

[Furthermore,] a bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "By my power, may those beings who are blind in all the Buddha-fields throughout the world-systems in the upward direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, behold forms with their eyes."
Thus, it would be as if the deaf were to hear sounds with their ears; the insane were to regain their mindfulness; the naked were to obtain clothing; hungry beings were to have their bowls filled;
and beings born in the states of woe were to be liberated from all states of woe, regain a human body, and [be freed] from those of immoral conduct.

"I shall establish those who have not yet established themselves in the aggregate of ethical discipline; I shall establish those who are unconcentrated in the aggregate of concentration; I shall establish those with poor wisdom in the aggregate of wisdom; I shall establish those who are unliberated in the aggregate of liberation;

I shall establish those lacking the knowledge and vision of liberation in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; I shall establish those who have not seen the truths in the fruit of stream-entry."

A bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "I shall establish them in the fruit of once-returning, in the fruit of non-returning, and in arhatship; I shall establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; I shall establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. [Thus ends the simile of the river's current, accompanied by the path of the single way.]
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the deportment of a Tathāgata should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore,
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way:

Thinking, "When indeed shall I behold the gaze of the Naga-kings? How might I walk upon the earth without my feet touching it by even four finger-breadths?"— thus should one train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way:
"How might I [attain] the four..."
[He was surrounded] by the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods,

the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Brahmapāriṣadya gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Anabhraka gods, and the Puṇyaprasava gods.

Thinking, "May I approach the foot of the Bodhi tree surrounded and honored by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sons of gods— by those of the Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Śuddhāvāsa, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, and Sudarśana heavens"— one should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way:
"How is it that the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trayastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin [gods]..."

The Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Brahmapāriṣadya gods; the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara gods; the Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna gods; the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala gods; the Asaṃjñisattvas; and the Śuddhāvāsa gods—the Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, and Sudarśana gods.
"And may the Akaniṣṭha gods spread out [their garments] at the foot of the tree of enlightenment"—
thus should one train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way:

"How may that portion of earth where I go, stand, sit, or lie down after I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment become composed of diamond?"— thus should one train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way:
"How might I, on the very same day that I go forth, attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment on that very same day?"
"On that very day, may I set in motion the wheel of Dharma;
and as I am setting the wheel of Dharma in motion,
may countless and immeasurable beings obtain the stainless, long-cleansed Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena."
"May [they] be liberated.
May the minds of incalculable and immeasurable sentient beings be liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
"In order that incalculable and immeasurable beings may become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, one should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should investigate the perfection of wisdom in this way: 'How might...'"

"May I have an immeasurable and incalculable assembly of disciples," and "may immeasurable and incalculable beings, through the teaching of a single dharma, become bodhisattvas seated upon a single seat who are irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
May the community of bodhisattvas be incalculable and immeasurable;
may the measure of their lifespan be limitless;
and may their excellence of radiance be boundless.
One should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should investigate the perfection of wisdom in this way:
"How shall it be for me when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"In that buddha-field, may the bases of passion, hatred, and delusion not exist at all, in every way and in every respect"— thus should one train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should investigate the perfection of wisdom in this manner.

"How may sentient beings come to be endowed with such wisdom when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, residing in other Buddha-fields, might utter this inspired exclamation?"

"Excellent is tranquility, excellent is self-control, excellent is restraint; excellent is the dwelling in the practice of celibacy, and excellent is non-violence toward all living beings—one should train in the perfection of wisdom in this way.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should investigate the perfection of wisdom in this manner."

"How may there be no disappearance of my True Dharma even after I have entered final nirvana, and how may those beings in world-systems throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges become fixed in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment upon merely hearing my name?"— thus should one train in the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom,
produces these qualities, then those great kings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system think thus: "We shall offer four bowls to this bodhisattva."
We shall give [this gift], just as it was given by former great kings to the former Tathāgatas;
and the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven will be delighted, while the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati,
and Paranirmitavaśavartin gods will become eager.
"We shall perform services and attend upon this bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Thus spoke the asuras.
The [inferior] bodies will diminish,
while the divine bodies will increase; and they shall become joyful throughout the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.
The gods of the Brahma-pariṣadya, the Brahma-purohita,
and the Mahābrahmans become joyful,
as do the Parīttābhas and the Apramāṇābhas.
The Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Śuddhāvāsa, Avṛha, Atapa,
Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha realms— among those [beings], it occurs thus:
"We shall entreat him, once he has attained full awakening, to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Śāriputra, at the time when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva [practices] in the perfection of wisdom...

As he practices and increases by means of the six perfections, at that time the sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle become joyful, thinking: "We shall be his mother and father; we shall be his wife, children, kinsmen, and blood relations."
The Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three,
the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods,
the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmans, the Brahmapāriṣadya gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, and the Apramāṇaśubha gods become joyful.
The Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Śuddhāvāsa, Aspr̥ha, Atapa,
Sadr̥śa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha devas [are attained] by a bodhisattva mahāsattva through the complete avoidance of the practice of sexual intercourse.
Furthermore, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is a celibate practitioner does not associate with things that lead to fetters;
it occurs to him: "This is for one who is not a celibate practitioner."
Furthermore, for one who indulges in sensual pleasures, even rebirth in the Brahma-world becomes an obstacle,
let alone the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, then—

A bodhisattva mahāsattva must awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment only after having gone forth from the home life as one who practices celibacy, and not as one who does not practice celibacy.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One in this way:

"Furthermore, Blessed One, must a bodhisattva necessarily have a mother and father? Must he necessarily have a wife, sons, kinsmen, and blood relations? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
Śāriputra, for some bodhisattva mahāsattvas, there exist parents, or wives, sons, kinsmen, and blood relations; however,
for other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, from the first production of the thought of awakening (prathamacittotpāda) onwards, [there are none].
At the conclusion of their undertaking of the conduct, while practicing the bodhisattva path as youths,
some bodhisattvas, great beings, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through skillful means.
And by means of skillfulness, having enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasure and then gone forth, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra, it is just as if, for example, there were a skilled illusionist...
Or suppose there were a master illusionist, or a well-trained apprentice of an illusionist, who,
having conjured up the five strands of sensual pleasure, would delight in, play with, and enjoy those five strands of sensual pleasure. That...
"What do you think, Śāriputra? Would that illusionist or the apprentice of an illusionist have actually tasted or enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasure?
Śāriputra said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "It is even so, Śāriputra."
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skill in means, enjoys the five strands of sensual pleasure for the sake of maturing sentient beings; however,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not [enjoy them] out of attachment to the strands of sensual pleasure.
In this manner, the bodhisattva mahāsattva speaks in dispraise of sensual desires:
"Sensual desires are ablaze; sensual desires are loathsome; sensual desires are murderers; sensual desires are adversaries."
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes up the five strands of sensual pleasure for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Thus, accompanied by the desire for the Dharma,
it is like a great cloud.
[Thus has the production of the thought of awakening been explained.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"How, Blessed One..."
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom. When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra.
In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, while being a bodhisattva indeed, does not perceive a bodhisattva,
nor does he perceive even the name "bodhisattva."
He does not perceive even the conduct of a bodhisattva; he does not perceive even the perfection of wisdom;
he does not perceive even form.
He does not perceive it; likewise, he does not even fully perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
For what reason?
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by way of the intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva, [does not perceive it].
It is empty, being empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
This is its very nature.
For in this way, form is not empty by means of emptiness; nor is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness empty by means of emptiness.

Emptiness is not other than form, nor is there emptiness other than feeling, nor is there emptiness other than perception, nor is there emptiness other than mental formations, nor is there emptiness other than consciousness.
For what reason? Form itself is emptiness; feeling itself is emptiness; perception itself is emptiness;
mental formations themselves are emptiness; consciousness itself is emptiness; emptiness itself is form; emptiness itself is feeling.
Emptiness itself is perception; emptiness itself is mental formations; emptiness itself is consciousness.
For what reason?
Because that which is called "bodhisattva" here is merely a name.
This which is called "perfection of wisdom" is a mere name; this which is form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is a mere name.
For form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like an illusion, and an illusion is a mere name.
Neither abiding in a location nor abiding in a specific part, this false vision arises without a cause; for that which has the nature of a magical illusion is neither produced nor ceased.
There is neither affliction nor purification. Thus,
practicing in the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive even arising,
nor does he perceive even cessation.
He does not perceive affliction, nor does he perceive purification. For what reason?
For names are artificial with respect to their respective objects,
and those [names] are conceptual constructs.
They are designated by adventitious names;
when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any of those names,
and not perceiving them, he does not become attached to them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not examine it in this way: "This which is called 'bodhisattva' is a mere name;
this which is called 'awakening' (bodhi) is also a mere name."
"This so-called 'perfection of wisdom' is a mere name;
this so-called 'practice in the perfection of wisdom' is a mere name."
"This so-called 'form' is merely a name;
this so-called 'feeling' is merely a name; this so-called 'perception' is merely a name."
"This is merely a name, namely 'formations' (saṃskāra);
this is merely a name, namely 'consciousness' (vijñāna).
Śāriputra, it is just as, for example, that which is called 'self' (ātman)."
And a self is not apprehended;
neither a sentient being, nor a living soul, nor a nourisher, nor a person, nor an individual, nor a human being is apprehended,
based on the emptiness of non-apprehension.
For what reason? Because a bodhisattva does not even perceive that by which he might become attached.
Practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva—
He courses in the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra, if this Jambudvīpa were filled with monks like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, as densely as a thicket of reeds or a grove of bamboo—

Whether it be a forest of sugarcane, a forest of reeds, a forest of rice, or a forest of sesame— the wisdom of those [beings] does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor any number, fraction, or calculation of the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom.
It does not even approach a comparison, a likeness, a secret essence, or a subtle resemblance.
Thus, Śāriputra, the wisdom cultivated by a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom for even a single day surpasses [the wisdom] of all śrāvakas—
It surpasses the wisdom of the Pratyekabuddhas.
For what reason?
Because, Śāriputra, it is thus.

The wisdom of a bodhisattva is present for the sake of the nirvāṇa of all sentient beings. Let alone this Jambudvīpa filled with monks like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, suppose this three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system were filled with [monks like] Śāriputra...
Even if there were monks like Maudgalyāyana’s son as numerous as a grove of reeds,

a grove of bamboos, a grove of sugarcane, a grove of *śara* grass, a grove of rice, or a grove of sesame seeds— the wisdom possessed by all of them would not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
It does not bear comparison even with a number, a fraction, a calculation, a likeness, a secret essence, or even a minute part. Let alone, Śāriputra,
a trichiliocosm world-system filled with beings like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—
If, Śāriputra, world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were filled with monks like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— [that]...
Just as, for example, a grove of *nalas*, a grove of bamboos, a grove of sugarcane, a grove of reeds, a grove of rice, or a grove of sesame seeds—

whatever wisdom those possess does not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom; nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor any number, fraction, or calculation.
It does not even admit of a comparison, nor a secret teaching, nor a subtle analogy. Śāriputra, if the world-systems in the southern direction were as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā,
and were filled with monks equal to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— just like a thicket of reeds— }

Whether it be a bamboo forest, a sugarcane forest, a reed forest, a rice field, or a sesame field— the wisdom of all those [beings] does not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom; nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor any number, fraction, calculation, or comparison.
It does not even approach a fraction, nor even a small part. Śāriputra, if the world-systems in the western direction were as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā,
and were filled with monks such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— just like a thicket of reeds—

Whether it be a bamboo grove, a sugarcane grove, a reed grove, a rice field, or a sesame field— the wisdom of those [beings] does not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom;
nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor any number, nor any fraction, nor any calculation, nor any comparison.
It does not even come close to a fraction, nor even a small part. Śāriputra, if in the northern direction there were world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā,
filled with monks like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, just as, for example, a thicket of reeds or a grove of bamboo.

Or a grove of sugarcane, or a grove of reeds, or a grove of rice, or a grove of sesame— whatever wisdom they possess does not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom; it does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part,
nor any number, nor a fraction, nor a calculation, nor a comparison, nor a likeness, nor even a resemblance.

If, Śāriputra, world-systems in the northeastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were filled with monks equal to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— just as, for example, a forest of reeds, or a forest of bamboos, or a forest of sugarcane, or a forest of *śara* grass, or a forest of rice, or a forest of sesame seeds— the wisdom possessed by them all...
The wisdom of that [other] Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom;
it does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor any number, nor a fraction, nor a calculation, nor a comparison, nor a resemblance, nor even a point of reference.
Śāriputra, if in the southeastern direction there were world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā,

filled with monks equal to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— just as, for example, a forest of reeds, or a forest of bamboos, or a forest of sugarcane, or a forest of *śara* grass, or a forest of rice, or a forest of sesame— whatever wisdom they possessed;
The wisdom of that [other] Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom;
it does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor any number, nor a fraction, nor a calculation, nor a comparison, nor a likeness, nor even a resemblance.

If, Śāriputra, world-systems in the southwestern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were filled with monks equal to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— just as, for example, a forest of reeds, or a forest of bamboos, or a forest of sugarcane, or a forest of *śara* grass, or a forest of rice, or a forest of sesame seeds— the wisdom possessed by them all...
The wisdom of that [other] person does not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom;
it does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor any number, nor a fraction, nor a calculation, nor a comparison, nor a likeness, nor even a resemblance.
Śāriputra, if in the northwestern direction there were world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges,

filled with monks equal to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— just as, for example, a forest of reeds, or a forest of bamboos, or a forest of sugarcane, or a forest of *śara* grass, or a forest of rice, or a forest of sesame— whatever wisdom they possessed...
The wisdom of that [other] Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom;
it does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor any number, nor a fraction, nor a calculation, nor a comparison, nor a likeness, nor even a resemblance.
If, Śāriputra, world-systems in the downward direction were as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā,
and were filled with monks equal to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— just as, for example, a thicket of reeds, or a bamboo grove,
or a field of sugarcane, or a field of *śara* grass, or a field of rice, or a field of sesame— whatever wisdom they possessed would [be compared] to the perfection of wisdom.
The wisdom of a Bodhisattva who is thus practicing does not approach even a hundredth part of it; nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part;
nor any number, fraction, calculation, comparison, likeness, or resemblance.
Śāriputra, if worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were filled in the upward direction—

Even if there were monks equal to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, as numerous as a grove of reeds, a grove of bamboo, a grove of sugarcane, a grove of *śara* grass, a grove of rice, or a grove of sesame seeds— the wisdom they possess would not approach even a hundredth part of the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
It does not approach even a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part; it does not admit of any number, fraction, calculation, comparison, likeness, or resemblance.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
Blessed One, that which is the wisdom of a stream-enterer, the wisdom of a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha,
the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and the wisdom of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—

All these wisdoms are undifferentiated, secluded, unarisen, devoid of intrinsic nature, and empty. Furthermore, O Blessed One, no differentiation or distinction is perceived within that which is undifferentiated, secluded, unarisen, devoid of intrinsic nature, and empty.

In that case, Blessed One, how is it that the wisdom cultivated by a bodhisattva in a single day surpasses the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas when he is practicing the perfection of wisdom?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:

"What do you think, Śāriputra? For what purpose is the wisdom—endowed with the excellence of all aspects—that has been cultivated for even a single day by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, now present?"
While practicing for the sake of omniscience and acting for the benefit of all sentient beings, having awakened to all phenomena in all their aspects, [he thinks]:
"All sentient beings must be led to final nirvana.
Now, Śāriputra, by that very task—
"It is present for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra said, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Śāriputra? Do all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ever think:
"Having awakened to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment by ourselves..."
"All sentient beings are to be led to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder. Śāriputra said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, Śāriputra, by this method also you should understand it thus:
that which is the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is [inferior] awakening (bodhi).

It does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor any number, fraction, calculation, comparison, resemblance, or likeness of the wisdom of a single being cultivated for even a single day.
"What do you think, Śāriputra? Do all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ever think:

'Having practiced the six perfections, having matured sentient beings, having purified a buddha-field, and having fulfilled the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eight..."
"Having fulfilled the ten unique qualities of a Buddha and awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
we shall lead immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvāṇa. Śāriputra said, "Certainly not so, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: 'Having practiced the six perfections, I [shall lead] sentient beings...'"

"Having matured [beings], having purified the Buddha-field, having fulfilled the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I shall lead immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvāṇa."
It is just as if,
Śāriputra, a firefly, a mere kind of insect, were to think, "May Jambudvīpa be illuminated by my light," or "May Jambudvīpa be filled with my light. Even so, [it is impossible].
Śāriputra, it does not occur to any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas: "Having practiced even a single one of the six perfections,

having matured sentient beings, having purified a buddha-field, and having fulfilled the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha..."

"Having fulfilled [the perfections] and awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall lead immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvāṇa. Śāriputra, it is just as when the orb of the sun rises over all Jambudvīpa—
Just as [the sun] makes things manifest by its radiance,
even so, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
having practiced the six perfections, having brought sentient beings to maturity, and having purified a buddha-field, [establishes] the ten...

Having fulfilled the powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, [he delivers] immeasurable, incalculable,
and infinite sentient beings.
[He] causes [them] to attain final nirvāṇa.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"How, Blessed One..."

The bodhisattva mahāsattva, having transcended the entire stage of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, attains the stage of non-retrogression and purifies the path to awakening. When this had been said, the Blessed One—
He said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Here, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, practicing the six perfections, [dwells] in emptiness and the signless— "
Abiding in these wishless phenomena, he transcends the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, attains the irreversible level, and purifies the path to enlightenment.
When this had been said, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, abiding on which stage does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become a constant and perpetual object of offerings for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, while practicing the six perfections, until he reaches the seat of awakening— in the interval between these times— a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly and continuously [cultivates] all..."
He becomes one worthy of offerings for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
For what reason? Because, Śāriputra, it is by depending upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that all wholesome dharmas appear in the world.
There is a manifestation,
namely: of the ten paths of wholesome action,
of the five trainings, of the poṣadha endowed with eight factors, and of the four meditative absorptions and the four immeasurables.
of the four formless attainments, the five superknowledges, the four noble truths,
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
The appearance of the path occurs in the world;
the appearance of the four grounds of self-confidence occurs in the world;
the appearance of the four analytical knowledges occurs in the world.
The manifestation in the world of the six perfections, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha occurs.
And through the manifestation of these wholesome qualities in the world,
the great kshatriya clans become known, the great brahmin clans become known,
the great householder clans become known, and the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings become known.
The Trāyastriṃśa gods are known;
the Yāma gods are known;
the Nirmāṇarati gods are known.
The gods who wield power over the creations of others are known;
the gods of the Brahma-realm are known;
the gods who are ministers of Brahmā are known.
The Mahābrahmā gods are known;
the Brahmapāriṣadya gods are known;
the Parīttābha gods are known.
The gods of Immeasurable Light are known;
the gods of Radiant Purity are known;
the gods of Limited Virtue are known.
The gods of Immeasurable Purity are known;
the gods of Universal Purity are known;
the gods of Cloudless Radiance are known.
The Puṇyaprasava gods are known;
the Bṛhatphala gods are known;
the Asaṃjñisattva gods are known.
The Śuddhāvāsa gods are known;
the Aspr̥ha gods are known;
the Atapa gods are known.
The Sadṛśa devas are known;
the Sudarśana devas are known;
the Akaniṣṭha devas [are known].
The gods of the sphere of infinite space are known; the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness are known.
The gods of the sphere of infinite space are known; the gods of the sphere of nothingness are known;
the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are known.
Stream-enterers arise in the world;
once-returners arise in the world; non-returners arise in the world.
Arhats arise in the world;
pratyekabuddhas arise in the world; bodhisattvas arise in the world; likewise, Tathāgatas...
"Arhats, the perfectly awakened ones, appear in the world.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"But what, Blessed One?"
“Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā), or not?
The Blessed One said, “No indeed, Śāriputra; a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not purify the sacrificial gift.”
For what reason?
Because the gift of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is absolutely pure.
For what reason? Because he is a donor.
Śāriputra, of what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva a giver? He is a giver of wholesome dharmas.
He is a giver. Of which wholesome dharmas is he a giver?
Namely, of the ten paths of wholesome action, the five precepts, the *poṣadha* endowed with eight factors, and the four...

of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five superknowledges, the four noble truths, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
He is the giver of the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the six perfections, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
[Thus ends the instruction on practice.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"How should one apply oneself?"
“Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva be said to be ‘engaged’ in the perfection of wisdom?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: “In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is engaged in the emptiness of form should be said to be ‘engaged.’”

One who is engaged in the emptiness of feeling should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of perception should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of mental formations should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of consciousness should be said to be "engaged.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is engaged in the emptiness of the eye should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the ear should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the nose should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the tongue should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the body should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the mind should be said to be "engaged.
One who is engaged in the emptiness of form should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of sound should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of odor should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of taste should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the tangible should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of phenomena should be said to be "engaged.
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the eye-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged.
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the ear-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the nose-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged.

One who is engaged in the emptiness of the tongue-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of the body-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the mental-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged.
One who is engaged in the emptiness of suffering should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of origination should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of cessation should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the path should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of ignorance should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of volitional formations should be said to be "engaged.
One who is engaged in the emptiness of consciousness should be said to be "engaged.
One who is engaged in the emptiness of name-and-form should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the six sense bases should be said to be "engaged.
One who is engaged in the emptiness of contact should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of feeling should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of craving should be said to be "engaged.
One who is engaged in the emptiness of grasping should be said to be "engaged. One who is engaged in the emptiness of existence should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of birth should be said to be "engaged.
One who is engaged in the emptiness of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair should be said to be "engaged."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
if he is engaged in internal emptiness, he should be said to be "engaged";
if he is engaged in external emptiness, he should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in internal-and-external emptiness should be said to be "engaged"; likewise,
one who is engaged in the emptiness of other-existence should be said to be "engaged."

In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom who is engaged in all these forms of emptiness is to be called "engaged. While practicing the perfection of wisdom through these emptinesses, he does not [attain] awakening— yet.
Should that being, that great being, be said to be "engaged" or "disengaged"?
For what reason?
Because he does not regard form as engaged, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness as engaged.
Or he perceives it as being improper.

[Thus ends the instruction on the Truth of Suffering. He does not perceive form as having the nature of arising or the nature of cessation; he does not perceive feeling as having the nature of arising or the nature of cessation; nor does he perceive perception as having the nature of arising—
He does not perceive a subject that has the nature of arising or the nature of cessation; nor does he perceive conditioned phenomena as having the nature of non-arising or the nature of cessation;
nor [does he perceive] consciousness as arising—
He does not perceive a phenomenon that has the nature of cessation, nor does he perceive form as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification.
He does not perceive feeling as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification. Nor does he...
He does not perceive perception as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification;
he does not perceive volitional formations as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification;
he does not perceive consciousness as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive that form merges into feeling;
nor does he perceive that feeling merges into perception.
He does not perceive that perception merges into mental formations;
he does not perceive that mental formations merge into consciousness.
He does not perceive that consciousness enters into phenomena; he does not perceive that a phenomenon enters into any phenomenon.
Why is that? Because there is no one whatsoever...
Dharma is sometimes subsumed within dharma, based on the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Why is that?
For, Śāriputra, that which is the emptiness of form is not that form.
That which is the emptiness of feeling is not that feeling;
that which is the emptiness of perception is not that perception.
That which is the emptiness of the formative forces is not those formative forces;
that which is the emptiness of consciousness is not that consciousness. Why is that?
For this reason: for that which is the emptiness of form does not form;
that which is the emptiness of sensation does not feel.
That which is the emptiness of perception does not perceive;
that which is the emptiness of formations does not form.
That which is the emptiness of consciousness does not cognize. For what reason? Because, Śāriputra, form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than [form].
Form is emptiness; emptiness is indeed form.
Feeling is not other than emptiness;
emptiness is not other than feeling.
Feeling itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is feeling. Perception is not other than emptiness,
and emptiness is not other than perception.
Perception itself is emptiness;
emptiness itself is perception.
There are no formations other than emptiness, nor is there any emptiness other than them.
Emptiness is not other than conditioned phenomena;
conditioned phenomena themselves are emptiness, and emptiness itself is conditioned phenomena. It is not something else.
Consciousness is not other than emptiness;
emptiness is not other than consciousness. Consciousness itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself is consciousness;
[thus is the instruction on the truth of the origin]. Śāriputra, emptiness is neither produced nor does it cease.
It is neither afflicted nor purified; it neither decreases nor increases;
it is not past, not future, and not present. And that which...
In that [state], there is no such thing as form, no sensation, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness;
no earth element, no water element, no fire element, no air element, no space element, and no consciousness element;
no eye sense-field, no form sense-field, no ear sense-field, no sound sense-field, and no nose sense-field.
The sphere of odor, not the sphere of tongue, not the sphere of taste, not the sphere of body, not the sphere of the tangible, not the sphere of mind,
not the sphere of mental phenomena;
not the eye-element, not the form-element, not the eye-consciousness—
There is no eye-element, no ear-element, no sound-element, and no ear-consciousness-element;
no nose-element, no odor-element, and no nose-consciousness-element.
There is no tongue element, no taste element, no tongue-consciousness element; no body element, no tangible object element, no body-consciousness element;
no mind element.
The realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is not the mind-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu).
There is no arising of ignorance, nor the cessation of ignorance;
there is no arising of formative forces (saṃskāra), nor the cessation of formative forces.
There is no arising of consciousness, nor cessation of consciousness;
no arising of name-and-form, nor cessation of name-and-form;
no arising of the six sense bases, nor cessation of the six sense bases.
There is no arising of contact, nor cessation of contact;
no arising of feeling, nor cessation of feeling;
no arising of craving, nor cessation of craving.
There is no arising of grasping, nor cessation of grasping;
no arising of becoming, nor cessation of becoming;
no arising of birth, nor cessation of birth.

There is no arising of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair; there is no cessation of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair; there is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; there is no attainment, no realization, no stream-enterer, and no [stream-entry].

There is no offense, nor the fruit of once-returning; no once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; no non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; no arhatship, nor the fruit of arhatship; no solitary buddha, nor solitary awakening; no Buddha, nor awakening.
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom is to be called "joined" (yukta), "joined.
[Thus ends the instruction on the truth of cessation.]
While practicing the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with the perfection of generosity;
nor does he perceive himself as being engaged with the perfection of ethical discipline.
He does not perceive [himself] as "engaged" or "disengaged";
he does not perceive [himself] as "engaged" or "disengaged" in the perfection of patience; he does not perceive [himself] as "engaged" or "disengaged" in the perfection of vigor. He does not...
He does not perceive himself as being engaged in the perfection of meditation, nor as being disengaged from it;
he does not perceive himself as being engaged in the perfection of wisdom, nor as being disengaged from it; he does not perceive himself as being engaged in form, nor as being disengaged from it.
He does not perceive [it] as being either engaged or disengaged with regard to feeling; he does not perceive [it] as being either engaged or disengaged with regard to perception. He does not...
He does not perceive the formative forces as being either "engaged" or "disengaged.
He does not perceive consciousness as being either "engaged" or "disengaged.
He does not perceive the eye as being either "engaged" or "disengaged. Nor...
He does not perceive the ear as being engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the nose as being engaged or disengaged;
he does not perceive the tongue as being engaged or disengaged; nor [does he perceive] the body.
He does not perceive it as "engaged" or "disengaged";
he does not perceive the mind as "engaged" or "disengaged";
he does not perceive form as "engaged" or "disengaged."
He does not perceive sound as either "joined" or "disjoined"; he does not perceive odor as either "joined" or "disjoined";
he does not perceive taste as either "joined" or "disjoined."

He does not perceive that one is "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the tangible; he does not perceive that one is "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to mental phenomena (*dharma*); he does not perceive that one is "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

He does not perceive whether one is "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the right efforts; he does not perceive whether one is "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the bases of psychic power; he does not perceive whether one is "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the faculties.
He does not perceive the powers as being either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the factors of enlightenment as being either engaged or disengaged.

He does not perceive [himself] as being "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the paths; nor does he perceive [himself] as being "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the four truths; nor does he perceive [himself] as being "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the four grounds of self-confidence.

He does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); nor does he perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as either "engaged" or "disengaged," nor does he perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as either "engaged" or "disengaged."
As long as he does not perceive whether he is engaged or disengaged with the knowledge of all aspects,
nor does he perceive whether he is engaged or disengaged with the knowledge of the omniscient one.
Therefore, Śāriputra, by this method also, it should be understood that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus engaged with the perfection of wisdom is to be called "engaged."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not join emptiness with emptiness, nor does he join the application of emptiness; nor does he [join] the signless with the signless...
He does not join the signless with the signless,
nor does he join the wishless with the wishless, nor does he join the yoga of the wishless with the wishless.
For what reason?
Because emptiness is neither conjunction nor non-conjunction; likewise, the signless and the wishless are neither conjunction nor non-conjunction. Thus...
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus engaged should be said to be "engaged" when he is engaged in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the perfection of wisdom...
He enters into the emptiness of the specific characteristics of phenomena.
Entering thus, he neither joins nor disjoins form; he neither joins nor disjoins sensation.
He neither joins nor disjoins perception;
he neither joins nor disjoins volitional formations;
he neither joins nor disjoins consciousness.
One does not associate form with the past limit, nor does one dissociate it from it;
one simply does not perceive the past limit itself. One does not associate form with the future limit, nor does one dissociate it from it.
He does not perceive the future limit at all;
he neither joins nor disjoins form with the present.
He does not perceive even the present;
he neither joins nor disjoins feeling with the past limit,
for he does not perceive even the past limit itself— not feeling, nor...
He does not join the future with the past, nor does he separate them; he does not even perceive the future itself.
He does not join feeling with the present, nor does he separate them; he does not even perceive the present itself.
He does not join perception with the past limit, nor does he disjoin it;
he does not even perceive the past limit itself.
He does not join perception with the future limit, nor does he disjoin it.
He does not perceive the future limit;
he neither joins nor disjoins perception with the present, nor does he perceive the present itself;
he neither joins nor disjoins the formative forces with the past limit.
He does not perceive a prior limit;
he neither joins nor disjoins the formative forces with a posterior limit;
and he does not perceive a posterior limit itself.
One does not associate formative forces with the present, nor does one dissociate them; one does not even perceive the present itself.
One does not associate consciousness with the prior limit, nor does one dissociate it;
one does not even perceive the prior limit itself.
One does not associate consciousness with the future limit, nor does one dissociate it from it;
one does not even perceive the future limit itself.
One does not associate consciousness with the present, nor does one dissociate it from it; one does not even perceive the present itself.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not join the past with the future, nor does he join the future with the past; nor does he join the present with either the past or the future.
One does not join the future limit with the past limit or the present;
nor does one join the past limit with the future limit or the present.

Or he applies it by means of the emptiness of the internal; relying on the emptiness of the paths, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who applies himself in this way should be said to be "engaged in the perfection of wisdom."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he applies himself in such a way that, while so applying himself, he does not join all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) with the past.
Since he does not even perceive the past, how could he join all-knowledge with the past?
One does not join omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) with the future;
for one does not even perceive the future itself.
How, then, could one join omniscience with the future?
He does not join omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) with the present; since he does not even perceive the present itself, how could he join omniscience with the present?
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this manner should be said to be engaged in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not associate form with the knowledge of all aspects; he does not even perceive form itself. He does not associate feeling with the knowledge of all aspects; he does not even perceive feeling itself. He does not associate perception...

He joins perception with the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not perceive perception itself; he does not join formative forces with the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not perceive formative forces themselves;
he does not join consciousness with the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not perceive consciousness itself.
He does not join the eye with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the eye itself; he does not join the ear with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the ear itself;
he does not join the nose with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the nose itself.
He does not join the tongue with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the tongue; he does not join the body with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the body;
he does not join the mind with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the mind.

He does not join form with omniscience; he does not even perceive form itself. He does not join sounds with omniscience; he does not even perceive sounds themselves. He does not join odors with omniscience; he does not even perceive odors themselves.
He does not associate tastes with omniscience, for he does not even perceive tastes; he does not associate tangible objects with omniscience, for he does not even perceive tangible objects.
He does not apply phenomena to the knowledge of all aspects, nor does he even perceive phenomena as such.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this manner is to be called one who is engaged in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not associate the perfection of giving with omniscience, nor does he even perceive the perfection of giving itself.

He does not join the perfection of ethical discipline with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the perfection of ethical discipline itself. He does not join the perfection of patience with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the perfection of patience itself.

He does not join the perfection of vigor with omniscience, nor does he perceive the perfection of vigor itself; he does not join the perfection of meditation with omniscience, nor does he perceive the perfection of meditation itself;
he does not join the perfection of wisdom with omniscience, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom itself.
He does not join the applications of mindfulness with the knowledge of all aspects; he does not even perceive the applications of mindfulness themselves.
He does not join the right efforts with the knowledge of all aspects; he does not even perceive the right efforts themselves.
He does not join the bases of psychic power with the knowledge of all aspects; he does not even perceive the bases of psychic power themselves.

He does not join the faculties with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the faculties themselves; he does not join the powers with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the powers themselves;
he does not join the factors of enlightenment with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the factors of enlightenment themselves.

He does not unite the paths with the knowledge of all aspects, nor does he perceive the paths themselves; he does not unite the analytical knowledges with the knowledge of all aspects, nor does he perceive the analytical knowledges themselves;
he does not unite the grounds of self-confidence with the knowledge of all aspects, nor does he perceive the grounds of self-confidence themselves.
He does not join the superknowledges with the knowledge of all aspects, nor does he perceive the superknowledges themselves.
He does not join the ten powers of a Tathāgata with the knowledge of all aspects, nor does he perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata themselves.
