When this Bodhisattva has fully awakened to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, there will be no assembly of Bodhisattvas;
this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will practice difficult austerities,
whereas this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will not practice difficult austerities.
He will practice. This bodhisattva is in his final existence;
this bodhisattva is not in his final existence. This bodhisattva shall sit at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
This bodhisattva will not sit upon the seat of awakening;
Māra will arise for this bodhisattva.
Māra will not exist for this bodhisattva;
for in this way, Śāriputra,
the Dharma-eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is completely pure.
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, what is the completely pure Buddha-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, immediately after the thought of awakening, enters the diamond-like samādhi and, through wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind, attains the knowledge of all aspects,
he becomes endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
He is endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion.

And by means of that eye, Śāriputra, there is nothing whatsoever that has not been seen, heard, sensed, or known by the bodhisattva mahāsattva in all its aspects; such indeed is the perfectly pure Buddha-eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to purify the five eyes should apply himself to the six perfections.
Why is that?
For it is thus, Śāriputra:

all wholesome dharmas, all the dharmas of the śrāvakas, all the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, and all the dharmas of the bodhisattvas are included within the six perfections. Indeed, Śāriputra, one who speaks correctly...
If they were to speak correctly, those who would say "the collection of all wholesome dharmas" would indeed be speaking of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Because, Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom is the mother of them all.
Śāriputra, by training in these perfections and in these five eyes of the bodhisattvas, bodhisattva mahāsattvas [attain] unsurpassed, perfect...
They fully awaken to perfect enlightenment.
[Thus ends the instruction on the five eyes.
Here, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom [attains] the superknowledges—
He cultivates the perfection [of wisdom] and experiences various kinds of miraculous powers; he even causes the earth to tremble.
Having been one, he becomes many;
having been many, he becomes one.
He experiences both manifestation and disappearance;
he passes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and even through mountains, just as if they were open space.
In the sky he is like a winged bird;
on the earth he performs emerging and submerging just as if it were water.
He walks upon water without breaking through it, just as if on solid earth;
he even emits smoke and blazes forth, just like a great mass of fire;
he also pours forth water from his body, just like a great cloud. These two...

He touches and strokes with his hand even the sun and moon, who possess such great psychic power (*maharddhika*) and majesty (*mahānubhāva*); he wields mastery over his body even as far as the Brahma-world,
yet by means of that supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he does not...
He does not conceive [it]. For he does not apprehend that supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) by which he might conceive;

nor does he even conceive that [power], because of its emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), because of its isolation from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viviktatā*), and because of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhitā*).
He does not even give rise to the thought of supernatural power, nor the thought of accomplishing supernatural power, except for the mental engagement with omniscience.
It is thus, Śāriputra.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, brings forth the knowledge that realizes the supernormal power of miraculous transformations.
With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he [hears] sounds.
He hears both divine and human sounds,
yet by means of that divine ear, he does not conceive the thought, "I am hearing sounds."
For he does not perceive even that sound,
by reason of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, by reason of the isolation of intrinsic nature, and by reason of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature;
he does not even give rise to the volition for the divine ear, nor the volition for the accomplishment of the divine ear.
Or otherwise, except for the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom realizes the superknowledge of the divine ear (*divyaśrotrābhijñā*).
He brings forth knowledge;
with his own mind, he understands the minds of other beings and other persons as they truly are.
He understands a mind possessed of passion as "a mind possessed of passion," knowing it as it truly is.
He understands, as it truly is, a mind free from passion as "a mind free from passion";
he understands a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred."
One understands the mind as it truly is: a mind free from hatred, a deluded mind, and a mind free from delusion.
Deluded; possessed of craving;
free from craving;
with grasping.
The mind that is without grasping,
concentrated, distracted, and limited.
Vast, expansive, and concentrated.
Unconcentrated,
secluded, unsecluded,
and with outflows.
Untainted;
with blemish; without blemish;
surpassable; unsurpassable.
And he does not conceive [an idea] by means of that,
because that mind is non-mind,
based on its inconceivability.
Thus, he does not conceive the thought, "I know.
He does not apprehend that very mind, because it is empty of intrinsic nature and because it is isolated from intrinsic nature.
Or, by virtue of non-apprehension,
he does not even produce the volition of another's mind,
nor the volition of accomplishing another's mind, except for the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects.

In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom brings forth the knowledge that realizes the supernormal cognition of the mental conduct of all sentient beings.
Through the knowledge of recollecting former abodes, he recollects one birth, two, three, and so forth.
He recollects even up to hundreds of thousands of births;
he recollects even a single thought,
up to a hundred thoughts.
Even for a single day or even for a hundred days; even for a single month or even for a hundred months;
even for a single year or even for a hundred years.

For even one eon, for even a hundred eons, for many hundreds of eons, for many thousands of eons, for many hundreds of thousands of eons, or even for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
He recollects, even as far back as the limit of the past:
"In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a caste, such food, such a duration of stay, and such a lifespan."
"...up to that limit: 'Having passed away from there, I was reborn there; having passed away from there, I am reborn here.

In this way, he recollects his manifold previous existences with their modes, details, and specific circumstances. And by means of that superknowledge of recollecting former existences, he does not become conceited."
For that knowledge is non-knowledge by virtue of its inconceivability;
it does not conceive, "I am one who understands," nor does it conceive that very [knowledge].
He does not perceive knowledge, by reason of its emptiness of intrinsic nature, by reason of its isolation from intrinsic nature,
and by reason of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature.
He does not even perceive the volition for recollecting past lives.
He does not produce the volition for accomplishing the recollection of past lives, except through mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects.
It is in this way, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [acts].
Practicing the perfection of wisdom, he brings forth the knowledge that realizes the recollection of past lives.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he beholds sentient beings.
He discerns beings as they pass away and are reborn— whether beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior, in happy destinies or miserable destinies— according to their karma;
"These worthy beings, by body..."

Endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind, they do not revile the noble ones and possess right view; by reason of that good conduct of body, speech, and mind, they are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world. These...
Furthermore, sirs, these beings are possessed of misconduct of body,
possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind; they are revilers of the noble ones.

Those with wrong views, because of their undertaking of actions based on wrong views, after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in the hells. Thus indeed, by means of divine [vision]...

With the purified divine eye, which transcends that of humans, he understands, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of beings belonging to the six realms of existence throughout all world-systems in the ten directions of the world— reaching to the limit of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and extending to the end of the realm of space (ākāśadhātu).
And by that he does not conceive [such a thought];
for that eye is a non-eye, based on its inconceivability; thus he does not conceive, "I see. That very [eye]...
Based on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, based on the isolation from intrinsic nature, and based on the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature, one does not apprehend the eye;
nor does one even give rise to the volition for the divine eye.
He does not produce the volition for the accomplishment of the divine eye, nor any other [volition], except for the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For it is in this way, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, accomplishes the knowledge of the direct realization of the superknowledge of the divine eye.
He brings forth the superknowledge that realizes non-arising,
and he does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Nor does he aspire to any other dharma whatsoever, except for the thought: "I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Through that destruction of the outflows...
He does not conceive [a notion of self] through his skill in the actualization of the knowledge of supernormal powers;
for that knowledge is non-knowledge by virtue of its inconceivability.
Thus he thinks: "I understand."

He does not conceive [of it]; he does not apprehend that very knowledge, by reason of its emptiness of intrinsic nature, by reason of its isolation from intrinsic nature, and by reason of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature. He is not one who possesses outflows—
He even generates the volition for the destruction [of the outflows], yet he does not generate the volition for the actualization of the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows,
except through the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects.
It is in this way, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] wisdom—
While practicing the perfection [of wisdom], he brings forth the knowledge that realizes the superknowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, his six superknowledges are fulfilled and purified.
Śāriputra, the supernormal knowledges, when completely purified, lead to the knowledge of all aspects. Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who [practice] in the perfection of wisdom.

Practicing while established in the perfection of generosity, they purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness, and not by way of grasping. Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing in the perfection of wisdom who, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness.
08906 By virtue of being beyond reproach,

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom who, abiding in the perfection of patience, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness,
by virtue of being unshakeable.

"Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of vigor, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness, on account of their non-laxity in physical and mental vigor.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom..."

"Abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, they purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness, on account of their undistracted minds. Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom, abide in the perfection of wisdom and purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness,
on account of their total relinquishment."
In this way, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing in the perfection of wisdom, abiding in the six perfections, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness.
Generosity is designated in dependence upon grasping;
ethical discipline is designated in dependence upon immorality;
patience is designated in dependence upon impatience.
Vigor is designated in dependence upon laziness;
meditative concentration is designated in dependence upon lack of concentration;
wisdom is designated in dependence upon faulty wisdom.
He does not think, "I have crossed over," nor does he think, "I have not crossed over. He does not think, "This is a gift," nor does he think, "This is an acceptance."
He does not conceive of ethical discipline as immorality; he does not conceive of patience as agitation; he does not conceive of vigor as laziness.
He does not conceive [the thought], "I am";
he does not conceive that "concentration is unconcentrated";
he does not conceive that "wisdom is lack of wisdom"; when reviled...
He does not think, "I am honored"; he does not think, "I am saluted"; he does not think, "I am revered"; he does not think, "I am neglected."
He does not think, "I am.
For what reason?
Because, Śāriputra, non-arising is not reviled.
He does not think, "I am honored";
he does not think, "I am saluted";
he does not think, "I am revered"; [he does not think,] "I am not...".
He does not think, "I have been made [so].
For what reason? Because the perfection of wisdom completely cuts off all conceits.

In this regard, Śāriputra, those qualities that belong to a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom do not all exist among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Perfecting these qualities, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies a buddha-field.
He purifies [them] and attains the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) generates a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Having generated a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, one attains the equality of all phenomena;
having attained the equality of all phenomena, [one...]
He establishes all sentient beings in the equality of all phenomena;
in this very life, he becomes dear and pleasing to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
He becomes dear and pleasing to all bodhisattvas, as well as to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Wherever he is reborn, there he never perceives with his eyes any unpleasant forms.
He sees; he does not hear unpleasant sounds with his ear;
he does not smell unpleasant odors with his nose.
He does not taste unpleasant tastes with the tongue; he does not touch unpleasant tangibles with the body;
he does not [perceive] unpleasant [objects] with the mind.
He understands all phenomena and does not fall away from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, while this teaching on the perfection of wisdom was being expounded, three hundred bhikṣuṇīs covered the Blessed One with their robes as they were worn and conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then, at that very moment, the Blessed One smiled.
Thereupon, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat.
Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground,
and bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason..."
There is a specific cause for the manifestation of a smile;
the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not manifest a smile without a cause or without a condition.
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, these three hundred bhikṣuṇīs,
in the sixty-first aeon, will become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Mahākeu."
Fully enlightened ones will arise in the world.
Having passed away from here during the aeon known as Tārakopama, they will be reborn in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya. And sixty...
Those thousands of sons of gods who have been brought to maturity by this teaching of the Dharma will attain final nirvana in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya.

Then, indeed, by the power of the Blessed One, at that very moment, the four assemblies, from the circle of the assembly of the Blessed Śākyamuni, beheld a thousand Buddhas in the eastern direction; likewise,
they beheld a thousand Buddhas in the southern direction, and in the western direction.

They see a thousand Buddhas in the northern direction; they see a thousand Buddhas in the northeastern direction; they see a thousand Buddhas in the southeastern direction; they see a thousand Buddhas in the southwestern direction; they see a thousand Buddhas in the northwestern direction.

Below and above, in each direction, they behold a thousand Buddhas; they behold the magnificent arrays of qualities of great Buddha-fields, yet they do not behold such magnificent arrays of qualities of Buddha-fields here in this Sahā world-system as those belonging to the Blessed Buddhas in each of the ten directions.
They beheld the magnificent arrays of qualities of the Buddha-fields.
Then, indeed, ten thousand living beings from the circle of the assembly of the Blessed One Śākyamuni made these aspirations: "May we..."
"We shall perform those meritorious deeds by which merits we shall be reborn in these Buddha-fields.
Then the Blessed One, knowing the intention of those sons of good family,
at that moment smiled.
Ānanda said: "O Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this smile?"
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, do you see these ten thousand living beings?"
Ānanda said, "I see them, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Ānanda, these ten thousand living beings, having passed away from here, will be reborn in thousands of Buddha-fields in those ten directions;
and they shall never again be separated from the Tathāgatas.
Thereafter, Tathāgatas named Vyūharāja will arise in the world.
Then, indeed, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, and these and many other well-known [disciples]—
The renowned monks, as well as the bodhisattvas, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen,
said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, this is a great perfection for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
That is to say, the perfection of wisdom.
This is the foremost perfection, this is the distinguished perfection, this is the excellent perfection,

this is the unsurpassed perfection, this is the peerless perfection, this is the incomparable perfection, this is the space-like perfection, this is the perfection of the emptiness of self-characteristic, [and] the equality of all qualities—

"O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that has reached the further shore; it is the invincible perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas—namely, the perfection of wisdom. For herein, O Blessed One, by the bodhisattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom..."
By those great beings, incomparable generosity was bestowed; by them, the incomparable perfection of generosity was fulfilled;
by them, an incomparable physical form was attained;
they are the possessors of the incomparable Dharma.
They will become [destined] for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By them, morality equal to the unequaled has been guarded;
by them, the perfection of morality equal to the unequaled has been fulfilled; by them, a physical existence equal to the unequaled has been attained.
They will become attainers of the Dharma that is peerless and equal to the peerless, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. By them, peerless patience has been cultivated;
the peerless perfection of patience has been fulfilled; by them, a peerless physical form has been attained.

They will become attainers of the Dharma that is unequaled; that is to say, of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. They have exerted unequaled vigor; they have fulfilled the perfection of unequaled vigor; they have obtained an unequaled physical existence;
they will become attainers of the Dharma that is unequaled; that is to say, of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. They [have attained] the unequaled...

They have cultivated meditative concentration; they have fulfilled the perfection of meditative concentration that is unequaled and equal to the unequaled. They have attained a physical existence that is unequaled and equal to the unequaled; they will become possessors of the Dharma that is unequaled and equal to the unequaled, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

They have cultivated wisdom that is unequaled and equal to the unequaled; they have fulfilled the perfection of wisdom that is unequaled and equal to the unequaled. They [have attained] the unequaled and equal...

They will have attained a physical existence that shall be the recipient of the peerless Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. And in this very regard, O Blessed One, while practicing in this perfection of wisdom, you have become a recipient of peerless form, peerless feeling, peerless perception, peerless mental formations, and peerless...

Having attained the realization of consciousness, he has fully awakened to peerless, equal enlightenment and turned the peerless, equal wheel of Dharma. In this very same way, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present [are established] in this very perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, they have awakened, will awaken, and are awakening to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, O Blessed One, one who wishes to go to the further shore of all dharmas—

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom. O Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who course in this perfection of wisdom are to be revered by gods and humans alike.
When this had been said by the world of gods,
the Blessed One spoke thus to those many śrāvakas and those bodhisattvas:
"So it is, noble sons; so it is.
Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who [abide] in this perfection of wisdom are to be honored by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras."
They move about. For what reason?
Śāriputra, it is because by depending upon the bodhisattva that the appearance of the world in the world occurs.
Of the human world, the divine world, the great noble families of kṣatriyas, the great noble families of brahmins, the great noble families of householders, the universal monarchs,
and the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Of the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods,
the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Brahmapārṣadya gods, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, and the Parīttaśubha gods.

the gods of the Apramāṇaśubhas, the gods of the Śubhakṛtsnas, the gods of the Anabhrakas, the gods of the Puṇyaprasavas, the gods of the Bṛhatphalas, the gods of the Asaṃjñisattvas, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsas, the gods of the Aspr̥has, the gods of the Atapas, the gods of the Sudr̥śas, the gods of the Sudarśanas, and the gods of the Akaniṣṭhas.
There is no appearance in the world of gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
nor of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, or arhats.
Śāriputra, it is by depending upon the bodhisattva that the appearance of pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, and tathāgatas, arhats,
perfectly awakened ones, occurs in the world. For it is by depending upon the bodhisattva, Śāriputra, [that these appear].
The manifestation of the three jewels occurs in the world,
as well as all worldly requisites for life, such as food, drink, clothing, bedding, seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
Śāriputra, it is because of this that there appears in the world the manifestation of gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, and silver,
as well as all divine and human articles of comfort.
And, Śāriputra, it is by depending upon the bodhisattva that the appearance of all the gateways to existence and the gateways to nirvāṇa occurs in the world. Why is that?
For, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva practices the conduct of the six perfections, he engages beings in giving,
causes them to undertake ethical discipline, establishes them in patience, and engages them in vigor.
He establishes them in meditative concentration and directs them toward wisdom;
and all sentient beings, having approached the bodhisattva, practice the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One extended his tongue-faculty and—
He covered the trichiliocosm, the great thousandfold world system, with his tongue-faculty. Then,
from that tongue-faculty, rays of light of many colors and various hues issued forth,
illuminating with their radiance world systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.
In this way, they illuminated world-systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with their light. Likewise,
they illuminated world-systems in the western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with their light.

They illuminated world-systems in the northern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with their radiance; they illuminated world-systems in the northeastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with their radiance;
they illuminated world-systems in the southeastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with their radiance.
In the southwestern direction, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with their radiance;
in the northwestern direction, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with their radiance;
and in the downward direction, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with their radiance.
They illuminated with their radiance world-systems in the upward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
Then, indeed, from the eastern direction up to the upward direction, [as many as] the sands of the river Gaṅgā—
Bodhisattvas, immeasurable and incalculable in number, from Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
having seen those arrays of light, questioned the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in their respective Buddha-fields: "Blessed One, whose power is this, by which such a radiance of splendor is seen?"
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, spoke thus to those bodhisattva mahāsattvas:
"O sons of good family, in the western [direction]..."
Furthermore, as far as the downward direction, in the Sahā world-system, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni resides,
remains, and maintains his life; having extended his tongue-faculty,
he has filled all the world-systems in every direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, with light.

As far as the upward direction— in this way, throughout the ten directions, world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges were pervaded by light for the purpose of teaching and elucidating the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to the bodhisattvas, the great beings (*mahāsattvas*).
Those bodhisattvas said this to those Tathāgatas:
"O Blessed One, we shall go to that Sahā world-system to behold and pay homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni."
For the sake of attending upon him and for the sake of hearing that Perfection of Wisdom from those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have assembled from the ten directions,
those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, said:
"Go, sons of good family, whenever you deem it the right time.
Then those bodhisattva mahāsattvas from the ten directions...
Taking flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards,
and taking baskets of various jewels, gold, silver, and flowers, they approached the Blessed One Śākyamuni with a great performance of music, cymbals, and song.
Then indeed, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods,
the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, and the Brahmapurohita gods—
the gods of the Retinue of Brahmā, the gods of Limited Radiance, the gods of Immeasurable Radiance, the gods of Utmost Radiance, the gods of Limited Purity,

the gods of Immeasurable Purity, the gods of Universal Purity, the Cloudless gods, the gods of Merit-Born, the gods of Vast Fruit, the gods of Non-percipient Beings, the gods of the Pure Abodes, the Uncontentious gods, the Untroubled gods, the Fair-Sighted gods, and the Good-to-See gods.

And the Akaniṣṭha gods, taking divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags— blue lotuses, white lotuses, red lotuses, mandārava flowers, kesaras, and tamāla leaves— approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Then indeed those bodhisattvas and those gods scattered flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha.
Then, those flowers, leaving the ground and rising up, formed above this trichiliocosm a flower-pavilion;
it was four-pillared, square in shape, well-proportioned, beautiful, and delightful.

Then, indeed, from that assembly, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, they addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, in a future time, may we become recipients of such qualities as those of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha."
"And thus we would lead a community of disciples and thus teach the Dharma in the assembly,
just as the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, teaches the Dharma at present.
Then the Blessed One [spoke] to them...

Having understood the intention of the sons of good family, and having realized the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding the non-arising, non-ceasing, non-conditioning, and non-manifestation of all phenomena, he smiled. Then, from the Blessed One’s mouth, rays of light of many colors issued forth, pervading the entire world.
Having circumambulated [him], they returned once more and vanished into the crown of the Blessed One's head. Then,
the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground.
Having established himself upon the earth, he bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this smile?
Then the Blessed One—
He said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, after sixty-eight hundred thousand million billion eons, these hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings will become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Bodhyaṅgapuṣpa."
Fully awakened Buddhas will arise in the world during the Puṣpākara eon.
[Thus ends the instruction on the six superknowledges.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti:
"May it occur to you, Subhūti, to speak concerning the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, as to how..."
"...that the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, would set out for the perfection of wisdom.
Then, indeed, this [thought] occurred to those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, to those great śrāvakas, and to those sons of the gods:

[He] was. Now, will the venerable Subhūti teach the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to the bodhisattvas, the great beings (*mahāsattva*), by means of the power of his own wisdom and eloquence (*prajñāpratibhāna-bala*), or rather through the majestic presence of the Buddha? Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, through the majestic presence of the Buddha, [addressed] those bodhisattvas, the great beings...
And having known with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those great śrāvakas and those sons of gods, he said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, whatever..."
Whatever the disciples of the Blessed One speak, teach, or instruct—all that should be understood as the personal effort of the Tathāgata.
For what reason? Because it is within that Dharma taught by the Tathāgata [that they abide].

Training in the teaching of the Dharma, they realize that very nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Having realized that nature of phenomena, whatever they speak, teach, or instruct, all of it is not in contradiction with the nature of phenomena.

Touch is the Bodhisattva; the Bodhisattva is not other than touch; the Bodhisattva is in touch, and touch is in the Bodhisattva; yet the Bodhisattva is untouched.

"Dharma is the bodhisattva; apart from dharma there is no bodhisattva. In dharma there is the bodhisattva, and in the bodhisattva there is dharma; [otherwise] it would be a non-dharma that is the bodhisattva. What do you think, Subhūti? Are the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness the bodhisattva, or is he apart from these, or within them? These...
In that regard, apart from the eye, forms, and visual consciousness, there is no "bodhisattva.
What do you think, Subhūti? Apart from the ear, sounds, and auditory consciousness, is there a bodhisattva elsewhere than these, or is he within them?
Without these—namely, the ear, sound, and ear-consciousness—he is a bodhisattva.
What do you think, Subhūti? Are the nose, odor, and nose-consciousness the bodhisattva, or is he elsewhere than these, or within them?
Without these—namely, the nose, odor, and nose-consciousness—he is a bodhisattva.

What do you think, Subhūti? Is the Bodhisattva apart from the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness, or is he within them? Is he the Bodhisattva without the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness?
What do you think, Subhūti? Is the Bodhisattva apart from the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness, or is he within them?
"Without body, tangibles, and body-consciousness, is there a bodhisattva in that?
What do you think, Subhūti? Is a bodhisattva apart from mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness, or is he within them?
Without mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness, is there a bodhisattva in that?"
Subhūti said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Is the earth element a bodhisattva, apart from the earth element?"
In that regard, Subhūti, regarding the element of earth: is the bodhisattva the element of earth, or is the bodhisattva not the element of earth?

What do you think, Subhūti, regarding the element of water: is the bodhisattva other than the element of water, or in that regard, within the bodhisattva, is the element of water the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva not the element of water?

What do you think, Subhūti? Is the fire-element a bodhisattva, or is there a bodhisattva apart from the fire-element? In that case, is the bodhisattva in the bodhisattva the fire-element, or is the bodhisattva one who is not the fire-element? What do you think, Subhūti? Is the wind-element a bodhisattva, or is there a bodhisattva apart from the wind-element? In that case, is the bodhisattva in the bodhisattva the wind-element, or is the bodhisattva one who is not the wind-element?

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the space-element the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva other than the space-element? In that case, is the bodhisattva the space-element, or is the bodhisattva a non-space-element? What do you think, Subhūti? Is the consciousness-element the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva other than the consciousness-element? In that case, is the bodhisattva the consciousness-element, or is the bodhisattva a non-consciousness-element?
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is a bodhisattva other than ignorance?"
"In ignorance there is a bodhisattva; in the bodhisattva there is ignorance; ignorance is not ignorance, yet it is the bodhisattva.

What do you think, Subhūti? Is the bodhisattva the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), or is the bodhisattva apart from the formative forces, or is the bodhisattva within the formative forces, or are the formative forces within the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva the absence of formative forces (*asaṃskāra*)?

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is consciousness the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than consciousness? Is the Bodhisattva in consciousness, or is consciousness in the Bodhisattva? Or is the Bodhisattva one who is without consciousness? What do you think, Subhūti? Is name-and-form the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than name-and-form? Is the Bodhisattva in name-and-form, or is name-and-form in the Bodhisattva? Or is the Bodhisattva one who is without name-and-form?"

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is a bodhisattva the six sense-bases, or is a bodhisattva apart from the six sense-bases? Is a bodhisattva within the six sense-bases, or are the six sense-bases within the bodhisattva? Are the six sense-bases a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva not the six sense-bases?

What do you think, Subhūti? Is contact a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva apart from contact? Is a bodhisattva within contact, or is contact within the bodhisattva? Is contact a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva not contact?"

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is feeling the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than feeling? Is the Bodhisattva in feeling, or is feeling in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva without feeling? "What do you think, Subhūti? Is craving the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than craving? Is the Bodhisattva in craving, or is craving in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva without craving? "What do you think, Subhūti? Is grasping the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than grasping? Is the Bodhisattva in grasping, or is grasping in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva without grasping?"

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is existence the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than existence? Is the Bodhisattva in existence, or is the Bodhisattva existence or non-existence? What do you think, Subhūti? Is birth the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than birth? Is the Bodhisattva in birth, or is the Bodhisattva birth or non-birth? What do you think, Subhūti? Is old age and death the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than old age and death? Is the Bodhisattva in old age and death, or is the Bodhisattva old age and death or non-old-age-and-death?"
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One. [Thus ends the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.]
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of form the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of form? Is the suchness of form in the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of form?"
"Suchness, the suchness of formlessness, is the bodhisattva.
What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of feeling the bodhisattva, or is it the suchness of feeling apart from the suchness of feeling?"
"A Bodhisattva is the suchness of feeling in a Bodhisattva, which is the suchness of non-feeling.

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of perception the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of perception? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of perception? Is the suchness of perception in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva the suchness of perception, which is the suchness of non-perception?"

What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of formations (saṃskāra-tathatā) the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva other than the suchness of formations? Is the suchness of formations in the suchness of formations the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva in the bodhisattva the suchness of formations? Is the suchness of formations the bodhisattva? What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of consciousness (vijñāna-tathatā) the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva other than the suchness of consciousness? Is the bodhisattva in the suchness of consciousness? Is the suchness of consciousness in the bodhisattva? Is the suchness of consciousness the bodhisattva?
"Is 'non-cognition-tathatā' the Bodhisattva? Subhūti said,
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
If there is no Bodhisattva in the [skandhas] taken individually, would he exist in them taken collectively? That which is the suchness (tathatā) of the skandhas—"
"A bodhisattva is not other than the suchness of the aggregates; the bodhisattva is in the suchness of the aggregates, and the bodhisattva is in the bodhisattva.
The suchness of the aggregates is neither the suchness of the aggregates nor the bodhisattva.
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, this is so."
"Blessed One," [Subhūti replied]. The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness the Bodhisattva, or is it elsewhere than the suchness of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness? "The eye..."

In the suchness of form, eye, and eye-consciousness, the Bodhisattva [perceives] the Bodhisattva; the suchness of eye, form, and eye-consciousness, the suchness of non-eye, form, and eye-consciousness, is the Bodhisattva.
Thus [it is with] the ear and sound—
The suchness of ear-consciousness, the suchness of nose, odor, and nose-consciousness, and the suchness of tongue, taste, and tongue-consciousness—
Suchness is the suchness of body, tangibles, and body-consciousness;
it is the suchness of mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness.
Subhūti said,
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the earth element the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of the earth element? Is the suchness of the earth element within the Bodhisattva? Or is the suchness of the earth element not the earth element?

"Suchness is the bodhisattva. "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the water-element the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of the water-element? Is the bodhisattva in the suchness of the water-element? Is the suchness of the water-element in the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva not the suchness of the water-element?"

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the fire element the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of the fire element? Is the Bodhisattva within the suchness of the fire element? Is the suchness of the fire element within the Bodhisattva? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the fire element? "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the wind element the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of the wind element?"

In the suchness of the wind-element, there is neither a bodhisattva nor a bodhisattva in the suchness of the wind-element; there is no such thing as "the suchness of the wind-element is the bodhisattva.

What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the space-element the bodhisattva? Is there a bodhisattva apart from the suchness of the space-element? Is there a bodhisattva in the suchness of the space-element? Is there a bodhisattva in the bodhisattva? Is the suchness of the space-element not the suchness of the space-element, or is it the bodhisattva?

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the suchness of the consciousness-element the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of the consciousness-element? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of the consciousness-element? Is the suchness of the Bodhisattva the suchness of the consciousness-element? Is the suchness of the Bodhisattva the suchness of non-consciousness? Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
If the Bodhisattva does not exist in the elements taken separately, nor in them taken together—let it be so!

That which is the suchness of the elements is the Bodhisattva; yet the Bodhisattva is not other than the suchness of the elements. Within the suchness of the elements there is the Bodhisattva, and within the Bodhisattva there is the suchness of the elements. There is no suchness of the elements apart from the Bodhisattva, and there is no Bodhisattva apart from the suchness of the elements.
Subhūti said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the eye the Bodhisattva?"

Apart from the suchness of the eye, there is no such thing as a "bodhisattva" in the suchness of the eye, nor is there a "suchness of the eye" in a "bodhisattva," nor is there a "bodhisattva" in the suchness of the eye.
Thus it is with the suchness of the ear, the suchness of the nose, and the suchness of the tongue.
Suchness is the suchness of the body.

What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the mind the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of the mind? Is the bodhisattva in the suchness of the mind, or is the suchness of the mind in the bodhisattva?

"Non-mental suchness is the bodhisattva. "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of form the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva other than the suchness of form? Is the bodhisattva within the suchness of form? Is the suchness of form within the bodhisattva? Or is the bodhisattva the suchness of non-form?"

What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of sound the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of sound? Is the suchness of sound in the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of sound? Is the suchness of sound the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva the suchness of non-sound? What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of odor the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of odor? Is the suchness of odor in the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of odor? Is the suchness of odor the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva the suchness of non-odor?

"The non-odor-tathatā is the bodhisattva. What do you think, Subhūti: is that which is the taste-tathatā the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva other than the taste-tathatā? Is the bodhisattva in the taste-tathatā? Is the taste-tathatā in the bodhisattva? Is the taste-tathatā the bodhisattva? Or is the bodhisattva the taste-tathatā? Or is the bodhisattva the non-taste-tathatā? Or is the bodhisattva the bodhisattva?

What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the tangible the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of the tangible? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of the tangible, or is the suchness of the tangible in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva the suchness of the tangible, or is the suchness of the tangible not the Bodhisattva? What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of phenomena (dharma) the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of phenomena? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of phenomena, or is the suchness of phenomena in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva the suchness of phenomena, or is the suchness of phenomena not the Bodhisattva?
"O Subhūti, if there is no bodhisattva in the sense bases when they are separate,
let it be so; O Subhūti, that which is the suchness of the sense bases is the bodhisattva."

Apart from the suchness of the sense bases, within the suchness of the sense bases, there is no "bodhisattva" in a bodhisattva, no "suchness of the sense bases," no "non-suchness of the sense bases," and no "bodhisattva.
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti?"
The suchness of ignorance—apart from the suchness of ignorance, there is no bodhisattva; within the suchness of ignorance, there is the bodhisattva;
and within the bodhisattva, there is the suchness of ignorance. It is neither non-ignorance-suchness nor is it the bodhisattva. Thus, as far as...

The suchness of formative forces, the suchness of consciousness, the suchness of name-and-form, the suchness of the six sense bases, the suchness of contact, the suchness of feeling, the suchness of craving, the suchness of grasping, the suchness of becoming, the suchness of birth, and the suchness of aging and death.
If the Bodhisattva does not exist in the individual members of dependent origination,
nor in them collectively, then let the suchness of dependent origination be the Bodhisattva; yet, apart from the suchness of dependent origination,
there is no Bodhisattva in the suchness of dependent origination, nor is the suchness of dependent origination in the Bodhisattva.
"The suchness of dependent origination, the suchness of non-dependent origination, is the bodhisattva.
Subhūti said,
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
Furthermore, Subhūti, on what basis do you say this:
that "form is not a bodhisattva," nor is feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness?
There is no earth element, no water element, no fire element, no wind element, no space element, and no consciousness element;
there are no forms and no sounds.
There are no odors, no tastes, no tangibles, and no mental phenomena;
there is no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, and no mind.

There is no eye, no form, no visual consciousness; no ear, no sound, no auditory consciousness; no nose, no odor, no olfactory consciousness; no tongue, no taste, no gustatory consciousness; no body, no tangible object, no tactile consciousness;
no mind, no mental phenomenon, no mental consciousness; and likewise, no ignorance, no volitional formations, no consciousness, and no name-and-form.
The six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are not the bodhisattva;
likewise, up to the point that the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination are not the bodhisattva; and the suchness of form is not the bodhisattva.

There is no suchness of feeling, no suchness of perception, no suchness of mental formations, and no suchness of consciousness; there is no suchness of the earth element, no suchness of the water element, no suchness of the fire element, no suchness of the wind element, no suchness of the space element, and no suchness of the consciousness element;
there is no suchness of the eye.
There is no suchness of the ear, no suchness of the nose, no suchness of the tongue, no suchness of the body, and no suchness of the mind;
no suchness of form, no suchness of sound, no suchness of odor, no suchness of taste, no suchness of the tangible, and no suchness of phenomena; and no suchness of the eye.
The suchness of form, eye, and visual consciousness is not the suchness of ear, sound, and auditory consciousness;

it is not the suchness of nose, odor, and olfactory consciousness; it is not the suchness of tongue, taste, and gustatory consciousness; it is not the suchness of body, tangible object, and tactile consciousness; it is not the suchness of mind, mental phenomena, and mental consciousness; it is not the suchness of ignorance; it is not the suchness of volitional formations; it is not the suchness of consciousness; it is not the suchness of name-and-form; it is not the suchness of the six sense bases.
There is no suchness of contact, no suchness of feeling, no suchness of craving, no suchness of grasping,
no suchness of becoming, no suchness of birth, and no suchness of aging and death; indeed, there is no suchness of the aggregates, elements, or sense-fields.
"The suchness of dependent origination is the Bodhisattva.
Subhūti said,
"In an ultimate sense..."
Blessed One, a bodhisattva does not exist and is not apprehended;
how then could form be a bodhisattva?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness will become a bodhisattva.
However, Blessed One, a bodhisattva does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense. How then could the earth element be a bodhisattva?
In this way, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element,
and the consciousness element will become a bodhisattva.
However, Blessed One, because of their absolute non-existence, a bodhisattva neither exists nor is apprehended.
How then could form be a bodhisattva? Likewise, how could sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomena be a bodhisattva?
In this way, will the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind become a bodhisattva?
How then could the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness become a bodhisattva?
In this way, the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness;

the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness; the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness; the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness; and the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness will be the bodhisattva. Ignorance will be the bodhisattva.
In this way, formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death will become a bodhisattva.
Yet, Blessed One, because of their absolute non-existence, a bodhisattva does not exist and is not apprehended.
How, then, could the suchness of form be apprehended in it?
How could the suchness of feeling,
the suchness of perception, the suchness of mental formations, and the suchness of consciousness be apprehended?
“O Blessed One, ultimately a bodhisattva does not exist and is not apprehended.

How then could the suchness of the earth element be apprehended? Likewise, the suchness of the water element is not apprehended; the suchness of the fire element is not apprehended; the suchness of the wind element is not apprehended; the suchness of the space element is not apprehended; and the suchness of the consciousness element is not apprehended.”

“O Blessed One, since a bodhisattva absolutely does not exist and is not apprehended, how could the suchness of form be apprehended? Likewise, how could the suchness of sound be apprehended, the suchness of odor be apprehended, the suchness of taste be apprehended, the suchness of tangible objects be apprehended, or the suchness of phenomena be apprehended? Likewise, [the suchness of] the eye—”

The suchness of the ear is apprehended; the suchness of the nose is apprehended; the suchness of the tongue is apprehended; the suchness of the body is apprehended; the suchness of the mind is apprehended.

In this way, the suchness of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness will be apprehended; the suchness of the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness will be apprehended; the suchness of the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness will be apprehended.

One will not apprehend the suchness of the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness; one will not apprehend the suchness of the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness; one will not apprehend the suchness of the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness.
For, Blessed One, a bodhisattva does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense. Therefore...
From where will its suchness of ignorance be apprehended?
In this way, its suchness of formations will be apprehended; its suchness of consciousness will be apprehended; its suchness of name-and-form will be apprehended;
its suchness of the six sense bases will be apprehended; its suchness of contact will be apprehended; its suchness of feeling will be apprehended; its suchness of craving will be apprehended.

The suchness of grasping will be apprehended; the suchness of existence will be apprehended; the suchness of birth will be apprehended; the suchness of aging and death will be apprehended. Thus, O Blessed One, in each and every instance—whether individually or collectively—among the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination, a bodhisattva absolutely does not exist and is not apprehended.
How then could the suchness of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination be apprehended by him?
"This is not possible. The Blessed One said,
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the non-apprehension of sentient beings, should train in the non-apprehension of the perfection of wisdom. [Thus ends the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.]
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is 'bodhisattva' a designation for form? Is 'bodhisattva' a designation for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?"
Thus it was said. Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Subhūti? Is "bodhisattva" a designation for the permanence of form, or for the impermanence of form;
for the pleasure of form, or for the suffering of form; for the self of form, or for the non-self of form; or for the peace of form?
"Form-peacefulness" is a designation for "bodhisattva.
What do you think, Subhūti? Is "sensation-impermanence," or rather "the impermanence of sensation," a designation for "bodhisattva"? Sensation—"

"Bodhisattva" is a designation for the pleasantness of feeling, the painfulness of feeling, the selfhood of feeling, the non-selfhood of feeling, the peacefulness of feeling, and the non-peacefulness of feeling. "Bodhisattva" is a designation for the pleasantness of perception, the painfulness of perception, the selfhood of perception, the non-selfhood of perception, the peacefulness of perception, and the non-peacefulness of perception.

"Bodhisattva" is a designation for the pleasantness of formations, the suffering of formations, the selfhood of formations, the non-selfhood of formations, the peace of formations, and the non-peace of formations.

"Bodhisattva" is likewise a designation for the pleasantness of consciousness, the suffering of consciousness, the selfhood of consciousness, the non-selfhood of consciousness, the peace of consciousness, and the non-peace of consciousness.
What do you think, Subhūti, regarding the emptiness of form?
The term "bodhisattva" is a designation for the emptiness of form, the signlessness of form, the wishlessness of form, and the non-wishlessness of form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations.

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is 'bodhisattva' a designation for the emptiness of consciousness, the non-emptiness of consciousness, the characterized nature of consciousness, the uncharacterized nature of consciousness, the wishless nature of consciousness, or the non-wishless nature of consciousness?"
Subhūti said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Furthermore, Subhūti, on what basis do you say this:
that the designation "permanence" for form,
nor the designation "impermanence," is the "bodhisattva"?
Thus, it is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering;

not a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self; not a designation for non-self; not a designation for peace, nor a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; not a designation for signs, nor a designation for signlessness; nor is it a designation for the directedness of form.
"Bodhisattva" is not a designation for the wishless;
"Bodhisattva" is not a designation for the permanence of feeling, nor is it a designation for impermanence.
Thus, "Bodhisattva" is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering; it is not a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self;
it is not a designation for peace, nor a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; it is not a designation for signs, nor a designation for signlessness;
and it is not a designation for the wishless regarding feeling, nor a designation for the non-wishless. It is "Bodhisattva."
It is not that "bodhisattva" is a designation for permanence, nor is it a designation for impermanence.
Likewise, it is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering; it is not a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self;
it is not a designation for peace, nor a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness, nor a designation for signs.
"Bodhisattva" is not a designation for the signless, nor is it a designation for the wishless, nor is it a designation for the non-wishless.
"Bodhisattva" is not a designation for the permanence of conditioned phenomena, nor is it a designation for their impermanence.
Likewise, it is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering, nor a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self. It is not a designation for non-self.

"Bodhisattva" is not a designation for peace, nor a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; it is not a designation for signs, nor a designation for signlessness; it is not a designation for the conditioned as being with aspiration, nor a designation for the conditioned as being without aspiration.
"Bodhisattva" is not a designation for the permanence of consciousness, nor a designation for its impermanence.

Thus, "Bodhisattva" is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering; it is not a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self; it is not a designation for peace, nor a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; it is not a designation for signs, nor a designation for signlessness; and it is not a designation for the directedness of consciousness, nor a designation for the absence of directedness.
Subhūti said: "Ultimately, form does not exist and is not apprehended; how then can there be a designation for form?"
“Blessed One, since ultimately there is no such thing as ‘non-coming’ and it is not apprehended, how could there be a designation for ‘feeling’ that would be a bodhisattva?”
“O Blessed One, in an ultimate sense, non-arising does not exist and is not apprehended. How, then, could there be the designation ‘bodhisattva’?
O Blessed One, in an ultimate sense, non-arising does not exist and is not apprehended.”
How could there be the designation "bodhisattva" for conditioned phenomena?
Blessed One, because they are ultimately non-existent, they are neither found nor perceived.
How could there be the designation "bodhisattva" for consciousness?
"O Blessed One, in an ultimate sense, impermanence does not exist and is not apprehended.
O Blessed One, in an ultimate sense, permanence does not exist and is not apprehended. How much less, then, can there be a conceptualization of the impermanence of form?"
“O Blessed One,
since that which is ultimately impermanent does not exist and is not apprehended,
how could the designation ‘the impermanence of form’ be a bodhisattva?”
Thus, it is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering; not a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self; not a designation for peace, nor a designation for non-peace;
not a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; not a designation for signs, nor a designation for signlessness; not a designation for aspiration—
“...will not be a designation for the beneficial, nor will it be a designation for the wishless;
so too for feeling, perception, and mental formations. Blessed One, because they are absolutely non-existent and unapprehendable, how could there be...”
"Blessed One, a Bodhisattva will be a designation for the impermanence of consciousness;
for, in the ultimate sense, that which is permanent neither exists nor is apprehended."
From where could there be the designation "bodhisattva" for the impermanence of consciousness? Likewise, there is no designation of suffering, no designation of non-suffering;
no designation of self, no designation of non-self; no designation of peace, no designation of emptiness, and no designation of non-emptiness.

"A Bodhisattva will not be one who has the designation of signs, nor one who has the designation of signlessness; he will not have the designation of the conditioned nature of form, nor the designation of the unconditioned nature of form.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!

For it is thus, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not perceive the designation of form, nor perceive the designation of feeling, nor perceive the designation of perception."
By not apprehending [it], [one does not apprehend] the designation of formative forces; by not apprehending [it], the designation of consciousness;

by not apprehending [it], the designation of the permanence or impermanence of form; by not apprehending [it], the designation of pleasure or pain; by not apprehending [it], the designation of the peaceful or the unpeaceful; by not apprehending [it], the designation of emptiness or non-emptiness.
By not apprehending the designation of "sign" and "signless"; by not apprehending the designation of "wishful" and "wishless";

by not apprehending the designation of "permanent" and "impermanent" regarding feeling; by not apprehending the designation of "pleasure" and "pain"; by not apprehending the designation of "peaceful" and "unpeaceful"; and by not apprehending the designation of "empty" and "non-empty."
By not apprehending the designation of the signless as having signs; by not apprehending the designation of the wishless as having wishes;

by not apprehending the designation of permanence or impermanence regarding perception; by not apprehending the designation of pleasure or pain; by not apprehending the designation of peace or non-peace; and by not apprehending the designation of emptiness or non-emptiness.
By not apprehending the designation of the signless as having signs; by not apprehending the designation of the wishless as having wishes;

by not apprehending the designation of conditioned phenomena as permanent or impermanent; by not apprehending the designation of pleasure or pain; by not apprehending the designation of the peaceful or the unpeaceful; and by not apprehending the designation of emptiness or non-emptiness.
By not apprehending the designation of the signless as having signs; by not apprehending the designation of the wishless as having wishes;
by not apprehending the designation of consciousness as permanent or impermanent; and by not apprehending the designation of it as pleasure or pain.

One should train in the perfection of wisdom by not apprehending the designation of "peaceful" and "unpeaceful," by not apprehending the designation of "emptiness" and "non-emptiness," by not apprehending the designation of "signless" and "non-signless," and by not apprehending the designation of "wishless" and "non-wishless."
[Thus is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as for what you said:
"I do not perceive that dharma which is called a bodhisattva."
Thus it is said: Subhūti, for a phenomenon does not perceive the realm of phenomena,
nor does the realm of phenomena perceive a phenomenon.
[Thus is the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path.
Subhūti, the form-realm does not perceive the dharma-realm,
nor does the dharma-realm perceive the form-realm.
He does not perceive the element of sensation as the element of phenomena; nor does he perceive the element of phenomena [as the element of sensation].
He does not perceive the element of feeling as the element of phenomena;
nor does he perceive the element of phenomena as the element of perception.
He does not perceive the element of mental formations as the element of phenomena.
Nor does the dharma-element perceive the formation-element;
nor does the consciousness-element perceive the dharma-element;
nor does the dharma-element perceive the consciousness-element.
The eye-element does not perceive the dharma-element,
nor does the dharma-element perceive the eye-element.
The ear-element does not perceive the dharma-element.
Nor does the dharma-element perceive the ear-element;
nor does the nose-element perceive the dharma-element;
nor does the dharma-element perceive the nose-element.
The tongue-element does not perceive the dharma-element,
nor does the dharma-element perceive the tongue-element;
the body-element does not perceive the dharma-element.
Nor does the dharma-element perceive the body-element;
nor does the mind-element perceive the dharma-element;
nor does the dharma-element perceive the mind-element.
The form element does not perceive the dharma element,
nor does the dharma element perceive the form element;
the sound element does not perceive the dharma element.
Nor does the dharma-element perceive the sound-element; nor does the odor-element perceive the dharma-element;
nor does the dharma-element perceive the odor-element.
The taste-element does not perceive the dharma-element,
nor does the dharma-element perceive the taste-element;
the tangible-object-element does not perceive the dharma-element.
Nor does the dharma-element perceive the tangible-element;
nor does the dharma-element perceive the dharma-element;
nor indeed does the dharma-element perceive the dharma-element.
[Thus is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
Subhūti, the conditioned realm does not perceive the unconditioned realm,
nor does the unconditioned realm [perceive it].
He perceives the conditioned realm.
[Thus is the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.]
[Thus concludes the instruction on the path of vision.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is not possible to designate the unconditioned as being distinct from the conditioned;
nor is the unconditioned—
Apart from that, it is impossible to designate anything as "conditioned.
For in this way, Subhūti, a mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever.
Not perceiving [them], he is not terrified, not frightened, and does not fall into fear;
nor does his mind sink back into any phenomenon.
He becomes remorseful in his mind.
For what reason? Because, Subhūti, the mahāsattva...
Practicing in the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive form;
one does not perceive feeling;
one does not perceive perception.
He does not perceive volitional formations;
he does not perceive consciousness;
he does not perceive the eye.
One does not perceive the ear;
one does not perceive the nose;
one does not perceive the tongue.
One does not perceive the body; one does not perceive the mind;
one does not perceive form.
He does not perceive sound;
he does not perceive odor;
he does not perceive taste.
He does not perceive tangible objects;
he does not perceive phenomena;
he does not perceive the element of eye-consciousness.
He does not perceive the ear-consciousness element;
he does not perceive the nose-consciousness element;
he does not perceive the tongue-consciousness element.
He does not perceive the element of mental consciousness;
he does not perceive ignorance;
he does not perceive volitional formations.
One does not perceive consciousness;
one does not perceive name-and-form;
one does not perceive the six sense bases.
He does not perceive contact;
he does not perceive sensation;
he does not perceive craving.
He does not perceive grasping;
he does not perceive becoming;
he does not perceive birth.
He does not perceive aging and death;
he does not perceive passion;
he does not perceive hatred.
He does not perceive delusion; he does not perceive a self;
he does not perceive a being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer.
He does not perceive the desire realm;
he does not perceive the form realm;
he does not perceive the formless realm.
He does not perceive the element of space;
he does not perceive a śrāvaka.
He does not perceive a pratyekabuddha; he does not perceive a bodhisattva;
[he does not perceive] the dharmas of the śrāvakas.
He does not perceive the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha;
he does not perceive the dharmas of a bodhisattva.
He does not perceive a Buddha;
he does not perceive the qualities of a Buddha;
he does not perceive awakening.
As long as he does not perceive any dharmas,
by not perceiving any dharmas, he is not terrified, not frightened, and will not fall into fear.
Subhūti said: "For what reason, Blessed One, does the mind of a mahāsattva not become dejected or discouraged? The Blessed One replied:
For in this way, Subhūti, a mahāsattva does not apprehend and does not perceive mental states and mental factors;
it is thus, Subhūti, that the mind of a mahāsattva does not become despondent.
He does not shrink back. Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not become terrified?"
The mind. The Blessed One said:
"For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend, nor does he perceive, the mind and the mind-element."

For in this way, Subhūti, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not tremble. For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom through the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom,

does not apprehend nor perceive that perfection of wisdom; and if he does not apprehend nor perceive that bodhisattva, that designation "bodhisattva," and that thought of awakening— this very [is the practice].
This is the instruction for a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
this indeed is the teaching regarding the perfection of wisdom.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand form should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand feeling should train in the perfection of wisdom.

O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand perception (*saṃjñā*) should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) should train in the perfection of wisdom. O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand consciousness (*vijñāna*) should train in the perfection of wisdom. [The same applies to] the eye (*cakṣus*).
“O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand [the eye] should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand the ear should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand the nose should train in the perfection of wisdom.”

O Bhagavān, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand the tongue should train in the perfection of wisdom; O Bhagavān, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand the body should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Bhagavān, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand the mind should train in the perfection of wisdom.
“O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand form should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand sound should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand odor should train in the perfection of wisdom.”

O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand taste should train in the perfection of wisdom; O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand tangible objects should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand phenomena should train in the perfection of wisdom.
“Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand eye-consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand ear-consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand nose-consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom.”
O Bhagavat, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand tongue-consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Bhagavat, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand body-consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Bhagavat, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand mind-consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom.

“Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand eye-contact and the feeling born of eye-contact should train in the perfection of wisdom. Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand ear-contact and the feeling born of ear-contact should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand nose-contact and the feeling born of nose-contact should train in the perfection of wisdom.”
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand the contact of the tongue and the feeling born of the contact of the tongue should train in the perfection of wisdom.

O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand the contact of the body and the feeling born of the contact of the body should train in the perfection of wisdom. [Likewise,] the contact of the mind...
“O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand the feeling born of mental contact should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abandon passion, hatred, and delusion should train in the perfection of wisdom.”

"Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abandon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), ill will (*vyāpāda*), attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*)— all these fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and outbursts (*paryutthāna*)— must train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
