the perfection of meditation does not exist and is not apprehended; the perfection of vigor does not exist and is not apprehended; the perfection of patience does not exist and is not apprehended; the perfection of ethical discipline does not exist and is not apprehended;
the perfection of generosity does not exist and is not apprehended, based on internal emptiness and external emptiness.

By relying on internal and external emptiness; by relying on great emptiness; by relying on the emptiness of emptiness; by relying on ultimate emptiness; by relying on conditioned emptiness; by relying on unconditioned emptiness; by relying on absolute emptiness;
by relying on the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end; by relying on the emptiness of non-dispersal; and by relying on the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Based on the emptiness of all phenomena, based on the emptiness of specific characteristics, based on the emptiness of non-apprehension,

based on the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, based on the emptiness of existence, based on the emptiness of non-existence, based on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and based on the emptiness of extrinsic nature, O Venerable Śāriputra, form does not exist and is not apprehended.
Venerable Śāriputra, feeling does not exist and is not apprehended; Venerable Śāriputra, perception does not exist and is not apprehended;
Venerable Śāriputra, mental formations do not exist and are not apprehended; Venerable Śāriputra, consciousness does not exist and is not apprehended;
Venerable Śāriputra, internal emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended; external emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended.
Internal-and-external emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended; great emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended;
the emptiness of emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended; the emptiness of the ultimate does not exist and is not apprehended;
the emptiness of the conditioned does not exist and is not apprehended; the emptiness of the unconditioned does not exist and is not apprehended.

Extreme emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended; the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end does not exist and is not apprehended; the emptiness of non-dispersal does not exist and is not apprehended; the emptiness of intrinsic nature does not exist and is not apprehended; the emptiness of all phenomena does not exist and is not apprehended; the emptiness of specific characteristics does not exist and is not apprehended; the emptiness of non-apprehension...
The emptiness of non-existence is not found and is not apprehended; the emptiness of existence is not found and is not apprehended;

the emptiness of non-existence is not found and is not apprehended; the emptiness of self-nature is not found and is not apprehended; the emptiness of other-nature is not found and is not apprehended; and so on, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The factors conducive to enlightenment do not exist and are not apprehended;

the superknowledges do not exist and are not apprehended; the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not exist and are not apprehended; suchness does not exist and is not apprehended.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not exist and is not apprehended; the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*) does not exist and is not apprehended; the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*) does not exist and is not apprehended.
The limit of reality is neither found nor apprehended; O Venerable Śāriputra, even a Buddha is neither found nor apprehended;
O Venerable Śāriputra, even omniscience is neither found nor apprehended.

Based on internal emptiness, and so on, up to based on the emptiness of other-nature, if, moreover, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom examines in this way and meditates in this way,
then as he thus examines and thus meditates, his mind does not sink and does not become despondent.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into fear should be known as one who is never separated from the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus ends the specific distinction of the object and aspect of the superior stage of the higher progression.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "For what reason, venerable Subhūti, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva not separated from the perfection of wisdom?"
It should be understood thus.
Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, form is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form; in this same way..."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness,
venerable Śāriputra, are devoid of the intrinsic nature of consciousness;
even the perfection of generosity, venerable Śāriputra, is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity.

"Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of ethical discipline is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline; the perfection of patience, Venerable Śāriputra, is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of patience; the perfection of vigor, Venerable Śāriputra, is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of vigor; and the perfection of meditation, Venerable Śāriputra, is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of meditation."

Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom; the applications of mindfulness, Venerable Śāriputra, are also devoid of the intrinsic nature of the applications of mindfulness; the right efforts, Venerable Śāriputra, are also devoid of the intrinsic nature of the right efforts; and the bases of psychic power, Venerable Śāriputra, are also devoid [of their intrinsic nature].

Venerable Śāriputra, even the faculties are devoid of the intrinsic nature of the faculties; Venerable Śāriputra, even the powers are devoid of the intrinsic nature of the powers; Venerable Śāriputra, even the factors of enlightenment are devoid of the intrinsic nature of the factors of enlightenment; Venerable Śāriputra, even the paths are devoid of the intrinsic nature of the paths.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, the immeasurable meditative absorptions are devoid of the intrinsic nature of the immeasurable meditative absorptions; the formless attainments, Venerable Śāriputra, are also devoid of the intrinsic nature of the formless attainments; the ten powers, Venerable Śāriputra, are also devoid of the intrinsic nature of the ten powers; and the grounds of self-confidence, Venerable Śāriputra, are also devoid of the intrinsic nature of the grounds of self-confidence.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, the analytical knowledges are devoid of the intrinsic nature of the analytical knowledges; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are devoid of the intrinsic nature of the qualities of a Buddha.
"Even the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), venerable Śāriputra, is devoid of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the limit of reality.
Śāriputra said:
"But how, venerable Subhūti, is there the intrinsic nature of form?"
How [is it] with respect to feeling, perception, and mental formations?
How is the intrinsic nature of consciousness, and how [are they] individually and collectively?
The intrinsic nature of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination;
and so on in detail, up to: how is the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality?
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, non-existence is the intrinsic nature of form; non-existence is the intrinsic nature of feeling."
The absence of perception is its intrinsic nature;
the absence of mental formations is their intrinsic nature;
the absence of consciousness is its intrinsic nature.
Non-existence is the intrinsic nature of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination, whether taken individually or collectively;
non-existence is the intrinsic nature born of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and lack of formative activity;
non-existence is the intrinsic nature of suchness, the realm of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the fixed order of phenomena. Thus...
In detail, up to: non-existence is the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Therefore, venerable Śāriputra, by this method it should be understood thus.

Just as form is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form, feeling is devoid of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception is devoid of the intrinsic nature of perception, mental formations are devoid of the intrinsic nature of mental formations, and consciousness is devoid of the intrinsic nature of consciousness;
so it is in detail.
One should practice with respect to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination, both individually and collectively, up to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, form is devoid of the characteristic of form.

Feeling is devoid of the characteristic of feeling; perception is devoid of the characteristic of perception; mental formations are devoid of the characteristic of mental formations; consciousness is devoid of the characteristic of consciousness.

In this way, it should be applied in detail to the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination, both individually and collectively, up to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), which is itself devoid [of its own characteristic].
By way of the characteristic of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
even the characteristic is devoid of the nature of characteristics; by way of the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even intrinsic nature is devoid [of characteristics].
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this will go forth to all-aspect omniscience."
Subhūti said: "It is so, venerable Śāriputra.
For whoever trains here in this way will go forth to omniscience. [Thus ends the section on the weak.]
[The distinction of the object and aspect of patience:
For what reason?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, they are unborn.
"All dharmas are unproduced.
Śāriputra said: "For what reason, venerable Subhūti, are they unarisen?"
"All dharmas have gone forth.
Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; of that..."
Neither arising nor departure is perceived;
for, Venerable Śāriputra, feeling is empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling,
and thus neither its arising nor its departure is perceived.
Perception, venerable Śāriputra, is empty of the intrinsic nature of perception;
neither its birth nor its departure is apprehended.
Volitional formations, venerable Śāriputra, are empty of the intrinsic nature of volitional formations.
Neither their birth nor their departure is perceived;
consciousness, O Venerable Śāriputra, is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness,
and neither its birth nor its departure is perceived.

In this same manner, it should be applied in detail to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination, both individually and collectively, up to the point that the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality; for that [limit of reality], there is neither birth nor...
...the departure [from saṃsāra] is apprehended.
For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom draws near to all-aspect omniscience; and in whatever measure he draws near to all-aspect omniscience—

In whatever way he practices, in that same way he attains purification of body, purification of mind, and purification of the marks. And in whatever way he attains purification of body, purification of mind, and purification of the marks,
in that same way the mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not arise accompanied by form.
A mind accompanied by hatred does not arise; a mind accompanied by delusion does not arise;
a mind accompanied by pride does not arise;
a mind accompanied by greed does not arise; and a mind accompanied by wrong view does not arise.
Because he does not give rise to a mind of passion, because he does not give rise to a mind of hatred,

because he does not give rise to a mind of delusion, because he does not give rise to a mind of pride, and because he does not give rise to a mind of wrong views, he is never again born from a mother’s womb; he is constantly and continuously [free from them].
He travels wearing sandals,
proceeding from buddha-field to buddha-field,
and he attends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
He brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field;
he is never separated from those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
...until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
For in this way, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws near to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
[Thus ends the specific characteristics of the object and the aspect of the medium degree of patience.
Then, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
If, Blessed One,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is unskilled in means, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, practices with respect to form, he practices with respect to a sign;
he does not practice in the perfection of wisdom.
If he courses in feeling, he courses in a sign; he does not course in the perfection of wisdom. If he courses in perception, he courses in a sign; he does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If he courses in formations, he courses in a sign; he does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If he courses in consciousness, he courses in a sign; he does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If he courses with the thought that form is permanent...

If he courses in the notion that "feeling is permanent," he courses in a sign; he does not course in the perfection of wisdom. If he courses in the notion that "perception is permanent," he courses in a sign; he does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in a sign, one does not course in the perfection of wisdom; if one courses with the thought that conditioned phenomena are permanent,
one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses with the thought that consciousness is permanent,
one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses with the thought that form is pleasure or pain...
If one courses in the notion that "feeling is pleasant or painful," one courses in a sign; one does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in the notion that "perception is pleasant or painful," one courses in a sign; one does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in a sign— that formations are either pleasant or painful— one does not course in the perfection of wisdom;
if one courses in a sign, one does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in the notion that consciousness is either pleasure or pain,
one courses in signs and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in the notion that form is self or non-self...
If one courses in the notion that "feeling is self" or "feeling is not-self," one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom;
if one courses in the notion that "perception is self" or "perception is not-self," one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in signs, one does not course in the perfection of wisdom;
if one courses with the thought that formations are either self or non-self,
one courses in signs and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in the thought that consciousness is self or non-self,
one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in the thought that form is peaceful or unpeaceful, [one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom].
If one courses in the notion that "feeling is peaceful or not peaceful," one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom;
if one courses in the notion that "perception is peaceful or not peaceful," one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in signs—
that is, if one courses with the thought that "formative factors are either tranquil or not tranquil"—
one courses in signs and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in the thought that consciousness is either peaceful or not peaceful,
one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in the thought that form is either secluded or not secluded, [one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom].
If one courses in [the notion that] "feeling is secluded or not secluded," one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom;
if one courses in [the notion that] "perception is secluded or not secluded," one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in a sign, one does not course in the perfection of wisdom;
if one courses with the thought that "conditioned phenomena are either secluded or not secluded," one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
If one courses in the thought that consciousness is either secluded or not secluded,
one courses in a sign and does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, is unskilled in means regarding the thirty-seven [factors of enlightenment]...
If one practices among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), one practices with signs (*nimitta*) and does not practice in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Likewise, up to the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the perfections, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the five eyes, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and so on, up to the eighteen [unique qualities of a Buddha]— [if one practices these, one practices with signs and does not practice in the perfection of wisdom].
He courses in the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), he courses in signs, and he does not course in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through a lack of skill in means (*anupāyakauśalya*), while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, thinks thus:
To think, "I am practicing the perfection of wisdom," is to practice in apprehension; to think, "I am practicing," is to practice in signs.
If it should occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "He who practices in this way practices in the perfection of wisdom; he cultivates the perfection of wisdom," then, indeed, the venerable...
Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"For what reason, venerable Subhūti, should this lack of skill in means on the part of a bodhisattva mahāsattva be understood?"
Subhūti said:
"For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom establishes himself in form..."
One perceives and resolves upon feeling; one presides over perception, perceives it, and resolves upon it. One presides over perception, perceives it, and resolves upon it.
He presides over, perceives, and resolves upon the formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
he presides over, perceives, and resolves upon consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Presiding over, perceiving, and resolving upon that form (*rūpa*), [he acts].
Abiding in feeling, perceiving it, and resolving upon it; abiding in perception, perceiving it, and resolving upon it;
abiding in volitional formations, perceiving them, and resolving upon them.
When one abides in consciousness, perceiving it and being resolved upon it,
one courses in the formative activity of form; I declare that this brings about birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair for such a person.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, is lacking in skillful means, he does not dwell upon, perceive, or resolve upon the eye; he does not dwell upon, perceive, or resolve upon the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; he does not dwell upon or perceive form.

He does not resolve upon sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; he does not preside over them, does not perceive them, and does not resolve upon them. He does not preside over visual consciousness, does not perceive it, and does not resolve upon it; [likewise] auditory consciousness and olfactory consciousness.
He presides over tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness, yet he does not perceive them and does not resolve upon them.

He presides over eye-contact, yet he does not perceive it and does not resolve upon it; he presides over ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact, yet he does not perceive them and does not resolve upon them.
He presides over the feeling conditioned by eye-contact, yet he does not perceive it and does not resolve upon it; he presides over the feeling conditioned by ear-contact,

the feeling conditioned by nose-contact, the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, the feeling conditioned by body-contact, and the feeling conditioned by mind-contact, yet he does not perceive them and does not resolve upon them.

Whether it be pleasure, pain, neither-pain-nor-pleasure, or equanimity, he does not dwell upon it, does not perceive it, and does not resolve upon it. If he does not dwell upon, perceive, or resolve upon the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*),
and likewise the five eyes, the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the six perfections (*pāramitā*), and the four—
He does not preside over, does not perceive, and does not resolve upon the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the four immeasurables, the four meditative concentrations,
the four formless attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood,
the state of a bodhisattva, or the Buddha-qualities.
Blessing, perceiving, and resolving upon all the qualities of a Buddha, he courses in the formative activity of the qualities of a Buddha;
coursing in formative activity, he is not liberated from birth, nor from old age and death.

And I say that he is not liberated from suffering through sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. Furthermore, Śāriputra, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is incapable of falling to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha;
how much less could he fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? Such a thing is impossible. Thus it is.
“Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should be known as one lacking skill in means.
Śāriputra asked:
“Venerable Subhūti, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [lacks skill in means] while practicing the perfection of wisdom?”
One who practices in this way should be known as skillful in means.
Subhūti said:
"O Venerable Śāriputra, that bodhisattva..."
The Mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, does not dwell upon form, does not perceive it, and does not resolve upon it;

he does not dwell upon feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he perceive them or resolve upon them. Likewise, up to the Buddha-qualities, he does not dwell upon them, does not perceive them, and does not resolve upon them.
He [does not dwell] upon form...
He does not course in feeling, he does not course in perception, he does not course in volitional formations,

nor does he course in consciousness; he does not course in the sign of form, he does not course in the sign of feeling, he does not course in the sign of perception, he does not course in the sign of volitional formations, nor does he course in the sign of consciousness.
He does not course [in the thought] that form is permanent, nor that it is impermanent; he does not course [in the thought] that feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness are permanent, nor that they are impermanent.
He does not course [in the notion] that form is pleasure, nor that it is suffering; nor that it is self, nor that it is non-self; nor that it is peaceful, nor that it is unpeaceful.
It is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations.

He does not course [with the thought] that consciousness is pleasure, nor that it is the self, nor that it is not the self, nor that it is peaceful, nor that it is not peaceful; he does not course with the thought that form is empty, nor that it is not empty, nor that it has signs, nor that it is signless, nor that it is wishless, nor that it is not wishless, nor that it is secluded, nor that it is not secluded.

Thus, he does not course [thinking] "feeling is not empty" nor "it is not non-empty"; he does not course [thinking] "perception is not empty" nor "it is not non-empty"; he does not course [thinking] "formations are not empty" nor "they are not non-empty"; he does not course [thinking] "consciousness is not empty" nor "it is not non-empty"; he does not course [thinking] "there is a sign" nor "there is no sign."

He does not course [thinking] "it is not wishless," nor does he course [thinking] "it is not non-wishless"; he does not course [thinking] "it is secluded," nor does he course [thinking] "it is not secluded. For what reason? Because, venerable Śāriputra, that which is the emptiness of form is not form, nor is it other than form.

Form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is form itself, and form is emptiness. Whatever is the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of mental formations, and the emptiness of consciousness—that is consciousness. And consciousness is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than consciousness.
Emptiness itself is consciousness, and consciousness itself is emptiness.

Thus it is with respect to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination— whether taken individually or collectively— as well as the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the paths, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique [buddha-qualities].
Regarding the Buddha-qualities, up to the point of the emptiness of the Buddha-qualities: those are not the Buddha-qualities, nor are the Buddha-qualities elsewhere than in emptiness;
emptiness is not elsewhere than in the Buddha-qualities.
Emptiness itself is the Buddha-qualities, and the Buddha-qualities themselves are emptiness.

Emptiness. Thus, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should be known as one skilled in means. Thus, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practicing] the perfection of wisdom—
Practicing within the *Amitāyus* [sūtra], one is capable of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, if while practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) one approaches any dharma, one does not practice the perfection of wisdom; if one does not approach it, one does not practice.
One neither approaches nor does not approach, one does not practice, and one neither approaches nor does not not approach;
thus one does not practice in the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra said: "For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, not approach [anything]?"
Subhūti said: "For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended."
For what reason?
Because, Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom has non-existence as its intrinsic nature; it is by this method, O Venerable Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [is so called].

One does not approach the thought, "I am practicing the perfection of wisdom," nor does one approach the thought, "I am not practicing," nor does one approach the thought, "I both practice and do not practice."

He does not approach the thought "I am practicing," nor does he approach the thought "I am neither practicing nor not practicing. Why is that? Because he has followed after and attained the realization that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.

If, while practicing thus in the perfection of wisdom, the mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not become despondent, does not tremble, does not fear, and does not fall into terror, then, O Venerable Śāriputra, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is close to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
[Thus is the distinction of the object and aspect of supreme patience.
Furthermore, O Venerable Śāriputra, that omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is non-dual and without division.
Based on the fact that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature,
this samādhi of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas called "the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" is vast, preeminent, immeasurable, certain, and unassailable.
"By dwelling in this samādhi, O Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra said:
"By means of which concentrations, Venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling [in them] quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Subhūti replied:

"Venerable Śāriputra, there exists for bodhisattvas mahāsattvas a samādhi called Śūraṅgama, by dwelling in which samādhi a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. There is also a samādhi called Ratnamudrā."
There is a samādhi called "Excellent Moon";
there is a samādhi called "Moon Banner Crest";
there is a samādhi called "Seal of All Dharmas."
There is a samādhi called Avalokitamūrdhā;
there is a samādhi called Dharmadhātuniyata;
there is a samādhi called Niyatadhvajaketu.
There is a samādhi called "diamond-like" (vajropama);
there is a samādhi called "the seal of entry into all phenomena" (sarvadharmapraveśamudra);
there is a [samādhi] called "equipoised" (samāhita).
There is the samādhi called "Neither Abiding Nor Non-abiding";
there is the samādhi called "Royal Seal";
there is the samādhi called "Powerful Heroism."
There is a samādhi called "Exalted Above All Dharmas";
there is a samādhi called "Entrance into the Certainty of Etymological Explanations";
there is a samādhi called "Entrance into the Inexhaustible."
There is a samādhi called "Surveying the Directions"; there is a samādhi called "Seal of the Dhāraṇī";

in which, when training, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Among these, what is the meditative concentration called "Heroic Progress" (*śūraṅgama*)?
That concentration by which one experiences the range of all concentrations is called the concentration named Śūraṅgama.
In that regard, what is the concentration named Ratnamudrā?
This is the samādhi. By means of this samādhi, all samādhis are sealed; this is called the "jewel-seal" (ratnamudra) samādhi.
Likewise, up to: what is the samādhi called "unstained liberation from attachment to space"?
It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one attains the state of being unstained by and liberated from attachment to space regarding all phenomena.
It is called the samādhi named "unstained by attachment to space and liberated. [Thus ends the specific object and aspect of the lowest stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas.]
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, through the power of the Buddha, said this to the venerable Śāriputra:

Furthermore, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who currently reside, abide, and maintain themselves in the worlds of the ten directions— they too prophesy that bodhisattva mahāsattva.
He who dwells by means of these concentrations does not perceive even concentration;
nor does he conceive himself on account of that concentration.
"I am concentrated," "I shall enter into concentration," "I have entered into concentration."
"I enter into meditative absorption.
All these conceptual constructions do not exist and are not perceived by the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Thus ends the distinction regarding the object and aspect of the supreme mundane dharmas.
Śāriputra said:

[The Tathāgatas], the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened Buddhas, prophesy [it].
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, venerable Śāriputra."
For what reason?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom is not one thing, the samādhi another, and the bodhisattva another; they are not distinct from one another. A bodhisattva is...
This very concentration is the Bodhisattva, and the Bodhisattva is indeed this very concentration.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, if the concentration is not one thing and the Bodhisattva another..."
"Samādhi itself is the bodhisattva, and the bodhisattva himself is samādhi, based on the equality of all phenomena. Is it possible to demonstrate that samādhi? Subhūti said:
"For it is not so, Venerable Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"But then, Venerable One, does that son of good family perceive that samādhi?"
Subhūti said:
"No, venerable Śāriputra, that son of good family does not perceive that samādhi.
Śāriputra said:
"How does he not perceive?
Subhūti replied,
"In the same way that he does not conceptualize."
Śāriputra asked: "In what way does one not conceptualize?
Subhūti replied:
Because all phenomena are non-existent, he does not conceptualize even samādhi.
Venerable Śāriputra, it is by this method that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive.
Śāriputra said:
"How does he not perceive it?
Subhūti replied,
"By virtue of the non-conceptuality of that samādhi, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive it."
[Thus ends the specific object and aspect of the supreme mundane dharmas.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the venerable Subhūti:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just as you have been designated by me as the foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-contention."
This is the instruction. Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom;
thus should he train in the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity;
and thus in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.
One should train in the dharmas, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Then, indeed, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, training in this way..."
The bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom.
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, training in this way..."
The bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension;
likewise, he trains in the perfection of meditative concentration by way of non-apprehension, he trains in the perfection of vigor by way of non-apprehension,
he trains in the perfection of patience by way of non-apprehension, and he trains in the perfection of ethical discipline by way of non-apprehension.

He trains in the perfection of generosity by way of non-apprehension; and so on, in detail, he trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment by way of non-apprehension, up to the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments, training in them by way of non-apprehension.
He trains in the ten powers, the four forms of fearlessness, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
Śāriputra asked:
"Lord, why does he not apprehend them?"
The Blessed One said:

"Śāriputra, one does not apprehend a self; one does not apprehend anything up to a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer, because of their absolute purity."
Starting from [the individual] up to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination— whether taken separately or as a whole—
one does not perceive them, on account of their absolute purity;
one does not perceive suffering, on account of its absolute purity.
One does not apprehend the origin, because of its absolute purity;
one does not apprehend cessation, because of its absolute purity;
one does not apprehend the path, because of its absolute purity.
One does not apprehend the realm of form, on account of its absolute purity; one does not apprehend the formless realm, on account of its absolute purity;
[nor does one apprehend] the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, or the formless attainments.
One does not apprehend the meditative attainments, on account of their absolute purity;

one does not apprehend the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, on account of their absolute purity;
one does not apprehend the perfections, on account of their absolute purity.
One does not apprehend the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, on account of their absolute purity;
one does not apprehend the stream-enterer, on account of their absolute purity.
One does not apprehend a once-returner, on account of ultimate purity;
one does not apprehend a non-returner, on account of ultimate purity;
one does not apprehend an arhat, on account of ultimate purity.
One does not apprehend a pratyekabuddha, because of ultimate purity;
one does not apprehend a bodhisattva, because of ultimate purity;
one does not apprehend a buddha, because of ultimate purity.
Śāriputra said:
"But what, Blessed One, is purity?
The Blessed One replied:
"Non-arising, Śāriputra, non-manifestation, non-apprehension, and non-conditioning— this is called purity.
[Thus concludes the section on the general association with conceptual construction.]
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, in which dharmas does he train?"
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this way does not train in any phenomena whatsoever."
For what reason?
Śāriputra, these phenomena do not exist in the way that foolish ordinary people are attached to them.
Śāriputra said:
"How is it, Blessed One, that these phenomena do not exist?
The Blessed One replied:
They do not exist in the way that foolish ordinary persons are attached to them.
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, how is it that these dharmas do not exist?"
The Blessed One said:
"They exist in such a way that they do not exist; thus, while they do not exist, they exist."
Therefore, it is called ignorance (avidyā).
[Thus ends the first conceptualization of ignorance within the association with the conceptualizations of the stage of heat.
Śāriputra asked: "For what reason is it said that ignorance is non-existent?"
The Blessed One said: "Śāriputra, form does not exist, by reason of internal emptiness, by reason of external emptiness,
by reason of internal and external emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of phenomena."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Śāriputra,
do not exist, by way of internal emptiness and by way of external emptiness.
Based on internal and external emptiness,
up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment do not exist, and up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not exist, based on internal emptiness.
Based on external emptiness;
based on internal-external emptiness.
Thus, therein is the second [section] concerning the aggregates of form and so forth.
[...conceptual construction... In this regard, fools are attached to ignorance and craving.
Having conceptualized ignorance and craving as things to be conceptualized, they become attached to both through ignorance and craving.
Attached to both extremes, they neither know nor see that phenomena do not exist as they appear. Having conceptualized those phenomena, they are attached to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so on,
up to being attached to the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*).

[Thus ends the third conceptualization of attachment to name-and-form in that very context. Attached to these phenomena, they conceptualize both non-existent extremes; having conceptualized them, they neither know nor see.
Do they not know, do they not see?
They do not know form, they do not see it; they do not know feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do they see them.
As long as they do not know and do not see the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination,
and as long as they do not know and do not see the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, by that they are reckoned as "fools. [Thus it is said.]
In that very context, the fourth conceptualization is the attachment to the two extremes.
They do not know and do not see that [form] has ignorance and craving as its conditions; they do not know and do not see that form is afflicted;
likewise, they do not know and do not see that form is purified.
They do not know and do not see that feeling, perception, and consciousness are afflicted;
likewise, they do not know and do not see that consciousness is purified.
They will not go forth; from what will they not go forth? They will not go forth from the desire realm.
They will not emerge from the realm of form; they will not emerge from the realm of formlessness;
they will not emerge from the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
[Thus ends the fifth conceptualization regarding the knowledge of affliction and purification in that very context. They do not have faith. Why do they not have faith?
They do not have faith that form is empty of form,
up to and including that awakening is empty of the nature of awakening.
They do not abide. Why do they not abide?
They do not abide in the perfection of generosity; they do not abide in the perfection of ethical discipline; they do not abide in the perfection of patience.
They do not abide in the perfection of vigor; they do not abide in the perfection of meditation; they do not abide in the perfection of wisdom.
They do not abide on the stage of non-retrogression, nor do they abide in the qualities of a Buddha.
For this reason they are called "fools.
They are attached.
To what are they attached?
They are attached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
they are attached to passion, hatred, and delusion;
they are attached to the products of views, and so forth.
[They] are attached to awakening.
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way..."
"He trains in the perfection of wisdom and will emerge into the knowledge of all aspects.
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the perfection of wisdom."
[He] will not set out for the knowledge of all aspects.
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva..."
The mahāsattva, lacking skill in means, conceptualizes and adheres to the perfection of wisdom;
he conceptualizes and adheres to the perfection of meditative concentration; he conceptualizes and adheres to the perfection of vigor; he conceptualizes and adheres to the perfection of patience.

He conceptualizes and adheres to the perfection of ethical discipline; he conceptualizes and adheres to the perfection of generosity; likewise, he conceptualizes and adheres to the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments. He conceptualizes and adheres to the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path. [He conceptualizes and adheres to] the ten powers...

He conceptualizes and adheres to the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he conceptualizes and adheres to everything up to all phenomena and the knowledge of all modes.
Śāriputra, by this method, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the perfection of wisdom.
"He will not set out for the knowledge of all aspects. Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way does not train in the perfection of wisdom."
"He will not set out for the knowledge of all aspects.
The Blessed One said:
"Training in this manner..."
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the perfection of wisdom; he will not emerge into all-aspect omniscience.
[Thus ends therein the sixth conceptualization regarding the establishment in the Noble Path.
Śāriputra said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom?"
"In what way will one training [in this] emerge into the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said,
"When, Śāriputra..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend nor perceive the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom and training in the perfection of wisdom will emerge into omniscience by means of non-apprehension.

In this way, one does not apprehend and does not perceive the perfection of meditation; one does not apprehend and does not perceive the perfection of vigor; one does not apprehend and does not perceive the perfection of patience; one does not apprehend and does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline.
He does not apprehend nor perceive the perfection of generosity, up to and including awakening and the knowledge of all aspects;
he does not apprehend nor perceive them. It is in this way, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom and training in the perfection of wisdom, [proceeds].
He will set out for the knowledge of all modes by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
[Thus ends the seventh conceptualization of apprehension in that very context.
Śāriputra asked: "By means of the non-apprehension of what?"
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, one does not apprehend nor perceive a self, by virtue of its absolute purity."
[Thus ends the eighth conceptualization regarding the self and so forth.
Śāriputra, non-arising is non-manifestation, non-conditioning, and purity.
[Thus ends, in that very same place,
the ninth conceptualization concerning purification, arising, and so forth.]
[Thus ends the first conceptualization of the apprehended.
14913 He, being unskilled in means, conceptualizes and adheres to form, up to and including consciousness; he conceptualizes and adheres to it.

[Thus ends, in that very same place,
the sixth conceptualization regarding the meaning of the perfections.]

[Thus ends, in that very same place,

[Thus ends the ninth discrimination regarding the path of training in that very same context.]
[Thus ends the second conceptualization of the apprehended.
Śāriputra, one does not perceive a self.
In this way, one does not perceive a being, a soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer.
