For, in an absolute sense, the self does not exist and is not perceived.
[Thus ends] the first independent conceptualization of a self (*svatantrātmavikalpa*) in association with conceptualizations accompanied by receptivity (*kṣānti*).
“Śāriputra, one does not apprehend form, nor does one apprehend anything up to consciousness.
Thus ends the second conceptualization of a single self in that very same section.
Śāriputra, one does not apprehend the eye, and so on up to the mind; one does not apprehend form, and so on up to the qualities of a Buddha.

[Thus ends the third conceptualization of the self as cause in that very context. Śāriputra, one does not apprehend eye, form, or visual consciousness, up to and including mind, mental objects, or mental consciousness. [Thus ends the fourth conceptualization of the self as the seer and so forth in that very context.]
Śāriputra, one does not apprehend dependent origination, up to and including the formless attainments; one does not apprehend them.
[Thus ends, in that very same place, the sixth conceptualization concerning the basis of detachment.]
[He] does not perceive the noble truths.
[Thus ends, in that very context, the seventh conceptualization of the self as the support for seeing.]
He does not apprehend the eight liberations or the nine successive meditative attainments.
[Thus ends the eighth conceptualization regarding the basis of cultivation in that very same context.]
[He] does not apprehend the ten powers, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
How does he not apprehend them?
As the self. For what reason? On account of the absolute purity of the self.
[Thus ends, in that very same context, the ninth conceptualization of the self as the stream of one who has accomplished his purpose.]
[Thus ends the first conceptualization of the grasper.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if someone were to ask—"
"Will this illusory person, having trained in the perfection of wisdom, emerge into the knowledge of all aspects?
To one who asks this, how should it be explained?
Likewise regarding the perfection of meditative concentration...
"Having trained in this, one will set out for the knowledge of all aspects; having thus trained in the perfection of vigor, one will set out for the knowledge of all aspects;
having thus trained in the perfection of patience, one will set out for the knowledge of all aspects."
"Having thus trained in the perfection of ethical discipline, one will set out for the knowledge of all aspects.

"Having trained in the perfection of generosity, one will set out for the knowledge of all aspects. To him who asks in this manner, how should it be explained, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment?
"Having trained in the dharmas up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he will set out toward the knowledge of all aspects; he will attain the knowledge of all aspects.
To him who asks thus, how should it be explained?
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, Subhūti, I shall question you on this matter;
you should answer as you see fit."
What do you think, Subhūti? Is form one thing and illusion another?
Is feeling one thing, perception another, mental formations another, and consciousness another, while illusion is yet another?
Subhūti said, "No, Blessed One."
[Thus ends the first conceptualization regarding the designation of the aggregates, occurring in conjunction with the conceptualization pertaining to the supreme dharmas.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
Illusion is one thing and the eye another;

illusion is one thing and the ear, nose, tongue, and body another; illusion is one thing and the mind another; illusion is one thing and visible form another; illusion is one thing and sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects another.
"Is illusion one thing and phenomena another?
Subhūti replied, "No, Blessed One."
[Thus ends the second conceptualization of the designation of the sense-bases (āyatana-prajñapti-vikalpa) in that very same section.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? Is illusion one thing and eye-consciousness another? Is illusion one thing and ear-consciousness another? Is illusion one thing and nose-consciousness another? Is illusion one thing and tongue-consciousness another? Is illusion one thing and body-consciousness another? Is illusion one thing and mind-consciousness another?
Illusion is one thing, and the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness are another; illusion is one thing, and the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness are another;
illusion is one thing, and the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness are another; illusion is one thing, and the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness are another;
illusion is one thing, and the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness are another; illusion is one thing, and the mind, mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness are another.
Illusion is one thing, eye-contact another; illusion is one thing, ear-contact another; illusion is one thing, nose-contact another; illusion is one thing, tongue-contact another;
illusion is one thing, body-contact another; illusion is one thing, mind-contact another.
Subhūti said, "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? Is illusion one thing, and is the feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that arises conditioned by the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, another?
Subhūti said, "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? Is illusion one thing and the earth element another? Is illusion one thing and the water element another? Is illusion one thing and the fire element another? Is illusion one thing and the wind element another? Is illusion one thing and the space element another? Is illusion one thing and the consciousness element another?
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One. The earth element is not one thing and illusion another;
the earth element itself is illusion, and illusion itself is the earth element."
"No, Blessed One, the water element is not one thing and illusion another;
the water element itself is illusion, and illusion itself is the water element.
No, Blessed One, the fire element is not one thing and illusion another."
The fire element itself is illusion, and illusion itself is the fire element.
No, Blessed One, the wind element is not one thing and illusion another;
the wind element itself is illusion, and illusion itself is the wind element.
"No, Blessed One, the space-element is not one thing and illusion another;
the space-element itself is illusion, and illusion itself is the space-element.
No, Blessed One, the consciousness-element is not one thing and illusion another."
The consciousness element itself is illusion, and illusion itself is the consciousness element.
[Thus ends the third conceptualization regarding the designation of the elements in that very context.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Is illusion one thing and dependent origination another?
Subhūti replied, "No, Blessed One, they are not different."
Is ignorance different from illusion?
Is ignorance itself illusion, and illusion itself ignorance?
"No, Blessed One, conditioned formations are not one thing and illusion another."
Formations themselves are illusion, and illusion itself is formations.
No, Blessed One, consciousness is not one thing and illusion another;
consciousness itself is illusion, and illusion itself is consciousness.
"No, Blessed One, name-and-form is not one thing and illusion another;
name-and-form itself is illusion, and illusion itself is name-and-form.
No, Blessed One, the six sense-bases are not one thing and illusion another."
The six sense bases themselves are illusion, and illusion itself is the six sense bases.
No, Blessed One, contact is not one thing and illusion another;
contact itself is illusion, and illusion itself is contact.
"No, Blessed One, feeling is not one thing and illusion another;
feeling itself is illusion, and illusion itself is feeling.
No, Blessed One, craving is not one thing and illusion another."
Craving itself is illusion, and illusion itself is craving.
No, Blessed One, grasping is not one thing and illusion another;
grasping itself is illusion, and illusion itself is grasping.
"No, Blessed One, existence is not one thing and illusion another;
existence itself is illusion, and illusion itself is existence.
No, Blessed One, birth is not one thing and illusion another."
Birth itself is illusion, and illusion itself is birth. O Blessed One, aging and death are not one thing and illusion another;
aging and death themselves are illusion, and illusion itself is aging and death.
[Thus ends the fourth conceptualization regarding the designation of dependent origination.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Is illusion one thing and the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening another?
Subhūti replied, "No, Blessed One."
[Thus ends the fifth conceptualization regarding the designation of purification.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
Illusion is one thing, emptiness is another;
illusion is one thing, the sign is another; illusion is one thing, the wishless is another.
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One."
[Thus ends the sixth conceptualization regarding the designation of the path of seeing.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Is illusion one thing and the meditative absorptions and formless attainments another?
Subhūti replied, "No, Blessed One."
[Thus ends therein the seventh conceptualization regarding the designation of the path of cultivation.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Is illusion one thing and all-emptiness another?
Subhūti replied,
"No, Blessed One."
Right there, the eighth conceptualization concerning the designation of the path of distinction [is as follows].
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Is illusion one thing and the ten powers another? Is illusion one thing and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha another? Subhūti said:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Is illusion one thing and awakening another?
Subhūti replied, "No, Blessed One, they are not different."

“Māyā is another form and form is indeed māyā, Blessed One; māyā is indeed Blessed One, form. Māyā is not other than feeling, Blessed One; feeling is indeed māyā, Blessed One; māyā is indeed Blessed One, feeling. Māyā is not other than perception, Blessed One; perception is indeed māyā, Blessed One; māyā is indeed Blessed One, perception.”

“Venerable Lord, perception is not one thing and illusion another; the conditioned factors are not different from illusion. Venerable Lord, the conditioned factors themselves are illusion, and illusion itself, Venerable Lord, is the conditioned factors. Venerable Lord, illusion is not one thing and consciousness another; consciousness itself, Venerable Lord, is illusion, and illusion itself, Venerable Lord, is consciousness.”
"No, Blessed One, the eye is not one thing and illusion another; no, Blessed One, form is not one thing and illusion another. No, Blessed One, the ear is not one thing and illusion another;

no, Blessed One, sound is not one thing and illusion another. No, Blessed One, the nose is not one thing and illusion another; no, Blessed One, odor is not one thing and illusion another. No, Blessed One, [the tongue is not one thing and illusion another...]

The tongue is not other than illusion, O Blessed One; taste is not other than illusion, O Blessed One; the body is not other than illusion, O Blessed One; the tangible is not other than illusion, O Blessed One; the mind is not other than illusion, O Blessed One;
phenomena are not other than illusion, O Blessed One; and auditory consciousness is not other than illusion, O Blessed One.

"O Blessed One, auditory consciousness is not other than illusion; O Blessed One, olfactory consciousness is not other than illusion; O Blessed One, gustatory consciousness is not other than illusion; O Blessed One, tactile consciousness is not other than illusion; O Blessed One, mental consciousness is not other than illusion; O Blessed One, visual consciousness, arising from the eye and visible forms, is not other than illusion."

“O Blessed One, the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness are not one thing and illusion another; O Blessed One, the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness are not one thing and illusion another; O Blessed One, the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness are not one thing and illusion another; O Blessed One, the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness are not one thing and illusion another; O Blessed One, the mind, mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness are not one thing and illusion another; O Blessed One, visual contact is not one thing [and illusion another].”
"O Blessed One, illusion is not one thing and ear-contact another; O Blessed One, illusion is not one thing and nose-contact another;
O Blessed One, illusion is not one thing and tongue-contact another; O Blessed One, illusion is not one thing and body-contact another;
O Blessed One, illusion is not one thing and mind-contact another."

“Blessed One, there is no feeling—whether pleasant, painful, neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, other than that [feeling] itself.
Blessed One, illusion is not one thing and the factors of enlightenment another; the factors of enlightenment are themselves illusion.”
"O Blessed One, it is an illusion.
O Blessed One, the factors conducive to awakening are indeed an illusion.
They are not [real], O Blessed One."
"Is illusion one thing and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha another?
O Blessed One, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are themselves illusion; O Blessed One, illusion itself is the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
“O Blessed One, illusion is not one thing and awakening another; awakening itself is illusion, and illusion itself, O Blessed One, is awakening.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there indeed the arising or the cessation of an illusion?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Is there either affliction or purification of illusion?
Subhūti said, "No, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Regarding that which has no arising..."
There is no cessation, no affliction, and no purification. He trains in the perfection of wisdom; he trains in the perfection of meditation;
he trains in the perfection of vigor; he trains in the perfection of patience; he trains in the perfection of ethical discipline; he trains in the perfection of generosity;
[and he trains] in the immeasurables, the meditations, and the formless attainments.

He trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; he trains in the superknowledges, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
he will emerge into omniscience, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects.
[He] will attain it. Subhūti said:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Subhūti?
Is this designation, appellation, conceptualization, and conventional usage "bodhisattva" [applied] to these five aggregates of clinging?
Subhūti said, "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? Is the arising, the cessation, the defilement, or the purification of the five aggregates of clinging merely a designation, a convention, a conceptual construction, and a worldly transaction?
[It] is perceived.
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? For that which has no perception, no designation, and no conceptualization..."
There is no conventional designation, no conceptual designation of names, no body, no bodily action, no speech,
no verbal action, no mind, no mental action, no arising, no cessation, no affliction, and no purification; yet,
having trained in this perfection of wisdom, one will emerge into the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti said, "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In this way indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in the perfection of wisdom, will set out for the knowledge of all aspects by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
Subhūti said:
Thus, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom should train in unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment just like an illusory person. Why is that?
For it is thus, Blessed One: those very five aggregates of clinging are to be understood as a person created by illusion. The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Subhūti? Will these five aggregates of clinging,
having trained in the perfection of wisdom, emerge into the knowledge of all aspects?
Subhūti said:
"No, Blessed One.
For what reason?
For in this way, Blessed One, the five aggregates of clinging have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
Thus, the five aggregates are like a dream; and just as a dream, which has non-existence as its intrinsic nature, is not apprehended, so too the five aggregates are non-existent.
They are not perceived by way of intrinsic nature.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
The five aggregates are like an echo, like a mirage, like a magical creation, and like a reflection; having trained in the perfection of wisdom,
one will emerge into the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti said, "No, Blessed One.
For what reason? Because:

O Blessed One, the five aggregates, being of the nature of non-existence, are not apprehended; they are like an echo, a mere appearance, a magical creation, and a reflection, for their intrinsic nature is non-existent.
For in this way, O Blessed One, form is like an illusion.
Feeling is like an illusion; perception is like an illusion; mental formations are like an illusion; consciousness is like an illusion.
That which is consciousness is the six sense faculties; those are the five aggregates, and they are not apprehended through internal emptiness.

They are not apprehended through external emptiness; they are not apprehended through internal-external emptiness; and so on, up to: they are not apprehended through the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
If, Blessed One, when this is being spoken, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not shrink back, does not cower, does not become regretful,
and does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into terror—
It should be known, Blessed One, that this person will set forth toward omniscience and will attain the knowledge of all aspects.
[Thus ends, in that very place, the ninth conceptualization regarding the designation of the path of those beyond training.
[Thus ends the second conceptualization of the grasper.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
May it not be, Blessed One, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the vehicle, upon hearing this teaching, should become discouraged, cowed, or full of regret.
He would be terrified, tremble, and fall into a state of fear.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the vehicle, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, lacks skillful means—"
He might be skillful, yet he would not have fallen into the hands of a spiritual friend; he would tremble, be terrified, and fall into a state of dread.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is it for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom..."
Skill in means is that wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing, does not tremble, is not terrified, and does not fall into fear.
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),"
He contemplates that form is impermanent, yet he does not apprehend it.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he contemplates that feeling is impermanent, yet he does not apprehend it.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that perception is impermanent, yet he does not apprehend it. [He contemplates] the formations...
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that [form] is impermanent, yet he does not apprehend it.

He contemplates that consciousness is impermanent with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not apprehend it. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Skill in means should be understood [in this way].
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects,
contemplates that form is suffering, yet he does not apprehend it.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates feeling as suffering, yet he does not apprehend it;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates perception as suffering, yet he does not apprehend it;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates formations as suffering, yet he does not apprehend them.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he contemplates consciousness as suffering, yet he does not apprehend it.
Subhūti, this should be known as the skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects...

He contemplates that form is empty, yet he does not apprehend it; with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that feeling is empty, yet he does not apprehend it; with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that perception is empty, yet he does not apprehend it.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are empty and does not perceive them;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is empty and does not perceive it.
Subhūti, this should be known as the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, contemplates that form is selfless and does not apprehend it; with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that feeling is selfless and does not apprehend it.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates perception as selfless and does not apprehend it;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates formative forces as selfless and does not apprehend them;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates consciousness as selfless and does not apprehend it.
Subhūti, this should be understood as the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates form as peaceful, yet does not apprehend it; [likewise] he contemplates feeling with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects... [and so on].
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that feeling is peaceful, yet he does not apprehend it;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that perception is peaceful, yet he does not apprehend it;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that formations are peaceful, yet he does not apprehend them.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes, he contemplates that consciousness is peaceful, yet he does not apprehend it.
Subhūti, this should be known as the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes...

With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that form is secluded, yet he does not apprehend it; with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that feeling is secluded, yet he does not apprehend it;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that perception is secluded, yet he does not apprehend it.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are secluded, yet he does not apprehend them.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is secluded, yet he does not apprehend it.
Subhūti, this should be known as the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, contemplates form as signless and does not apprehend it; with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates feeling as signless and does not apprehend it.
With a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates perception as signless and does not apprehend it;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates volitional formations as signless and does not apprehend them;
with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he contemplates consciousness as signless and does not apprehend it.
Subhūti, this should be understood as the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that form is wishless, yet he does not apprehend it; [likewise] he contemplates feeling with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects... [and so on].

He contemplates that the mind is wishless by means of a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not apprehend it. He contemplates that perception is wishless by means of a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not apprehend it. He contemplates that volitional formations are wishless by means of a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not apprehend them.
He contemplates that consciousness is wishless by means of a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, yet he does not apprehend it.
Subhūti, this should be known as the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom [regarding] the knowledge of all aspects—

That teaching of the Dharma which he performs through mental applications associated with non-apprehension by way of the yoga of non-apprehension— this is the perfection of giving of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Of those very mental applications associated with the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā)—
This thorough grasping [of those mental attentions] is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

This endurance, proclamation, and discernment of those very mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The non-abandonment of those very mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)— this is the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, it is the refusal to grant any opportunity to those mental attentions associated with the level of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, or to any other unwholesome states.
This is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva regarding all phenomena.
For in this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he is not startled, not terrified, and does not fall into terror.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom contemplates in this way: form is not empty by means of the emptiness of form;
rather, form itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself is form.
It is not that feeling is empty because of emptiness;
rather, feeling is empty.
Feeling itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is feeling;
it is not that perception is empty because of the emptiness of perception.
Perception itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is perception.
It is not by means of the emptiness of volitional formations that volitional formations are empty.
Formations themselves are emptiness, and emptiness itself is formations.
It is not by means of the emptiness of consciousness that consciousness is empty; [consciousness is empty of itself].
Consciousness itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is consciousness.
It is not by means of the emptiness of the eye that the eye is empty.
The eye itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is the eye.
It is not by means of the emptiness of the ear that the ear is empty.
The ear itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is the ear.
It is not by means of the emptiness of the nose that the nose is empty.
The nose itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is the nose.
It is not by means of the emptiness of the tongue that the tongue is empty.
The tongue itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is the tongue.
It is not by means of the emptiness of the body that the body is empty.
The body itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is the body;
it is not that the mind is empty because of the emptiness of the mind.
Mind itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is mind.
Form is not empty by virtue of the emptiness of form.
Form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form.
Sound is not empty because of the emptiness of sound.
Sound itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is sound.
It is not that sound is empty by means of the emptiness of smell.
Odor itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is odor.
Taste is not empty by virtue of the emptiness of taste.
Taste itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is taste.
It is not by means of the emptiness of the tangible that the tangible is empty.
Tangibility itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is tangibility.
It is not by means of the emptiness of phenomena that phenomena are empty; rather, phenomena are empty of themselves.
Dharma is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself dharma.
It is not by means of the emptiness of visual consciousness that visual consciousness is empty.
Visual consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is visual consciousness.
It is not by means of the emptiness of auditory consciousness that auditory consciousness is empty.
Auditory consciousness itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is auditory consciousness.
Auditory consciousness is not empty by virtue of the emptiness of olfactory consciousness.
Olfactory consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is olfactory consciousness.
Olfactory consciousness is not empty by virtue of the emptiness of olfactory consciousness.
Tongue-consciousness itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is tongue-consciousness.
It is not by means of the emptiness of body-consciousness that body-consciousness is empty.
Body-consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is body-consciousness.
Body-consciousness is not empty by virtue of the emptiness of mind-consciousness; rather, mind-consciousness is empty [by its own nature].
Mental consciousness itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is mental consciousness.
It is not by means of the emptiness of eye-contact that eye-contact is empty.
Eye-contact itself is emptiness,
and emptiness itself is eye-contact.
It is not by means of the emptiness of ear-contact that ear-contact is empty.
Auditory contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is auditory contact.
Auditory contact is not empty by virtue of the emptiness of auditory contact; rather, auditory contact is empty.

Nose-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is nose-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of tongue-contact that tongue-contact is empty; rather, tongue-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is tongue-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of body-contact that body-contact is empty; rather, body-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is body-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of mind-contact that mind-contact is empty; rather, mind-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is mind-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of eye-consciousness that eye-consciousness is empty; rather, eye-consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is eye-consciousness. It is not by means of the emptiness of ear-consciousness that ear-consciousness is empty; rather, ear-consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is ear-consciousness. It is not by means of the emptiness of nose-consciousness that nose-consciousness is empty; rather, nose-consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is nose-consciousness. It is not by means of the emptiness of tongue-consciousness that tongue-consciousness is empty; rather, tongue-consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is tongue-consciousness. It is not by means of the emptiness of body-consciousness that body-consciousness is empty; rather, body-consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is body-consciousness. It is not by means of the emptiness of mind-consciousness that mind-consciousness is empty; rather, mind-consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is mind-consciousness. It is not by means of the emptiness of eye-contact that eye-contact is empty; rather, eye-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is eye-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of ear-contact that ear-contact is empty; rather, ear-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is ear-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of nose-contact that nose-contact is empty; rather, nose-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is nose-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of tongue-contact that tongue-contact is empty; rather, tongue-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is tongue-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of body-contact that body-contact is empty; rather, body-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is body-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of mind-contact that mind-contact is empty; rather, mind-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is mind-contact. It is not by means of the emptiness of eye-element that eye-element is empty; rather, eye-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is eye-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of ear-element that ear-element is empty; rather, ear-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is ear-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of nose-element that nose-element is empty; rather, nose-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is nose-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of tongue-element that tongue-element is empty; rather, tongue-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is tongue-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of body-element that body-element is empty; rather, body-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is body-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of mind-element that mind-element is empty; rather, mind-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is mind-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of form-element that form-element is empty; rather, form-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of sound-element that sound-element is empty; rather, sound-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is sound-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of odor-element that odor-element is empty; rather, odor-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is odor-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of taste-element that taste-element is empty; rather, taste-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is taste-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of tangible-object-element that tangible-object-element is empty; rather, tangible-object-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is tangible-object-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of mental-object-element that mental-object-element is empty; rather, mental-object-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is mental-object-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of eye-consciousness-element that eye-consciousness-element is empty; rather, eye-consciousness-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is eye-consciousness-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of ear-consciousness-element that ear-consciousness-element is empty; rather, ear-consciousness-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is ear-consciousness-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of nose-consciousness-element that nose-consciousness-element is empty; rather, nose-consciousness-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is nose-consciousness-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of tongue-consciousness-element that tongue-consciousness-element is empty; rather, tongue-consciousness-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is tongue-consciousness-element. It is not by means of the emptiness of body-consciousness-element that body-consciousness-element is empty; rather, body-consciousness-element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is body-consciousness-element. Tongue-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is tongue-contact.

Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, who are the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
"Those by whom this teaching of the perfection of wisdom has been embraced, having heard it, do not tremble, do not fear, and do not fall into terror.
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, these are the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who [are his]..."
They teach the Dharma that "form is impermanent," and they do so by way of non-apprehension; furthermore,
they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
They teach the Dharma that "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent," and they do so by way of non-apprehension; furthermore,
they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas,
but rather [dedicate them] to omniscience in all its aspects.
Subhūti, these are the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who teach him the Dharma that "form is suffering," and that "form is non-self, peaceful, and secluded."
They teach the Dharma as "empty," "signless," and "wishless," and by way of non-apprehension,
they do not dedicate those roots of merit to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas,
but rather to omniscience in all its aspects.
They teach the Dharma that feeling, perception, mental formations, and whatever consciousness there may be are suffering;
they teach the Dharma that consciousness is selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless— and they do so by means of non-apprehension.

And those roots of merit he does not dedicate to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, these are the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—
The spiritual friends of that being are those who teach him the Dharma that "the eye is impermanent," and they do so by way of non-apprehension;
furthermore, he does not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
They teach the Dharma that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent, and they do so by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (sarvākārajñatā).
Subhūti, these are the good friends of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who teach him the Dharma that the eye is suffering.
They teach the Dharma that "the eye is non-self," "it is peaceful," "it is secluded," "it is empty," "it is signless," and "it is wishless," and they do so by means of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience in all its aspects.
They teach the Dharma that "the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are suffering."
They teach the Dharma that "the mind is non-self," "it is peaceful," "it is secluded," "it is empty," "it is signless," and "it is wishless," and they do so by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience in all its aspects.
Subhūti, these are the good friends of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are those who teach him the Dharma that eye-consciousness is impermanent, and they do so by way of non-apprehension;
and he does not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
They teach him the Dharma that ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are impermanent, and they do so by way of non-apprehension.
And those roots of goodness he does not dedicate to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Subhūti, these are the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who teach him the Dharma thus: "Eye-consciousness is suffering";
they teach the Dharma that eye-consciousness is "selfless," "peaceful," "secluded," "empty," "signless," and "wishless," and they do so by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yogena*).
And they do not dedicate those roots of goodness to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
They teach the Dharma that auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness are suffering;
they teach the Dharma that mental consciousness is selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless—and they do so by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*).
And those roots of goodness he does not dedicate to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Subhūti, these are the good friends of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the good friends of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva are those who teach him the Dharma that "eye-contact is impermanent," and that by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yogena*).
And they do not dedicate those roots of goodness to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
They teach the Dharma that "ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-consciousness-contact, and mind-contact are impermanent," and they do so by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
And they do not dedicate those roots of goodness to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience.
Subhūti, these are the good friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who teach him the Dharma thus: "Eye-contact is suffering";
they teach the Dharma that "eye-contact is non-self," "peaceful," "secluded," "empty," "signless," and "wishless," and this by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience in all its aspects.
They teach the Dharma that ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are suffering;
they teach the Dharma that mind-contact is non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless—and this by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience in all its aspects.
These, Subhūti, are the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are those who teach him the Dharma that the feeling conditioned by eye-contact is impermanent;
and they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but rather to omniscience alone.
They teach the Dharma that the feeling conditioned by ear-contact, the feeling conditioned by nose-contact, the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact,
the feeling conditioned by body-contact, and the feeling conditioned by mind-contact are impermanent,
and they do so through the application of non-apprehension.
And those roots of merit he does not dedicate to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Subhūti, these are the good friends of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who teach him the Dharma thus: "Feeling conditioned by eye-contact is suffering";

they teach the Dharma that feeling conditioned by eye-contact is "selfless," "peaceful," "secluded," "empty," "signless," and "wishless," and they do so through the application of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yogena*).
And they do not dedicate those roots of goodness to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).

They teach the Dharma that the feeling conditioned by ear-contact, the feeling conditioned by nose-contact, the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, the feeling conditioned by body-contact, and the feeling conditioned by mind-contact are suffering.
They teach the Dharma that the feeling conditioned by mental contact is selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless—and they do so through the application of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience in all its aspects.
Subhūti, these are the spiritual friends of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are those who teach him the Dharma that the applications of mindfulness are impermanent, and they do so by way of non-apprehension;
and he does not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience.
These, Subhūti, are the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who teach him the Dharma that the applications of mindfulness are suffering.
They teach the Dharma that the applications of mindfulness are selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless, and they do so by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience in all its aspects.
Subhūti, these are the spiritual friends of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the good friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are those who teach him the Dharma that the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are impermanent, and they do so by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
And he does not dedicate those roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) to the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
These, Subhūti, are the good friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who teach him the Dharma that these right efforts are suffering.
They teach the Dharma that the right efforts are selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless, and they do so by way of non-apprehension;
furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas,
but rather toward omniscience in all its aspects.
In this way, they teach that the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers,
the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path are impermanent— and they do so by means of non-apprehension. Furthermore,
they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather [dedicate them] to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).

In this way, they teach the Dharma that the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, and the superknowledges are impermanent, and they do so by means of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience in all its aspects.
In the same way, [they teach the Dharma regarding] the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They teach the Dharma that [all things] are impermanent; they teach the Dharma that they are suffering, and this by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, they do not dedicate those roots of virtue to the level of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but rather to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, these are the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by whom he is sustained in this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Having heard this teaching, he is not startled, not terrified, and does not fall into terror.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is unskilled in means regarding the perfection of wisdom?"
He will fall into the hands of evil friends;
whoever, having heard this exposition of the perfection of wisdom, shall be terrified, greatly terrified, and fall into a state of terror.
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates and apprehends the perfection of wisdom through mental engagements that are dissociated from all aspects of omniscience."
And thus, by means of the perfection of wisdom,
one conceives [of it];
one cultivates the perfection of meditation and perceives it.
And thus he conceives of himself through the perfection of meditation;
he cultivates the perfection of vigor and apprehends it,
and likewise he conceives of himself through the perfection of vigor.
He cultivates the perfection of patience and apprehends it;
likewise, he conceives of himself by means of that perfection of patience.
He cultivates the perfection of ethical discipline and apprehends it.
And likewise, he conceives [himself] by means of the perfection of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, with mental attentions dissociated from all-aspect omniscience, attends to form as "internally empty."
He attends to form as empty externally, up to attending to form as empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
He attends to feeling as empty internally;
he attends to feeling as empty externally, up to attending to feeling as empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
He attends to the thought that perception is empty of the internal;
he attends to the thought that perception is empty of the external; and so on, up to attending to the thought that perception is empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
He attends to the thought that volitional formations are empty of the internal.
He attends to the fact that formations are empty externally, up to attending to the fact that formations are empty of the nature of non-existence.
He attends to the fact that consciousness is empty internally;
he attends to the fact that consciousness is empty externally, up to attending to the fact that consciousness is empty of the nature of non-existence.
With mental engagements dissociated from all aspects of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), he perceives internal emptiness, external emptiness,

internal-and-external emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); yet, by means of those forms of emptiness, he conceives [of them] through the application of apprehension (*upalambha*).

He attends to the eye as "empty internally," he attends to it as "empty externally," and he attends to it as "empty both internally and externally," up to attending to it as "empty of the nature of non-existence.
And he perceives those emptinesses, and he conceives them by way of that perception.
In this way, he attends to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as empty of the internal;
he attends to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as empty of the external;
and so on, up to attending to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as empty of the nature of non-existence.

He attends to form as "empty internally," he attends to it as "empty externally," he attends to it as "empty both internally and externally," and so on, up to attending to it as "empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Yet he perceives those emptinesses and conceives of them by way of apprehension.
In this way, he attends to sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena as empty of the internal;
he attends to sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena as empty of the external;
and so on, until he attends to sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena as empty of the nature of non-existence.

He attends to eye-consciousness as "internally empty," he attends to it as "externally empty," he attends to it as "both internally and externally empty," and so on, up to attending to it as "empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Yet he perceives those emptinesses and conceives of them by way of apprehension.
In this way, one attends to ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness as empty of the internal;
one attends to ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness as empty of the external;
and so on, up to attending to ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness as empty of the nature of non-existence.

He attends to eye-contact as empty of the internal, he attends to it as empty of the external, he attends to it as empty of both the internal and the external, up to attending to it as empty of the nature of non-existence;
and he perceives those emptinesses, conceiving them by way of apprehension.
In this way, he attends to ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact as empty of the internal;
he attends to ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact as empty of the external;
and he attends to ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact as empty of the nature of non-existence.

He attends to the feeling conditioned by eye-contact as "empty internally," he attends to it as "empty externally," he attends to it as "empty both internally and externally," and so on, up to attending to it as "empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Yet he perceives those emptinesses and conceives of them by way of apprehension.

In this way, one attends to the feeling conditioned by ear-contact, the feeling conditioned by nose-contact, the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, the feeling conditioned by body-contact, and the feeling conditioned by mind-contact as being empty internally.
[One attends to] the feeling conditioned by ear-contact, the feeling conditioned by nose-contact, the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact...
He attends to the feeling conditioned by bodily contact as empty of the external;
likewise, he attends to the feeling conditioned by auditory contact, the feeling conditioned by olfactory contact, the feeling conditioned by gustatory contact,
the feeling conditioned by tactile contact, and the feeling conditioned by mental contact as empty of the nature of non-existence.
Thus he attends to it:

in this way, from ignorance up to old age and death, he attends to them as "internally empty"; he attends to old age and death as "externally empty," and so on, up to attending to old age and death as "empty of the nature of non-existence."

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he cultivates the applications of mindfulness with mental attentions that are dissociated from all-aspect omniscience;
yet he perceives those applications of mindfulness and, by way of apprehension, conceives himself in relation to them.

In the same way, [he perceives] the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the limbs of enlightenment, the paths, the analytical knowledges, the grounds of self-confidence, the superknowledges, the powers of a Tathāgata, and the Buddha-qualities.
And he perceives those Buddha-qualities and conceives himself by means of them through the application of perception.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] in the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing without skill in means, upon hearing this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, he becomes terrified, trembles, and falls into a state of fear.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva come to be taken hold of by a bad friend?"
"Because of being under the influence of evil friends, having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, they become afraid, terrified, and fall into a state of terror.
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, [the Buddha] distinguishes the bodhisattva mahāsattva from the perfection of wisdom."

He discriminates against the perfection of meditation, he discriminates against the perfection of vigor, he discriminates against the perfection of patience, he discriminates against the perfection of ethical discipline, and he discriminates against the perfection of generosity, saying, "One should not train in this;
this was not spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha; these are merely the works of poets."
These poetic works are not to be heard, nor taken up, nor mastered, nor retained, nor recited, nor attended to with the mind, nor even taught to another.
Subhūti, this should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s evil friend.
Furthermore, Subhūti, another evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who does not instruct him regarding the deeds of Māra.
He does not point out the faults of Māra; for indeed, Māra the Evil One approaches the bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a Buddha and speaks thus:
"Noble son, what is the use to you of cultivating the perfection of wisdom?"
"What is the use of your having cultivated the perfection of meditation? What is the use of your having cultivated the perfection of vigor?
What is the use of your having cultivated the perfection of patience?"
"What is the use of your cultivating the perfection of ethical discipline? What is the use of your cultivating the perfection of generosity?
Subhūti, this should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s evil friend."

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, in the guise of a Buddha, will teach, proclaim, analyze, clarify, and fully illuminate sūtras associated with the level of the Śrāvaka— namely, the Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Nidāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, Avadāna, and Upadeśa.
If one does not understand that these very kinds of deeds of Māra have been thus described,
Subhūti, this too should be known as a bad friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva and speak to him in this way:
"Son of good family, you do not possess any thought of awakening at all; nor are you irreversible, nor will you be able to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening."
If one does not understand these aforementioned deeds of Māra, Subhūti, this too should be known as a spiritual friend of evil for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a Buddha, will say: "The eye, noble son—"
O son, it is empty of self and of what belongs to self;

likewise, the ear is empty of self and of what belongs to self; the nose is empty of self and of what belongs to self; the tongue is empty of self and of what belongs to self; the body is empty of self and of what belongs to self;
the mind is empty of self and of what belongs to self.

And by which [realization] one understands that form is empty of self and of what belongs to self; sound is empty of self and of what belongs to self; odor is empty of self and of what belongs to self; taste is empty of self and of what belongs to self;
the tangible is empty of self and of what belongs to self; mental phenomena are empty of self and of what belongs to self; and eye-consciousness is empty of self.
Ear-consciousness is empty of self and of what belongs to self; nose-consciousness is empty of self and of what belongs to self;
tongue-consciousness is empty of self and of what belongs to self; body-consciousness is empty of self and of what belongs to self;
mind-consciousness is empty of self and of what belongs to self; and eye-contact is empty of self.
Ear-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self; nose-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self;

tongue-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self; body-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self; mind-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self; and feeling conditioned by eye-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self.

The sensation conditioned by ear-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self; the sensation conditioned by nose-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self; the sensation conditioned by tongue-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self;
the sensation conditioned by body-contact is empty of self and of what belongs to self.
And feeling conditioned by mind-contact is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self.
The perfection of generosity is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self; the perfection of ethical discipline is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self;

the perfection of patience is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self; the perfection of vigor is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self; the perfection of meditative concentration is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self.

The perfection of wisdom is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self; the applications of mindfulness are empty of a self and of what belongs to a self. Likewise, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the paths, and so on up to the unique qualities of a Buddha, are empty of a self and of what belongs to a self. Why is this?
"Subhūti, one who does not point out nor teach such deeds of Māra as these, even while intending to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening—
this should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s evil friend."
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a pratyekabuddha and say this:
"O son of good family, in the eastern direction there is emptiness; there, by the Buddhas, Blessed Ones, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas, there is no Buddha, no awakening, no bodhisattva, and no śrāvaka."

Thus, the ten directions all around are empty of Buddhas, Blessed Ones, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas; herein there is no Buddha, no awakening, no Bodhisattva, and no Śrāvaka. He who does not point out such deeds of Māra as these—[is one who does not teach].

Subhūti, these should be known as the evil friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a śramaṇa, diverts the bodhisattva mahāsattva from mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects and [instead] [engages them] with mental attentions associated with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
He will instruct and advise [others],
yet he will not point out such deeds of Māra as these.
Subhūti, this should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s evil friend.

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a preceptor or a teacher, will alienate the bodhisattva mahāsattva from the conduct of a bodhisattva; he will alienate him from mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects,
and will instead enjoin him to the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power.
He will apply them to the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the paths; he will apply them to emptiness, the signless, and the wishless.
Having realized these very kinds of dharmas, he will realize the stage of a śrāvaka.
"Practice! What will the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment do for you, if [this person] neither points out nor teaches such deeds of Māra?
Subhūti, this should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s evil friend."
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One, approaching a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a father or mother, will say this to him:
"Come, son of good family, apply yourself to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; apply yourself to the realization of the fruit of once-returning;
apply yourself to the realization of the fruit of non-returning; [apply yourself to] arhatship—"
"Apply yourself to the yoga for the direct realization of the fruits [of the śrāvaka path].

What is the use to you of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, for the sake of which you would have to wander through saṃsāra for incalculable and immeasurable eons with your hands..."
He will have to experience the cutting off of his hands and the cutting off of his feet—
he who does not point out or declare such deeds of Māra as these.
"Subhūti, this should be known as a bad friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a monk, will teach that form is impermanent by way of apprehension."
He will teach that form is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension;
he will teach that feeling is impermanent by way of apprehension.
He will teach that feeling is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by means of apprehension; he will teach that perception is permanent by means of apprehension;
he will teach that perception is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by means of apprehension.
He will teach that "formations are impermanent" by way of apprehension;
he will teach that "formations are suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by way of apprehension;
he will teach that "consciousness is impermanent" by way of apprehension.
He will teach that consciousness is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by means of apprehension;
he will teach that the eye is impermanent by means of apprehension;
he will teach that the eye is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by means of apprehension.
He will teach that "the ear is impermanent" by way of apprehension;
he will teach that "the ear is suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by way of apprehension;
he will teach that "the nose is impermanent" by way of apprehension.
He will teach, by way of apprehension, that the nose is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless; he will teach, by way of apprehension, that the tongue is impermanent;
he will teach, by way of apprehension, that the tongue is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless.
He will teach that "the body is impermanent" by way of apprehension;
he will teach that "the body is suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by way of apprehension;
he will teach that "the mind is impermanent" by way of apprehension.
He will teach that the mind is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by means of apprehension;
he will teach that form is impermanent by means of apprehension;
he will teach that form is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by means of apprehension.
He will teach that "sound is impermanent" by means of apprehension;
he will teach that "sound is suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by means of apprehension;
he will teach that "odor is impermanent" by means of apprehension.
He will teach that "odor is suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by means of apprehension;
he will teach that "taste is impermanent" by means of apprehension;
he will teach that "taste is suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by means of apprehension.
He will teach that "the tangible is impermanent" by way of apprehension;
he will teach that "the tangible is suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by way of apprehension;
he will teach that "phenomena are impermanent" by way of apprehension.
He will teach that "phenomena are suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by means of apprehension;
he will teach that "eye-consciousness is impermanent" by means of apprehension;
he will teach that "eye-consciousness is suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by means of apprehension.
He will teach that auditory consciousness is impermanent by way of apprehension;
he will teach that auditory consciousness is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension;
he will teach that olfactory consciousness is impermanent by way of apprehension.
He will teach that olfactory consciousness is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension;
he will teach that gustatory consciousness is impermanent by way of apprehension;
he will teach that gustatory consciousness is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension.
He will teach that body-consciousness is impermanent by way of apprehension;
he will teach that body-consciousness is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension.
He will teach that mental consciousness is impermanent by way of apprehension;
he will teach that mental consciousness is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension.
In this same manner, up to the applications of mindfulness—

He will teach that the [four] foundations of mindfulness are permanent by way of apprehension; he will teach that they are suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension.
Likewise, he will teach that the [four] right efforts are impermanent by way of apprehension.
He will teach that the applications of mindfulness are suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless, by way of apprehension.
He will teach that the bases of psychic power are impermanent, by way of apprehension.
He will teach that conditioned phenomena are suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless, by way of apprehension.
He will teach that the sense faculties are impermanent by way of apprehension;
he will teach that the applications of mindfulness are suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension;
he will teach that the powers are impermanent by way of apprehension.
He will teach that the applications of mindfulness are suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless, by way of apprehension.
He will teach that the factors of enlightenment are impermanent, by way of apprehension.
[He will teach] that the applications of mindfulness are suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless, by way of apprehension. The path—
He will teach that "it is permanent" or "it is impermanent" by way of apprehension;
he will teach that "the path is suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by way of apprehension;
and so on, until he teaches that "even the Buddha-qualities are impermanent" by way of apprehension.
He will teach that "formations are suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless" by way of apprehension.
Subhūti, one should know that whoever does not point out or declare such deeds of Māra as these is also a bad friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva; having recognized him, he should be avoided.
[Thus ends the second section on being accompanied by a spiritual friend.
[Thus have been explained the four factors conducive to penetration.]
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, it is said, 'Bodhisattva, Bodhisattva. [What is] a bodhisattva?"
"Lord, what is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'? The Blessed One replied, "Subhūti, the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' is that it has no referent."
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, neither arising nor existence nor non-existence is found or apprehended in awakening. Therefore, Subhūti, the referent "bodhisattva" is a non-referent.
[Thus is the essential nature of the lineage.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the track of a bird in the sky does not exist and is not perceived; even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not perceived.
A track for a dream does not exist and is not apprehended; even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
A track for an illusion does not exist and is not apprehended; even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
A track for a mirage does not exist and is not apprehended; even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
"Subhūti, just as no trace of an echo is found and is not apprehended, even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' is neither found nor apprehended.
Just as no trace of a reflection is found and is not apprehended, even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' is neither found nor apprehended.
Just as no trace of a mirrored image is found and is not apprehended, even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' is neither found nor apprehended."
The track of a city of the Gandharvas does not exist and is not apprehended; even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
The track of a magical creation does not exist and is not apprehended; even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
16101 [Thus ends the support for the stage of heat.]
"Subhūti, it is just as, for example, no trace of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) exists and is not apprehended;
even so, the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, no trace of suchness (tathatā) exists and is not apprehended."
In the same way, the referent of a "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Likewise, the referent of suchness, non-other-suchness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*),
the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), and truth (*satyatā*) does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
[Thus ends the support reaching the summit.
16104 {Just as, Subhūti, for example, no trace of the form of an illusory person exists and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva...}
For one practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the referent of the consciousness of an illusory person does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Just as, Subhūti, the track of a phantom person’s eye does not exist and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
The same applies to the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body.
Subhūti, just as, for example, no track of a phantom person's mind exists and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, no referent for the term "bodhisattva" exists and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, no footprint of an illusory person's form exists and is not apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
It is the same for sound, smell, taste, and the tangible.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, no trace of the phenomenon of an illusory person is found and cannot be apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, no referent for the term "bodhisattva" is found and cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, no trace of the visual consciousness of an illusory person is found and cannot be apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
It is the same for ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness.
Just as, Subhūti, for the mind-consciousness of an illusory person, no footing exists and none is apprehended.

In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended. [Thus ends the support for the stage of patience.
Just as, Subhūti, for an illusory person practicing in internal emptiness, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist...
It exists, yet it is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Just as, Subhūti, for an illusory person practicing in external emptiness, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
for one practicing the emptiness of the internal and external,
the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
this continues in detail until: "Just as, Subhūti, it is as follows."
