When a phantom person practices the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, the referent "Bodhisattva" is neither found nor perceived.
In the same way, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent "Bodhisattva" is neither found nor perceived.
Just as, Subhūti, with respect to a phantom—
For a person, [there is no attainment] regarding the perfections, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power,

the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the paths, the analytical knowledges, the grounds of self-confidence, the superknowledges, the powers of a Tathāgata, the Buddha-qualities, the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-bases.

In those instances of dependent origination, while practicing the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, and the superknowledges, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
[Thus ends the section on the basis for those who have reached the supreme dharmas.
16116 Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the referent of the term "form" does not exist and is not apprehended in a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended. 16117

In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, and mental formations [are non-existent]. Just as, for example, the referent of the term "consciousness" does not exist and is not apprehended in a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the referent of the term "eye" does not exist and is not apprehended in a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
It is the same for the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the referent of the term "Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha" does not exist and is not apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the referent of the term "form" (rūpa) does not exist and is not apprehended for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
likewise for sound, odor, taste, and the tangible.
Just as, Subhūti, the referent of the term "Dharma" does not exist and is not apprehended by a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Just as, Subhūti, for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the referent-object "visual consciousness" does not exist and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

In the same way, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, and tactile consciousness [are non-existent]. Just as, Subhūti, the referent of the term "mental consciousness" does not exist and is not apprehended in the case of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, while a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha practices from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, the referent-object of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Just as, Subhūti, for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who practices all the factors of enlightenment, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Just as, Subhūti,
in the unconditioned realm, the term for the conditioned realm does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the conditioned realm, the term "unconditioned realm" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
[Thus ends the basis for the path of vision.
"Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, the referent of the term 'non-arising' does not exist and is not apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist and is not apprehended."
"Just as, Subhūti, the referent-object (padārtha) of non-ceasing, non-conditioning, non-manifestation, non-apprehension, and non-defilement does not exist and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object 'bodhisattva' does not exist and is not apprehended."
"Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the entity of non-purification does not exist and is not apprehended;
in the very same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the entity of 'bodhisattva' does not exist and is not apprehended."
For what reason?
Subhūti, the referent for the arising of form does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, the referent for the arising of feeling does not exist and is not apprehended; Subhūti, the referent for the arising of perception does not exist and is not apprehended;
Subhūti, the referent for the arising of volitional formations does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, the referent of the arising of consciousness does not exist and is not apprehended.
Why is that?
Subhūti, the referent of the cessation, conditioned formation, manifestation, apprehension, and affliction of form does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, regarding feeling (*vedanā*), the category of phenomena consisting in cessation, volitional formation, manifestation, apprehension, and affliction does not exist and is not perceived.

Subhūti, regarding perception (*saṃjñā*), the category of phenomena consisting in cessation, volitional formation, manifestation, apprehension, and affliction does not exist and is not perceived. Subhūti, regarding mental formations (*saṃskāra*), the category of phenomena consisting in cessation, volitional formation, manifestation, apprehension, and affliction does not exist and is not perceived.
Subhūti, regarding consciousness, there exists no such thing as cessation, volitional formation, manifestation, apprehension, or affliction, nor is any such thing found.
Why is that?
Subhūti, regarding form, there exists no such thing as purification, nor is any such thing found.
Subhūti, the state of non-purification regarding feeling does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, the state of non-purification regarding perception does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, the state of non-purification regarding mental formations does not exist and is not apprehended.

Subhūti, for consciousness there exists no state of non-purification, nor is it apprehended. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, for the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, and dependent origination— whether taken individually or collectively— there exists no state of arising, nor is it apprehended.
To the extent that the term for purification does not exist and is not apprehended within the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination;
likewise [it does not exist] within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments.

The referent of the terms for the meditative attainments, the superknowledges, the analytical knowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a buddha does not exist and is not apprehended;
likewise, up to the point that the referent of the term for purification does not exist and is not apprehended.
In this very way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

"Just as, Subhūti, in the case of the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma), up to the point that the referent-object of affliction and purification does not exist and is not apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object of 'bodhisattva' does not exist and is not apprehended."
"Subhūti, it is just as, for example, because form (*rūpa*) is absolutely secluded, no basis for signs (*nimitta-pada*) exists and is not apprehended.
In the very same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist and is not apprehended.
Because feeling (*vedanā*) is absolutely secluded, no basis for signs exists and is not apprehended."
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
because perception is absolutely secluded, the basis for signs does not exist and is not apprehended.
In this very way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are absolutely secluded, the locus of signs (*nimitta-pada*) does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the very same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Because consciousness (*vijñāna*) is absolutely secluded, the locus of signs does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Just as, Subhūti, because the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination— whether taken individually or collectively— are absolutely secluded, the referent of the term "sign" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Just as, Subhūti, because the applications of mindfulness are absolutely pure, the referent of the term "sign" does not exist and is not apprehended; even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

In this way, because the right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path, powers, fearlessnesses, analytical knowledges, and unique qualities of a Buddha are absolutely pure, the term "sign" does not exist and is not apprehended. In just the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

"Subhūti, it is just as, for example, in the purification of the self, sentient being, living soul, nourisher, person, individual, human, man, agent, experiencer, knower, and seer, no such term exists and is not apprehended, because of the non-existence of a self, sentient being, living soul, nourisher, person, individual, human, man, agent, experiencer, knower, and seer. In the very same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object 'bodhisattva' does not exist and is not apprehended."
[Thus ends the basis for the path of cultivation.
"Subhūti, it is just as, for example, when the sun rises, no trace of its radiance exists and is not perceived;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist and is not perceived. [Thus it is said.]
[The support for the counteragent:
"Subhūti, it is just as, for example, when the conflagration at the end of an eon is occurring, no trace of any conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra) exists and none is perceived;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the referent-object (padārtha) of 'bodhisattva' does not exist and is not perceived."
16311 // [Thus ends the support for the abandonment of opposing factors.
16312 {Subhūti, it is just as if} in the morality of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, no basis for immorality exists and is not apprehended;
16313 even so, Subhūti, for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object of the term "Bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, in the meditative absorption of a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, no basis for distraction exists and is not apprehended;
in the wisdom of a Tathāgata, no basis for faulty wisdom exists and is not apprehended;
and in the liberation of a Tathāgata, no basis for non-liberation exists and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Just as, Subhūti, the referent of the term "liberation-knowledge-and-vision" of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
[Thus is the basis for the abandonment of conceptualizations regarding the counter-factors and their opposites.
16317 {Subhūti, it is just as if, for example,} no track of the light of the sun and moon exists and is not apprehended;

{in the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom,} the referent-object of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended. [Thus is the perfection of wisdom—]
[The Support of Compassion:
"Subhūti, it is just as, for example, no trace or basis for the light of the moon, the sun, the planets, the stars, or the light of precious jewels can be found or apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, no referential object (padārtha) for the term 'bodhisattva' exists or is apprehended."
[Thus, the locus of uncommon qualities.

16403 “Subhūti, it is just as, for example, with the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.”

Just as no trace of the radiance of the gods of the Brahma’s Retinue, the gods of Brahma’s Ministers, the gods of the Great Brahmas, and so on up to the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven is found or perceived, even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is neither found nor perceived.
[Thus concludes the basis for the sequence of the welfare of others.
"Subhūti, it is just as, for example, no footprint of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha can be found or apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' cannot be found or apprehended."
For what reason?

Because, Subhūti, that awakening by which the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is constituted, and that which is the referent of the term "bodhisattva"—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and one.
They have characteristics, that is to say, they are without characteristics.
For, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the non-attachment and the non-existence of all dharmas.
Subhūti, by means of both non-conceptualization and the state of non-conceptualization, all dharmas must be realized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Thus, there is no basis for knowledge that has arisen in the absence of appearances.]
[Thus has been explained the basis for acceptance.
Subhūti said:
"What, O Blessed One, are all phenomena?
How, O Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the non-existence of all phenomena?"
“Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva realize all dharmas?
The Blessed One replied:
"All phenomena" refers to those that are wholesome and unwholesome, determinate and indeterminate, mundane and supramundane, with outflows and without outflows, conditioned and unconditioned,
and common and uncommon.
These, Subhūti, are called all dharmas, in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in their lack of true existence.
These, Subhūti, are all dharmas that must be fully understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Thus ends the nature of the object.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the wholesome worldly dharmas?"
The Blessed One said:
"Worldly wholesome dharmas are said to be:
motherliness, fatherliness, the state of being a recluse, and the state of being devoted to Brahmā."
In the family, there is the honoring of elders;
the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline,
and the basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation.
Skillful means accompanied by service;
the ten paths of wholesome action;
and the nine worldly perceptions.

The perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a bloody corpse, the perception of a bluish-black corpse, the perception of a gnawed corpse, the perception of a scattered corpse, the perception of bones, and the perception of a burnt corpse; the four worldly dhyānas, the four immeasurables,
the four formless attainments, the five worldly superknowledges, and the ten worldly recollections.

Namely: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of relinquishment, recollection of the deities, recollection of inhalation and exhalation, recollection of death, recollection of disenchantment, and recollection directed toward the body.
[These are called the wholesome worldly dharmas.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the unwholesome worldly dharmas?"
The Blessed One said:

"Taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view—these are the ten unwholesome paths of action; as well as anger and enmity."
Concealment, spite, cruelty, envy, avarice, pride, and false pride.
[These are called the worldly unwholesome dharmas.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, what are the indeterminate phenomena?
The Blessed One replied: “Indeterminate bodily action; indeterminate vocal action.”
The mental action is indeterminate;
the four great elements are indeterminate;
the five sense faculties are indeterminate.
The six sense bases are indeterminate;
the formless aggregates, elements, and sense bases are indeterminate.
The [mental] formations are indeterminate.
"All these are called indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*).
Subhūti asked:
"Blessed One, what are the mundane wholesome phenomena (*laukika-kuśala-dharma*)?"
The Blessed One said:
"The five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the ten paths of wholesome action,
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five superknowledges, and whatever others..."
The mundane dharmas.
[These are called mundane wholesome dharmas.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the supramundane wholesome dharmas?"
The Blessed One said:
"The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path— emptiness..."

The gateways to liberation: the gateway of signlessness, the gateway of wishlessness, and the gateway of emptiness; the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known;
and concentration accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought.
Concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought;
knowledge, liberation, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and appropriate mental attention.
What are the eight liberations? Which eight? One who possesses form sees forms; this is the first liberation.
Being internally percipient of the formless, one sees external forms.
This is the second liberation. One becomes resolved upon emptiness;
this is the third liberation. In every respect...

By transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] "space is infinite," one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space;
this is the fourth [dhyāna].

The fifth liberation: by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation. Completely...
By transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, [thinking] "there is nothing whatsoever," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness;
this is the sixth liberation.
By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, neither...
Having attained and dwelt in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
this is the seventh liberation. Completely [transcending] that, neither...
By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling;
this is the eighth liberation.
These are the eight liberations.

The nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling: [1] secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*),
and born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is characterized by rapture and bliss.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by rapture and bliss.

Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in happiness, possessing equanimity and mindfulness"— thus he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna.
And through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain,
and with the previous disappearance of joy and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Through the complete transcending of perceptions of form, through the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance,
and through non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space.
Through the complete transcending of the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," [he dwells having attained] the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Having attained and dwelt in that,
by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness.
Having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, he dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he [dwells having attained] the cessation of perception and feeling.
He dwells having attained the cessation [of perception and feeling].
These are the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling.
Internal emptiness, external emptiness...
Internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the four analytical knowledges.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
[These are called the supramundane wholesome dharmas.
Subhūti said:
"Which, Blessed One, are the tainted phenomena?
The Blessed One said: "The five aggregates."

The twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four meditative absorptions (dhyānas), the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments— these are called the phenomena with outflows (sāsrava-dharmas).
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the untainted phenomena?
The Blessed One replied: "The four..."

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
[These are called the untainted phenomena.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, what are conditioned phenomena?
The Blessed One replied: “The realm of desire, the realm of form, the formless realm, and whatever other phenomena are included within the three realms.”
The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening and so forth are the dharmas; these are called conditioned dharmas.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the unconditioned phenomena? The Blessed One said: "Those which..."
In phenomena, neither arising, nor cessation, nor alteration is perceived; rather, there is the exhaustion of passion, the exhaustion of hatred, and the exhaustion of delusion.
It is suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness, the nature of phenomena, the realm of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the fixed order of phenomena, and the limit of reality.
[These are called the unconditioned phenomena.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, which are the common phenomena?"
The Blessed One said: "The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges— these are called the common dharmas."
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the uncommon dharmas?
The Blessed One replied:

The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the three gateways to liberation, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
[These are called the uncommon dharmas.

In that regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form any attachment toward dharmas that are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), and all dharmas should be realized through the yoga of non-duality.
"Based on both conceptualization and non-conceptualization. [Thus has been stated the objective support for practice.
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, as for what is called 'a bodhisattva mahāsattva,' for what reason, O Blessed One, is a bodhisattva called a 'mahāsattva'?
The Blessed One replied:
In this regard, Subhūti, he will bring about the leadership of a great mass of beings, a great multitude of beings;
for that reason, Subhūti, [he is called] a bodhisattva.
...is called a *mahāsattva*.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is that mass of great beings (*mahāsattva-rāśi*), that collection of great beings (*mahāsattva-nikāya*), of which [it is said]?"
The bodhisattva mahāsattva will bring about preeminence.
The Blessed One said:
"O mass of mahāsattvas—"

"Subhūti, what is called the 'great assembly of beings' refers to those beginning from the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the eighth stage (*aṣṭamakabhūmi*), the stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*), the non-returner (*anāgāmī*), the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha, up to the stage of irreversibility (*avinivartanīya*), starting from the first production of the thought of awakening."
This is a great mass of beings, a great multitude of beings;
herein, the bodhisattva mahāsattva shall exercise leadership.
In this regard, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, [a state] like a diamond must be cultivated.
"Having generated the thought [of awakening], one should bring about leadership for the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the diamond-like generation of the thought?"
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates such a thought:
'I shall don the armor in an immeasurable saṃsāra.'"
Having donned the armor, one must be one who does not abandon any sentient being;
one must generate a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
"I must lead all sentient beings to final nirvana by means of the three vehicles.
Yet, even after I have led all sentient beings to final nirvana, not a single sentient being has been led to final nirvana.
Why is that?"
I must realize the non-arising of all phenomena;
with a mind of omniscience that is unadulterated, I must practice the six perfections.
I must train in the perfection of the penetration of all phenomena that is omnipresent;
I must bring about the realization of all phenomena as a single unity.
One must awaken [to this]: "I must train in all dharmas for the sake of the realization and penetration of the accomplishment of the perfections;
I must train in all dharmas for the sake of the realization and penetration of the accomplishment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."

I must train in all dharmas for the sake of realizing and penetrating the immeasurable meditations, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, and the gnosis; I must train in all dharmas for the sake of realizing and penetrating the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
Subhūti, this is the diamond-like production of the thought of awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
established in which, the bodhisattva mahāsattva shall exercise leadership over the great mass of beings and the great multitude of beings.
And that is by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates this thought:
"As many beings as there are who experience painful sensations—whether they be in the hells, among the animals, or in the realm of Yama..."
"I would experience that painful sensation.
In that situation, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate the following thought:

For the sake of even a single sentient being, I would endure the suffering of the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, until that sentient being has attained final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
By this means, for the sake of all sentient beings,
may I experience that suffering of the hells and so forth until those beings have attained final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder; thereafter,
having planted the roots of merit for myself, for ten million eons—
"Subhūti, by means of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions [of eons], may I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

This, Subhūti, is the diamond-like production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; established in this, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will bring about leadership over a great mass of beings, a great multitude of beings."
And that is by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates this thought:
"May I experience all those painful feelings experienced by as many beings as there are—whether they be in the hells, or among the animals, or in the world of Yama."
In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate the following thought:

"For the sake of even a single sentient being, I would endure the suffering of the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of aeons, until all those sentient beings have entered the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"May they enter final nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should possess a noble mind, by which mind he should bring about preeminence for all sentient beings.
In this regard, the noble-mindedness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists in this: from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, he does not give rise to a mind of passion,
nor does he give rise to a mind of hatred.
He does not give rise to a mind of delusion;
he does not give rise to a mind of malice;
he does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka.

He does not give rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha. Subhūti, this is the noble-mindedness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by which he will bring about the state of preeminence for all sentient beings, and by that—
He does not conceive with the mind.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must possess an unshakable mind. In this regard, the unshakability of the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is this: that he does not even attend to mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti, this is the unshakable state of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should possess a mind of welfare and happiness toward all sentient beings.
In that regard, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s state of mind of welfare and happiness: that which is the protection of all sentient beings.
Not abandoning all sentient beings, and not being conceited because of that—
Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s state of mind characterized by the desire for their welfare and happiness.
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom will bring about the state of preeminence for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should possess passion for the Dharma.
One who has attained a love for the Dharma through that [practice] should be devoted to the application of yoga.
In this regard, what is the Dharma? It is the non-differentiation of all phenomena.
This is called the Dharma.
In that regard, what is delight in the Dharma? That which is joy in the Dharma is called delight in the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the state of delighting in the Dharma? That which is the cultivation and frequent practice of that Dharma is called the state of delighting in the Dharma.
Delight in the Dharma.

For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should bring about leadership over the great mass of beings and the great multitude of beings by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having stood in internal emptiness, having stood in external emptiness,
having stood in internal-and-external emptiness, and so on up to having stood in the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, [should cultivate] the great...

"By means of the yoga of non-apprehension, one should bring about preeminence over the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having stood in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, in the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities..."
Abiding in the qualities of a Buddha, one should bring about leadership for the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, abiding in the diamond-like samādhi, [should do so] as far as the unattached liberation like space and the stainless [state].

Abiding in this samādhi, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom must bring about the leadership of the great mass of beings, the great collection of beings. Subhūti,
it is by abiding in these dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom brings about the leadership of the great mass of beings, the great collection of beings.
He should cause [this] to be done;
therefore he is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Thus ends the greatness of the mind that is supreme among all sentient beings.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"It occurs to me as well, Blessed One, for what reason the term 'bodhisattva mahāsattva' is used.
The Blessed One said:
"May it be clear to you, Śāriputra, in what sense a bodhisattva mahāsattva [is so called].
Śāriputra said:

O Blessed One, [it is so] because of the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a creature, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer; because of the view of annihilationism, the view of eternalism, the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of the aggregates, the view of the elements, the view of the sense-bases, the view of dependent origination, and the view of the factors of enlightenment.

The vision of phenomena, the vision of the powers and fearlessnesses, the vision of the unique qualities of a Buddha, the vision of maturing sentient beings, the vision of purifying the buddha-field, the vision of a bodhisattva, the vision of a Buddha, and the vision of turning the wheel of Dharma—
of all these, [he has no perception].
He teaches the Dharma for the abandonment of views by means of non-apprehension;
for that reason, he is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Subhūti said: "For what reason, venerable Śāriputra, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva have a view of form, a view of feeling, a view of perception, a view of mental formations, and a view of consciousness?"
Śāriputra said:
"In this regard, venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom may be unskilled in means."
Having perceived form,
he generates a view by means of that perception;
in this way, [he proceeds] in detail with respect to the aggregates, elements, and bases, both individually and collectively.
Having perceived dependent origination, up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair,
he produces a view by means of apprehension.
Likewise [regarding] the applications of mindfulness, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path—
Having apprehended the perfections, the superknowledges, the syllables, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments,

one produces a view by means of apprehension. Likewise, having apprehended the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one produces a view by means of apprehension.
[Thus ends the greatness of abandonment.
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, it occurs to me as well."
"For what reason is a bodhisattva called a 'mahāsattva'?
The Blessed One said,
"Let your inspiration flow, Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, even with respect to that bodhicitta— the mind of equality that is peerless, the mind that is not shared by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas— one is unattached even to that mind."
For what reason?
Because that mind of omniscience is untainted and not included within the three realms; since he is unattached even to that mind, he is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
...it enters into calculation.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, what is the 'unequaled' [state] of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The mind is an uncommon mind, not shared with any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti said:
"In this regard, venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought..."
Relying on this, one does not perceive the arising or the cessation of any dharma whatsoever;
nor decrease or increase, nor coming or going, nor defilement or purification— wherein [these do not exist].
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, there is neither affliction nor purification, neither going nor coming, neither decrease nor increase, neither arising nor cessation;
and that is neither the mind of a śrāvaka nor the mind of a pratyekabuddha.
Śāriputra, this mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is an unequaled mind, a mind that is not shared with any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, when you say that one is unattached even to the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— "
"Indeed, venerable Subhūti, is form also unattached, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature?
Is feeling also unattached, perception also unattached, mental formations also unattached, and is consciousness also unattached?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is, venerable Śāriputra: form is unattached; feeling is unattached; perception is unattached; mental formations are unattached; consciousness is unattached.
Even so, up to the individual and collective aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination, even up to old age and death, all are unattached."

In this way, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments are also unattached; likewise, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and even the unique qualities of a Buddha— the unique qualities of a Buddha are also unattached.
17321 Śāriputra said: "Even though the Venerable Subhūti has said this,
as for that omniscience— "
"The mind is untainted and unconditioned.
"But, Venerable Subhūti, is not even the mind of ordinary foolish people untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature? Is it not so for all [minds]?"
The minds of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and samyaksaṃbuddhas as well are untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of their being empty by nature.
Subhūti said: "It is so, Venerable Śāriputra."
Śāriputra said:
"Subhūti, form also, Subhūti, is without outflows and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Feeling also, Subhūti, is without outflows and unconditioned, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature."
Subhūti, perception also is untainted and unattached, by virtue of its natural emptiness.
Subhūti, volitional formations also are untainted and unattached, by virtue of their natural emptiness.
Consciousness also, O Venerable One...
Subhūti, [it is] because they are untainted and unconditioned by virtue of their intrinsic emptiness.
Is it not the case, Venerable Subhūti, that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,

the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the three gateways to liberation, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are untainted and unconditioned?
Based on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, Subhūti said:
"It is just so, Venerable Śāriputra, as you say; even for ordinary worldlings..."
The mind is untainted and unconditioned, by virtue of its intrinsic emptiness;
this applies even to the minds of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and perfectly enlightened buddhas, which are likewise untainted and unconditioned by virtue of their intrinsic emptiness.

Up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the three gateways to liberation, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— these are untainted, unconditioned, and empty by nature. Śāriputra said:
Furthermore, as for what the Venerable Subhūti said: "Because it is non-mind, one is unattached even to that mind."

"Venerable Subhūti, is it not the case that even in form, form is unattached; even in feeling, feeling is unattached; even in perception, perception is unattached; even in formations, formations are unattached; and even in consciousness, consciousness is unattached? Subhūti replied:
"It is so, venerable Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"But, venerable Subhūti, are there not even applications of mindfulness within the applications of mindfulness?"
They are unattached. Likewise, even among the right efforts, the right efforts are unattached;

even among the bases of psychic power, the bases of psychic power are unattached; even among the faculties, the faculties are unattached; even among the powers, the powers are unattached; even among the factors of enlightenment, the factors of enlightenment are unattached; even among the paths, the paths are unattached; and even among the grounds of self-confidence...

The grounds of self-confidence are unattached; even the analytical knowledges are unattached; even the perfections are unattached; even the powers of a Tathāgata are unattached; even the unique qualities of a Buddha are unattached.

Subhūti said: "It is so, Venerable Śāriputra, just as you say. Venerable Śāriputra, form is unattached even in form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise unattached even in consciousness."

In this way, even when taken individually or collectively, the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), sense-bases (āyatanas), truths (satyas), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), the immeasurables (apramāṇas), the meditative absorptions (dhyānas), and the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpattis) [are likewise empty].

The perfections, the superknowledges, the factors of enlightenment, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, and the unique qualities of a Buddha are unattached.
It is thus, venerable one.

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, he does not conceive pride nor does he become attached even to that bodhicitta— the mind equal to the unequaled, the mind not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas— by way of apprehending all phenomena.
[Thus ends the greatness of realization.]
[Thus ends the summary of practice.
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said:
"O Blessed One, it occurs to me as well for what reason a bodhisattva..."
...is called a *mahāsattva*.
The Blessed One said:
"May you find delight in this, Pūrṇa."
Pūrṇa said: "O Blessed One, that being is one clad in the great armor; O Blessed One, that being has set out in the Great Vehicle;
that being has mounted the Great Vehicle; O Blessed One, for that reason he is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Pūrṇa, to what extent is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to be 'armed with the great armor'?"

Pūrṇa said: "In this case, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing for the sake of awakening does not give gifts while abiding in the perfection of generosity for the sake of limited beings; rather, [he gives] for the sake of all sentient beings."
Having established himself through what has been done in the perfection of generosity, he gives gifts;
likewise in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
One who practices for the sake of awakening does not, while abiding in the perfection of wisdom, cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of limited beings;
rather, one cultivates the perfection of wisdom for the sake of all beings.
He cultivates [this]. A bodhisattva mahāsattva clad in the great armor does not don that armor by means of a limitation of sentient beings, thinking:

"I shall lead this many sentient beings to final nirvāṇa, and I shall not lead this many sentient beings to final nirvāṇa"; or "I shall establish this many sentient beings in awakening, and I shall not establish this many sentient beings in awakening."
Furthermore, he indeed dons the armor for the sake of all sentient beings, and he thinks:

"I myself shall fulfill the perfection of generosity and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of generosity. He also thinks: "I myself shall fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of ethical discipline."
And thus it occurs to him: "I myself shall fulfill the perfection of patience and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of patience.
And thus it occurs to him: "I myself shall fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of meditative concentration.
And thus it occurs to him: "I myself shall fulfill the perfection of wisdom and I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom."
"In this way, I myself shall cultivate the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments, and I shall establish all sentient beings in them."

"Until I myself abide in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and until I establish all sentient beings in those as well."
To this extent, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor. [Thus ends the nature of practice.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom while giving gifts...
The dedication of giving, having made it common to all sentient beings through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment—
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s [practice] in the perfection of wisdom.
While practicing and giving gifts, there is the armor of the perfection of generosity.
Furthermore,
Śāriputra, while a bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing and giving gifts within the perfection of wisdom—
The avoidance of the mental orientations of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects—
this is the armor of the perfection of ethical discipline for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore,

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift, his forbearance, encouragement, and investigation regarding those [gifts] are associated with the mental attentions directed toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This is the armor of the perfection of patience for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom gives a gift with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, that which is the absence of slackening in vigor— this is [the armor of the perfection of vigor].
Having made the roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

This is the armor of the perfection of vigor for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom gives a gift...

That state of one-pointedness of mind, through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which allows no opportunity for the minds of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*,

he dedicates that root of virtue— having made it common to all sentient beings— for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*). This is the armor of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) for one who gives a gift.
Furthermore,

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift with mental applications associated with the knowledge of all aspects, the perception of an illusion is established, yet there is no giver at all.

He perceives neither a recipient nor a gift. This, O Venerable Śāriputra, is the armor of the perfection of wisdom for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, when that bodhisattva mahāsattva [engages] in all modes—
With a mind associated with the knowledge of suchness, he does not take those six perfections as signs and does not apprehend them.

In this way, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom becomes one who is armored with the great armor. [Thus ends the first hexad on the armor of the perfection of generosity.]

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline gives a gift with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he dedicates it to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment after having made it common to all sentient beings, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. This, Subhūti, is [the perfection of ethical discipline] of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline,
the perfection of generosity consists in the lack of longing for the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects.

How much more so, Śāriputra, is this the perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline who has already transcended the level of ordinary beings?

Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, that which constitutes their forbearance through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects— this is [the perfection of patience].
Thorough investigation is the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline...

Through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all modes, whatever lack of slackening and lack of despondency in vigor there may be, he makes that root of virtue common to all sentient beings and dedicates it to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline,

he does not allow any opportunity for the arising of thoughts associated with the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. By virtue of that root of merit, his mind attains one-pointedness through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, [thereby abandoning] the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Without making room for [any other thought], he dedicates that root of merit to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment after having made it common to all sentient beings.

This is the perfection of meditation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline. Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, [that which consists of] mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects—}
The perception of "created by illusion" arises;
yet he does not conceive of that morality, nor does he apprehend it.
This, venerable one, is...
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline, this is indeed the perfection of wisdom.
For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline encompasses all six perfections. By means of that—
He is reckoned as one who is "armed with the great armor."
[Thus ends the second hexad on the armor of the perfection of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience gives a gift, he does so with [thoughts] associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

With mental attentions not associated with the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, he dedicates that root of merit— having made it common to all sentient beings— for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the perfection of generosity of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of patience.
In this way, for one practicing the perfection of patience, there are the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience [cultivates] the collection of all Buddha-dharmas.

He applies himself to the training in giving and to the maturation of all sentient beings through wisdom; by means of mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not by means of mental attentions associated with the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, he makes that root of virtue common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This, Śāriputra, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience.
Thus indeed, Śāriputra.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience, he encompasses the six perfections; by that, he comes to be reckoned as one who is "armed with the great armor."
[Thus ends the third section, the sixfold armor of the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor gives gifts with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not with mental attentions associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas.
By means of mental applications, he makes that root of virtue common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor.
Thus, for one practicing the perfection of vigor, there are the perfection of ethical discipline,
the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] the perfection of vigor...
Practicing in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* and cultivating the perfection of wisdom, one establishes the perception that all phenomena are like illusions.

With mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects— and not with mental attentions associated with the level of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas— one takes that root of merit and, having made it common to all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor.
For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor embraces all six perfections;
therefore, he is reckoned as one who is "armed with the great armor."
17814 // [Thus ends the fourth section, the sixfold armor of the perfection of vigor.
17815 Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditation gives a gift,
he does so with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not with mental attentions associated with the disciples or pratyekabuddhas.
By means of mental attentions, he makes that root of virtue common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
In this way, for one practicing the perfection of meditation,
there are the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva—
Practicing the perfection of meditative concentration and cultivating the perfection of wisdom, he establishes the perception that all phenomena are like illusions;
through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas.
By means of mental attentions, he makes that root of merit common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration encompasses all six perfections.
Therefore, he is reckoned as "one who is armored with the great armor."
[Thus ends the fifth hexad of the armor of the perfection of meditation.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom [regards] the threefold circle—

He gives a completely pure gift with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, not with mental orientations associated with the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; and having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This is the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom.

Likewise, for one practicing in the perfection of wisdom, there are the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom [practices] the perfection of wisdom.

He cultivates [this]. For him, there arises the perception that all the perfections, all phenomena, and all mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā)—and not those associated with the Disciples or Pratyekabuddhas—are like an illusion, a dream, a reflection, an echo, a mirror-image, or a magical creation. And that root of virtue...
Having made it common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. It is in this way, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [dedicates].

While practicing the perfection of wisdom, he fulfills the perfection of wisdom. Venerable Śāriputra, it is because when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he is one who has donned the great armor. And thus...
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by abiding in each individual perfection, fulfills all six perfections.
[Thus ends the sixth section on the sixfold armor of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), yet he does not relish those absorptions, nor is he captivated by them, nor is he reborn under their influence.
In this way, he enters the immeasurables and the formless attainments, yet he does not relish them, is not captivated by them,
and is not reborn under their influence.
This should be understood as the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva that has entered into skill in means.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells with the vision of seclusion within the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and dwells with the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); yet he does not personally realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is the armor of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya-sannāha*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Thus, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who has donned the great armor; therefore, he is called a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva.
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva, Venerable Śāriputra, who has thus donned the great armor—"
In the ten directions, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, utter inspired exclamations, proclaim their praise, and,
while extolling the name of that bodhisattva mahāsattva, cause his voice to be heard and raise their cry.
In that expanse of world-systems, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the great armor,
brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the buddha-field.
[Thus concludes the summary of the sixfold armor. 17923 [Thus has been explained the practice of armor.
18001 Śāriputra said:
"To what extent, venerable Pūrṇa, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the Mahāyāna and mounted upon the Mahāyāna?
Pūrṇa replied:

In this case, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of generosity, dwells having attained the first dhyāna, which is secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, and which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with joy and happiness.
In this way, he enters and dwells in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; likewise,
he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

These are the meditations and formless attainments of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. When the bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, enters into and emerges from these meditations and these formless attainments by way of the aspects, marks, and signs of space, and having made those roots of merit common to all sentient beings, [dedicates them] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—
He inclines [the mind]. This is the perfection of giving of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In the same way, it is spoken of regarding the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,

he enters the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and enters the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). When the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in these meditative concentrations and these formless attainments, [he does so without apprehending them].
Entering and emerging from these meditative absorptions and formless attainments, he attends to the forms, signs, and marks of space.
While practicing the perfection of wisdom, he [dedicates] those roots of virtue and all other [roots of virtue] toward omniscience.

By means of mental attentions associated with [the three doors of liberation], having made [these roots of merit] common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

For in this way, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, armored with the great armor, brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the buddha-field. [Thus ends the section on emerging from and entering the meditative absorptions and formless attainments.]

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the mental application associated with the knowledge of all aspects, gives rise to the thought, "I shall teach the Dharma to all sentient beings in order to destroy their afflictions," this is the [perfection of wisdom] of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The perfection of generosity:
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of those very mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, enters the first dhyāna,
teaches it, and abides therein, he allows no opportunity for other thoughts to arise.
This is the unattached perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva associated with the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) through mental attentions (*manasikāra*) associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it occurs to him:
"I shall teach the Dharma for the sake of the exhaustion of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings," and so on, until those mental attentions [are fully realized].
Forbearance, delighting, thorough investigation, awakening, and profound reflection—
this is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having made all roots of virtue common to all sentient beings through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, dedicates them toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment and does not slacken his vigor;
this is the [practice] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The perfection of vigor:
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, enters into the meditative absorptions and formless attainments, yet does not perceive them.
This is the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), [cultivates] the factors of the first dhyāna, as well as the factors of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
He contemplates by way of the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, the aspect of selflessness, the aspect of peace, the aspect of emptiness,
the aspect of signlessness, and the aspect of wishlessness, yet he does not apprehend them;
this is the [great]— of the bodhisattva.
The perfection of wisdom of a being—
this, venerable Śāriputra, is the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Thus concludes the undertaking of the six perfections.]
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is that which cultivates all aspects of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.
He cultivates in every aspect the meditative concentrations on the gateways to liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
and the powers and fearlessnesses in every aspect.
He cultivates the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
This, venerable Śāriputra, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Thus concludes the setting forth of the noble path.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness— vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rival, unobstructed, harmless, all-pervading, and well-spoken— [dwells].

In this world, which is supreme as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and terminates at the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), he dwells having pervaded and attained the entire world in one direction, and likewise pervading and attaining it throughout the ten directions.
Thus is compassion—

With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, accompanied by compassion, accompanied by sympathetic joy, and accompanied by equanimity— a mind that is vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rival, unobstructed, harmless, all-pervading, well-spoken, reaching the limit of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and extending as far as the realm of space—
he dwells having suffused one direction with this entire world, and likewise having suffused the ten directions.

He dwells [in this way]. These are called the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and directs it [with the thought]: "I must protect all sentient beings."

He enters the meditative absorption of compassion (*karuṇā-samādhi*) and directs a state of compassionate concern toward sentient beings; he enters the meditative absorption of sympathetic joy (*muditā-samādhi*) and directs the thought, "I alone shall gladden them," toward sentient beings.
And he enters into the meditative absorption of equanimity and directs the destruction of the outflows toward all sentient beings;
this is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the immeasurables.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into and emerges from the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and their aspects, signs, and marks, yet does not dedicate [the merit] to the level of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but rather [dedicates it] solely to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is the ungrasped perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the immeasurables.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells unmixed with those meditative concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments, he does not [fall] into these two levels:
either the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.

For this bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the immeasurables, it is precisely omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) that he endures and finds pleasing— this is his ungraspable perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

When the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells with a sense of duty never abandoned, through mental states associated with omniscience, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome dharmas and for the attainment of wholesome dharmas.
This is the unattached perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*):
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into these meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), as well as these immeasurables and formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Nor does he take rebirth through the power of the meditative absorptions, the immeasurables, or the formless attainments;
nor does he relish them, nor is he captivated by them.

This is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), which is ungraspable; when the bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), enters into those meditative concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

He enters and emerges from them, and he contemplates them through the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, the aspect of non-self, the aspect of peace, the aspect of emptiness, the aspect of signlessness, and the aspect of wishlessness; yet he does not enter the fixed course of the Śrāvakas or the fixed course of the Pratyekabuddhas.
This is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables, which is free from grasping;
this, venerable one, is the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Thus ends the section on the practice of the immeasurables. Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that which is the internal emptiness—
The knowledge regarding that [internal emptiness] is not by way of apprehension;
the knowledge regarding external emptiness is not by way of apprehension;
the knowledge regarding internal and external emptiness is not by way of apprehension.
That knowledge regarding emptiness which does not function through the mode of apprehension—
this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
That mind which does not train in any phenomena is a concentrated mind; that is knowledge.
This too is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that in which the cognition "it is permanent" does not arise, nor does the cognition "it is impermanent";
neither "it is suffering" nor "it is not suffering" arises.

Knowledge proceeds neither as "it is pleasure" nor as "it is not pleasure," neither as "it is self" nor as "it is not-self," neither as "it is peaceful" nor as "it is not peaceful," neither as "it is empty" nor as "it is not empty," neither as "it has signs" nor as "it is signless," and neither as "it is with aspiration" nor as "it is without aspiration. Subhūti, this too is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is that knowledge which does not operate with respect to the past,
and knowledge which does not operate with respect to the future.
Knowledge does not operate in the present time,
nor does its knowledge operate in the three times;
and that is by way of non-apprehension.
This too, Śāriputra, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
that knowledge does not operate in the realm of desire, knowledge does not operate in the realm of form, and knowledge does not operate in the formless realm.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, his knowledge does not operate within the realms of desire, form, or formlessness, and that occurs by way of non-apprehension.
This, too, Śāriputra, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Moreover, Śāriputra, this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
There is no cognition that operates with respect to mundane or supramundane phenomena;

it does not operate with respect to tainted phenomena nor untainted phenomena, nor with respect to conditioned or unconditioned phenomena; and there is no cognition of his that operates with respect to mundane or supramundane, tainted or untainted, conditioned or unconditioned phenomena.
And that is by way of non-apprehension.
This, venerable Śāriputra, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

{a mere name, namely} consciousness, by virtue of the non-apprehensibility of consciousness.

18414 By virtue of their non-apprehensibility: thus, the aggregates, the elements, the sense-bases, dependent origination, the perfections, the superknowledges,
