Furthermore, Śāriputra, from the first production of the thought of awakening until reaching awakening, in the interval between these, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because of the perfection of the superknowledges, matures sentient beings and travels from buddhafield to buddhafield.
In every buddha-field, he honors, reveres, respects, and worships the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
according to the appropriate methods of worship and honor for each respective Buddha.
And from those Blessed Buddhas he hears the Dharma, namely this very Mahāyāna.

Having mounted that Bodhisattva vehicle, he travels from buddha-field to buddha-field, purifies the buddha-fields, and brings sentient beings to maturity; yet, in him, no perception of a buddha-field arises, nor does a perception of sentient beings arise.
Abiding on the stage of non-duality, he intentionally assumes such a physical form as would enable him to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings;
he is never thereafter separated from that Great Vehicle.
Until he attains the knowledge of all modes.
[Thus concludes the section on the application of the superknowledges.

Having attained the knowledge of all aspects, he turns the wheel of Dharma, which cannot be turned by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor by the world of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or asuras.

When he has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, shall speak his praise, proclaim his voice,

Having mounted [the Great Vehicle], they have attained all-aspect omniscience; having attained all-aspect omniscience, they have set the wheel of Dharma in motion.
In this same way, in the southern direction—in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak his praise, raise their voices, and proclaim his glory:

What do you think, Subhūti? Would he, by this [act], [generate much merit]?
"Suppose a magician or a magician’s apprentice were to give something to someone. Subhūti said, 'No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:"

In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having manifested an array as vast as that of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), gives food to those seeking food, and so on, up to giving various human requisites to any sentient being whatsoever— up to any other such things.
Having given human requisites, they become [merit].
For what reason?
Subhūti, this is the nature of things (dharmatā).
Based on the illusory nature of all phenomena,
Subhūti, it is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor."
[Thus concludes the equipment of generosity.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the intentional assumption of rebirth in the perfection of ethical discipline, is born into a family of universal monarchs.
Abiding there, he establishes sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action;

in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five [powers].
He establishes them in the seven powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the thirty-seven dharmas conducive to enlightenment;
he establishes them even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
And those beings are never deprived of that teaching of the Dharma until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
it is just as if, for example:

Subhūti, suppose a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create a great multitude of people at a major crossroads and establish them in the ten paths of wholesome action; indeed, he might establish them as far as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, encourages beings toward patience,

Abiding in patience, he encourages, settles, and establishes others in it.

Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, dons this armor: "Even if all sentient beings were to strike me with blows of sticks, clods of earth, fists, or weapons..."
"In that situation, I must not give rise to even a single thought of agitation, and I must establish all sentient beings in such patience as this.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create, at a great crossroads, a vast multitude of people by means of an illusion.

Even if all of them were to strike that illusionist with sticks, clods of earth, fists, or weapons, he would not give rise to even a single thought of agitation toward them; rather, he would establish those created beings in such patience as this.
Having established that many beings in patience, not a single being has been established;
even so, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, those many beings [are established] in patience.
Having established [them], not a single sentient being has been established in patience.
Why is that?
Subhūti, it is because this is the very nature of phenomena, based on the illusory nature of all things.
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "one who has donned the great armor."

[Thus ends the equipment of patience. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of vigor, encourages, introduces, and establishes all sentient beings in the perfection of vigor.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled magician or a magician’s apprentice were to conjure up a great multitude of people at a crossroads and [then] attend to them with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects.

yet, even by establishing that many beings in physical and mental vigor, not a single being would have been established in physical and mental vigor.

For it is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor."
[Thus is the equipment of vigor.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, encourages all sentient beings, leads them into, and establishes them in the perfection of meditative concentration.

And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, cause all sentient beings to take up, enter, and become established in the perfection of meditative concentration?
Here, Subhūti, the bodhisattva...
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the equality of all phenomena, does not perceive the distraction or non-distraction of any phenomenon whatsoever.

It is, for example, as follows:

Subhūti, suppose a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to conjure a great multitude of people at a major crossroads and establish that multitude in the perfection of meditative concentration;
by establishing that many beings in the perfection of meditative concentration, not even a single being would have been established in the perfection of meditative concentration.

In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes all sentient beings in the perfection of meditative concentration, not a single sentient being has been established in the perfection of meditative concentration. Why is that?
This is the true nature of phenomena, Subhūti, based on the illusory nature of phenomena.
For it is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor."
[Thus is the equipment of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, encourages, introduces, and establishes all sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, encourage, introduce, and establish all sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom?
It is because, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom...
He does not apprehend the further shore or the near shore of any dharma whatsoever;
in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes established in the perfection of wisdom.
In that very same way, he also encourages, establishes, and settles all sentient beings therein.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist were to create a great multitude of people at a major crossroads.

If one were to establish a multitude of people in the perfection of wisdom, by having established that many beings in the perfection of wisdom, not even a single being would have been established in the perfection of wisdom. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has established all beings in the perfection of wisdom, no being at all has been established in the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Subhūti, this is the true nature of phenomena, based upon the illusory nature of phenomena.
It is for this reason, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "one who has donned the great armor."
[Thus is the equipment of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the great armor, [regarding] as many beings as there are in world-systems in the eastern direction equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā— just as he himself has practiced the perfection of giving—

he encourages, introduces, and establishes them in the perfection of meditation; he encourages, introduces, and establishes them in the perfection of wisdom; and he teaches the Dharma, namely, this very teaching associated with the six perfections.

likewise in the perfection of ethical discipline.

he encourages, introduces, and establishes them in the perfection of vigor;
he encourages, introduces, and establishes them in the perfection of meditation; he encourages, introduces, and establishes them in the perfection of wisdom, and he teaches the Dharma.

and having heard it, they shall never again be separated from the six perfections until they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

likewise, he encourages them, leads them, and establishes them in the perfection of ethical discipline and the perfection of patience.

he encourages, introduces, and establishes them in the perfection of meditation; he encourages, introduces, and establishes them in the perfection of wisdom; and he teaches the Dharma, namely, this very teaching associated with the six perfections.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice, having conjured a great multitude of people at a crossroads, were to encourage, establish, and settle them in the six perfections. That...
"What do you think, Subhūti? Has any sentient being at all been incited, established, or settled by that illusionist or the illusionist’s apprentice in the six perfections?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In just this way, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
Even if one were to establish that many beings in the six perfections, not a single being would have been established in the six perfections.
Why is that?
This is the true nature of phenomena, Subhūti, based on the illusory nature of phenomena.
For it is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the great armor, [proceeds] with that which is associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Dwelling with such a mind, he allows no opportunity for other mental states to arise,
thinking: "I must establish this many sentient beings in the perfection of generosity."
"So many beings must I establish in the perfection of ethical discipline;
so many beings must I establish in the perfection of patience;
so many beings must I establish in the perfection of vigor."
"I must establish this many sentient beings in the perfection of meditative concentration;
I must establish this many sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom;
I must establish this many sentient beings in the factors conducive to enlightenment."
"I must establish this many sentient beings in the unique qualities of a Buddha;
I must establish this many sentient beings in the fruit of stream-entry;
I must establish this many sentient beings in the fruit of once-returning."
"I must establish this many beings in the fruit of non-returning; I must establish this many beings in arhatship;
I must establish this many beings in the state of a pratyekabuddha."
"‘I must establish this many sentient beings in omniscience’—
but rather, indeed, incalculable and immeasurable sentient beings must be established in the six perfections."

In this way, incalculable and immeasurable sentient beings should be established in the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; [and they should be established] in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and in arhatship.
They should be established in Buddhahood.
[Thus ends the equipment for calm abiding.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create a great multitude of people at a crossroads of four great roads and establish them in the six perfections, up to and including establishing them in the knowledge of omniscience endowed with the excellence of all aspects; even so, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva—
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has established those countless and immeasurable beings in the six perfections,
and even up to establishing them in the knowledge of omniscience endowed with the excellence of all aspects, not a single being has actually been established in the six perfections.
For what reason?
Subhūti, this is the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā), namely, that they are based upon this illusory nature of phenomena.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken,
this bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one who is, in fact, armored with a non-armament, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics."

For what reason? Because, Blessed One, form is empty of form; feeling is empty of feeling; perception is empty of perception; volitional formations are empty of volitional formations; consciousness is empty of consciousness;
and the eye is empty of the eye.
The ear is empty of the ear; the nose is empty of the nose; the tongue is empty of the tongue;
the body is empty of the body; the mind is empty of the mind. Form is empty of form; sound is empty of sound;
odor is empty of odor; taste is empty of taste; the tangible is empty of the tangible; phenomena are empty of phenomena.
Eye-consciousness is empty of eye-consciousness; ear-consciousness is empty of ear-consciousness;
nose-consciousness is empty of nose-consciousness; tongue-consciousness is empty of tongue-consciousness;
body-consciousness is empty of body-consciousness; mind-consciousness is empty of mind-consciousness; and the feeling conditioned by visual contact is [empty].

The feeling conditioned by eye-contact is empty of the feeling conditioned by eye-contact; the feeling conditioned by ear-contact is empty of the feeling conditioned by ear-contact; the feeling conditioned by nose-contact is empty of the feeling conditioned by nose-contact;
the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact is empty of the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact; the feeling conditioned by body-contact [is empty of the feeling conditioned by body-contact].
The feeling conditioned by bodily contact is empty of the feeling conditioned by mental contact; the feeling conditioned by mental contact is empty of the feeling conditioned by mental contact.

The perfection of generosity is empty of the perfection of generosity; the perfection of ethical discipline is empty of the perfection of ethical discipline; the perfection of patience is empty of the perfection of patience; the perfection of vigor is empty of the perfection of vigor; the perfection of meditative concentration is empty of the perfection of meditative concentration.

The perfection of wisdom is empty; the perfection of wisdom is empty of the perfection of wisdom. Internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness; external emptiness is empty of external emptiness; internal-and-external emptiness is empty of internal-and-external emptiness; the emptiness of emptiness is empty of the emptiness of emptiness; great emptiness is empty of great emptiness; the emptiness of the ultimate is empty of the emptiness of the ultimate.
Conditioned emptiness is empty of ultimate emptiness;
unconditioned emptiness is empty of conditioned emptiness; absolute emptiness is empty of absolute emptiness;
emptiness without beginning or end is empty of emptiness without beginning or end; emptiness of non-dispersal is empty of emptiness of non-dispersal; and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is [empty].

The emptiness of all phenomena is empty by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the emptiness of all phenomena is empty by virtue of the emptiness of all phenomena; the emptiness of specific characteristics is empty by virtue of the emptiness of specific characteristics; the emptiness of non-apprehension is empty by virtue of the emptiness of non-apprehension; the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is empty by virtue of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
the emptiness of existence is empty by virtue of the emptiness of existence; the emptiness of non-existence is empty by virtue of the emptiness of non-existence.
Emptiness of intrinsic nature is empty of emptiness of intrinsic nature; emptiness of other-nature is empty of emptiness of other-nature;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are empty of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;

the ten powers of a Tathāgata are empty of the ten powers of a Tathāgata; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
It is empty. Blessed One, even the armor of the Great Vehicle is empty of the armor of the Great Vehicle.
Blessed One, by this method, it is so.
"A bodhisattva should be known as one who is armored with armor.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti; it is just as you say."
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, all-aspect omniscience is uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned.
"Those beings, too, are uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned, for whose sake the bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned this great armor. Subhūti said:
For what reason, Blessed One, is omniscience uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned?
Those sentient beings for whose sake the bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor are likewise uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, based on the non-apprehension of an agent, omniscience in all its aspects is uncreated, unmodified, and unconditioned."
Those beings, too, are uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned.
Why is that? Because, Subhūti, form is not [created].
It does not act, it does not transform, it does not form. Feeling does not act, it does not transform, it does not form. Perception does not act, it does not transform, it does not form.

Formations do not act, do not transform, and do not perform formative activity; consciousness does not act, does not transform, and does not perform formative activity; the eye does not act, does not transform, and does not perform formative activity.
The ear does not act, does not transform, and does not construct; the nose does not act, does not transform, and does not construct;
the tongue does not act, does not transform, and does not construct.
The body does not act, does not transform, and does not construct;
the mind does not act, does not transform, and does not construct;
form does not act, does not transform, and does not construct.
Sound does not act, does not transform, and does not construct; odor does not act, does not transform, and does not construct;
taste does not act, does not transform, and does not construct.

Tangibility does not act, does not transform, and does not construct; phenomena do not act, do not transform, and do not construct; visual consciousness does not act, does not transform, and does not construct.
It does not produce ear-consciousness, nor does it transform it, nor does it construct it; it does not produce nose-consciousness, nor does it transform it, nor does it construct it;
it does not produce tongue-consciousness, nor does it transform it, nor does it construct it.
It does not produce, transform, or construct body-consciousness;
it does not produce, transform, or construct mind-consciousness;
it does not produce, transform, or construct the feeling conditioned by eye-contact.
He does not produce, does not transform, and does not construct the feeling conditioned by ear-contact;
he does not produce, does not transform, and does not construct the feeling conditioned by nose-contact;
he does not produce, does not transform, and does not construct the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact.
He does not produce, does not transform, and does not construct the feeling conditioned by bodily contact;
he does not produce, does not transform, and does not construct the feeling conditioned by mental contact.
For what reason?
Because, in this way, all these do not exist and are not apprehended in an ultimate sense.

Subhūti, the self does not act, does not transform, and does not construct. Likewise, the sentient being, the life-principle, the nourisher, the person, the individual, the human, the youth, the agent, the experiencer, the knower, and the seer do not act, do not transform, and do not construct.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, they do not exist and are not apprehended in an ultimate sense;
a dream neither acts, nor transforms, nor performs any conditioned formation.
An echo, a reflection, a mirrored image, a mirage, and a magical creation do not act, do not transform, and do not perform formative activity.
Why is that?
For they do not exist and are not apprehended in an ultimate sense:
namely, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness,
the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, and the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end.

Non-dispersal emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence,
the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of other-nature do not act, do not transform, and do not construct.
For what reason? Because,
in an ultimate sense, they do not exist and are not apprehended—
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the four [grounds of self-confidence].
Subhūti, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
suchness, the realm of space, the limit of reality, the inconceivable realm, awakening, and the knowledge of all aspects do not act, do not transform, and do not perform any formative activity.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, they do not exist and are not apprehended in an ultimate sense. By this method, all—
The knowledge of all aspects is uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned;
for the sake of these, the bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have donned the great armor.
[Thus ends the equipment of insight.
Subhūti said:
As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken:
O Blessed One, form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, O Blessed One, are neither bound nor liberated.
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, you say that form is neither bound nor liberated.
Venerable Subhūti, you say that feeling is neither bound nor liberated."
"Venerable Subhūti, do you say that perception is neither bound nor liberated?
Venerable Subhūti, do you say that volitional formations are neither bound nor liberated?
Venerable Subhūti, do you say that consciousness is neither bound nor liberated?"
Subhūti said: "It is so, Venerable Pūrṇa.
Pūrṇa asked: "Venerable Subhūti, what is that form which is neither bound nor liberated?"
"Venerable Subhūti, what is that feeling which is neither bound nor liberated?
Venerable Subhūti, what is that perception which is neither bound nor liberated? Venerable Subhūti, what are those formations which are neither bound nor liberated?"
"Venerable Subhūti, what is that consciousness which is neither bound nor liberated?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Pūrṇa, that form which is like a dream is neither bound nor liberated. [And so it is with] those which...
Feelings are like a dream; they are neither bound nor liberated.
That perception which is like a dream is neither bound nor liberated.
Those formations which are like dreams are unbound and unliberated.

That consciousness which is like a dream is neither bound nor liberated. Likewise, O Venerable Pūrṇa, that form which is like an echo, like an illusion, like a mirage, like a reflection, and like a magical creation, is neither bound nor liberated.
Those feelings which are like a magical creation are neither bound nor liberated;
that perception which is like a magical creation is neither bound nor liberated.
These conditioned phenomena, which are like magical illusions, are neither bound nor liberated.
This consciousness, which is like a magical illusion, is neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, O Venerable Pūrṇa, future and present form is neither bound nor liberated.
Present feeling is neither bound nor liberated;
present perception is neither bound nor liberated.
Present conditioned phenomena are neither bound nor liberated;
present consciousness is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason?

Because of its non-existence, Venerable Pūrṇa, form is neither bound nor liberated. Likewise, because of the non-existence of feeling, perception, and mental formations, Venerable Pūrṇa, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Because of the non-existence of consciousness, Venerable Pūrṇa, that consciousness is thus neither bound nor liberated;
likewise, because it is secluded, peaceful, empty, and signless—

Because it is signless, wishless, unconditioned, and unarisen, O Venerable Pūrṇa, form— whether wholesome or unwholesome, afflicted or free from affliction, blameworthy or blameless, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, defiled or purified— is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason?
Because form is non-existent, in this way that form is neither bound nor liberated; so too are feeling and perception.
Formations, O Venerable Pūrṇa, are neither bound nor liberated; consciousness is defiled and purified, yet it is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that?
Because consciousness is non-existent, in this way that consciousness is neither bound nor liberated.
All dharmas, too, Venerable Pūrṇa, are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that?
Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Thus, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Furthermore, O Venerable Pūrṇa, even internal emptiness is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason? Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
External emptiness, too, O Venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason?
Because it is non-existent, it is neither bound nor liberated.
Thus, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even internal and external emptiness, venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.

Because they are non-existent, they are neither bound nor liberated.

Even absolute emptiness, venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that?
Because it does not exist, it is neither bound nor liberated.
Thus, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even beginningless and endless emptiness, venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that?
Because they are non-existent, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even the emptiness of non-dispersal, O Venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason? Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even the emptiness of intrinsic nature, venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason?
Because it is non-existent, it is neither bound nor liberated.
Thus, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even the emptiness of all phenomena, O Venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.

Because they are non-existent, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even the emptiness of specific characteristics, O Venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason? Because they are non-existent, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even non-apprehension emptiness, venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason?
Because of its non-existence, it is neither bound nor liberated.
Thus, because they are secluded and so forth, up to being unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that?
Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even the emptiness of entities, O Venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason? Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even non-existence emptiness, venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that?
Because of its non-existence, it is neither bound nor liberated.
Thus, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Furthermore, O Venerable Pūrṇa, even the emptiness of intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that?
Because they are non-existent, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even the emptiness of other-being (*parabhāva-śūnyatā*), O Venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
For what reason? Because they are non-existent, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Venerable Pūrṇa, even the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that?
Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated."
Thus, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
In this same way, it applies to the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The knowledge of all aspects,
suchness, the realm of phenomena, and the limit of reality—
thus it is, O Venerable One.
Pūrṇa, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither bound nor liberated.
In this same way, the six perfections are also neither bound nor liberated;
indeed, even the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is neither bound nor liberated.
Even those sentient beings whom he will lead to final nirvana are neither bound nor liberated;
even those buddha-fields which he will purify are likewise neither bound nor liberated.
The Buddhas, Blessed Ones, whom he will attend upon are also unbound and unliberated;
the Dharma which he will hear is also unbound and unliberated.

He shall never be separated from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; he is neither bound nor liberated. He shall not be separated from the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); he is neither bound nor liberated.
He shall not be separated from the five eyes; he is neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, he will not be separated from other meditative concentrations; unbound and unliberated,
he will produce the knowledge of the aspects of the path which is itself unbound and unliberated.
He will realize omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) which is neither bound nor liberated; he will turn the wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) which is neither bound nor liberated;
and he will lead beings—who are neither bound nor liberated—into final nirvana by means of the three vehicles (triyāna).
He will awaken, being neither bound nor liberated.
For in this way, venerable Pūrṇa, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being neither bound nor liberated by the six perfections, will fully awaken to all dharmas on account of their non-existence.
Thus, from seclusion up to non-arising;
for in this way, O Venerable Pūrṇa, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither bound nor liberated.
The great armor of the Mahāyāna is to be understood.
[Thus ends the equipment for the path of union.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the [great]..."
[This is] the Mahāyāna of a being.
Blessed One, how is it to be understood that a bodhisattva mahāsattva has set out in the Mahāyāna?
From where will that vehicle set out?
Where will that vehicle abide? Or who will set out by means of that vehicle?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, as to what you have asked— 'What is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?'—
it is the six perfections."
Subhūti, what is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva? It consists of the six perfections. What are the six? The perfection of giving... [and so forth].
The perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of generosity?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects; that is to say, he gives internal and external things, and those..."
Having made these common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and he encourages others therein by way of non-apprehension.
This, Subhūti, is [the perfection of wisdom] of a bodhisattva.
[This is] the perfection of giving of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the perfection of ethical discipline of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, personally undertakes and abides in the ten paths of wholesome action,
and encourages others to undertake the ten paths of wholesome action by means of the yoga of non-apprehension."
"This, Subhūti, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s ungrasped perfection of ethical discipline.
Subhūti said,
"Lord, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of patience?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, personally attains patience and also encourages others toward patience.
This, Subhūti, is the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells with the burden not laid down in the five perfections, through mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and he encourages others to take up those five perfections by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
This, Subhūti, is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the perfection of meditative concentration of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One said:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with mind-sets associated with the knowledge of all aspects, personally enters the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*). Yet, he is not reborn under their influence, and he encourages others to enter the meditative concentrations by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-yoga*).
This, Subhūti, is the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects, does not adhere to any phenomena and contemplates the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
And while contemplating their intrinsic nature, he encourages sentient beings [toward that same contemplation] by means of non-apprehension.
This, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. This...
Subhūti, this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

[Thus is the equipment of skill in means. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
emptiness of the conditioned, ultimate emptiness, emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, emptiness of non-dispersal, emptiness of intrinsic nature,

emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of non-apprehension, emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence, emptiness of existence, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of self-nature, and emptiness of other-nature.
In that regard, what is internal emptiness?
Internal phenomena are said to be the eye,
the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind.
In that regard, the eye is empty of the eye, based on its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
Because this is its very nature.
The ear is empty of the ear, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its very nature:
the nose is empty of the nose, by reason of its being neither immutable nor indestructible.
Why is that?
This is its very nature:
the tongue is empty of a tongue, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its very nature:
the body is empty of the body, by reason of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its very nature:
the mind is empty of mind, by virtue of being neither immutable nor indestructible.
Why is that?
This is its very nature.
This is called internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is external emptiness (*bahirdhāśūnyatā*)?
Those external phenomena, namely: forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmas*).
Among these, form is empty of form, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that?
For what reason? This is its very nature:
sound is empty of sound, by virtue of being neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason?
This is its very nature:
odor is empty of odor, by virtue of being neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason?
This is its very nature:
flavor is empty of flavor, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason?
This is its very nature:
the tangible is empty of the tangible, by virtue of being neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason?
This is its very nature:
a phenomenon is empty of a phenomenon, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its very nature; this is called external emptiness (*bahirdhāśūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā*)?
The six internal sense bases and the six external sense bases—
this is called internal-and-external emptiness.
In this regard, what are internal phenomena that are empty of external phenomena? The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are internal;
they are empty of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, [this being so] by virtue of their being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason?
This is their intrinsic nature.
In this regard, which external phenomena are empty of internal phenomena? They are:
form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
The dharmas are empty of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, because they are neither immutable nor indestructible.
Why is that? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
This is called internal-and-external emptiness.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of emptiness?
That which is the emptiness of all phenomena is empty by means of that very emptiness, because it is neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of emptiness.
In that regard, what is the great emptiness?
The eastern direction is empty of the eastern direction; likewise the southern and the western directions.

The northern, the northeastern, the southeastern, the southwestern, the northwestern, the downward, and the upward direction are empty of the upward direction, by virtue of being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason?
This is its very nature.
This is called the great emptiness.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of the ultimate?
The ultimate is said to be nirvāṇa.
And that [nirvana] is empty of nirvana,
by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason?
This is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of the conditioned?
The conditioned refers to the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
In that regard, the desire realm is empty of the desire realm, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason? Because this is its very nature.
The realm of form is empty of the realm of form, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible.
Why is that? Because this is its very nature.
The formless realm is empty of the formless realm, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason?
This is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of the conditioned.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of the unconditioned?
The unconditioned is said to be that which has neither arising nor cessation.
There is neither stability nor alteration;
this is called the unconditioned.
The unconditioned is empty of the unconditioned.
19616 {On account of its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason? Because this is its very nature.}
This is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)?
That for which no end is perceived is the ultimate; it is empty by way of the ultimate.
19618 {Based on its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
Why is that? Because this is its very nature.}
This is called absolute emptiness (*atyantaśūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end (*anavarāgraśūnyatā*)?
It is that for which neither a beginning nor an end is perceived.
Its nature is that of being without middle. And for that which neither beginning, nor middle, nor end is perceived, there is neither coming nor going.
Even the beginning, middle, and end are empty of beginning, middle, and end, by virtue of being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason? Because this is their very nature.
This is called the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.
In this regard, what is the emptiness of non-dispersal?
It is that dharma for which there is no dispersal whatsoever.
"Scattering" (avakāra) means dispersing, casting away, or relinquishing.
Non-scattering is empty of non-scattering, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason? Because this is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of non-dispersal.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of intrinsic nature?
That which is the nature of all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned—is not made by Śrāvakas, nor made by Pratyekabuddhas, nor made by Tathāgatas, Arhats, or Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
it is not unmade. Nature is empty of nature, because it is neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason? Because this is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
19706. In that regard, what is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*)?
All phenomena are said to be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
19707 the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible.
Dharmas are: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact;

as well as the feeling conditioned by eye-contact, the feeling conditioned by ear-contact, the feeling conditioned by nose-contact, the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, and the feeling conditioned by body-contact.
19708 Feeling conditioned by mental contact, conditioned phenomena, and unconditioned phenomena—
these are called all phenomena.
19709 In that regard, phenomena are empty of phenomena, because they are neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason? Because this is their very nature.
This is called the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*).
19710 {In this context, what is} the emptiness of specific characteristics? Form has the characteristic of being affected;
feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; perception—
Perception has the characteristic of grasping;
formations have the characteristic of volitional construction;
consciousness has the characteristic of discernment.

In detail, that which is the characteristic and non-characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and that which is the characteristic and non-characteristic of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)— all these phenomena are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), because they are neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
Why is that?
This is their intrinsic nature;
this is called the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of non-apprehension?
Those phenomena which are past, future, and present are not apprehended.
For what reason?
The future is not perceived in the past,
nor are the past [dharmas] perceived in the future; the past and the future are not perceived in the present.
Nor are those [dharmas] past or future;
these are non-apprehensible because they are pure from the beginning, by virtue of being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason?
This is their intrinsic nature;
this is called the emptiness of non-apprehension (anupalambha-śūnyatā).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā)?
The nature of a phenomenon that brings about conjunction does not exist, because it is dependently originated.
Conjunction is empty of conjunction, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason? Because this is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*).
19.7.1 What is the emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*)? Existence is said to be the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*).
And that existence is [empty] by means of existence.
It is empty, by virtue of being neither immutable nor indestructible.
For what reason?
This is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*)?
Non-existence is said to be the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
And that unconditioned is empty of the unconditioned, by reason of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its intrinsic nature;
this is called the emptiness of non-existence.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of intrinsic nature?

For intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the fundamental state (*prakṛti*), which is non-perversion; its emptiness [is established] by means of that very state, on account of its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
Why is that?
This is its very nature;
it was not created by means of knowledge or vision.
For what reason?
This is its nature;
this is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of other-nature (*parabhāva-śūnyatā*)?

Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), this fixed order of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), and this limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) remain established; the emptiness of that [nature] by means of itself is [the emptiness of non-alteration],
because it is neither immutable nor subject to destruction.
For what reason?
This is its very nature;
it was not created by another.
For what reason?
This is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of other-nature (*parabhāva-śūnyatā*).
This, Subhūti, is called the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

the concentration called "the accomplishment of non-attachment to mental aspects";
the concentration called "the non-admission of mental aspects."
The concentration named "Scattering the Entire Ground of Existence Without Exception," the concentration named "Entry into Conventional Sounds," and the concentration named "Possessing Sound."
The concentration named "Liberation from Syllables," the concentration named "Possessing Radiance," and the concentration named "Blazing Torch."
The samādhi called "protective complete drying up";
the samādhi called "untroubled patience";
the samādhi called "entry into all modes."
The concentration named "Rejoicing in Neither All Pleasure nor Pain," the concentration named "Inexhaustible Form," and the concentration named "Retention-Intelligence."
The samādhi called "Comprehension of Rightness and Wrongness," the samādhi called "Anger, Hostility, and Counter-Hostility," and the samādhi called "Stainless Radiance."
The concentration named Śāravatī; the concentration named Paripūrṇavimalacandraprabha;
the concentration named Vidyutprabha.
The concentration named Great Array;
the concentration named Illuminator of All Worlds;
the concentration named Essence of Concentration.

The concentration called "liberated from the methods of misconduct and good conduct," the concentration called "following and converging with all," and the concentration called "unrestricted as the wind."
The samādhi called "Certainty Established in Suchness," the samādhi called "Thoroughly Crushing the Defilement of Body," and the samādhi called "Destroying the Defilement of Speech."
The samādhi called "resembling space";
the samādhi called "unattached liberation like space and free from all defilement."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Heroic Progression" (śūraṅgama)?
That concentration by which one experiences the range of all concentrations is called the concentration named "Heroic Progression.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Jewel Seal" (ratnamudra)?
That concentration by which all concentrations are sealed is called the concentration named "Jewel Seal. In that regard, what is the concentration named "Lion’s Play"?
19815 Samādhi: Abiding in which samādhi, one sports with all samādhis;
this is called the samādhi named "The Lion’s Sport" (siṃhavikrīḍita). 19816
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Beautiful Moon" (*sucandra*)?
When one abides in this samādhi, one illuminates all samādhis;
this is called the samādhi named "Beautiful Moon."
In this regard, what is the samādhi called *candradhvajaketu*?
It is that which upholds the banner of all samādhis.
This is called the samādhi named *candradhvajaketu*.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Surpassing All Phenomena"?
It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one rises above all samādhis.
This is called the samādhi named "Exalted Above All Phenomena.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Beholding the Crown of the Head"?
Abiding in which concentration one beholds the summit of all concentrations—
this is called the concentration named "Beholding the Summit" (*avalokitamūrdha*).
In that regard, what is the "Determined by the Realm of Phenomena" (*dharmadhātuniyata*)?

[This is] the concentration named [Dharmadhātuniyata]. Abiding in which concentration, one attains certainty regarding the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). This is called the concentration named "Certainty in the Realm of Phenomena."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "the banner of certainty" (*niyatadhvajaketu*)?
It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one maintains the banner of certainty of all samādhis.
This is called the samādhi named "the banner of certainty."
In this regard, what is the concentration called "diamond-like"?
It is that concentration, abiding in which,
one cannot be broken by any concentrations.
This is called the concentration named "diamond-like" (*vajropama*).
In that regard, what is the concentration named "seal of entry into phenomena" (*dharmapraveśamudrā*)?
It is that concentration, by abiding in which [one enters] all concentrations.
One enters the 19,095 mudrās;
this is called the samādhi named "Seal of Entry into the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Well-Established King of Samādhis"?
Abiding in which concentration, one becomes firmly established through the supreme establishment of all concentrations;
this is called the concentration named "Supremely Established King of Concentrations."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Emission of Rays"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one emits the rays of all concentrations.
This is called the concentration named "Emission of Rays.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Array of Powers"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, [one masters] all concentrations.
It maintains the array of powers;
this is called the concentration named "Array of Powers.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Exalted"?
That concentration, abiding in which all concentrations arise—
this is called the concentration named "Samudgata" (The Emergent).
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Entry into the Exposition of Etymologies"?
Abiding in which concentration one enters into the explanation of the etymologies of all concentrations—
this is called the concentration named "Entry into the Explanation of Etymologies.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Thorough Entry into Designations"?
Abiding in which concentration, one enters into the designations and names of all concentrations;
this is called the concentration named "Entry into Designations."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Surveying the Directions"?
It is that concentration by remaining in which all directions of all concentrations are surveyed.
This is called the samādhi named "Surveying the Directions.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Seal of Sustenance"?
It is the seal of all samādhis when one abides in this samādhi.
19913 He sustains;
this is called the samādhi named "the seal of sustaining.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named "unfailing"?
Abiding in which concentration all concentrations are not forgotten—
this is called the concentration named "Unforgotten.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Seal of the Ocean, the Convergence of All Dharmas"?
Abiding in which concentration, all concentrations emerge as a collection and a convergence;
this is called the concentration named "The Ocean Seal of the Convergence of All Dharmas."
In this regard, what is the concentration called "pervading space"?
It is that concentration in which, having remained, one pervades all concentrations by means of the pervasion of space.
This is called the concentration named "pervading space."
In this regard, what is the samādhi called "Possessing Radiance" (*tejovatī*)?
It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one causes all samādhis to blaze with brilliance and wisdom.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "Possessing Radiance.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Immeasurable Illumination"?
Abiding in which samādhi, immeasurable radiance shines forth; therefore, it is called the samādhi named "Immeasurable Radiance.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Unattached and Unobstructed"?
Abiding in which samādhi, by virtue of being free from all attachments, one shines forth unobstructed.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "unattached and unobstructed.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "the complete severance of the activity of all phenomena"?
It is that concentration by remaining in which one completely severs the activity of all phenomena.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "the complete severance of the activity of all phenomena.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "the abandonment of conflict"?
It is that concentration by remaining in which one abandons even the signs of all concentrations.
All other signs of the afflictions [are abandoned] even beforehand; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Abandoning Conflict.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Illumination"?
It is that concentration in which, having remained—
It illuminates, heats, and shines upon all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration named Vairocana.
In that regard, what is the concentration named Animiṣa?
It is that concentration wherein, having remained—
20004 No one seeks after any dharma; therefore it is called the "unblinking" (*animiṣa*) samādhi.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "abiding without a dwelling place" (*aniketasthita*)?
It is that samādhi, abiding in which, [one does not abide] in any samādhis.
Does he perceive any dharma as being without abode? By this it is called the concentration named "Abiding Without Abode.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Thoughtless"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one [perceives] the inferior...
Because it does not cause the mental states and mental factors to arise, it is called the "mindless" (*niścitta*) samādhi.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Stainless Lamp" (*vimalapradīpa*)?
It is that samādhi in which, having remained—
It maintains the lamp of all samādhis; therefore, it is called the samādhi named "Stainless Lamp.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Infinite Radiance"?
It is that samādhi, abiding in which—
It produces infinite radiance; therefore, it is called the "Infinite Radiance" samādhi.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Light-Maker"?
It is that samādhi, abiding in which [one perceives] all samādhis...
It produces radiance; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Light-Maker.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Universal Illumination"?
Upon the simultaneous attainment of which concentration—
The gateways of concentration shine forth; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Universal Illumination.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Pure Essence"?
It is that concentration wherein, having remained, [one perceives] all concentrations...
One attains pure equanimity; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Pure Essence.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Stainless Radiance"?
It is that concentration by abiding in which [one perceives] all concentrations...
It draws forth power and manifests all meditative absorptions; therefore, it is called the meditative absorption named Vimalaprabha (Stainless Light).
In that regard, what is the meditative absorption named Ratikara (Delight-Maker)?
It is that meditative absorption in which, having remained, [one attains] all—
One experiences delight in these concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Producer of Delight.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Lightning Lamp"?
It is that concentration wherein, having remained, [one perceives] all concentrations...
One produces a lamp; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Lightning Lamp.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Inexhaustible"?
It is that concentration wherein, by abiding in which, one does not perceive the exhaustion or non-exhaustion of concentrations.
Because one sees [thus], it is called the concentration named "Inexhaustible.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Vajra-maṇḍala"?
It is the concentration by abiding in which one maintains all maṇḍalas of concentration.
Therefore, it is called the samādhi named Vajramaṇḍala.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named Akṣayāpagata?
It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one perceives the exhaustion of all samādhis, and likewise...
When one perceives that one does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon, it is therefore called the "samādhi free from exhaustion.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "immovable"?
It is that samādhi, abiding in which—
It does not move all meditative absorptions, it does not conceive of them, it does not vibrate, and it does not proliferate; therefore, it is called the "unshakeable" (*aniñjya*) samādhi.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "opened" (*vivṛta*)?
Abiding in which concentration one perceives all concentrations as opened; therefore it is called the concentration named "The Opened.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "The Sun-Lamp"?
Abiding in which concentration illuminates the gateway of the rays of all concentrations, it is therefore called the concentration named "Sun-Lamp.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Stainless Moon"?
Abiding in which concentration dispels the darkness of all concentrations, it is therefore called the concentration named "Stainless Moon."
In this regard, what is the concentration called "Pure Radiance"?
It is that concentration in which, having abided, one attains the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of all concentrations; therefore it is called the concentration named "Pure Radiance."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Light-Maker"?
When one abides in this concentration, one produces light for the gateways of concentration; therefore it is called the concentration named "Light-Maker.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Action-Maker"?
Abiding in which concentration one performs the function of being the cause for all concentrations— therefore it is called the concentration named "The Performer" (*kārākāra*).
In that regard, what is the concentration named "The Banner of Knowledge" (*jñānaketu*)?
Abiding in which concentration one perceives the banner of knowledge of all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Banner of Knowledge.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Diamond-like"?
Abiding in which concentration one penetrates all phenomena and yet does not perceive even that concentration— therefore it is called the concentration named "diamond-like" (*vajropama*).
In that regard, what is the concentration named "stability of mind" (*cittasthiti*)?

Abiding in which concentration, one does not describe the mind, it does not turn back, it does not appear, it does not fall into destruction, and the thought "this is mind" does not occur; therefore, it is called the concentration named "abiding of the mind."
In this regard, what is the concentration called "Universal Illumination"?
It is that concentration in which, having remained, one perceives the universal illumination of all concentrations; therefore it is called the concentration named "Universal Illumination."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "well-established"?
When one abides in this concentration, one becomes established in all concentrations; therefore it is called the concentration named "well-established."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Jewel-Crest" (*ratnakoṭi*)?
When one abides in this concentration, all concentrations are seen from every side like a jewel-crest; therefore it is called the concentration named "Jewel-Crest."
In this regard, what is the samādhi called the "Seal of the Supreme Dharma"?
It is that samādhi in which, by remaining therein, all samādhis are sealed—
beginning with the seal of the primordial seal— and for that reason it is called the samādhi named the "Seal of the Supreme Dharma."
In this regard, what is the samādhi called "the equality of all phenomena"?
It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever as being apart from equality; therefore it is called the samādhi "the equality of all phenomena."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Abandoning Delight"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one abandons all delight in concentrations and all delight in phenomena; therefore it is called the concentration "Abandoning Delight."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Arising and Fulfillment of All Dharmas"?
When one abides in this concentration, one arises above all dharmas and is filled by all dharmas; therefore, it is called the concentration "Arising and Fulfillment of All Dharmas."
In this regard, what is the concentration called "Scattering"?
When one abides in this concentration, one scatters and disperses all phenomena by means of all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Scattering."
In this regard, what is the concentration called "the differentiation of the words of all phenomena"?

It is that concentration by abiding in which one differentiates the words of all concentrations and all phenomena; therefore, it is called the concentration "the differentiation of the words of all phenomena."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Equal Syllable"?
It is the concentration in which, by abiding therein, one attains the state of equal syllables regarding all concentrations; therefore it is called the concentration named "Equal Syllable.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Beyond Syllables"?
When one abides in this samādhi, one does not perceive even a single syllable of any samādhi; therefore, it is called the "samādhi free from syllables" (*akṣarāpagata*).
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "severing the objective support" (*ālambanaccheda*)?
When one abides in this samādhi, the objective support of all samādhis is severed; therefore, it is called the "samādhi of severing the objective support."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "unchanging"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive any change in all phenomena; therefore it is called the concentration named "unchanging."
In this regard, what is the concentration called "without mode"?
It is that concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive even the mode of any phenomena; therefore it is called the concentration "without mode."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "non-entry into names and signs"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the names and signs of any concentrations; therefore it is called the concentration "non-entry into names and signs."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "wandering without a dwelling"?
When one abides in this concentration, one does not perceive a dwelling place for any concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration "wandering without a dwelling."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Free from Obscuration"?
When one abides in this concentration, one purifies the obscuration of all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration "Free from Obscuration."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Possessing Conduct" (*cāritravat*)?
When one abides in this concentration, one perceives the conduct of all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration "Possessing Conduct."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "immovable"?
When one abides in this concentration, one does not perceive any movement of sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "immovable" concentration.
What is the concentration called "Transcending the Object"?
It is that concentration by remaining in which one transcends the object of all concentrations; therefore it is called the concentration "Transcending the Object."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Attaining the Accumulation of All Qualities"?

It is the concentration by abiding in which one attains the state of accumulation of all qualities and all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration "Attaining the Accumulation of All Qualities."
In this regard, what is the concentration called "ascertained stability of mind"?
When one abides in this concentration, the mind does not engage with any other concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration "ascertained stability of mind."
In this regard, what is the concentration called "Purity of Blooming Beauty"?
Abiding in which concentration, one attains the purity of blooming beauty within all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration "Purity of Blooming Beauty."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "possessing the factors of enlightenment"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one attains the seven factors of enlightenment; therefore it is called the concentration "possessing the factors of enlightenment."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "infinite manifestation"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the two extremes; therefore it is called the concentration "infinite manifestation.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "the peerless equal"?
When, by abiding in this samādhi, one does not attain the equality of all samādhis, it is therefore called the "samādhi equal to the unequaled.
What is the samādhi called "Transcending All Phenomena"?
When, by abiding in this samādhi, one transcends the entire triple world, it is therefore called the "samādhi transcending all phenomena."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "the maker of discernment"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one will effect the discernment of all concentrations and all phenomena.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "The Maker of Delimitation.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "The Dispeller of Doubt"?
It is that concentration by abiding in which one dispels doubt regarding all concentrations.
One attains it; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Dispeller of Doubt.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Without Basis"? It is that concentration in which, having remained, one perceives the non-abiding of all phenomena.
Therefore, it is called the "supportless" (*niradhiṣṭhāna*) samādhi.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "single array" (*ekavyūha*)?
It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one does not perceive the duality of any phenomenon whatsoever.
Therefore, it is called the samādhi named "Single Array.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named "Manifestation of Aspects"?
It is that samādhi, abiding in which [one perceives] all samādhis and all dharmas...
When one perceives the manifestation of the letter *ca*, it is therefore called the concentration named "Manifestation of the Letter *ca*.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Single Array of Forms"?
It is the concentration wherein, having remained—
One perceives the single mode of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the "concentration named Array of a Single Mode.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Non-occurrence of Modes"?
Abiding in which concentration one perceives the non-duality of all phenomena; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Non-occurrence of Aspects.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Mastery over the Foundation of All Penetrating Entities"?
Abiding in which concentration [one perceives] all concentrations...

One attains penetrative knowledge (*nirvedhika-jñāna*), by the attainment of which nothing whatsoever remains unpenetrated. Therefore, it is called the concentration named "The Sovereignty over the Foundation of All Phenomena through Penetration.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Entry into Conventional Sounds"?
Abiding in which concentration one enters into the conventional sounds and expressions of all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Entry into Conventional Sounds.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Voice-Sound Free from Syllables"?
Abiding in which concentration one perceives all concentrations as being free from syllables.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "Sound of Speech.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Blazing Torch"?
It is the concentration wherein, having remained, one illuminates and radiates all concentrations with splendor.
Because it shines forth, it is therefore called the concentration named "Blazing Torch.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Purification of Characteristics"?
It is that concentration by abiding in which one purifies all characteristics.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "Purification of Characteristics.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Uncharacterized"?
It is the concentration wherein, having remained, one characterizes all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Uncharacterized."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Endowed with the Excellence of All Aspects"?
It is the concentration by abiding in which one becomes endowed with the excellence of all aspects; therefore, it is called the concentration "Endowed with the Excellence of All Aspects."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "not delighting in any pleasure or pain"?

It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive pleasure or pain within any concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration "not delighting in any pleasure or pain."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "the aspect of the inexhaustible"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the exhaustion of any concentrations; therefore it is called the concentration called "the aspect of the inexhaustible."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "the practice of retention" (*dhāraṇī-pratipatti*)?
It is the concentration by remaining in which one retains all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration named "the practice of retention."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Comprehension of All Correctness and Incorrectness"?

It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive the correctness or incorrectness of concentrations; therefore it is called the concentration "Comprehension of All Correctness and Incorrectness."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "the pacifier of all obstructions and cessations"?
It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one does not [perceive] the obstructions or cessations of any samādhis.
When one perceives [it] thus, it is called the concentration named "the pacifier of the cessation of all obstructions.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "following and counter-following"?
It is that concentration wherein, having abided, one follows after all concentrations.
Because he does not perceive any further pursuit, it is therefore called the "concentration on the non-pursuit" (*anusārapratisāra*).
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Stainless Radiance" (*vimalaprabha*)?
It is that concentration, abiding in which [one perceives] all concentrations...
No circle of light is perceived; therefore, it is called the concentration named Vimalaprabha (Stainless Light).
In that regard, what is the concentration named Sāravatī (Possessing Essence)?
It is that concentration wherein, having remained, [one perceives] all concentrations—
20308 Since its lack of essence is not perceived, it is therefore called the concentration named "Possessing Essence.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Stainless Full Moon"?
Abiding in which concentration, his entire—
The concentrations become fully perfected, just as the moon on the full-moon day; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Stainless Full Moon.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Great Array"?
When one abides in this concentration, all concentrations become endowed with a great array; therefore, it is called the concentration named "Great Array.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Illuminator of All Aspects"?
When one abides in this concentration, one produces the radiance of all concentrations and of all phenomena.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "Illuminator of All Aspects.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Sameness of Concentrations"?
It is that concentration wherein, having remained, there is neither distraction nor one-pointedness of all concentrations.
Because he perceives thus, it is called the concentration named "equality of concentration.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "convergence into the passionless"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, [one perceives] all—

One attains the state in which all concentrations converge into the non-contentious (*araṇa*) and the contentious (*saraṇa*); therefore, it is called the concentration named "Convergence into the Non-contentious.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "No Abode in the Wind" (*anilāniketa*)?
When one abides in this concentration, one does not perceive a dwelling place (*ālaya*) for any concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration named "No Abode in the Wind."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "firmly established in suchness"?
Abiding in which concentration, one does not deviate from the suchness of all concentrations; therefore, it is called the concentration "firmly established in suchness.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "thoroughly crushing the defilement of the body"?
