When one abides in this samādhi, one does not perceive the body of all samādhis; therefore, it is called the "samādhi that thoroughly crushes the defilement of the body.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "the destruction of the defilement of speech"?
When one abides in this samādhi...
One perceives all samādhis through vocal action; therefore, it is called the "samādhi that destroys the defilement of speech.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "resembling space"? It is that samādhi in which, having remained—gagana-
It shines like a mare’s flame; therefore it is called the concentration named "resembling space.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "unattached liberation like space and free from defilement"?
Abiding in which concentration, [one perceives] all phenomena—

He attains that which is called the liberation through non-attachment to space and being unstained; therefore, it is called the "concentration named liberation through non-attachment to space and being unstained.
Subhūti, this is the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus concludes the equipment of merit.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows:
namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?
They are the application of mindfulness to the body, the application of mindfulness to feelings, the application of mindfulness to the mind, and the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
Among these, what is the application of mindfulness to the body?
In this way, up to: what is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the internal body.
And he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with the body, by way of non-apprehension;
he dwells contemplating the body in the external body.
And he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with the body, by way of non-apprehension;
he dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body,
and he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with the body, by way of non-apprehension.
Ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world;
thus [he dwells] with regard to internal feelings and the mind.
He dwells observing phenomena among internal phenomena,
yet he does not engage in discursive thoughts associated with phenomena, by means of non-apprehension;
ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness for the world.
[He dwells] with covetousness and dejection.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell contemplating the body within the body?
Here, Subhūti...
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, when walking, clearly knows, "I am walking";
when standing, he clearly knows, "I am standing"; when sitting, he clearly knows, "I am sitting."
Lying down, he knows, "I am lying down.
In whatever way his body is positioned— whether in a refined or unrefined manner— he knows it accordingly.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body within the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body within the body; whether moving forward or moving backward, he acts with clear comprehension; whether looking ahead or looking aside, whether bending or stretching his limbs, or in carrying his outer robe, inner robe, bowl, and robes, or in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting.

Whether lying down to dispel the fatigue of sleep, or when coming, going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, remaining silent, or dwelling in seclusion— he thus acts with clear comprehension. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body within the body;
ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world—by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Bodhisattva...

The Mahāsattva, breathing in mindfully, knows as it really is: "I am breathing in mindfully. Breathing out mindfully, he knows as it really is: "I am breathing out mindfully. Or, breathing in long, he knows as it really is: "I am breathing in long."
He understands it as it truly is:
breathing out long, he understands as it truly is, "I am breathing out long"; or breathing in short, he [understands] "I am breathing in short."
He understands as it truly is: "I am breathing in," and when breathing out short, he understands as it truly is: "I am breathing out short.
It is just as follows:
Subhūti, it is as if a potter or a potter’s apprentice, while spinning a wheel, were to throw the rod long and know, "I am throwing it long," according to reality;
or were to throw it short and know, "I am throwing it short," according to reality.

In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, breathing in mindfully, knows as it really is: "I am breathing in mindfully"; breathing out mindfully, he knows as it really is: "I am breathing out mindfully."

Breathing in long, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in long. Breathing out long, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out long. Breathing in short, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in short."
Breathing out short, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out short.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates this very body according to its elements as they really are: "There exists—
In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example,
a butcher or a butcher’s apprentice were to kill a cow with a sharp weapon, and having killed the cow, [were to cut it up].
One should prepare four planks;
having prepared the four planks, one should examine them while either standing or sitting.
In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates this very body, part by part, as it truly is:
"In this body there is the earth element, the water element..."
[The element of fire] or the element of wind.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body within the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
And that is by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by the nails, body hair, and skin, as full of various kinds of—
One contemplates the impure as it truly is: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, hide, flesh, sinews,
blood, bones, marrow, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, spleen, undigested food, intestines,
mesentery, stomach, excrement, urine, tears, sweat, fat, saliva, snot, pus, and blood."
He contemplates this body as it truly is: bile, phlegm, fat, filth, brain matter, eye-secretion, and ear-secretion.
Subhūti, it is just like a workman’s basket full [of refuse].
Suppose there were various kinds of grain— rice, paddy, sesame, husked rice, mung beans, black gram, barley, wheat, lentils,
and even mustard seeds— and another man with sight, having been released and examining them, should recognize them thus: "This is rice."
This is rice;
these are sesame seeds; these are grains; these are mung beans.
These are beans, these are barley,
these are wheat.
"These are antelope herds;
these are mustard seeds.
In this very same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [regards] this very body, upwards...

From the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, including the nails, body hair, and skin, he contemplates this body as it truly is, full of various kinds of impurities: "In this body there are head-hairs and body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, inner skin, flesh, sinews,
blood, bones, marrow, heart, kidneys, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, stomach, and feces."
feces, urine, tears, sweat, fat, saliva, snot, pus, blood, bile, phlegm, muscle-fat, dirt, brain-matter, eye-secretion, and ear-wax.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom dwells contemplating the body within the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has gone to a cemetery and sees various forms in the cemetery...
Cast away upon a cemetery, discarded— whether dead for one day, dead for two days, dead for three days,
dead for four days, or dead for five days; swollen, or livid, or festering,
or being devoured, or skeletal— he applies this very body to that [state].
This body, too, has such a nature, such a self-nature, and does not transcend this natural law.
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the external body— ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
Regarding mental distress:
furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees dead bodies discarded in a cemetery,
deceased for six nights or seven nights, being devoured by crows;

Or being devoured by ospreys, or vultures, or jackals, or wolves, or dogs, or by various other kinds of living beings—there he applies this very body [to that example]: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character; it has not transcended this natural law. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees those dead bodies abandoned in a cemetery—eaten by animals, impure, putrid, and foul-smelling—he applies this very body to that [vision]: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character; it has not transcended this natural law."

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees on a charnel ground a heap of bones, smeared with flesh and blood, held together by tendons, and having seen it...
He applies this very body to that [external body], thinking: "This body, too, is of such a nature, such a character, and has not transcended this natural law.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...

When he sees those dead bodies on the charnel ground—skeletons from which the flesh and blood have departed, with only the binding of tendons remaining—he compares this very body to them: "This body, too, is of such a nature, such is its inherent character; it has not transcended this natural law.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees on a charnel ground a skeleton, with its bonds of the body severed and disjoined,

scattered upon the earth according to their respective positions, he applies this very body to that [sight], thinking: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and it does not transcend this natural law."

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees bones scattered in the various directions and intermediate directions on a charnel ground— namely, here one [bone], there another...

With one [hand] he takes the bones of the feet, with another the bones of the shanks, with another the bones of the thighs, with another the bones of the pelvic basin, with another the bones of the spine, with another the bones of the ribs, with another the bones of the neck, with another the bones of the arms, and with another the bones of the skull. He then applies this very body to that [skeleton], thinking: "This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and does not transcend this natural law."

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees bones in a charnel ground that have been there for many years, many—

For one hundred and seven thousand years, they have been overcome by wind and sun, becoming white like conch shells; he compares this very body to them, thinking: "This body, too, is of such a nature, such is its inherent character, and it cannot transcend this natural law.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the external body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees bones on a cemetery ground that are more than a year old—bluish, pigeon-colored, putrid, reduced to powder, and leveled with the dust of the earth—he applies this very body to that [vision]: "This body, too, is of such a nature, such is its inherent character; it has not transcended this natural law."

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
In the same way, he dwells contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
Regarding mental distress, that too is by way of non-apprehension.
Subhūti, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Namely, the four right efforts.
What are the four?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [exerts himself] regarding evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen...

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and applies himself correctly for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen dharmas; he generates desire, exerts himself, takes hold of the mind, and applies himself correctly for the sake of the abandoning of arisen evil and unwholesome dharmas.
He generates desire, exerts himself, takes hold of the mind, and applies right effort for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;
he generates desire for the stability, increase, non-confusion, and non-decline of wholesome states that have already arisen.
He generates [the mind], exerts himself, takes hold of the mind, and correctly applies it,
and that by way of non-apprehension.
This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
What are the four?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the application of effort (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) associated with the concentration of desire (*chandasamādhi*).

He cultivates the basis of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, and culminating in relinquishment; likewise, he cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment— the concentration of energy, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation— dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion,
and dependent on cessation, culminating in relinquishment.
And that is thoroughly understood through the application of non-apprehension.
This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the five faculties. What are the five? They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. And these are practiced through the yoga of non-apprehension.
This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows:
namely, the five powers. What are they?

Furthermore, Subhūti, there are five powers: the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom; and these are practiced through the yoga of non-apprehension. This, too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Moreover, Subhūti, another [aspect] of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is the seven factors of enlightenment.

Which are the seven? The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
In that regard, what is the limb of awakening of mindfulness, up to the limb of awakening of equanimity?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom...

He cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; and he does so through the yoga of non-apprehension. Subhūti, this too is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, another aspect of the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the noble eightfold path.
What is the noble eightfold path? It is as follows:
right view, right intention, right action, right livelihood, right effort, [right mindfulness,] and right concentration.
Mindfulness and right concentration;
and that by way of non-apprehension.
This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, another aspect of the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the three concentrations. What are the three concentrations? They are the concentration on emptiness—
The signless and the wishless.
In that regard, what is the concentration on emptiness?
It is [the meditation] on those things which are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The stability of the mind of one who contemplates all phenomena as empty, which is the gateway to liberation known as emptiness— this is called the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
[One contemplates] all phenomena as signless (*animitta*).
The stability of the mind for one who is contemplating [all phenomena] as signless is called the signless liberation door; this is called the signless samādhi.
The stability of the mind for one who is contemplating all phenomena as wishless is called the wishless liberation door; this is called the wishless samādhi.
These three gateways to liberation are the three concentrations. This also, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
One should train in these three gates of liberation.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows:
namely, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
The knowledge of destruction, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of mastery,
and the knowledge according to the literal expression.
Among these, what is the knowledge of suffering?
The knowledge of the non-arising of suffering is the knowledge of suffering. {In that regard, what is} the knowledge of origination?
It is the knowledge of the abandonment of origination.
In that regard, what is the knowledge of cessation? It is the knowledge of the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the knowledge of the path?
Regarding the knowledge of the realization of cessation:
therein, what is the knowledge of destruction?
It is that which [concerns] passion, hatred—
The knowledge of the destruction of delusion.
In that regard, what is the knowledge of non-arising?
It is the knowledge of non-arising with respect to non-arising.
In that regard, what is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
It is the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena regarding the five aggregates.
In that regard, what is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
The eye is impermanent; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent.
Thus it continues, up to the individual and collective [analysis] of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and dependent origination—
And there is knowledge regarding the [twelve] dependent originations.
In that regard, what is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
It is that which, by means of the mind alone, [knows] the minds of other sentient beings and other persons.
Knowledge of the mind.
In that regard, what is the knowledge of mastery?
It is the knowledge of mastery in practice.
In that regard, what is knowledge according to the letter?
It is that knowledge of the Tathāgata’s omniscience in all its aspects, and that by way of non-apprehension.
This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, another aspect of the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is this:
namely, the three faculties.
What are the three?
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known.
In that regard, what is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
The faculty of those persons in training who have not yet attained full realization, which is without illumination and has not been disciplined—

the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom— this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
In that regard, what is the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*)?

It is the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom belonging to those persons who are in training (*śaikṣa*) and who have already known; this is called the faculty of having known.
In that regard, what is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)? It is as follows:

the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom belonging to those persons beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—namely, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones. This is called the faculty of one who has already known.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, this too is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by way of non-apprehension. Moreover, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought and with only sustained thought."
20920 Samādhi. {In that regard, what is} the samādhi with applied thought and sustained thought?

Here, {Subhūti}, a {bodhisattva} mahāsattva, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, enters the first [dhyāna], which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
Having attained and abiding in this dhyāna, it is called concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarkaḥ savicāraḥ samādhiḥ*). In that regard,
what is concentration without applied thought and with only sustained thought (*avitarko 'vicāramātraḥ samādhiḥ*)?

That which is intermediate between the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna is called the concentration without applied thought (*avitarka*) and with sustained thought only (*avicāramātra*). In that regard, what is the concentration without applied thought?

"Non-discursive concentration is that which is the second dhyāna; this should be explained in detail up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called non-discursive, non-discerning concentration.
This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
21005 by way of apprehension. 21006 Furthermore, Subhūti, another aspect of the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the ten recollections (daśānusmṛtayaḥ).
What are the ten? Namely:

mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of relinquishment, mindfulness of the deities, mindfulness of upward progress, mindfulness of death, and mindfulness of the body.

Mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation—this too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva by way of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless [attainments].
The eight attainments, the nine liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments—
this too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this is another [aspect] of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The ten powers of a Tathāgata.
What are the ten? Namely, in this regard, a bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva understands, as it truly is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible;
and he understands, as it truly is, the place, the cause, and the maturation of past, future, and present actions and the undertaking of actions.
He understands, as it really is, the world of diverse elements;
he understands, as it really is, the diversity of inclinations among other beings and other persons.
He understands, as it truly is, the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other beings and other persons;
he understands, as it truly is, the path leading everywhere;
[he understands] the meditations and liberations of other beings and other persons...
He understands, as it truly is, the defilement, purification, and emergence from meditative concentrations and attainments;
he recollects his manifold previous abodes.

And with the divine eye, he understands, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings. Through the destruction of the outflows, he dwells having realized, witnessed, and attained in this very life, by his own direct knowledge, the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom, [knowing]: "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished."
He understands, as it truly is, that "there is nothing further to be done" and that "this is not falsehood.
Subhūti, this too is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, another aspect of the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*). What are the four?

That is to say: "If anyone— whether a śramaṇa, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world— should rightfully challenge me, who claims, 'Indeed, these dharmas have been fully realized by me,' on this point, [I see] no such ground."
I do not perceive this.

Not perceiving any such ground for apprehension here, I dwell having attained security and having attained fearlessness; I recognize my place as the preeminent leader and roar the perfect lion’s roar in the assembly—the Brahma-roar.
"I set in motion the wheel that has not been set in motion by any ascetic, or brahmin, or deva, or Māra, or Brahmā,
or by anyone else in the world, together with its dharma.
For me, who declares, "My outflows are exhausted," these [are the grounds].

That the outflows (āsrava) are not completely exhausted— this is impossible. And herein, whether it be some ascetic or brahmin— and so forth, as before— I set in motion the Brahma-wheel, which has not been set in motion by any ascetic or brahmin, nor by a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else.
Or again,
it is not possible that what I have declared to be obstructive factors in the world would not be obstacles for one who indulges in them; such a case does not exist.
"In this regard, there is no ascetic or brahmin— [the rest as before]— nor anyone else in the world who can rightfully [reprove me]:
'The path declared by you is noble, leading to liberation, and conduces to the complete destruction of suffering for one who practices it'— yet having practiced that very path,"

"It is impossible that pride should not lead to the complete destruction of suffering; there is no such possibility. And herein, whether it be some śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa—or for that matter, anyone else in the world—it is not possible according to the Dharma [to challenge me]. These are the four grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya)."
This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Namely, the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Which are the four?
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid).
The analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Namely, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikā buddhadharmāḥ*).
What are these eighteen?

Namely, Subhūti, from the night the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, fully realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, until the night [he passes away]—taking that as the basis—[these qualities remain].

Subhūti, during this interval until he attains final nirvāṇa, there is no stumbling on the part of the Tathāgata; there is no lapse, no loss of mindfulness, no perception of diversity, no unconcentrated mind,
no equanimity lacking discernment, no decline in zeal, no decline in vigor, and no decline in mindfulness.
There is no falling away from concentration, no falling away from wisdom, and no falling away from liberation.
All bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge.
All verbal action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge;
all mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.
Unimpeded and unattached knowledge and vision regarding the past; unimpeded and unattached knowledge and vision regarding the future;
and unimpeded and unattached knowledge and vision regarding the present.
It proceeds.
These are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikā buddhadharmāḥ*).
This too, Subhūti, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
21207 by way of non-apprehension.
[Thus is the equipment for the path.
21208 Furthermore, Subhūti, there is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Namely, the gateways of dhāraṇī;

that is to say, the gateway of the equality of the method of syllables, the entrance into syllables. What is the equality of the method of syllables, the gateway of syllables, and the entrance into syllables?
The letter A is the gateway to all phenomena because they are unarisen from the very beginning;
the letter Ra is the gateway to all phenomena because they are free from dust.
The letter *pa* is a gateway to all phenomena because it indicates their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
The letter *ca* is a gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of their passing away and rebirth.
The letter *na* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are devoid of names;
the letter *la* is the gateway to all phenomena because they have transcended the world and because the causes and conditions for the creeper of craving have been uprooted.
The letter *da* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are delimited by self-control and discipline. The letter *ba* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are liberated from bondage.
The letter *ḍa* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are free from turmoil.
The letter *sa* is a gateway to all phenomena because attachment is non-apprehensible;
the letter *va* is a gateway to all phenomena because the path of speech and sound is utterly severed.
The letter *ta* is the gateway to all phenomena because their suchness is immovable;
the letter *ya* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are non-arising in accordance with reality.
The letter *sta* is the gateway to all phenomena because a pillar is not apprehended;
the letter *ka* is the gateway to all phenomena because an agent is not apprehended.
The syllable *sa* is a gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of their sameness;
the syllable *ma* is a gateway to all phenomena because of the non-apprehension of the sense of "mine."
The letter *ga* is the gateway to all phenomena,
because space is non-apprehendable.
The letter *stha* is the gateway to all phenomena, because a location is non-apprehendable.
The letter *ja* is a gateway to all phenomena, because birth is non-apprehensible. The letter *śva* is a gateway to all phenomena, because exhalation is non-apprehensible.
The letter *dha* is a gateway to all phenomena, because the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is not apprehended.
The letter *śa* is a gateway to all phenomena, because tranquility (*śamatha*) is not apprehended. The letter *kha* is a gateway...
The letter *sa* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are unapprehendable as being equal to space; the letter *kṣa* is the gateway to all phenomena because their exhaustion is unapprehendable;
all phenomena have the letter *ta* as their gateway because that [exhaustion] is also unapprehendable.
All phenomena have the letter *ja* as their gateway, because omniscience is non-apprehendable;
all phenomena have the letter *ha* as their gateway, because a cause is non-apprehendable; all phenomena have the letter *ccha* as their gateway, because even a thief is non-apprehendable.
All phenomena have the letter *sma* as their gateway, because recollection is unapprehendable.
All phenomena have the letter *ddha* as their gateway, because they are devoid of grasping.
All phenomena have the letter *sa* as their gateway... [and so forth].

All phenomena have the letter *gha* as their gateway because of the non-apprehension of enthusiasm; all phenomena have the letter *ṭha* as their gateway because of the non-apprehension of solidification;
all phenomena have the letter *ṭha* as their gateway because of the non-apprehension of fabrication.
All phenomena have the letter *ṇa* as their gateway because they are free from conflict; all phenomena have the letter *pha* as their gateway because no fruit is to be apprehended.
All phenomena have the letter *ska* as their gateway, because the aggregates (*skandha*) are non-apprehendable;
all phenomena have the letter *ja* as their gateway, because aging (*jarā*) is non-apprehendable.
All phenomena have the letter *ca* as their gateway, because movement is non-apprehensible; all phenomena have the letter *ṭa* as their gateway, because the syllable *ṭhaṃ* is non-apprehensible;
all phenomena have the letter *ḍha* as their gateway.
Because of the non-apprehension of the syllable *ḍaṃ*.
Beyond this, there is no further conventional expression.
For what reason? Because thus it is.
There is no name whatsoever by which it might be conventionally designated, or by which it might be expressed, or by which it might be pointed out, or by which it might be characterized,
or by which one might perceive it;
it is, Subhūti, just like space.
In this very way, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are to be understood. Subhūti, this entry into the dhāraṇī is the entry into the teaching of the letters beginning with *a*. Whosoever...

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who understands this entry into skill in the syllables beginning with *a* will not be obstructed by any sound whatsoever; he will bring all that into accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and will attain skill in the knowledge of sounds. Subhūti, any bodhisattva mahāsattva who hears this seal of the syllables beginning with *a*, and having heard it—
Whoever shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, teach it to others, and delight in it with such a continuity of practice, twenty benefits are to be expected for them. What are these twenty?
He will be possessed of mindfulness and possessed of intelligence.
He will be possessed of skillful means;
he will be possessed of steadfastness; he will be possessed of a sense of shame, wisdom, eloquence, and proficiency in the truths.
This entrance to the dhāraṇī will be attained with little difficulty, and he will not be full of doubt; furthermore, no uncertainty shall arise within him.
Nor, upon hearing pleasant speech,
will he become attached to others;
nor will he be repelled by harsh speech.
He will be neither haughty nor humble;
he will remain exactly as he is, and he will be skilled in sounds,
skilled in the aggregates, and skilled in the elements.
He will be skilled in the sense bases; he will be skilled in the truths; he will be skilled in dependent origination;
he will be skilled in causes; and he will be skilled in conditions.
He will be skilled in the Dharma,
and he will be skilled in the knowledge of the perfection of the faculties.
He will be skilled in the knowledge of others' minds; he will be skilled in the knowledge of the methods of supernatural power;
he will be skilled in the knowledge of the divine ear; and he will be skilled in the knowledge of recollecting former abodes.

He will be skilled in the knowledge of death and rebirth; he will be skilled in the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows; and he will be skilled in the exposition of what is possible and what is impossible.
"He will become skilled in transgressing [faults] and skilled in the modes of conduct (īryāpatha).
He will obtain these benefits.
Subhūti, this too is a gateway to the dhāraṇī for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, a gateway to the syllables, a gateway to the letter 'A'.
The Mahāyāna. [Thus concludes the equipment of dhāraṇīs.
Furthermore, as Subhūti has said:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out upon the Mahāyāna?"
...it comes to be so. Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the six perfections, passes from stage to stage.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva pass from stage to stage? That is to say—
Through the non-transmigration of all phenomena.
For what reason?
Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that comes.
He does not go, nor does he move, nor does he approach; rather,
regarding that which is the ground of phenomena,
he does not conceive of it, he does not reflect upon it, he performs the preparation of the ground, and yet he does not perceive the ground.
And what is the preparation of the stages for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the first stage must perform the ten preparations for the stages.
Which ten? The preparation of resolute intention through the yoga of non-apprehension;
the preparation of being a basis for benefit by way of the non-apprehension of signs.

The purification of the mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, by way of the non-apprehension of sentient beings; the purification of relinquishment, by way of the non-apprehension of the giver, the gift, and the recipient.

The cultivation of attending upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra-sevā*) by way of not being complacent with them; the cultivation of seeking the true Dharma (*saddharma-paryeṣṭi*) by way of the non-apprehension of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-anupalabdhi*);
and the cultivation of frequent renunciation (*abhīkṣṇa-naiṣkramya*) by way of the non-apprehension of the home (*gṛha-anupalabdhi*).
The preparation consisting of longing for the Buddha-body,

by virtue of the non-apprehension of the signs of the primary marks and secondary characteristics; the preparation consisting of the exposition of the Dharma, by virtue of the non-apprehension of the differentiation of phenomena.
The purification through truthful speech (satyavacanaparikarma),
by way of the non-apprehensibility of speech;
these, Subhūti, are the ten purifications for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas belonging to the first stage (bhūmi).
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the first stage must perform ten preparatory practices.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the second stage attends to eight qualities and practices accordingly.
What are the eight?
Namely: purity of ethical discipline, gratitude, thankfulness, establishment in the power of patience, the experience of joy through not abandoning any sentient being, and—
Bringing great compassion to manifestation;
through faith in the gurus, showing them reverence, regarding them as the Teacher, serving the gurus, and seeking the perfections and their application.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the second stage should practice by attending to these eight dharmas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the third stage [should attend] to five dharmas.
One should abide [in these].
In which five?
Namely, in insatiability regarding great learning, and therein, regarding the letters—

In establishing [himself] therein; in the exposition of the gift of the Dharma free from worldly motives and through non-conceit regarding that; in the dedication of roots of merit for the purification of the Buddha-field and through non-conceit regarding that; in not becoming weary of the immeasurable cycle of existence and through non-conceit regarding that; and in the establishment of moral shame and dread of blame and through non-conceit regarding that—in these, Subhūti, the bodhisattva [should train].
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the third stage should abide in five dharmas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the fourth stage should abide in ten dharmas.
And these ten should not be abandoned. Which ten?
Namely: dwelling in the forest.
Having few desires, contentment, not relinquishing the ascetic practices (*dhūtaguṇa*) and refinement, not abandoning the training, revulsion toward the qualities of sensual pleasure,
the arousal of the thought of mind accompanied by world-weariness, the renunciation of all things, a mind that is not cowed,
and indifference toward all material objects.
Subhūti, these ten dharmas should not be abandoned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the fourth bhūmi;
rather, he should abide in them.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the fifth stage must avoid ten things. What are the ten?
Namely, association with householders and renunciants must be avoided; [association with] families must...
One should avoid falsehood;
one should avoid places of social distraction;
one should avoid self-exaltation.
One should avoid disparaging others; one should avoid the ten unwholesome paths of action;
one should avoid arrogance and conceit.
The perversions are to be avoided; doubt is to be avoided;
the latencies of passion, hatred, and delusion are to be avoided.
Subhūti, these ten dharmas are to be avoided by a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding on the fifth bhūmi.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding on the sixth bhūmi must fulfill six dharmas.
What are the six? Namely, the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitāḥ) are to be fulfilled.
There are another six dharmas that are to be avoided. What are the six?
The mind of a śrāvaka should be avoided;
the mind of a pratyekabuddha should be avoided; the mind of despondency [should be avoided].
One should avoid [such thoughts];
seeing a beggar, one does not shrink back;
all things are to be relinquished, and there is no dejection.
One should generate this thought, and one must not cause distraction by the petitioner.
Subhūti, these six dharmas are to be fulfilled by a bodhisattva mahāsattva while abiding on the sixth ground.
Furthermore, Subhūti, another six dharmas are to be avoided.
Moreover, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding on the seventh bhūmi, there are twenty dharmas that [are not to be practiced].
They come to be. What are the twenty?
Namely: he has no grasping at a self, no grasping at a sentient being, no grasping at a life-force, no grasping at a person, no grasping at annihilation, and no grasping at permanence.
The perception of signs is the view of causality;
it is attachment to the aggregates, attachment to the elements, the sense bases, supernatural powers, and establishment within the three realms. The three realms—
21612 Adherence to the three realms, the *ālaya*, attachment to the view of relying on the Buddha, attachment to the view of relying on the Dharma, attachment to the view of relying on the Saṃgha,
attachment to the view of relying on ethical discipline, and the dispute that "all phenomena are empty"— for one who [holds these], there is no contradiction with emptiness. These, Subhūti, are...
There are twenty qualities that do not exist for a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding on the seventh stage;
therefore, those very same twenty qualities must be fully perfected by one established on the seventh stage.
What are these twenty?

Namely: the fulfillment of emptiness, the direct realization of the signless, the knowledge of the wishless, the purity of the three spheres, compassion and pity for all sentient beings, not despising them, seeing the equality of all phenomena and having no attachment therein; the penetration of the true principle and not being conceited because of it; the patient acceptance of non-arising and the knowledge of non-arising; and the single principle—
This is the exposition: the eradication of conceptualization regarding all phenomena;

the turning away from perceptions and views; the turning away from afflictions; the realization of tranquility (*śamatha*); skill in insight (*vipaśyanā*); the state of a tamed mind; and the state of a mind possessing unimpeded knowledge regarding all things.
The sphere of non-attachment is that wherein one travels at will to any field and, remaining there in the assembly circle of the Buddhas, manifests one's own body.
These twenty qualities are to be perfected by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the seventh stage.
[They] are to be fulfilled.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the eighth stage must completely fulfill four dharmas.
Which four? Namely: penetrating the minds of all sentient beings; sporting with the superknowledges (abhijñā);
beholding the Buddha-fields; and the accomplishment of those Buddha-fields exactly as they have been seen, as well as attending upon the Buddhas.
21704 The thorough contemplation of the body as it truly is.
Subhūti, these four dharmas must be fulfilled by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the eighth stage.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the eighth stage must fulfill four dharmas. What are these four?
Namely: the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties [of beings], and the purification of the buddha-field.

Through the frequent attainment of the illusion-like samādhi, he manifests various forms of existence according to the way in which the roots of virtue of sentient beings are brought to fruition; this is the intentional production of existence.
Subhūti, these [are the qualities] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding on the eighth stage must fulfill four qualities.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding on the ninth stage must fulfill twelve qualities. What are these twelve?
That is to say, it is the embracing of infinite vows.
In whatever way he makes his vow, in that very way it is fulfilled for him; he gains knowledge of the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans.

The knowledge of the teaching of eloquence consists of: the perfection of the descent into the womb, the perfection of birth, the perfection of lineage, the perfection of retinue, the perfection of birth, the perfection of renunciation, the perfection of the tree of enlightenment, and the perfection of the fulfillment of all qualities.
These, Subhūti, [are the perfections].
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the ninth stage must fulfill twelve dharmas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the tenth bodhisattva stage is to be called a Tathāgata indeed.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the purification of the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:

Subhūti, that which consists in the thorough acquisition of all roots of merit through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects—this is the preparation of the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. In that regard, what is the preparation of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s state of being a basis for benefit? It is when the bodhisattva mahāsattva—
A bodhisattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, applies himself to the quest for the knowledge of the Mahāyāna;
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the basis of welfare.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings?

It is the accomplishment of the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—by means of mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects; this is called the cultivation of a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation of relinquishment?

That which consists in giving gifts to all sentient beings without conceptual differentiation—this is called the preparation of relinquishment. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation of attending upon spiritual friends?
Those who are the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

who encourage them toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*),— the serving, honoring, attending upon, and obeying of those friends is called the "preparation consisting in the service of the spiritual friends" for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation for the search for the Dharma?

It is when one searches for the Dharma with a mental attention associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and does not fall into the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; this is it.
21806 {It is said: the preliminary preparation for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s quest for the Dharma}.
In that regard, {what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s} frequent preliminary preparation for renunciation?
It is that which is unmixed throughout all births—abhi-

When one goes forth from home into the teaching of the Tathāgata and enters the religious life, and no obstacle whatsoever arises for them— Subhūti, this is called the constant preparation for renunciation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation consisting of longing for the Buddha-body?
Subhūti, when one has seen the form of a Buddha, one never becomes separated from the mental engagement with the Buddha until one has attained all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is it.
It is said that [this is] the purification of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s longing for the Buddha-body.
In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s purification of the exposition of the Dharma?
It is when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in the presence of a Tathāgata—

Whether he has departed or has entered final nirvāṇa, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing; solitary, complete, pure, and pristine—the holy life (*brahmacarya*), namely: the discourses (*sūtra*), mixed prose and verse (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), historical narratives (*itivṛttaka*), and birth stories (*jātaka*).
The Nidānas, Avadānas, as well as the Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, and Upadeśas—
this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s preparation for the exposition of the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s truthful speech?
21815 Purification: namely, acting in accordance with what one has spoken. This is called the purification of truthful speech for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti, these are the ten purifications for a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the first stage.
In this regard, Subhūti, what are the eight purifications of a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the second stage?
Here, Subhūti, they are the purification of ethical discipline (*śīla*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely, that which pertains to the śrāvakas—
The non-mental engagement with the thoughts of pratyekabuddhas, and the non-mental engagement with whatever other factors cause immorality or create obstacles to awakening—
this is called the purification of ethical discipline of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

In that regard, what is the gratitude and thankfulness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, does not let even a small favor done perish until the end of saṃsāra, much less one that is great; this is called the gratitude and thankfulness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s establishment in the power of patience?
It is the state of a mind free from malice and non-violence toward all sentient beings; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s establishment in the power of patience.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s...
The experience of joy and gladness:
that which consists in the ripening of all sentient beings is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s experience of joy and gladness.
In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s...
The manifestation of great compassion occurs when a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva,
thinks: "For the sake of each and every sentient being, I shall remain in hell for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges."

"I shall continue to ripen [beings] until that being has been established in the wisdom of a Buddha. Such enthusiasm and lack of weariness for the sake of each and every single being is called the manifestation of the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the faith and reverence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is the state of being endowed with faith through having utterly subdued pride in all things; this is called the faith and reverence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s faithful obedience toward the guru?
That which consists of perceiving those who are one's gurus as the Teacher is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s faith and devotion in serving his gurus.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s pursuit of the perfections and their application?
That state of seeking the perfections with undivided attention is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s pursuit of the application to the perfections.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s insatiability regarding extensive learning?

Whatever has been spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, whether here in this world-system or throughout the worlds in the ten directions, the insatiability that thinks, "I shall master all of that," is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s insatiability regarding extensive learning.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s exposition of the gift of the Dharma free from worldly motives?
It is when the bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches the Dharma.
By means of that skill in the gift of Dharma, he does not even expect his own enlightenment;
this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s exposition of the non-material gift of Dharma.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s dedication of roots of merit for the purification of a buddha-field, by which roots of merit—
By purifying the Buddha-field through roots of merit, one purifies the minds of oneself and others;
that which is the dedication of those roots of merit is called the "dedication of the roots of merit for purifying the Buddha-field" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the "inexhaustibility of immeasurable saṃsāra" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

The support of the roots of virtue: being supported by those roots of virtue, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field, and never falls into weariness until he has fulfilled all dharmas and omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s indefatigability throughout immeasurable saṃsāra.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s establishment of moral shame and dread of blame?
It is the state of loathing all thoughts of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s establishment of moral shame and dread of blame.

In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of dwelling in the forest? It is that which transcends all the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of dwelling in the forest. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s fewness of desires?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not even desire awakening, this is called the "fewness of wishes" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the "contentment" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not even conceive pride regarding omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is called the "contentment" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of the ascetic qualities (*dhūtaguṇa*) and refinement (*saṃlekha*)?
That which is profound reflection and patience regarding deep dharmas—this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of the ascetic qualities and refinement. In that regard:
What is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of training?
It is the non-occurrence of all trainings; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-abandonment of training.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s loathing for the qualities of sensual pleasure?

The non-arising of a mind of desire is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s revulsion toward the qualities of sensual pleasure. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s production of the thought of awakening accompanied by world-weariness?
The non-conditioning of all phenomena is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s production of the thought of awakening accompanied by world-weariness.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s relinquishment of all things?
It is the non-appropriation of internal and external phenomena; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s relinquishment of all things.

In that regard, what is the non-dejected state of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is when his mind does not become dejected amidst the stations of consciousness; this is called the non-dejected state of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s lack of dependence on any thing?
That state of non-mental engagement with all things is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s lack of regard for all things.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of intimacy with householders? It is that which [arises from] the Buddha—

22013. Transmigrating from one field to another buddha-field, obtaining birth by transformation, and shaving the head and donning the saffron robes—this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of intimacy with householders.
22014. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of intimacy with monks and nuns?
It is when [one does not associate] together with a monk or a nun.
It does not remain for even the duration of a finger-snap, nor does he give rise to a mind of distress without them;
this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of intimacy with monks and nuns.
In that regard, how should the bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid stinginess regarding families?
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate the following thought:
"Whatever provision for the happiness of all sentient beings must be made by me, therein they [shall find it]."
"Sentient beings are happy through their own merits alone; I should not give rise to a mind of envy toward this. This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s avoidance of envy regarding family.
In that regard, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva avoid places of social distraction?"

Wherever a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while situated in a place of social gathering, might have discourse associated with the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, or should give rise to a thought associated therewith, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not remain there.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of places of social distraction.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid self-exaltation?
That which is the non-perception of internal phenomena—this is what must be avoided by the bodhisattva mahāsattva regarding self-exaltation.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of disparaging others? Namely, [the non-perception] of external phenomena.
This thorough observation is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of disparaging others.
In that regard, how [should] a bodhisattva mahāsattva [regard] the ten unwholesome paths of action?
They must be avoided;
for these create obstacles to the Noble Path, let alone to a good rebirth or to perfect enlightenment. Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must avoid the ten unwholesome paths of action.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid overweening pride?
For he does not perceive any dharma at all; how much less so anything superior by which he might be proud?
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should avoid overweening pride. Furthermore, Subhūti, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid arrogance?
It is because he does not perceive any such entity wherein [arrogance might arise].
Subhūti, in this way a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should indeed give rise to [the realization of] arrogance; for it is in this manner that arrogance must be avoided by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
In that regard, Subhūti, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva avoid the perversions?
Based on the non-apprehension of all things,
Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should completely avoid the perversions.
In that regard, Subhūti, how [should one proceed]?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva must avoid doubt;
for he perceives all phenomena as being free from uncertainty. Thus, Subhūti, must a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid doubt.
In that regard, Subhūti, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid the endurance of passion, hatred, and delusion?
It is because he does not perceive any objective basis for passion, hatred, and delusion. Thus...
For indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must avoid the endurance of passion, hatred, and delusion.

In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the six dharmas? Namely, the six perfections: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom. These six perfections are to be fulfilled.
They are to be fulfilled.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid six things?
Namely, the mind of a śrāvaka.
It should be avoided.
For what reason?
Because this is not the path to awakening.
The mind of a pratyekabuddha should be avoided. Why is that? Because this is not the path to awakening.
One should not harbor a mind of regret.
Why is that? Because this is not the path to awakening.
Upon seeing a beggar...
One should not give rise to a dejected mind.
Why is that? Because this is not the path to awakening;
even after relinquishing all one's possessions, one should not be despondent.
[This] occurs. Why is that? Because this is not the path to awakening.
One must not cause distraction by means of a petitioner.
Why is that? Because this is not the path to awakening.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not grasp at a self?
For what reason?
For in this way, since the self does not exist at all, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form a grasping for a self; likewise,
he should not form a grasping for a sentient being, a grasping for a soul, or a grasping for a person.

For what reason? Because these do not exist at all; thus, one should not grasp at a being (*sattva*), a life-principle (*jīva*), or a person (*pudgala*). In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid grasping at annihilation (*uccheda*)?
For what reason? Because indeed no phenomenon whatsoever is annihilated;
since all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, there is no annihilation. Thus, one should not form a grasping for annihilation.
In this regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid grasping at permanence?
For what reason? Because that dharma which is not produced cannot be permanent. Thus, one should not grasp at permanence.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not give rise to the perception of signs?
For what reason? Because, in an ultimate sense, affliction does not exist at all; thus, the perception of signs should not be produced.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not form a view of causes? For what reason? Because he does not perceive that view.
Thus, a view of causes should not be formed. Thus...
One should not form an attachment to the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-fields.
Why is that? Because those phenomena do not exist by way of their own intrinsic nature.
Thus, one should not form an attachment to the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid forming an attachment to the triple world?
For what reason? Because the intrinsic nature of the triple world does not exist;
thus, one should not form an attachment to the triple world.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not form an attachment to the three realms?
For what reason? Because that object is not apprehended.
Thus, one should not form an attachment to the three realms.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not form an attachment (*ālaya*) to the triple world?
For what reason?
Because it is precisely due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) that one should not form an attachment to the triple world in this way.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not rely upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
For what reason? Because it is not by relying on the view of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha that there is the vision of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
In this way, one should not rely on views regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not rely on views regarding ethical discipline?
For what reason? Because purity of ethical discipline does not arise from reliance on views regarding ethical discipline; thus, one should not rely on views regarding ethical discipline.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva engage in dispute concerning emptiness?
It should not be done.
For what reason? Because all phenomena are empty by their own nature, not by means of emptiness.
Thus, there is no dispute regarding emptiness.
It should not be done.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid contradicting emptiness?
For what reason? Because all phenomena are empty, but emptiness is not [a phenomenon].
[He] contradicts emptiness.
Thus, one must not contradict emptiness.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill emptiness?
Based on the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the fulfillment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed the fulfillment of emptiness; thus should emptiness be fulfilled.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s realization of the signless (*animitta-sākṣātkriyā*)?
That is to say, the state of non-attention toward all signs;
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s realization of the signless.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the wishless? It is the non-abiding of the mind within the entire triple world;
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the wishless.
In that regard, what is the purification of the three spheres for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is precisely the purification of the ten paths of wholesome action; such is the purification of the three spheres for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring to fulfillment compassion and pity toward all sentient beings?
It is by the attainment of great compassion.
In this way, one should bring to fulfillment compassion and pity for all sentient beings.
In that regard, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva not despise any sentient being?
Namely, through loving-kindness (maitrī).
For the sake of fulfillment. Thus, all sentient beings must not be despised.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s vision of equality? It is this:
namely, neither adding nor subtracting.
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s vision of the equality of all phenomena.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s penetration of the true method?
It is the non-penetration of all phenomena.
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s penetration of the true method.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding non-arising?
It is that which, for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena, [remains patient].
This patience regarding the absence of volitional construction is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience regarding non-arising.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of non-arising?
It is that which [is free from] name-and-form—
This is the knowledge of non-arising for a bodhisattva mahāsattva—[this is] the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of non-arising].
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s teaching on the single principle? It is the state of non-dual manifestation; this is it.
{This is the teaching on the single principle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.} In that regard,

{what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s eradication of conceptual construction?} It is the conceptual construction of all phenomena; this is {the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s eradication of conceptual construction}.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s turning away from perception and views?
It is the state of turning away from perception and views regarding the levels of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s turning away from perception and views.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s reversal of the afflictions?
It is the relinquishing of all afflictions along with their residual impressions and continuities; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s reversal of the afflictions.
In that regard, what is the stage of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
That which is the knowledge of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā-jñāna*)—this is the stage of calm abiding and insight of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the state of a tamed mind (*dānta-cittatā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
That which is non-delight in the three realms—
this is the tamed state of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the unimpeded [state] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Knowledge is the attainment of the Buddha-eye;
this is the unimpeded knowledge of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the removal of attachment?
That equanimity which pertains to the six sense-bases is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of how to withdraw from attachment.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s going to whichever field he desires?
That which does not move from a single buddha-field yet appears in all buddha-fields, and yet no perception of a "buddha-field" arises in him—
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s going to whichever field he desires.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s manifestation of his own body everywhere?
It is the manifestation of his own body within whichever assembly circle [he appears]. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s manifestation of his own body everywhere.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s penetration into the mental conduct of all sentient beings?
It is the knowledge of the mental conduct of all sentient beings by means of a single mind.
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s penetration into the mental conduct of all sentient beings.

In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s sport of the superknowledges (*abhijñāvikrīḍanā*)? It is when, sporting by means of these superknowledges, he travels from buddha-field to buddha-field in order to behold the Buddhas, yet he does not form the conceptual notion of a "Buddha."
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s sport of the superknowledges (*abhijñāvikrīḍanā*).
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of a buddha-field exactly as it has been seen?
It is that which [extends throughout] the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system...

The state of non-conceptualization regarding the renunciation of all world-systems by one who has become a sovereign wheel-turning monarch of a world-system—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of a buddha-field exactly as it has been seen.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attendance upon the Buddhas? It is that attendance upon the Buddhas which is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attendance upon the Buddhas.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s correct contemplation of the Buddha-body?
It is the correct contemplation of the Dharma-body as it truly is.
...this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s correct analytical observation of the Buddha-body.
In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties? It is that which, abiding in the ten powers, [perceives them].
The wisdom and knowledge regarding the perfection of the faculties of all sentient beings—
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s [knowledge of] the purification of the buddha-field?

Purification: that which is the purification of the minds of all sentient beings—this is the purification of the Buddha-field of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. In that regard, what is the illusion-like [samādhi] of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
This is the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like concentration). Abiding in this concentration, one performs all activities, yet there is no movement of the mind.
In that regard, what is the *abhīkṣṇa-samāpatti* (frequent attainment) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
That which is the maturation-born samādhi of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s frequent attainment.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s intentional assumption of a physical existence? It is when the bodhisattva...

In whatever way the roots of virtue of sentient beings reach full completion, in that very way the bodhisattva mahāsattva intentionally takes up a physical form. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s intentional taking up of a physical form.
In that regard, what is the infinite vow of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is when the bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the fulfillment of the six perfections, in whatever way...
In whatever way he makes a vow, it is fulfilled accordingly.
This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s infinite vow.
In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s [knowledge of] the sounds of all sentient beings?

The knowledge by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), penetrates the speech of gods and others— this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the speech of all sentient beings. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfected eloquence (*paripūrṇa-pratibhāna*)?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva penetrates the knowledge of teaching with perfected eloquence through the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*),
this is the perfected eloquence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the perfection of the descent into the womb of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Here, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is born by spontaneous generation (*upapāduka*) in all his births. This is...
The perfection of the descent into the womb of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the perfection of the family of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is born into great kṣatriya families or great brāhmaṇa families.
Or he is reborn into great *śāla* families;
this is the perfection of family of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the perfection of lineage (*gotra*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is reborn into that lineage from which previous bodhisattvas have arisen,
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of lineage.
In that regard, what is the perfection of the retinue of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having established sentient beings in awakening, possesses a retinue consisting solely of bodhisattvas; this is the perfection of the retinue of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the excellence of birth of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is when, as soon as he is born, the bodhisattva mahāsattva pervades all world-systems with his radiance and causes them all to tremble in six ways.
This is the perfection of birth of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, what is the perfection of the great departure of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is when the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having gone forth, [goes] together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings.
He departs from his home; this is the perfection of the Great Bodhisattva’s Great Departure.
In that regard, what is the perfection of the array of the Bodhi tree of the Great Bodhisattva?
It is that which belongs to the Bodhisattva...
The root of the Bodhi tree of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is made of gold; its trunk is made of lapis lazuli;
