its branches are composed of all kinds of jewels, and its leaves are likewise composed of all kinds of jewels. The fragrance and radiance of that tree’s flowers pervade infinite world-systems with their light. This is the perfection of the array of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s Bodhi tree.
In that regard, what is the perfection of the complete fulfillment of all qualities for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is that which consists in the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s maturation of sentient beings and the [purification of] the buddha-field.
This purity is the perfection of the complete fulfillment of all qualities of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
In that regard, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the tenth stage should be called a Tathāgata?
It is when the ten perfections of the bodhisattva mahāsattva are fulfilled, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

The qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*) become perfected, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*) is attained, the afflictions along with their latencies and continuities (*sarvavāsanānusandhikleśa*) are abandoned, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) arises, and all the qualities of a Buddha become perfected.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva...
Furthermore, a Mahāsattva beyond the tenth Bodhisattva stage is to be called a Tathāgata.
In that regard, what are the ten stages of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
They are those [stages] through which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of skill in means...

Practicing in all the perfections, trained in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, practicing in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments, practicing in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,

[he traverses] the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from passion, the stage of one who has completed what was to be done, and the stage of the Śrāvaka—

Having transcended the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the stage of the bodhisattva—having transcended these nine stages—the bodhisattva mahāsattva is established in the stage of a Buddha. This, Subhūti, is the tenth stage of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; in this way, indeed, the bodhisattva mahāsattva has set out upon the Mahāyāna.
[Thus ends the equipment for the stages.
Furthermore, as for what Subhūti said:
"From where will that vehicle set forth?"—it sets forth from the triple world.

He will go by way of that which is all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), and he will abide therein through the yoga of non-duality. Why is that? Because both the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) and all-aspect omniscience—these two dharmas—are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely: [the characteristic of emptiness].
These two are characterized by suchness. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, there are no two phenomena without characteristics that have emerged, are emerging, or will emerge from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).

Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from the signless dharmas would likewise desire the departure from suchness, from the limit of reality, from the inconceivable realm, from the realm of space,
from the realm of abandonment, from the limit of dispassion, from non-arising, from non-ceasing, and from non-existence.
Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure from the emptiness of form;

whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure from the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of mental formations, and the emptiness of consciousness. Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would [desire the departure] from them.

For what reason? Subhūti, it is because the emptiness of form will not depart from the triple world, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects; [the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of mental formations,] and the emptiness of consciousness will not depart from the triple world, nor will they abide in the knowledge of all aspects. For what reason?
For this reason, Subhūti, form is empty of form;
feeling is empty of feeling; perception is empty of perception; mental formations are empty of mental formations.
Subhūti, one who would desire the departure from the emptiness of the eye would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks.

In this way, Subhūti, one who desires the departure from the emptiness of the ear, the emptiness of the nose, the emptiness of the tongue, the emptiness of the body, and the emptiness of the mind, would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks.
Likewise for the emptiness of form, the emptiness of sound, the emptiness of odor, the emptiness of taste, the emptiness of the tangible, and the emptiness of mental objects.
The emptiness of eye-consciousness, the emptiness of ear-consciousness, the emptiness of nose-consciousness, the emptiness of tongue-consciousness,
the emptiness of body-consciousness, the emptiness of mind-consciousness; the emptiness of eye-contact, the emptiness of ear-contact,
the emptiness of nose-contact, the emptiness of tongue-contact, the emptiness of body-contact, and the emptiness of mind-contact.
Subhūti, one who would desire the departure from the emptiness of feeling born of eye-contact, the emptiness of feeling born of ear-contact, the emptiness of feeling born of nose-contact,
the emptiness of feeling born of tongue-contact, the emptiness of feeling born of body-contact,
and the emptiness of feeling born of mind-contact, would desire the departure from dharmas that are without marks.
For what reason? Subhūti,
it is because the emptiness of the eye will not depart from the triple world, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.

In this way, neither the emptiness of the ear, nor the emptiness of the nose, nor the emptiness of the tongue, nor the emptiness of the body, nor the emptiness of the mind will emerge from the three realms, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Likewise, neither the emptiness of form, nor the emptiness of sound, nor the emptiness of odor, nor the emptiness of taste, nor the emptiness of the tangible, nor the emptiness of phenomena will emerge from the three realms, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.

In this way, neither the emptiness of eye-consciousness, nor the emptiness of ear-consciousness, nor the emptiness of nose-consciousness, nor the emptiness of tongue-consciousness, nor the emptiness of body-consciousness, nor the emptiness of mind-consciousness will depart from the three realms, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Likewise, neither the emptiness of eye-contact, nor the emptiness of ear-contact, nor the emptiness of nose-contact [will do so].

Neither the emptiness of tongue-contact, nor the emptiness of body-contact, nor the emptiness of mind-contact will go forth from the three realms, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Likewise, neither the emptiness of feeling born of eye-contact, nor the emptiness of feeling born of ear-contact, nor the emptiness of feeling born of nose-contact, nor the emptiness of feeling born of tongue-contact [will do so].
The emptiness of the feeling born of body-contact does not depart from the three realms, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that?

For in this way, Subhūti, the eye is empty of the eye; the ear is empty of the ear; the nose is empty of the nose; the tongue is empty of the tongue; the body is empty of the body; the mind is empty of the mind.
Form is empty of form; sound is empty of sound; odor is empty of odor; taste is empty of taste.

Tangible objects are empty of tangible objects; phenomena are empty of phenomena; eye-consciousness is empty of eye-consciousness; ear-consciousness is empty of ear-consciousness; nose-consciousness is empty of nose-consciousness;
tongue-consciousness is empty of tongue-consciousness; body-consciousness is empty of body-consciousness; and mind-consciousness is empty of mind-consciousness.

Eye-contact is empty of mental consciousness; ear-contact is empty of eye-contact; nose-contact is empty of ear-contact; tongue-contact is empty of nose-contact; body-contact is empty of tongue-contact;
mind-contact is empty of body-contact; and that which is born of eye-contact is empty of mind-contact.
Feeling is empty of the feeling born of eye-contact; the feeling born of ear-contact is empty of the feeling born of ear-contact;

the feeling born of nose-contact is empty of the feeling born of nose-contact; the feeling born of tongue-contact is empty of the feeling born of tongue-contact; the feeling born of body-contact is empty of the feeling born of body-contact.

Feeling born of mental contact is empty of feeling born of mental contact; feeling born of mental contact is empty of feeling born of mental contact. Subhūti, one who would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of a dream.
This should be explained in detail.
Likewise, [the same applies] to a mirage, an illusion, an echo, a reflection, a shadow, a reflected image, a city of the Gandharvas, and a Tathāgata’s emanation.
Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of signless phenomena would desire the departure of that which has no signs.
Why is that?
Subhūti, it is because the intrinsic nature of a dream does not depart from the triple world.
He will not abide in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Likewise, there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a mirage, no intrinsic nature of an illusion, no intrinsic nature of an echo, no intrinsic nature of a reflection, no intrinsic nature of an image, and no intrinsic nature of a *gandharva*-city; nor is there [an intrinsic nature] of suchness (*tathatā*).
The intrinsic nature of that which has gone forth as a transformation will depart from the triple world and will not abide in omniscience.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of a dream is empty of the intrinsic nature of a dream; [likewise] the intrinsic nature of a mirage...

The nature of a mirage is empty of the nature of a mirage; the nature of an illusion is empty of the nature of an illusion; the nature of an echo is empty of the nature of an echo; the nature of an optical illusion is empty of the nature of an optical illusion;
the nature of a reflection is empty of the nature of a reflection; the nature of a city of the Gandharvas is empty of the nature of a city of the Gandharvas; and the emanation of a Tathāgata—
Intrinsic nature is empty of the intrinsic nature of a Tathāgata’s emanation. [Thus ends the antidote to the first conceptualization of the object on the path of seeing.]
"Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of the perfection of giving would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks.

Likewise, Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks."
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, that which is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of giving will not depart from the triple world, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.
In this same way, it is so for the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
For indeed, that which is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom will not depart from the three realms, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is that?
For in this way, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity;
the intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline.
The intrinsic nature of the perfection of patience is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of patience;
the intrinsic nature of the perfection of vigor is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of vigor;
the intrinsic nature of the perfection of meditative concentration is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of meditative concentration.
Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure from internal emptiness.
Why is that?
For the intrinsic nature of internal emptiness does not depart from the triple world, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is that?
For in this way, Subhūti, internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness;
external emptiness is empty of external emptiness; internal-external emptiness is empty of internal-external emptiness, and so on, up to...

The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is empty of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; the foundations of mindfulness are empty of the foundations of mindfulness; the right efforts are empty of the right efforts; the bases of psychic power are empty of the bases of psychic power;
the faculties are empty of the faculties; the powers are empty of the powers; the factors of enlightenment are empty of the factors of enlightenment.
The path is empty of the path; the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments are empty of the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata are empty of the ten powers of a Tathāgata; the four grounds of self-confidence are empty of the four grounds of self-confidence; the four analytical knowledges are empty of the four analytical knowledges.
For it is thus, Subhūti: the Buddha-dharmas are empty of Buddha-dharmas.
[Thus ends the second section on the conceptualization of the apprehended object within the path of vision.
Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from phenomena that are without marks would desire the departure of an Arhat.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, that which is the intrinsic nature of an arhat will not emerge from the triple world,
nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of an Arhat is empty of the intrinsic nature of an Arhat.
"Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of a pratyekabuddha, he would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks.
Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, he would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks.
Subhūti, whoever would desire the departure of a Tathāgata, he would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks. [Stream-enterer...]
"Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from the fruit of stream-entry would desire the departure from dharmas that are without marks.

Likewise, Subhūti, he who would desire the departure from the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects, would desire the departure from dharmas that are without marks."
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, that which is the intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry will not depart from the triple world, nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.
For what reason? Because...

The intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry. Likewise, the intrinsic nature of the fruit of once-returning, the intrinsic nature of the fruit of non-returning, the intrinsic nature of arhatship, and the intrinsic nature of pratyekabuddhahood— [are all empty].
That which is the intrinsic nature of Buddhahood, that which is the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the path, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects—
none of these will emerge from the three realms, nor will they abide in the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is that?
For thus, the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects is empty of the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects.
[Thus ends the antidote to the first conceptualization of the grasper on the path of seeing.
Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of names would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks.
Likewise, Subhūti, he who would desire the departure of signs, conventions, designations, and conceptual constructs would desire the departure of dharmas that are without marks.
For what reason?

Because, Subhūti, that which is the intrinsic nature of a name will not emerge from the three realms, nor will it abide in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). For what reason? Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of a name is empty of the intrinsic nature of a name.

Thus, whatever is the intrinsic nature of conventional designation, whatever is the intrinsic nature of worldly discourse, and whatever is the intrinsic nature of conceptual description— that will not emerge from the three realms,
nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.
For what reason?
Because that which has the nature of a designation is empty of the nature of a designation.
The nature of non-arising is empty of the nature of non-arising;
the nature of non-ceasing is empty of the nature of non-ceasing; for likewise, the nature of non-conditioning is empty of the nature of non-conditioning.
For in this way, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna will not depart from the triple world,
nor will it abide in the knowledge of all aspects.
That vehicle is immovable.
[Thus, in the path of seeing,
this is the antidote to the second conceptualization of the grasper.
Furthermore, as for what Subhūti has said:
"Where will that vehicle abide? "That vehicle will not abide anywhere. For what reason?"
For thus, Subhūti, all dharmas are non-abiding.
Moreover, Subhūti,
that vehicle will abide in a state of non-abiding, not by way of abiding.
Just as, Subhūti, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) neither stands nor does not stand,
even so, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle neither stands nor does not stand.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, non-arising, non-ceasing, non-defilement, non-purification, and non-conditioning are neither abiding nor non-abiding;
even so, Subhūti, [is this].
That Mahāyāna is neither abiding nor non-abiding.
For, Subhūti, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is empty of the realm of phenomena. Why is that?
For indeed, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm neither abides nor does not abide.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm is empty of the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm.
Thus, non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, non-purification, and non-conditioning are empty by virtue of non-conditioning.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of non-conditioning neither abides nor does not abide.
Or [it is not so]. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the nature of non-conditioning is empty of the nature of non-conditioning.
For in this way, Subhūti, that vehicle will not abide anywhere; it is unestablished by virtue of the principle of non-abiding and by virtue of the principle of immovability.
[Thus ends the antidote to the first conceptualization regarding the object of apprehension on the path of cultivation.
Furthermore, as for what Subhūti said:
"Who will set out by means of that vehicle?"
No one at all shall set forth by means of that vehicle.
For what reason?

For it is thus, Subhūti: that vehicle by which one will set forth, he who will set forth, and that from which one will set forth—all these phenomena do not exist. Since all phenomena are thus non-existent, what phenomenon will set forth by means of what phenomenon? That...
For what reason?

Because, Subhūti, neither a self is apprehended, nor a sentient being, nor a living soul, nor a nourisher, nor a person, nor an individual, nor a human, nor a youth, nor an agent, nor an experiencer, nor a knower, nor a seer is apprehended, on account of the absolute purity of the self. And so it continues, up to...
Based on the absolute purity of the seer, the dharmadhātu is not apprehended, because of its absolute purity. Likewise, non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, non-purification,
and non-conditioning are not apprehended, because of their absolute purity.
The aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are not apprehended, on account of their absolute purity;
dependent origination is not apprehended, on account of its absolute purity;
the perfection of generosity is not apprehended, on account of its absolute purity.

In this way, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom are not apprehended, by reason of their absolute purity. Internal emptiness is not apprehended, by reason of its absolute purity.
Up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, it is not apprehended on account of its absolute purity;
the applications of mindfulness are not apprehended on account of their absolute purity;
the right efforts are not apprehended on account of their absolute purity.
The bases of psychic power are not apprehended, by reason of their ultimate purity; the faculties are not apprehended, by reason of their ultimate purity;
the powers are not apprehended, by reason of their ultimate purity.
The factors of enlightenment are not apprehended, by virtue of their absolute purity;
the path is not apprehended, by virtue of its absolute purity;
the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments are not apprehended, by virtue of their absolute purity.
The ten powers of a Tathāgata are not apprehended, by virtue of their absolute purity;
the four grounds of self-confidence are not apprehended, by virtue of their absolute purity;
the four analytical knowledges are not apprehended, by virtue of their absolute purity.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not apprehended, by virtue of their absolute purity;
the Arhat is not apprehended, by virtue of his absolute purity;
the Pratyekabuddha is not apprehended, by virtue of his absolute purity.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is not apprehended, by virtue of ultimate purity;
the Tathāgata is not apprehended, by virtue of ultimate purity;
the fruit of stream-entry is not apprehended, by virtue of ultimate purity.
The fruit of once-returning is not apprehended on account of ultimate purity;
the fruit of non-returning is not apprehended on account of ultimate purity;
arhatship is not apprehended on account of ultimate purity.
Pratyekabodhi is not apprehended on account of its absolute purity;
mārgajñatā is not apprehended on account of its absolute purity;
sarvākārajñatā is not apprehended on account of its absolute purity.
The stage of the Joyous (*pramuditā bhūmi*) is not apprehended, on account of its absolute purity; likewise [are] the Immaculate (*vimalā*), the Radiant (*prabhākarī*), the Luminous (*arciṣmatī*),

the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), the Facing (*abhimukhī*), the Far-Reaching (*duraṅgamā*), the Immovable (*acalā*), the Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), and the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*) stages.
It is not apprehended on account of its absolute purity;
its prior limit is not apprehended on account of its absolute purity;
its posterior limit is not apprehended on account of its absolute purity.
The present is not apprehended, by virtue of its absolute purity;
likewise, coming is not apprehended,
and going is not apprehended.
Abiding is not apprehended, passing away is not apprehended, rebirth is not apprehended, decline is not apprehended, and supernatural power is not apprehended,
by virtue of absolute purity.
Through the non-apprehension of what is it that [these] are not apprehended?
It is not apprehended because the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is unapprehendable.
For what reason?
Subhūti, it is because the realm of phenomena is not apprehended; it is not apprehended by way of non-apprehension.
Through the non-apprehension of non-arising, non-ceasing, non-defilement, non-purification, and non-conditioning, conditioning is not apprehended.
Through the non-apprehension of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are not apprehended.
Through the non-apprehension of dependent origination, dependent origination is not apprehended. [The same applies to] the perfection of generosity...
Because the perfection of generosity is not apprehended, the perfection of generosity is not apprehended;

because the perfection of ethical discipline is not apprehended, the perfection of ethical discipline is not apprehended; because the perfection of patience is not apprehended, the perfection of patience is not apprehended; because the perfection of vigor is not apprehended, the perfection of vigor is not apprehended; because the perfection of meditative concentration is not apprehended...

The perfection of meditation is not apprehended because the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended; the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended because internal emptiness is not apprehended; internal emptiness is not apprehended because external emptiness is not apprehended;
external emptiness is not apprehended because internal-and-external emptiness is not apprehended; internal-and-external emptiness is not apprehended.

To the extent that the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; the applications of mindfulness are not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the applications of mindfulness; the right efforts are not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the right efforts;
the bases of psychic power are not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the bases of psychic power; and the faculties are not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the faculties.
The powers are not apprehended because of the non-apprehension of the powers; the factors of enlightenment are not apprehended because of the non-apprehension of the factors of enlightenment;

the path is not apprehended because of the non-apprehension of the path; the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments are not apprehended because of the non-apprehension of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments; and the ten powers of a Tathāgata are not apprehended because of the non-apprehension of the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

Through the non-apprehension of the four fearlessnesses, the four fearlessnesses are not apprehended; through the non-apprehension of the analytical knowledges, the four analytical knowledges are not apprehended;
[and] through the non-apprehension of the Buddha-qualities...
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not apprehended.
[Thus ends the antidote to the second conceptualization of the object of apprehension on the path of cultivation.
The stream-enterer is not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the stream-enterer.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, a stream-enterer is not apprehended, by virtue of absolute purity.

In this way, the once-returner is not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the once-returner; the non-returner is not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the non-returner; the arhat is not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the arhat; the pratyekabuddha is not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the pratyekabuddha; and so on, up to the Tathāgata, who is not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the Tathāgata.
Why is that?
For this reason, Subhūti, the Tathāgata is not apprehended, on account of absolute purity. [Thus ends the antidote to the first conceptualization of the grasper on the path of cultivation.
The fruit of stream-entry is not apprehended because the fruit of stream-entry is not apprehended.

In this way, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, the state of a pratyekabuddha, the state of a bodhisattva, and the state of a buddha are not apprehended because a buddha is not apprehended.
Thus is the stage of the Joyous (pramuditā).
The stage is not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the stage—namely, the Vimalā, Prabhākarī, Arciṣmatī, Sudurjayā, Abhimukhī, Duraṅgamā, Acalā, Sādhumatī, and Dharmameghā stages;
the Dharmameghā stage is not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the stage, by virtue of its absolute purity.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the ten stages are not apprehended through the non-apprehension of the stages.
What are the ten? The stage of bright insight,

the stage of the lineage, the stage of the eighth person, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from passion, the stage of one who has completed what was to be done, and the stage of the solitary realizer—
The stage of a Buddha, the stage of a Bodhisattva, the stage of a Buddha:
by way of internal emptiness, the first stage is not apprehended;
by way of external emptiness, the first stage is not apprehended.
By means of internal-external emptiness, the first stage is not apprehended;
up to and including by means of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, the first stage is not apprehended,
and so on up to the tenth stage.
By means of internal emptiness, the tenth stage is not apprehended;
by means of external emptiness, the tenth stage is not apprehended;
by means of internal-and-external emptiness, the tenth stage is not apprehended.

Up to the tenth stage, which is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, is not apprehended on account of its absolute purity; the ripening of sentient beings is not apprehended through internal emptiness,
nor is the ripening of sentient beings apprehended through external emptiness.
By means of internal-and-external emptiness, the ripening of sentient beings is not apprehended;
up to and including by means of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, the ripening of sentient beings is not apprehended, on account of ultimate purity.
By means of internal emptiness, the Buddha-field—
Purification is not apprehended; by means of external emptiness, the purification of the Buddha-field is not apprehended;
by means of internal-external emptiness, the purification of the Buddha-field is not apprehended;
and so on, up to: by means of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, the purification of the Buddha-field is not apprehended, on account of its absolute purity.
By means of internal emptiness, the five eyes are not apprehended;
by means of external emptiness, the five eyes are not apprehended;
by means of internal-and-external emptiness, the five eyes are not apprehended.
Up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, the five eyes are not apprehended, by reason of their absolute purity.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the yoga of non-apprehension of all phenomena, shall go forth toward the knowledge of all aspects by means of the Mahāyāna.
[Thus ends] the second conceptualization of the grasper on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and its antidote.
[Thus ends the practice of the accumulations.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"The Great Vehicle, the Great Vehicle—"
"O Blessed One, it is said:
'Having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, it will go forth'; therefore it is called the Mahāyāna."
That vehicle is equal to space. Just as, Blessed One, there is room in space for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings, even so—
"O Blessed One, in this Mahāyāna there is room for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings. For it is thus, O Blessed One, that the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva is;
just as, O Blessed One, [there is room] in space."
Nor is any coming seen, nor any going, nor is any staying seen.
In this very way, Blessed One, for this Great Vehicle, no coming is seen, no going, and no staying is perceived.
"Just as, Blessed One, no beginning of space is perceived, no end of space is perceived, and no middle of space is perceived, because of the equality of the time periods;
even so, Blessed One, for this Great Vehicle, no beginning is perceived, no end is perceived, and no middle is perceived, because of the equality of the time periods."
"Based on this, Blessed One, this Great Vehicle is called the 'Great Vehicle.
The Blessed One said:
'So it is, Subhūti; this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.'"

These six perfections—Subhūti, the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom—this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, all the gateways of dhāraṇīs and all the samādhis.
The Śūraṅgama samādhi should be explained in detail, up to the samādhi that is unattached, like space, liberated, and unstained. Subhūti, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, internal emptiness and external emptiness.

"Subhūti, from internal-external emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence—this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, and the five faculties."
The five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four analytical knowledges, the four grounds of self-confidence,
the six superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— Subhūti, this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, as for what Subhūti has said:
"That vehicle will set out having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras."
And what is the world with its gods, humans, and asuras? It is namely the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), the realm of form (rūpadhātu), and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
If, Subhūti, the realm of desire were suchness (tathatā), non-falsity (avitathatā), and non-otherness—
Suchness is non-erroneous, real, the truth, just as it is; it is eternal, stable, perpetual, and of an unchanging nature.
If it were a future entity and not a non-entity, this Mahāyāna would not have emerged, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Therefore, Subhūti, because the desire realm is imagined, constructed, and displayed as being unreal—
being entirely impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and non-existent— this Great Vehicle will emerge, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Subhūti, if the suchness of the form-realm (rūpadhātu)— its non-falsity, its non-otherness, its non-perversion, its reality, its truth,
and its being as it is— were an entity that is eternal, stable, perpetual, and of an unchanging nature, rather than a non-entity,
then this Great Vehicle would not transcend and emerge from the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

Therefore, Subhūti, because the realm of form is imagined, constructed, and displayed as it is not— being entirely impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and non-existent— this Great Vehicle will emerge, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Subhūti, if the formless realm were suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness, the unerring, the real, the truth,

as it is— permanent, stable, eternal, and of an unchanging nature, being an existent and not a non-existent— then this Mahāyāna would not have surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras and gone forth from it.
Therefore, Subhūti, because the formless realm is conceptualized, constructed, and displayed as being unreal—
being entirely impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and non-existent— this Great Vehicle will go forth, surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
"Subhūti, if form were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the non-erroneous, the real, the truth, the state of things as they are—

eternal, stable, perpetual, and of an unchanging nature— and were an existent thing rather than a non-existent thing, then this Great Vehicle would not transcend and depart from the world with its gods, humans, and asuras."

Therefore, Subhūti, because form is imagined, fabricated, and displayed as something unreal— being entirely impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and non-existent— it is for this reason that this Great Vehicle will emerge, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
In the same way, Subhūti, if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the unerring, the real, the truth,
as it is— permanent, stable, eternal, of an unchanging nature, an existent thing and not a non-existent thing— then this [teaching] would not exist.
The Mahāyāna will emerge, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. For this reason, Subhūti, because consciousness is imagined, fabricated, displayed, and shown to be unreal—
being entirely impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and non-existent— therefore this Mahāyāna surpasses the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
It will emerge having transcended the world.

Subhūti, if the eye were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the non-perverted, the real, the truth, as it is— permanent, stable, eternal, and of an unchanging nature, being an existent rather than a non-existent— then this Great Vehicle would not exist at all.

It will emerge having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. For this reason, Subhūti, because the eye is imagined, fabricated, and displayed as being unreal— being entirely impermanent, unstable, non-eternal,
subject to transformation, and a non-entity— therefore this Great Vehicle surpasses the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Having transcended the world, it will emerge.
It is the same for the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body.
If, Subhūti, the mind is suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the non-perverted, the real, the truth, and as-it-is;

If there were an entity that was eternal, stable, perpetual, and of an unchanging nature, it would be a non-entity; this Mahāyāna would not have emerged, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. But since, Subhūti, the mind is conceptualized, fabricated, manifested, and shown to be unreal—all is impermanent.
It is unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and characterized by non-existence; therefore, this Mahāyāna shall emerge having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Subhūti, if form were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the non-perverted, the real, the truth, and reality as it is—

If there were an entity that was permanent, stable, eternal, and of an unchanging nature, it would be a non-entity rather than an entity; this Mahāyāna would not have emerged, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. But since, Subhūti, form is imagined, fabricated, displayed, and unreal—as is all of it—it is entirely impermanent.
It is unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and characterized by non-existence; therefore, this Mahāyāna shall emerge having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
It is the same for sound, odor, taste, and the tangible.
Subhūti, if *dharma* were a real entity (*bhāva*)— if it were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the unerring, the real, the truth,

as-it-is, eternal, stable, perpetual, and of an unchanging nature— and were not a non-entity (*abhāva*), then this Mahāyāna would not transcend and emerge from the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

Therefore, Subhūti, because the Dharma is conceptualized, constructed, and demonstrated as being unreal— being entirely impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and non-existent— it is for this reason that this Mahāyāna shall go forth, surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Subhūti, if visual consciousness were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the non-perverted, the real, the truth, as it is—

being an entity that is eternal, stable, permanent, and of an unchanging nature, rather than a non-entity— then this Great Vehicle would not have transcended and departed from the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Therefore, Subhūti, because visual consciousness is imagined, fabricated, and displayed as being unreal—
being entirely impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and non-existent— this Mahāyāna will emerge, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

In the same way, [it applies to] ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness. Subhūti, if mental consciousness were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the unerring, the real, the truth,
as it is— permanent, stable, eternal, of an unchanging nature, an existent and not a non-existent— then this [teaching] would not even exist.

The Mahāyāna will emerge having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. For this reason, Subhūti, because mental consciousness is conceptualized, fabricated, and displayed as being unreal—
everything being impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and non-existent— therefore this Mahāyāna surpasses the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Having overcome the world, he will go forth.

Subhūti, if visual contact were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the non-perverted, the real, the truth, as it is, eternal, stable, perpetual, of an unchanging nature, an existent thing and not a non-existent thing; [then he would not go forth].

This Mahāyāna would not have emerged having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, were it not for the fact, Subhūti, that eye-contact is conceptualized, fabricated, and displayed as being unreal,
entirely impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and non-existent; therefore, this Mahāyāna has surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Having overcome the world, he will emerge from it.
In the same way, so it is with ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, and body-contact.
If, Subhūti, mind-contact is suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, and the unerring reality, [then it is not subject to arising or ceasing].
If reality were as it truly is—an entity that is eternal, stable, perpetual, and of an unchanging nature—then it would be a future existence and not a non-existence;
this Mahāyāna would never have emerged, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
However, Subhūti, because mental contact is conceptualized, fabricated, manifested, and is entirely unreal, [this Mahāyāna has emerged].

It is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and characterized by non-existence; therefore, this Mahāyāna shall emerge, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Subhūti, if the feeling born of eye-contact were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, and non-perversion...

If feeling born of eye-contact were real, as it truly is—eternal, stable, permanent, and of an unchanging nature; if it were to exist and not be non-existent—then this Mahāyāna would not have surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras to go forth. But since, Subhūti, feeling born of eye-contact is imagined, fabricated, and displayed as being unreal, [this Mahāyāna has surpassed the world].

"All is impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, subject to transformation, and characterized by non-existence; therefore, this Mahāyāna shall emerge, having surpassed the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
In the same way, so too are feelings born of ear-contact, feelings born of nose-contact, feelings born of tongue-contact, and feelings born of body-contact."
Subhūti, if the feeling born of mental contact were suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the unerring, the real, the truth,
as it is— permanent, stable, eternal, and of an unchanging nature, being an entity and not a non-entity—
then this Great Vehicle would not transcend and emerge from the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

For it is thus, Subhūti, that in this Mahāyāna there is room for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the self, and so forth, up to all dharmas—all these are non-apprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of the self and sentient beings, the non-existence of the knower and the seer should be understood.
To the extent that there is the non-existence of one who knows and sees,
so too should the non-existence of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, be understood.
By the existence of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, the non-existence of space is to be understood;
by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be understood;
and by the non-existence of the Mahāyāna, the non-existence of the immeasurable, the incalculable, and the infinite is to be understood.
Through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be understood.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings.
Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: the self, up to and including all dharmas—all these are non-apprehendable.

Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of the self and sentient beings, up to the non-existence of the knower and the seer, [all things] are to be known; and by the non-existence of the knower and the seer, [the same applies].
The non-existence of the foundations of mindfulness is to be understood; by the non-existence of the foundations of mindfulness, the non-existence of the right efforts is to be understood;
by the non-existence of the right efforts, the non-existence of the bases of psychic power is to be understood;
by the non-existence of the bases of psychic power, the non-existence of the faculties is to be understood; by the non-existence of the faculties, the non-existence of the powers is to be understood.

Through the non-existence of the powers, the non-existence of the factors of enlightenment is to be known; through the non-existence of the factors of enlightenment, the non-existence of the path is to be known; through the non-existence of the path, the non-existence of the grounds of self-confidence is to be known; through the non-existence of the grounds of self-confidence, the non-existence of the analytical knowledges is to be known; through the non-existence of the analytical knowledges, the non-existence of the perfections is to be known; through the non-existence of the perfections, the non-existence of the powers of a Tathāgata is to be known; through the non-existence of the powers of a Tathāgata...
The non-existence of the unique attributes of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) is to be understood;
by the non-existence of the unique attributes of a Buddha, the non-existence of space (ākāśa) is to be understood;
and by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be understood.
Through the non-existence of the Mahāyāna, the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings should be understood;
through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena should be understood.
For it is in this way, Subhūti, that there is room within that Mahāyāna for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the self and all phenomena, up to and including all of them, are not apprehended.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of the self and sentient beings, one should understand the non-existence of everything up to the knower and the seer.

To the extent that there is the non-existence of the one who knows and sees, the non-existence of the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi) is to be understood; to the extent that there is the non-existence of the stage of the lineage,
the non-existence of the stage of the eighth person (aṣṭamaka-bhūmi) is to be understood.

By the non-existence of the stage of the eighth person, the non-existence of the stage of vision is to be understood; by the non-existence of the stage of vision, the non-existence of the stage of refinement is to be understood;

by the non-existence of the stage of refinement, the non-existence of the stage of freedom from passion is to be understood; by the non-existence of the stage of freedom from passion, the non-existence of the stage of one who has accomplished what was to be done is to be understood;
by the non-existence of the stage of one who has accomplished what was to be done...
The non-existence of space is to be understood;
by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be understood;
by the non-existence of the Mahāyāna, the non-existence of the immeasurable, the incalculable, and the infinite is to be understood.
Through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be understood.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that there is room within that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings.
Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: the self, and so on, up to all dharmas—all these are not apprehended.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of the self and sentient beings, up to the non-existence of the knower and the seer, [it] should be known;
by the non-existence of the knower and the seer, the non-existence of the stream-enterer should be known, and of the stream-enterer—

By the non-existence of existence, the non-existence of the once-returner is to be known; by the non-existence of the once-returner, the non-existence of the non-returner is to be known; by the non-existence of the non-returner, the non-existence of the arhat is to be known; by the non-existence of the arhat, the non-existence of the pratyekabuddha is to be known;
by the non-existence of the pratyekabuddha, the non-existence of space is to be known;
by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be known.
Through the non-existence of the Mahāyāna, the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings is to be understood;
through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be understood.
For in this way, Subhūti, there is room in that Mahāyāna for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the self, and so forth, up to all dharmas—all these are non-apprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of a self and a sentient being, one should understand the non-existence of everything up to a knower and a seer.

To the extent that there is the non-existence of the one who knows and sees, the non-existence of the Śrāvaka vehicle should be understood; through the non-existence of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the non-existence of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle should be understood;

through the non-existence of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the non-existence of the Tathāgata should be understood; and through the non-existence of the Tathāgata, the non-existence of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) should be understood.
By the non-existence of the knowledge of all aspects, the non-existence of space is to be understood;
by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be understood.
Through the non-existence of the Mahāyāna, the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings should be understood;
through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena should be understood.
For in this way, Subhūti, there is room in that Mahāyāna for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the self, and so forth, up to all dharmas—all these are non-apprehendable.
It is just as if, Subhūti, in the realm of nirvāṇa, there were immeasurable, incalculable, and—
Just as there is room for immeasurable,
incalculable, and infinite sentient beings, so too, Subhūti, is there room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, there is room in space for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings.
In the same way, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings.
[Thus ends the departure for the benefit of sentient beings.
Furthermore, as Subhūti has said:
"Nor is the coming of that Great Vehicle seen, nor..."
"Its coming is not seen,
nor its staying; thus it is, Subhūti, that for this Great Vehicle neither its coming nor its going nor its staying is seen."
For what reason? Because, Subhūti, all dharmas are immovable;
they do not go anywhere, they do not come from anywhere, and they do not abide anywhere. For what reason?
For this reason, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of form does not come from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere;
nor does it do so for feeling, perception, or mental formations.

For indeed, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of consciousness does not come from anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere. For indeed, Subhūti, the suchness of form does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere.
[The same applies] to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
For indeed, Subhūti, the suchness of consciousness does not come from anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere.
For indeed, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of form does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere.
[The same applies] to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
For indeed, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of consciousness does not come from anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere.
For indeed, Subhūti, the characteristic of form does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere.
[The same applies] to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
For indeed, Subhūti, the characteristic of consciousness does not come from anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere.
Nor, Subhūti, [does it abide] in the eye.
Subhūti, intrinsic nature does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere; it is neither suchness, nor self-nature, nor characteristic.
It is likewise for the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body.

The nature of the mind is not suchness, nor its own-being, nor its characteristic; it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and stays nowhere. Subhūti, the nature of the earth element is not suchness, nor its own-being, nor its characteristic; it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and stays nowhere.

In this way, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the water element, the fire element, the wind element, and the space element does not come from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere; nor do their suchness, their own-being, or their characteristics come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere.
Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the dharma-element, its suchness, its own-being, and its characteristics do not come from anywhere, do not go anywhere, and do not abide anywhere.

In this way, Subhūti, the nature of suchness, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable realm does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere; nor is there any suchness, intrinsic nature, or characteristic therein.
Subhūti, the nature of the perfection of generosity does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere; nor is there any suchness, intrinsic nature, or characteristic therein.

In this way, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom— neither their suchness, nor their self-nature, nor their defining characteristic— comes from anywhere, goes anywhere, or abides anywhere.
Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the applications of mindfulness does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere; nor does its suchness, its self-nature, or its characteristic.

Likewise, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment—nor their suchness, their self-nature, or their characteristic—does not come from anywhere.
Nor does the intrinsic nature of the path, its suchness, its self-nature, or its characteristic come from anywhere.

It goes nowhere and stays nowhere. Subhūti, the nature of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it stay anywhere; such is their true nature, their suchness, their intrinsic being, and their characteristic. It is the same for the powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and, Subhūti, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The suchness of the Buddha-dharmas has no intrinsic nature and no defining characteristic; it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and stays nowhere.
Subhūti, the nature of awakening has no suchness, no intrinsic nature, and no defining characteristic; it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and stays nowhere.
Subhūti, neither the unconditioned, nor suchness, nor intrinsic nature, nor characteristic comes from anywhere, goes anywhere, or abides anywhere.
[Thus is the departure through effortlessness.
Furthermore, as Subhūti has said:
"No prior limit of this vehicle is apprehended, nor is a subsequent limit."
The middle is apprehended; that vehicle is equal to the three times. Therefore, it is called the "Great Vehicle," the Great Vehicle. It is so, Subhūti, it is so.
No prior limit of this vehicle is apprehended.
Neither a future limit nor a middle point is apprehended; that vehicle is equal throughout the three times. Therefore, it is called the "Great Vehicle," the Great Vehicle.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the past time—
The past time is empty of the past time;
the future time is empty of the future time;
the present time is empty of the present time.
The equality of the three times is empty by virtue of the equality of the three times;
the Great Vehicle is empty of the Great Vehicle; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva. Subhūti, emptiness is not one, nor two, nor three, nor four, nor five, nor six, nor seven, nor eight.

Whether nine or ten [times], this vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is equal throughout the three times; therein neither equality nor inequality is perceived, nor is passion perceived there, nor is the absence of passion;
neither hatred is perceived, nor is the absence of hatred.
Delusion is not apprehended, nor is non-delusion; a name is not apprehended, nor is non-name; and so on, up to: the wholesome is not apprehended, nor is the unwholesome.
Neither the contaminated is apprehended nor the uncontaminated; neither the faulty is apprehended nor the faultless; neither affliction is apprehended nor the absence of affliction.
Neither the destruction of afflictions nor the non-destruction of afflictions is apprehended;
neither the mundane nor the supramundane is apprehended.
Neither affliction nor purification is apprehended;
neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa is apprehended;
nor is anything permanent or impermanent apprehended therein.
Neither pleasure nor suffering is apprehended;
neither self nor non-self is apprehended;
neither the peaceful nor the non-peaceful is apprehended.
The desire realm is not apprehended, nor is the transcendence of the desire realm; the form realm is not apprehended, nor is the transcendence of the form realm;
the formless realm is not apprehended, nor is the transcendence of the formless realm. Why is that?
For what reason? Because its intrinsic nature is not apprehended. Subhūti, past form is empty of past form; future form is empty of future form;
present form is empty of present form.
In the same way, past feeling, perception, mental formations,
and past consciousness are empty of past consciousness.
Future consciousness is empty of future consciousness;
present consciousness is empty of present consciousness.
For what reason?
In emptiness, past form is not apprehended; since emptiness itself is empty, it is not apprehended within emptiness— how much less could past form be apprehended within emptiness?
In emptiness, past feeling is not apprehended;
for emptiness itself is empty, and it is not apprehended within emptiness— how much less, then, can [feeling] be apprehended in emptiness?
Past feeling will not be apprehended.
In emptiness, past perception is not apprehended;
for emptiness itself is empty, and it is not apprehended within emptiness.
How much less, then, will a past perception be found in emptiness?
In emptiness, past formations are not found.
Indeed, emptiness itself is empty; it is not found within emptiness.
How much less, then, could past conditioned phenomena be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, past consciousness is not apprehended;
for emptiness itself is empty, and it is not apprehended within emptiness.
How, moreover, could past consciousness be apprehended in emptiness?
Likewise, future form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not apprehended in emptiness;
nor is present form apprehended in emptiness.
Emptiness itself is empty; it is not apprehended within emptiness.
How, then, could present form be apprehended within emptiness?
Present feeling is not apprehended within emptiness.
Emptiness itself is empty; emptiness is not apprehended within emptiness.
How, then, could present feeling be apprehended within emptiness?
Present perception is not apprehended within emptiness.
Emptiness itself is indeed empty; even emptiness is not apprehended within emptiness.
How, then, could a present perception be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, present formative forces (saṃskāra) are not apprehended.
Emptiness itself is indeed empty; emptiness is not apprehended within emptiness.
How, then, could conditioned phenomena of the present be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, present consciousness is not apprehended.
Emptiness itself is empty; even emptiness is not apprehended within emptiness.
How, then, could present consciousness be apprehended within emptiness?
Nor is there past or future [consciousness] within emptiness.
Present form is perceived;
yet emptiness itself is empty, and it is not perceived within emptiness.
How much less, then, could past, future, or present form be perceived within emptiness?
In emptiness,
past, future, and present feeling are not apprehended;
for emptiness itself is empty, and within emptiness nothing is apprehended.
How much less, then, could past, future, or present feeling be apprehended within emptiness?
Past, future, or present perception is not apprehended within emptiness;
for emptiness itself is empty, and it is not apprehended within emptiness.
How much less, then, could the perception of the past, future, or present be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, the formations of the past, future, or present are not apprehended;
for emptiness itself is empty, and it is not apprehended within emptiness.
How much less, then, could past, future, or present conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, past, future, or present consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not apprehended.
Emptiness itself is empty; it is not apprehended within emptiness.
How much less, then, will past, future, or present consciousness be apprehended in emptiness?

Indeed, emptiness itself is empty; it is not apprehended within emptiness—how much less, then, [be apprehended] in emptiness? Subhūti, the perfection of generosity is not apprehended from the perspective of the prior limit.
Subhūti, the perfection of generosity is not apprehended from the perspective of the future; Subhūti, the perfection of generosity is not apprehended from the perspective of the present;
through the equality of the time periods, the perfection of generosity is not apprehended.

Subhūti, within the equality of the time periods, the past time period is not apprehended; indeed, even equality itself is not apprehended within equality. How much less, then, can there be [an apprehension of] that which is other than equality?

The perfection of generosity will not be apprehended as past, future, or present. Likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline is not apprehended within the three time periods— the prior limit, the subsequent limit, and the present.
In the past, future, and present time periods, the perfection of patience is not apprehended;
in the past, future, and present time periods, the perfection of vigor is not apprehended;
in the past, future, and present time periods, the perfection of meditative concentration is not apprehended.

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended from the perspective of the past; Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is also not apprehended from the perspective of the future; Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is also not apprehended from the perspective of the present.
The perfection of wisdom is not apprehended through the equality of the time periods.
Subhūti, within the equality of the time periods, the past time period is not apprehended; indeed, even equality itself is not apprehended within equality.
How much less, then, will the perfection of wisdom—past, future, and present—be apprehended within equality?
Furthermore, Subhūti, the foundations of mindfulness are not apprehended in the past, future, or middle;
in the equality of the three times,
the foundations of mindfulness are not apprehended.
Subhūti, within equality, the past, future, and present time periods are not apprehended;
indeed, even equality itself is not apprehended within equality.
How much less, then, could the applications of mindfulness of the past, future, and present be apprehended within equality?
The same applies to the right efforts.
The bases of psychic power are not apprehended in the past, future, or present time periods; the faculties are not apprehended in the past, future, or present time periods.
The powers are not apprehended in the past, future, or present time-periods;
the factors of enlightenment are not apprehended in the past, future, or present time-periods;
the path is not apprehended in the past, future, or present time-periods.
The immeasurable states, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments are not apprehended in the past, future, or present time periods.
The powers of a Tathāgata are not apprehended in the past, future, or present time periods.
The grounds of self-confidence are not apprehended in the past, future, or present time periods.
The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are not apprehended in the past, future, or present time-periods;
how much less, then, could the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikā buddhadharmāḥ*)— past, future, and present— be apprehended within such equality?

Furthermore, Subhūti, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not apprehended from the perspective of the past; an ordinary person is not apprehended from the perspective of the future; an ordinary person is not apprehended from the perspective of the present;
and an ordinary person is not apprehended through the equality of the three times.
For what reason? Because of the non-apprehension of sentient beings.
It is the same for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
The Tathāgata is not apprehended from the perspective of the past; the Tathāgata is not apprehended from the perspective of the future;
the Tathāgata is not apprehended from the perspective of the middle.
The Tathāgata is not apprehended due to the equality of the three times.
For what reason?
Because of the non-apprehension of sentient beings.
24209 ... [gift] / For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having stood in the perfection of wisdom and having trained in the three times, must fulfill omniscience in all its aspects.
This, Subhūti, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s [practice] regarding the three times—
The Mahāyāna is [characterized] by equality. Abiding therein, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras,
shall set forth toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
[Thus ends the departure from the extremes.
24213 Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, excellent, Blessed One!"
This well-spoken word of the Blessed One is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
In this Mahāyāna, O Blessed One,
by training themselves, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the past attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Future bodhisattva mahāsattvas as well, training in this Mahāyāna, will attain all-aspect omniscience.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who currently exist in the world-systems throughout the ten directions, in incalculable world-systems—
Having trained in this Great Vehicle, they too attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, Blessed One, this Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is indeed the equality of the three times. Then—
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Having trained in this Great Vehicle, the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present, [attain] the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
...have attained, will attain, and are attaining [it].
Then, indeed, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, this..."

The Elder Subhūti, having been exhorted by the Tathāgata on account of the perfection of wisdom, might consider himself qualified to teach the Mahāyāna. Then, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"May it not be so, Blessed One, that I should teach the Mahāyāna by transgressing the perfection of wisdom.
The Blessed One said:
For you do not, Subhūti, teach the Mahāyāna as being in conformity with the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, whatever wholesome factors conducive to awakening there may be—

Whether they be the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of the buddhas— all these go to inclusion and convergence within the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said:

“Blessed One, which are the wholesome factors conducive to awakening— whether they be the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of the buddhas— all of them proceed toward inclusion and convergence within the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said:
Namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts,
the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment,
and the noble eightfold path.
The gateways to liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the four immeasurables; the four meditative absorptions; the four formless attainments;
and the perfection of giving.

The perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom; the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, and—
Compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), the state of never forgetting the Dharma, and dwelling in constant equanimity.

Subhūti, these wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment— whether they be the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of the buddhas— all of them go toward inclusion and convergence within the perfection of wisdom.
And, Subhūti, that which is the Mahāyāna, as well as the perfection of meditation and the perfection of vigor...

The perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity; and form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness; and the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind; and form and sound.

Whatever odor, whatever taste, whatever tangible object, whatever mental phenomenon, whatever eye-consciousness, whatever ear-consciousness, whatever nose-consciousness, whatever tongue-consciousness, whatever body-consciousness, whatever mind-consciousness, whatever eye-contact, whatever ear-contact, and whatever nose-contact—

And whatever is tongue-contact, and whatever is body-contact, and whatever is mind-contact; and whatever feeling born of eye-contact, and whatever feeling born of ear-contact, and whatever feeling born of nose-contact, and whatever feeling born of tongue-contact, and whatever feeling born of body-contact, and whatever feeling born of mind-contact.
And those which are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments— those which...
and the powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the [three] gateways to liberation—
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— the unconditioned phenomena, suffering, its origin,
its cessation, and the path, as well as the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

And internal emptiness, and external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence; and those concentrations, and those gateways of dhāraṇī, and up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and that Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)—

That which is suchness, that which is the limit of reality, that which is the inconceivable realm, and that which is nirvāṇa—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
By this method, Subhūti, you describe the Mahāyāna as being in conformity with the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?

Subhūti, it is because the Great Vehicle is not other than the perfection of wisdom; nor is the perfection of meditation other, nor the perfection of vigor, nor the perfection of patience, nor the perfection of ethical discipline, nor the perfection of generosity other [than it].

Thus, indeed, the Mahāyāna and the perfections of wisdom, meditation, vigor, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are non-dual; they are not divided into two. Subhūti, it is not that the Mahāyāna is one thing and the applications of mindfulness another; for the Mahāyāna and the applications of mindfulness are non-dual; they are not divided into two.
In this way, the Mahāyāna is not other than the right efforts, and the right efforts are not other than the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna and the right efforts are non-dual and indivisible.

The Mahāyāna is not other than the bases of psychic power, and the bases of psychic power are not other than the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna and the bases of psychic power are non-dual and indivisible.
The Mahāyāna is not other than the faculties, and the faculties are not other than the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna and the faculties are non-dual and indivisible.
The Mahāyāna is not other than the powers, and the powers are not other than the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna and the powers are non-dual, this being an undivided unity.

The Mahāyāna is not other than the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of enlightenment are not other than the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna and the factors of enlightenment are non-dual, this being an undivided unity.
The Mahāyāna is not other than the paths, and the paths are not other than the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna and the paths are non-dual, this being an undivided unity.
The Mahāyāna is not other than the immeasurables and the meditative absorptions; for the Mahāyāna and the immeasurables and meditative absorptions are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.
The Mahāyāna is not other than the formless attainments; for the Mahāyāna and the formless attainments are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.
The Mahāyāna is not other than the ten powers; for the Mahāyāna and the ten powers are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.
The Mahāyāna is not other than the fearlessnesses, and the fearlessnesses are not other than the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna and the fearlessnesses are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.

The Mahāyāna is not other than the analytical knowledges, and the analytical knowledges are not other than the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna and the analytical knowledges are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.

The Mahāyāna is not other than the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not other than the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.
For this reason, Subhūti, you designate the Mahāyāna as being in conformity with the perfection of wisdom.
[Thus ends the departure through attainment.
Subhūti said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva does not approach from a prior limit."
A bodhisattva does not approach from the future limit;
a bodhisattva does not approach from the middle.
Due to the boundlessness of form, there is the boundlessness of the bodhisattva.

It should be understood that just as form is infinite, so too should the infinitude of the bodhisattva be understood through the infinitude of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Even the notion that "form is the bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended; it is thus.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva"—

even this is not found and is not apprehended. For in this way, O Blessed One, not apprehending and not perceiving a bodhisattva in any way whatsoever, in every respect, and in all manners, [I do not see one]."
"Which bodhisattva shall I instruct and admonish in which perfection of wisdom?
Furthermore, Blessed One, this so-called 'bodhisattva' is a mere name; just as it is said 'self, self,' yet in the ultimate sense, a self is not produced at all."
Thus, among phenomena whose intrinsic nature is non-existence, what is that form which is unarisen?
Likewise, what are those [feelings, perceptions, and mental formations], and what is that—
Knowledge is that which is unarisen;
