Blessed One, that which is the cessation of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is not that emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
“Blessed One, that which is the cessation of the emptiness of existence is not the emptiness of existence.
Blessed One, that which is the cessation of the emptiness of non-existence is not the emptiness of non-existence.
Blessed One, that which is the cessation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not the emptiness of intrinsic nature.”
"O Blessed One, that which is the passing away of the emptiness of other-nature is not that emptiness of other-nature.
O Blessed One, that which is the passing away of the applications of mindfulness is not those applications of mindfulness.
O Blessed One, that which is the passing away of the right efforts is not those right efforts."
O Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of the bases of psychic power is not those bases of psychic power; O Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of the faculties is not those faculties;
O Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of the powers is not those powers.
“Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of the factors of awakening is not those factors of awakening; Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of the paths is not those paths;
Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of the immeasurables and the meditative absorptions is not those immeasurables and meditative absorptions.”
Blessed One, that which is the cessation of the formless attainments is not those formless attainments;
Blessed One, that which is the cessation of the ten powers is not those ten powers; Blessed One, that which is the cessation of the grounds of self-confidence is not those grounds of self-confidence.

Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of the analytical knowledges is not those analytical knowledges; Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of the applications of mindfulness is not those applications of mindfulness;
Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is not those qualities of a Buddha.
Thus, indeed, the Buddha-qualities and cessation are non-dual; this is not a duality.
For what reason?
Because cessation is neither one, nor two, nor many, nor distinct. Therefore, that which...
There is no destruction of the Buddha-dharmas; those Buddha-dharmas do not exist. Furthermore, Blessed One, that which is called "form" is merely a designation applied to what is non-dual.

Feeling, perception, and mental formations—furthermore, that which is called "consciousness" is a designation made for this non-duality. As for what is further asked, "To whom does it belong? [it belongs to no one].
From form up to the knowledge of all aspects—this is the reckoning made regarding non-duality.
[Thus ends the refutation of the relationship between the attained and the attainer within the departure by attainment.
Then, indeed, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"How, venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, examine these phenomena? Which ones, venerable Subhūti?"
The Bodhisattva [asks]:
What is the perfection of wisdom?
What is its thorough investigation?
Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, as to what you have asked:
'Who is a bodhisattva?'—[it is] awakening—"
It is precisely because of that very being that one is called a "bodhisattva.
And by means of that awakening, one knows the aspect of all phenomena, yet one does not become attached to them.
Of which phenomena does he know the aspects?
He knows the aspects of form, and yet he does not become attached to them.
He knows the aspects of feeling, yet he does not adhere to them; he knows the aspects of perception, yet he does not adhere to them;
he knows the aspects of mental formations, yet he does not adhere to them.

He knows the aspects of consciousness and does not become attached to them. In this way, he knows the aspects of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields— both individually and collectively— as well as those of dependent origination and the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, and he does not become attached to them.

In this way, he knows the modes of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the perfections, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, yet he does not become attached to them.
Śāriputra said:
"Subhūti, what are those aspects of all phenomena?
Subhūti replied:

Venerable Śāriputra, those aspects, marks, and signs by which forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena— whether internal or external, conditioned or unconditioned— are characterized; by these aspects they are called the "aspects of all phenomena."
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as to what you asked:

"What is the perfection of wisdom?"—Venerable Śāriputra, it is because this is the state of having desisted and the act of having desisted that it is called the "perfection of wisdom. From what has it desisted?
Disenchantment and detachment from the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, the perfection of generosity,
the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom;
[disenchantment and detachment] from internal emptiness.

He has desisted from and refrained from external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence; he has desisted from and refrained from the applications of mindfulness.

They have desisted from and desisted in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the paths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Up to the point of being desisted from and having desisted from omniscience—
this is why it is called the perfection of wisdom. Venerable Śāriputra, by this method, this which is the perfection of wisdom is that which has desisted and has been desisted from.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as to what you asked:
"What is investigation? In this regard, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva—
When a Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not examine form as permanent, nor as impermanent;
not as pleasant, nor as painful; not as self, nor as non-self; not as peaceful, nor as unpeaceful;
not as empty, nor as non-empty; not as having signs, nor as signless; nor as being with aspiration.
He does not examine it as "wishless," nor does he examine it as "secluded" or "not secluded. He does not examine feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as permanent.

He does not examine [it] as "impermanent," nor as "pleasant," nor as "suffering," nor as "self," nor as "non-self," nor as "peaceful," nor as "not peaceful," nor as "empty," nor as "not empty," nor as "with signs," nor as "signless," nor as "with aspiration," nor as "without aspiration."
He does not examine [it] as "secluded" nor as "not secluded.
Likewise, he examines the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as "not permanent."

He examines it as not impermanent, not pleasant, not painful, not self, not non-self, not peaceful, not unpeaceful, not empty, not non-empty, not characterized by signs, not signless, not wishless, and not wishless-less.
They do not examine whether [things] are secluded or not secluded;
likewise, they examine that form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena are not permanent.

They do not examine them as "impermanent" or "not impermanent," nor as "pleasant" or "not pleasant," nor as "suffering" or "not suffering," nor as "self" or "not self," nor as "peaceful" or "not peaceful," nor as "empty" or "not empty," nor as "signless" or "not signless," nor as "wishless" or "not wishless";
they do not examine them as "secluded" or "not secluded."
In this way, one examines visual consciousness as neither permanent nor impermanent;
neither pleasant nor painful; neither self nor non-self; neither peaceful nor unpeaceful;
neither empty nor non-empty; neither with signs nor signless; and neither with aspiration nor without aspiration.
One does not examine it as "wishless," nor does one examine it as "secluded" or "not secluded.
One does not examine ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as "permanent."

He examines it as not impermanent, not pleasant, not painful, not self, not non-self, not peaceful, not unpeaceful, not empty, not non-empty, not characterized by signs, not signless, not wishless, and not wishless-less.
He does not examine it as "secluded" nor as "not secluded.
Likewise, he examines visual contact as neither permanent nor impermanent,
neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, and neither peaceful nor unpeaceful.
He examines it as neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, neither with aspiration nor aspirationless.
He examines it as neither secluded nor non-secluded.
He examines that ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are not permanent.

He examines it as not impermanent, not pleasant, not painful, not self, not non-self, not peaceful, not unpeaceful, not empty, not non-empty, not characterized by signs, not signless, not wishless, and not unwishless;
he examines it as neither secluded nor non-secluded.

In this way, one examines that feeling conditioned by eye-contact is neither permanent nor impermanent; neither pleasant nor painful; neither self nor non-self; neither calm nor uncalm; neither empty nor non-empty; neither with signs nor signless; neither wishless nor unwishless; and neither secluded nor non-secluded.

One examines that feeling conditioned by ear-contact is not permanent, nor impermanent; not pleasant, nor painful; not self, nor non-self; not peaceful, nor unpeaceful; not empty, nor non-empty; not characterized by signs, nor signless; not wishless, nor not wishless. One does not examine it as such. One does not examine that feeling conditioned by nose-contact... feeling conditioned by tongue-contact... feeling conditioned by body-contact... feeling conditioned by mind-contact as permanent, nor impermanent; not pleasant, nor painful; not self, nor non-self; not peaceful, nor unpeaceful; not empty, nor non-empty; not characterized by signs, nor signless; not wishless, nor not wishless. One does not examine it as such.
He examines it neither as secluded nor as non-secluded. Likewise, he examines the perfection of generosity neither as permanent nor as impermanent,

neither as pleasant nor as painful, neither as self nor as non-self, neither as peaceful nor as unpeaceful, neither as empty nor as non-empty, neither as having signs nor as signless, and neither as wishless nor as non-wishless.
One does not examine whether it is secluded or not secluded.

One does not examine whether the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom is permanent or impermanent;
nor as pleasant or painful; nor as self or non-self; nor as peaceful or unpeaceful; nor as empty or non-empty; nor as having signs or signless; nor as wishful or wishless.
He does not examine it as "secluded" nor as "not secluded.

Likewise, he does not examine internal emptiness as "permanent," nor as "impermanent"; nor as "pleasure," nor as "suffering"; nor as "self," nor as "non-self"; nor as "peaceful," nor as "not peaceful"; nor as "empty," nor as "not empty"; nor as "signless," nor as "not signless"; nor as "wishless," nor as "not wishless."
One does not examine it as "secluded" nor as "not secluded.

One does not [examine] external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, or the emptiness of non-dispersal.

One does not examine whether intrinsic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, or the emptiness of other-nature are permanent.

One does not examine them as "impermanent" nor as "suffering," nor as "self" nor as "non-self," nor as "peaceful" nor as "not peaceful," nor as "empty" nor as "not empty," nor as "signless" nor as "not signless," nor as "wishless" nor as "not wishless," nor as "secluded" nor as "not secluded.
In this way, they do not examine the applications of mindfulness as being permanent.

They do not examine them as impermanent, nor as pleasant, nor as painful; nor as self, nor as non-self; nor as peaceful, nor as unpeaceful; nor as empty, nor as non-empty; nor as having signs, nor as signless; nor as with aspiration, nor as without aspiration.
They do not examine them as secluded, nor as non-secluded.

In this same way, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the paths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges,
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and all the concentrations—
He examines that the gateways of dhāraṇīs and omniscience are neither permanent nor impermanent;
neither pleasant nor painful; neither self nor non-self; neither calm nor uncalm; neither empty nor non-empty; neither characterized by signs nor signless; neither wishless nor non-wishless;
and neither secluded nor non-secluded.
"In this way, Venerable Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom examines these phenomena.
Śāriputra said:
"For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you say this: 'That which is the non-arising of form is not that form;
that which is the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not that consciousness'?
Likewise [regarding] the individual and collective aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, the perfections, and all emptiness..."

Among all those factors conducive to enlightenment, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the gateways of concentration and mnemonic formulas, the superknowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—
that which is the non-arising of omniscience is not itself omniscience.
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty of form.
And that which is emptiness, Venerable Śāriputra, is not—"

That form is not an arising. By this method, O Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of form is not form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of consciousness.

That which is emptiness, Venerable Śāriputra, is neither consciousness nor its non-arising. By this method, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of consciousness is not consciousness. The perfection of giving, Venerable Śāriputra, is empty of the perfection of giving.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is emptiness is neither the perfection of giving nor its arising.

By this method, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of the perfection of giving is not the perfection of giving; it is not the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom;
for it is empty by means of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is emptiness is neither the perfection of wisdom nor arising.
By this method, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of the perfection of wisdom is not the perfection of wisdom.
Venerable Śāriputra, internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is emptiness is neither internal emptiness nor arising.
By this method, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of internal emptiness is not internal emptiness,
nor external emptiness, nor internal-and-external emptiness, nor the emptiness of emptiness, nor great emptiness, nor the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
The emptiness of the conditioned, the ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,

the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of other-nature— [all these] are empty by virtue of the emptiness of other-nature.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is emptiness is neither the emptiness of other-existence nor is it arising.
By this method, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of the emptiness of other-existence is not itself the emptiness of other-existence.
Venerable Śāriputra, the foundations of mindfulness are empty; they are the foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is emptiness is neither those applications of mindfulness nor their arising.

By this method, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of the applications of mindfulness is neither those applications of mindfulness, nor the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the paths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, or the formless attainments.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and omniscience are empty of omniscience.
And that which is emptiness, venerable Śāriputra, is neither omniscience nor arising.
"In this manner, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of omniscience is not omniscience.
Śāriputra said:
For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you speak thus:
"That which is the cessation of form is not that form"?
That which is the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not that consciousness.

In this way, [the same applies] to the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination, both individually and collectively; to the perfections, all the emptinesses, and all the factors conducive to enlightenment; and to the immeasurables, meditative absorptions, formless attainments, powers, and fearlessnesses.
Regarding the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and that which is the cessation of the knowledge of all aspects— that is not the knowledge of all aspects.
Subhūti said:

For in this way, O Venerable Śāriputra, that which is cessation, and that which is form, and that which is non-duality, and that which is feeling, and that which is perception, and those which are formations, and that which is consciousness—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined;
they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics. Thus it is.

In the individual and collective [treatments of] the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination; in the perfections; in all the emptinesses; in all the factors conducive to awakening;

in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments; in the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the analytical knowledges; in the Buddha-dharmas, the gateways of meditative concentration, and the gateways of dhāraṇī; and whatever is the exhaustion, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), and that which is non-duality—all these are [identical].
All phenomena are not conjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the absence of characteristics.
By this method, O Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the cessation of form is not form.

In the same way, that which is the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness. Likewise, among the individual and collective aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and emptinesses, as well as among the doors of concentration and the doors of dhāraṇī, up to that which is the cessation of the knowledge of all aspects is not the knowledge of all aspects.
Śāriputra said:
"For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you say this: that what is called 'form' is merely a designation made for that which is non-dual?"
Feeling, perception, and mental formations—
this which is called "consciousness" is a designation for non-duality; even this which is called "the knowledge of all aspects" is a designation for non-duality.
[It is] "done.
Subhūti said:
"For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, non-arising is not one thing and form another."
Non-arising itself is form; form itself is non-arising. [So too are] feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Non-arising is not one thing and consciousness another;
consciousness itself is non-arising, and non-arising itself is consciousness.
In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, that which is called "form" is designated as non-dual;
[the same applies to] feeling, perception, and mental formations.
This which is called "consciousness" is merely a designation for the non-dual.

In this same way, [this designation applies] to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination—whether taken individually or collectively; to the perfections; to all the emptinesses;

to all the factors conducive to awakening; to the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments; and to the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the analytical knowledges.
Regarding the gateways of the concentrations and dhāraṇīs, it is thus, O Venerable Śāriputra: non-arising is not one thing and omniscience another;
non-arising itself is omniscience, and omniscience itself is non-arising.
"By this method, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is called 'omniscience' (sarvākārajñatā) is designated as a reckoning of non-duality.
Furthermore, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
Blessed One, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, examines these phenomena, at that time he perceives the non-arising of form by way of its absolute purity.
He perceives the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, by virtue of their ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the self, by virtue of its ultimate purity.

In this way, based on ultimate purity, he perceives the non-arising of a being, a soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer. Likewise, based on ultimate purity, he perceives the non-arising of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, dependent origination, and the superknowledges, whether considered individually or collectively.
He perceives the non-arising of the perfection of generosity, by virtue of its ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the perfection of ethical discipline, by virtue of its ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the perfection of patience, by virtue of its ultimate purity.
He perceives the non-arising of the perfection of vigor, by virtue of its absolute purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the perfection of meditation, by virtue of its absolute purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the perfection of wisdom, by virtue of its absolute purity.
He perceives the non-arising of internal emptiness by way of its ultimate purity; he perceives the non-arising of external emptiness by way of its ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of internal-and-external emptiness by way of its ultimate purity.
He perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of emptiness, based on its ultimate purity; he perceives the non-arising of the great emptiness, based on its ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of the ultimate truth, based on its ultimate purity.
He contemplates the non-arising of conditioned emptiness by way of its absolute purity; he contemplates the non-arising of ultimate emptiness by way of its absolute purity;
he contemplates the non-arising of emptiness without beginning or end by way of its absolute purity.
He perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of non-dispersal by virtue of its ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of intrinsic nature by virtue of its ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of all phenomena by virtue of its ultimate purity.
He perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of specific characteristics, by virtue of its ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of the unapprehendable, by virtue of its ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, by virtue of its ultimate purity.
He perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of existence, based on its ultimate purity; he perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of non-existence, based on its ultimate purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, based on its ultimate purity.

He perceives the non-arising of the emptiness of other-nature, by virtue of its ultimate purity. He perceives the non-arising of the foundations of mindfulness, by virtue of their ultimate purity. Likewise [he perceives the non-arising] of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the limbs of enlightenment, the path, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
He perceives non-arising, by virtue of its absolute purity;
he perceives the non-arising of an ordinary person, by virtue of his absolute purity;
he perceives the non-arising of the dharmas of an ordinary person, by virtue of their absolute purity.

In this way, he perceives the non-arising of the stream-enterer, the qualities of the stream-enterer; the once-returner, the qualities of the once-returner; the non-returner, the qualities of the non-returner; the arhat, the qualities of the arhat; the pratyekabuddha, the qualities of the pratyekabuddha; the bodhisattva, the qualities of the bodhisattva; and the Buddha, based on their ultimate purity.
He perceives the non-arising of the Buddha-dharmas, by virtue of their ultimate purity.
Śāriputra said:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Venerable Subhūti has spoken, so it is with form—"
Non-arising is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; non-arising extends to the aggregates, whether taken individually or collectively;
the elements are non-arising;
the self is non-arising, the sentient being is non-arising, the life-principle is non-arising, the nourisher is non-arising, and the person is non-arising.
The person is non-arising; the human is non-arising; the youth is non-arising; the agent is non-arising; the experiencer is non-arising; the knower is non-arising; the seer is non-arising.
Thus, individually and collectively, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and the superknowledges are all non-arising.

The non-arising of the perfection of generosity, the non-arising of the perfection of ethical discipline, the non-arising of the perfection of patience, the non-arising of the perfection of vigor, the non-arising of the perfection of meditative concentration, and the non-arising of the perfection of wisdom;

the non-arising of internal emptiness, the non-arising of external emptiness, the non-arising of internal and external emptiness, the non-arising of the emptiness of emptiness, the non-arising of great emptiness, the non-arising of the emptiness of the ultimate, the non-arising of the emptiness of the conditioned, and the non-arising of absolute emptiness.

The non-arising of the emptiness of the ultimate limit, the non-arising of the emptiness of the non-dispersed, the non-arising of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the non-arising of the emptiness of all phenomena,

the non-arising of the emptiness of specific characteristics, the non-arising of the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the non-arising of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, the non-arising of the emptiness of existence, the non-arising of the emptiness of non-existence, the non-arising of the emptiness of self-nature, and the non-arising of the emptiness of other-nature.

The foundations of mindfulness are non-arising; the right efforts are non-arising; the bases of psychic power are non-arising; the faculties are non-arising; the powers are non-arising; the factors of enlightenment are non-arising; the paths are non-arising; the immeasurables and meditative absorptions are non-arising;
the formless attainments are non-arising; the ten powers are non-arising; the grounds of self-confidence are non-arising; and the analytical knowledges are non-arising.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) are non-arising; omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is non-arising. The ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is non-arising; the qualities of an ordinary person are non-arising. The stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) is non-arising; the qualities of a stream-enterer are non-arising. The once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) is non-arising; the qualities of a once-returner are non-arising. The non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is non-arising; the qualities of a non-returner are non-arising.
Non-arising is the Arhat; non-arising are the dharmas of the Arhat. Non-arising is the Pratyekabuddha; non-arising are the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddha.
Non-arising is the Bodhisattva; non-arising are the dharmas of the Bodhisattva.
Non-arising is the Buddha; non-arising are the dharmas of the Buddha.
"Venerable Subhūti, if form is non-arising, and even the qualities of a Buddha are non-arising,
then, Venerable Subhūti, has the disciple not already attained the enlightenment of a disciple, and [the enlightenment] of a Pratyekabuddha?"
By means of that vehicle, the awakening of a pratyekabuddha is attained;
by a bodhisattva, omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) is indeed attained,
and there will be no distinction among the five destinies.
Venerable Subhūti, if all dharmas are non-arisen, then the fivefold awakening has already been attained by the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
for what purpose, then, would one become a stream-enterer?
The path must be cultivated for the abandonment of the three fetters;
by a once-returner, the path must be cultivated for the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion.
The non-returner (anāgāmin) must cultivate the path for the abandonment of the five lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana);
the arhat [must cultivate it] for the five higher fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
The path must be cultivated for the sake of abandoning the various [afflictions];
by those belonging to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, the path must be cultivated for the attainment of Pratyekabodhi.
For what reason does a bodhisattva practice the course of difficult deeds, experiencing those various sufferings for the sake of sentient beings?
For what reason has the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha...
The Perfectly Awakened One has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
For what reason did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, set in motion the Wheel of Dharma?
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire the attainment of an unarisen dharma, nor its realization; I do not desire a stream-enterer who is characterized by non-arising."

I do not desire the fruit of stream-entry, nor the once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; I do not desire arhatship, nor the fruit of arhatship, nor the unarisen enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, nor pratyekabuddhahood. O Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire a bodhisattva practicing difficult austerities, nor does a bodhisattva [desire] difficult austerity.
He courses by means of perception.
Why is that?
For it is not possible, O Venerable Śāriputra, to remain established in the perception of difficult practices.

In order to accomplish the welfare of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings; furthermore, O Venerable Śāriputra, having generated the perception of a mother toward all sentient beings, as well as the perception of a father, the perception of a brother, the perception of a son, and the perception of oneself—
Having generated [this mind], it is possible to accomplish the welfare of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings.
Furthermore, O Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate the following thought:
"Just as that which is called 'self' and 'self' is ultimately unarisen, so too are all internal [phenomena]."
One should produce a perception regarding external phenomena;
if one produces such a perception, there will be no perception of difficulty.
For what reason?
Because those bodhisattvas do not produce nor perceive any phenomenon whatsoever, in any way, at all, or in any respect.

"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not accept an unarisen Tathāgata, nor supreme perfect enlightenment, nor the turning of the wheel of Dharma; nor do I accept that an unarisen attainment is being attained by means of an unarisen dharma."
Śāriputra said:
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, is an arisen attainment attained by means of an unarisen dharma?
Or is an unarisen attainment attained by means of an arisen dharma?"

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, I do not maintain that an unarisen attainment is being attained by means of an arisen dharma, nor that an arisen attainment is being attained by means of an unarisen [dharma]."
Śāriputra said:
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, do you desire attainment by means of an unarisen dharma,
or do you desire attainment by means of an arisen dharma?"
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire attainment by means of an unarisen dharma,
nor do I desire attainment by means of an arisen dharma."
Śāriputra said:
"But, Venerable Subhūti, is it that there is no attainment and no realization?
Subhūti replied:

"Venerable Śāriputra, there is attainment and there is clear realization, yet they are not two. Nevertheless, Venerable Śāriputra, it is by way of worldly convention that 'attainment' and 'clear realization' are designated;
it is by way of worldly convention that one is designated as a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha."
A bodhisattva or a Buddha is merely designated; however, in the ultimate sense, there is no attainment and no realization,
nor is there a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva, or a Buddha.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, it occurs to me to speak of a phenomenon that is unarisen.
Subhūti said:

"Venerable Śāriputra, when you say, 'An unarisen phenomenon is an unarisen phenomenon,' and that it occurs to you to speak thus— Venerable Śāriputra, even regarding non-arising, it occurs to you to speak."
For what reason?

Because, venerable Śāriputra, that which is an unarisen dharma, that which is eloquence, those which are mantras, and that which is non-arising—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless and invisible.
"Non-obstructive and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristicless.
Śāriputra said,
"Venerable Subhūti, even non-arising is a mantra."
"Non-arising is eloquence;
non-arising is the Dharma. Those dharmas, concerning which one has the eloquence to speak, are themselves unarisen. Subhūti said:
"So it is, Venerable Śāriputra: non-arising is the mantra;
non-arising is the eloquence, and non-arising are those phenomena concerning which one has the eloquence to speak. Why is that?"
For thus, venerable Śāriputra, form is non-arising;
likewise are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness is non-arising.

In this way, the aggregates and elements, both individually and collectively, as well as the sense bases, dependent origination, the perfections, all the emptinesses, and all the factors conducive to awakening— [are non-arising].
The immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the gateways of concentration and dhāraṇī, the superknowledges,
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and non-arising; the stream-enterer,
the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, the omniscient one, the knower of all aspects, and omniscience itself.
"Moreover, it is non-arising.
Śāriputra said: "It is so, Venerable Subhūti; non-arising is the mantra."

Non-arising is eloquence; non-arising is the Dharma. Those dharmas, concerning which one has the eloquence to speak, are themselves unarisen—namely, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields; dependent origination; the perfections; all the emptinesses; all the factors of enlightenment;
the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments; the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī.
The superknowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth, up to and including omniscience itself, are non-arising. Śāriputra said:

"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, just as attainment and clear realization exist by way of worldly convention, does the differentiation of the five destinies likewise exist by way of worldly convention, but not in the ultimate sense? Subhūti replied:

"So it is, Venerable Śāriputra, so it is. Just as attainment (*prāpti*) and clear realization (*abhisamaya*) exist by way of worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*), so too does the differentiation of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) exist by way of worldly convention; yet, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it does not exist.
Indeed, in this regard, there is nothing whatsoever by way of ultimate reality."
For what reason?
Because, O Venerable Śāriputra, in the ultimate sense there is neither karma nor its maturation, neither arising nor cessation, neither affliction nor purification.
Śāriputra said:
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, does an unarisen dharma arise, or rather,
does an arisen dharma arise?"
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire the arising of a dharma that has already arisen, nor do I desire the arising of a dharma that has not yet arisen."
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, which unarisen dharma is it that you do not wish to have arise?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not accept the arising of form—which is an unarisen phenomenon and empty of intrinsic nature. [I do not accept the arising] of feeling, perception, or mental formations.
Venerable Śāriputra, I do not accept the arising of consciousness—which is an unarisen phenomenon and empty of intrinsic nature."
I do not desire even a quarter [of it].
Thus, [I do not desire] the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, whether taken individually or collectively;
nor the dependent originations, the perfections, all the emptinesses, or all the factors conducive to awakening.

"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire the arising even of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī, the superknowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or even of awakening itself— which is unarisen and empty of intrinsic nature."
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, does arising arise, or does non-arising arise?
Subhūti replied:
For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, arising does not arise, nor does non-arising arise.
Why is that?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, both that which is arising and that which is non-arising—these two dharmas are [not distinct].

They are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being characterless. By this method, O Venerable Śāriputra, arising does not arise, nor does non-arising arise.
By this method, O Venerable Śāriputra, non-arising is the mantra, non-arising is the eloquence, non-arising is...
"Those dharmas, concerning which it occurs to you to speak, are also unarisen.
Śāriputra said:
"The Venerable Subhūti should be placed at the head of those who belong to the Dharma-body. That...
For what reason?
Because, Venerable Subhūti, whatever he is questioned about, from that very point he emerges.
Subhūti said:

"This is the nature of things, Venerable Śāriputra, for the disciples of the Tathāgata who are non-reliant upon all phenomena: from whatever they are questioned, from that very point they emerge. Why is that?"
For what reason? Because, as it were, all phenomena are non-dependent. Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, how are all phenomena non-dependent?"
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty by nature; it does not depend on the internal, it does not depend on the external, nor is it found between the two."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness,
O Venerable Śāriputra, are empty by nature;
they do not depend on the internal, they do not depend on the external, nor are they found between the two.
"Venerable Śāriputra, the eye is empty by nature; it does not depend on the internal, it does not depend on the external, nor is it found between the two.

The ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind, Venerable Śāriputra, are empty by nature; they do not depend on the internal, they do not depend on the external, nor are they found between the two."

"Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty by nature; it does not depend on the internal, it does not depend on the external, nor is it apprehended between the two. Sound, odor, taste, the tangible, and mental phenomena, venerable Śāriputra, are empty by nature; they do not depend on the internal, they do not depend on the external, nor are they apprehended between the two."
Eye-consciousness, venerable Śāriputra, is empty by nature; it does not depend on the internal, it does not depend on the external, nor is it apprehended between the two.

Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness, venerable Śāriputra, are empty by nature; they do not depend on the internal, they do not depend on the external, nor are they apprehended between the two.

"Venerable Śāriputra, the foundations of mindfulness are empty by nature; they do not depend on the internal, they do not depend on the external, and they are not apprehended between the two. The right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the paths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, Venerable Śāriputra, are empty by nature; they do not depend on the internal, they do not depend on the external, and they are not apprehended between the two."
In this manner, Venerable Śāriputra, all phenomena are non-reliant, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Thus, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections must purify form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are to be purified;
likewise, the aggregates and elements, both individually and collectively.

The bases, dependent origination, the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the gateways of concentration and mnemonic formulas,
the superknowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— [these] are purified.
They should be purified, up to and including the purification of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
[Thus is the departure toward the knowledge of all aspects.
Śāriputra said:
"How, Venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the six perfections, purify the path of a bodhisattva?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, there is a mundane perfection of generosity and there is a supramundane one.
Likewise, there is a mundane perfection of ethical discipline and a supramundane one; there is a mundane perfection of patience and a supramundane one;
there is a mundane perfection of vigor and a supramundane one; there is a mundane perfection of meditative concentration and a supramundane one; and there is a perfection of wisdom."
"It is both mundane and supramundane.
Śāriputra asked: "Venerable Subhūti, which is the mundane perfection of generosity, and which is the supramundane?"

Subhūti said: "Worldly, O Venerable Śāriputra, is the perfection of giving; herein a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes a donor, a master of giving, and a giver to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the wretched, beggars, travelers, and supplicants."
He gives food to those who desire food; and to those who desire drink,
vehicles, clothing, perfumes, garlands, ointments, flowers, incense, powders, dwellings, lodgings,
the necessities for life, utensils, bedding, seats, and medicines, he gives drink, vehicles, clothing, perfumes, garlands, ointments, flowers, incense, powders, dwellings, and so forth.
He becomes a donor of various dwellings, means of livelihood, requisites, and medicines;
to those who desire sons,
he gives a son.
To those who desire daughters, he gives his daughters;
to those who desire wives, he gives his wives;
to those who desire kingdoms, he gives his realms.
He gives his head to those who seek a head;
he gives his limbs to those who seek limbs.
To those who seek flesh, blood, and marrow, he gives flesh, blood, and marrow;
and he relinquishes them with a sense of dependence.
It occurs to him: "I am giving, and this person is receiving."
"Free from stinginess, I renounce my entire possession as this gift;
I carry out the command of the Buddha;
I practice the perfection of generosity."
Having made this gift common to all sentient beings,

I dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. And by this gift and the fruit of this gift, may all sentient beings be happy in this very life, without grasping.
May they attain parinirvāṇa.
He gives a gift while attached to three attachments.
To which three? Namely, [the attachment to] self—
Bound by these three attachments—by the notion of a self, the notion of another, and the notion of giving—one gives a gift.
"This is called the mundane perfection of generosity.
For it does not move away from the world, O Venerable Śāriputra, nor does it rise above it, nor does it transcend it."
Therefore, it is called the mundane perfection of giving.
In that regard, what is the supramundane perfection of giving? It is the complete purity of the three spheres.
In that regard, what is...
The purity of the three spheres:
here, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when giving a gift, does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a recipient.
He does not apprehend giving,
nor does he apprehend its maturation;
this, O Venerable Śāriputra, is the third [perfection] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore,
venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, he does not dedicate that gift to all sentient beings.
He does not perceive sentient beings,
nor does he perceive a self;
and that gift [is dedicated] to unsurpassed [enlightenment].
He dedicates it toward perfect enlightenment,
yet he does not apprehend enlightenment.
"This is called the supramundane perfection of generosity.
For what reason is it called the supramundane perfection of generosity?
For in this way, O Venerable Śāriputra,
it moves away from, rises above, and transcends the world;
for that reason, it is called the supramundane perfection of giving.
[It is] thus: the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, what is the mundane perfection of wisdom? What is [the supramundane]?"
[It is] supramundane.
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom is mundane."

In this case, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift while relying on apprehension, thinking, "I must subdue the mind of stinginess. Relying on the perception of self, sentient beings, and the act of giving, he relinquishes everything— whether external or internal.
There is no thing whatsoever—whether appropriated or unappropriated—that he does not relinquish;
and having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward enlightenment while relying on apprehension. He...
Established in the ascetic qualities (dhūtaguṇa), he practices moral discipline; yet,

relying on the apprehension of body, speech, and mind, and while practicing those ten paths of wholesome action, he remains dependent upon the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, and the view of wholesomeness.

Having apprehended awakening, he dedicates his morality—which is shared with all sentient beings—toward awakening, yet he does so by means of apprehension. He exalts himself and disparages others; though he endures the misdeeds of all sentient beings, he relies on a view of self and a view of sentient beings regarding patience, and he dedicates that wholesome root toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
Having made [that merit] common to all sentient beings by way of apprehension,
he exerts vigor while apprehending the body,
apprehending the mind, apprehending the accumulation of merit, apprehending the accumulation of gnosis, apprehending himself, and apprehending awakening.
And by means of that exertion of vigor, he conceives [pride];
and having made that common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment through the yoga of apprehension.
He cultivates loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
he enters into and emerges from the meditative attainments, and he relishes them. Relishing them, he...
He conceives thus: he dedicates to awakening the roots of goodness shared with all sentient beings while holding the view of apprehension. This is called the mundane perfection of wisdom.
While cultivating emptiness, he perceives that form is empty.
One perceives that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty.
As long as he perceives even the enlightenment of a Buddha through the application of apprehension,
he makes those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. That...
By means of the practice of apprehension,
he confesses all evil through the practice of apprehension; and he rejoices in the merit of both himself and others.
Perceiving [the merit] for the sake of both himself and others, he entreats all the Buddhas;
three times over, he dedicates that merit toward omniscience, having made it common to all sentient beings by means of skillful methods.
[This is called the mundane perfection of wisdom.
In that regard, what is the supramundane perfection of wisdom?
It is through the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, the gift, and awakening.
Through the purity of the three spheres, one purifies the perfection of giving.
For the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, and morality, and through the purity of the three spheres, one purifies the perfection of morality.

For the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, patience, and awakening— and by means of the complete purity of the three spheres— he purifies the perfection of patience.

And for the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, body, mind, vigor, merit, knowledge, and awakening— and by means of the complete purity of the three spheres— he [purifies] the perfection of vigor.

He purifies [the perfection of meditation]; for the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, meditative absorption, concentration, and the attainments of awakening, and by means of the complete purity of the three spheres, he purifies the perfection of meditation.

For the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, and all phenomena— and by means of the purity of the three spheres— he purifies the perfection of wisdom. For the sake of awakening, he dedicates all roots of merit toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of a dedication that is without distinction,
an unexcelled dedication, an incomparable dedication, an inconceivable and unequaled dedication, and an immeasurable dedication.
[This is called supramundane perfection of wisdom. For what reason is it mundane?
Because by means of these, one becomes part of the world.
Or those by which one turns back from the world;
or those which are equal to the world;
or those for the sake of the world by which one gives.
Those by which one emerges from the world,
or those which lead to the existence of the world,
or those existences within the world— these are the mundane (*laukikī*).
In this regard, what are the supramundane [faculties]?
They are those by which one crosses over the world;
they are those by which one causes the world to cross over.
Or that by which one is delivered from the world;
or that which serves as light;
or that by which one departs from the world.
Or, they are called "supramundane" because they lead to the transcendence of the world, or because they are superior within the world;
thus, O Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the six perfections [traverses] the path to enlightenment.
He purifies it.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, what is the path to enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, the four foundations of mindfulness are the path to awakening for a bodhisattva mahāsattva; so too are the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers."
The factors of enlightenment; the noble eightfold path; the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; all meditative concentrations; all gateways to the dhāraṇīs; the four immeasurables; the four dhyānas; and the four formless attainments.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion— this, O Venerable Śāriputra, is called the path to enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, of which perfection is this the human effort?
Subhūti replied:

Venerable Śāriputra, this is the human effort of the perfection of wisdom. For what reason? Because, Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom is the mother that gives birth to all wholesome dharmas:
the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the buddhas.
"Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom is the recipient of all wholesome dharmas— of the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas. The perfection of wisdom...

"Venerable Śāriputra, by training in this perfection of wisdom, those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly awakened Buddhas fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Venerable Śāriputra, so too will the future Tathāgatas, Arhats..."
The perfectly awakened ones, having trained in this very perfection of wisdom, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Moreover, O Venerable Śāriputra, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly awakened ones who currently abide, remain, and maintain themselves while teaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions— all of them likewise [have trained] in this very [perfection of wisdom].

Having trained in the perfection of wisdom, they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, if, while this perfection of wisdom is being spoken, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not experience doubt or hesitation, it should be known, Venerable One, that this is so.
Śāriputra, this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, never separated from this mental attention—
that is to say, the mental attention of not abandoning any sentient being and the mental attention of great compassion for the sake of protecting all sentient beings.
Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, as you have said, this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells by means of this."
"And he is not separated from this dwelling and this mental attention.
If that were so, Venerable Subhūti, then all sentient beings would also be bodhisattvas.
For what reason?
Because, venerable Subhūti, all sentient beings are never separated from mental attention.
Subhūti said:
"Excellent, excellent, venerable Śāriputra! I shall question you; the meaning has indeed been grasped by the venerable Śāriputra through his use of words that accord with reality."
For what reason? Venerable Śāriputra, one should know that because of the non-existence of sentient beings, there is the non-existence of mental attention.
Through the emptiness of sentient beings, the emptiness of mental attention should be understood;
through the lack of intrinsic nature of sentient beings, the lack of intrinsic nature of mental attention should be understood;
through the isolation of sentient beings, [the isolation of mental attention...]

Solitude is to be understood through the non-realization of sentient beings; the non-realization of mental attention is to be understood through the non-existence of form, the emptiness of form, the lack of intrinsic nature of form, and the solitude of form.
Through the non-realization of form, the non-realization of mental attention should be understood.

[The same applies to] feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. Through the non-existence of consciousness, through the emptiness of consciousness, through the lack of intrinsic nature of consciousness, through the solitude of consciousness, and through the non-realization of consciousness, the non-realization of mental attention [should be understood].

Thus, with respect to the aggregates, elements, bases, and dependent origination, both individually and collectively; with respect to the perfections, all the emptinesses, and all the factors conducive to awakening;

with respect to the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the gateways of samādhis and dhāraṇīs.

Through the existence of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), through the emptiness of omniscience, through the intrinsic nature of omniscience, through the seclusion of omniscience, and through the non-realization of omniscience, one should understand the non-realization of mental attention (*manasikāra*). By this dwelling and by this [practice], O Venerable Śāriputra... [the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and the superknowledges are to be understood].
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who is never separated from mental attention. Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the venerable Subhūti: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
It is indeed thus, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, should be taught, just as you teach it;
for it is through the very power of the Tathāgata that a bodhisattva, a mahāsattva, should course in the perfection of wisdom just as you teach it.

Furthermore, while this chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom was being spoken by the Venerable Subhūti, the trichiliocosm— the great trichiliocosm— trembled in six ways, rising and falling in the east, north, south, west, and the intermediate directions.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One smiled.
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this smile?
The Blessed One replied:

Subhūti, just as the Tathāgata here in this world-system teaches the perfection of wisdom, even so do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the incalculable and immeasurable world-systems in the eastern direction teach the perfection of wisdom to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.

They speak thus: "In this way, throughout the ten directions, in incalculable and immeasurable world-systems, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas teach the perfection of wisdom to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.
Now, while this teaching on the perfection of wisdom by Subhūti was being expounded,
Twelve myriads of beings, both divine and human, attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore,
from all sides in the world-systems of the ten directions, there were incalculable numbers of those Blessed Buddhas who were teaching this Perfection of Wisdom to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.
The minds of immeasurable sentient beings were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
[Thus, the departure by way of the path has been explained; the practice of departure has been explained; and omniscience has been explained.
This concludes the section on the Perfection of Wisdom within the *Ārya-pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-bodhisattvadharmā*.
In this [text] revised according to the *Samayālaṅkāra*, the first chapter, the Subhūti Chapter, belonging to the section on the Knowledge of All Aspects, is concluded.
